A committee then drew up rules on lending in May 1886. He argues the loan statute is flawed and says why in plain terms. The list of borrowers, he holds, stood outside the law itself.
38136-the-life-of-thomas-wanless-peasant:
An anonymous life of Thomas Wanless, a peasant, printed at Manchester and London. Its narrator explains how he found the story: on long vacations in a quiet Warwickshire village near Leamington, he preferred cottage folk and the bench at the alehouse door to fashionable society.

The contents run from a helot's nurture through a philanthropic parson, the allotment cure for hunger, and a chapter called Manufacturing Criminals. Jail life, sermons, men for a standing army, and Christian respectability all get chapters of their own. A peasant maiden, the lost one found, and the journey's end close it. Readers get a Victorian protest novel: a working man's whole life laid out as an argument about hunger, law, and class.
38177-the-passionate-elopement:
The Passionate Elopement is a novel by Compton Mackenzie, published by Putnam's Sons in New York in 1916. The tale is set at Curtain Wells, a fictional inland spa with a wide reputation. Its chapters bear mock-antique titles in the manner of an earlier century.

The action moves through the rooms and rituals of a spa season. Chapters visit the toilet, the pump room, the Blue Boar inn, and the publick breakfast. Then come Baverstock Barn, Sunday morning, the great rebellion, and the assembly, with the night after it. A Chinese masquerade and its grand minuet of Cathay follow. Quarts of Burgundy are drunk, and the dregs of the same. The love chase and a basket of roses advance the plot, until Sir George Repington appears. Mackenzie writes a comedy of costume and manners in high spirits.
39100-naples-past-and-present:
Naples Past and Present is a travel and history book by Arthur Norway, published by Methuen of London in 1901 and again in 1905. Twenty-five illustrations in colour by Maurice Grieffenhagen go with the text. Norway had written the Highways and Byways book on Devon and Cornwall. Here he gives Naples the same treatment. The book opens with the approach to the city by sea. The old marvels of the Phlegraean Fields come next.

Posilipo and its tales of Virgil the enchanter fill a chapter. The Riviera di Chiaia and the Castle of the Egg take the walk on. The kings who held the castle, and the cruelties of Ferdinand of Aragon, fill the history side. Norway mixes street by street notes with the city's long past. It is a guide for the traveller who wants the tale with the view.
39136-historical-romances-under-the-red-:
Historical Romances is a set of three tales of old France by Stanley Weyman. The three are named on the front leaf: past the red robe, a count of the wars of faith, and a man of France. The rights in the three were held in years that span from eighteen ninety three to nineteen twenty one. The host text gives the three in one pack. The same hand's more tales are list past them.

The first tale's parts are set out at the front. At a house of play, at a green post, and at a house in the wood head the run. A dame and her maid, a score paid back, and past a great peak fill the first part.
39139-a-letter-to-the-right-hon-lord-bex:
A Letter to the Right Honourable Lord Bexley, by Francis Cunningham, was published at London in 1827. Cunningham was rector of Pakefield in Suffolk when he wrote. Hatchard and Son issued the pamphlet from Piccadilly in that year. Its matter is a statement made to the committee of the British and Foreign Bible Society.

That statement concerned the relations of the society with lands on the continent. France, the valleys of Piedmont, Switzerland, and Germany are named in the title. Cunningham writes at the wish of Lord Bexley, kindly expressed to him in person. He sets down in writing the substance of what he stated to the committee by mouth. The state of religion in Europe, as tied to Bible work, is his theme throughout.
39143-the-making-of-a-saint:
The Making of a Saint is the second novel by William Somerset Maugham, published by Fisher Unwin in London in 1898. The publisher's pages lean hard on the success of his first book, quoting review after review of Liza of Lambeth. The Standard had called Liza the most powerful story of the lowest class since Kipling's Badalia Herodsfoot.

For this very different second novel Maugham chose an Italian motto: Lorenzo de Medici's carnival song on the beauty and brevity of youth. The story opens with a narrator presenting his friend Filippo, and the epigraph sets its key. Youth is beautiful but flees, and no man can be sure of tomorrow. The book is an early sign of Maugham's range: the Lambeth slums exchanged for Italy, and observation already turned toward the making and unmaking of character.
39184-checklist-a-complete-cumulative-ch:
Marion Zimmer Bradley edited and published a bibliography of fiction about women who love women. Gene Damon served as associate editor. The book came out in May 1960 from Rochester, Texas.

Bradley states the aim up front. The list means to name, document, and review every novel that deals, however slightly, with lesbian themes. It also takes in strong friendships between women, and many famed books on male themes. Entries give the date, the publisher, and the count of reprints. Short reviews judge most titles. Side lists cover poems on the theme, films, and the gay press. There are also addresses for paperback and hardcover houses. Made for collectors, students, and librarians, it stands as an early map of a hidden shelf of books.
39200-the-english-novel-and-the-principl:
A set of lectures on the English novel by Sidney Lanier. Charles Scribner's Sons published the book at New York in 1883. Lanier lectured at Johns Hopkins University. He also wrote The Science of English Verse. These chapters began as public lectures there. He delivered them in the winter and spring of 1881. An editor's note adds a sad fact. Lanier did not live to recast them for the press.

Lanier studies the great prose forms here. His earlier course treated verse in the same spirit. He hunts for the principle behind the novel's growth as an art. The lectures belong to a larger planned philosophy of beauty in literature. Death cut that project short. They remain an early American attempt to give fiction serious formal study.
39223-ortus-christi-meditations-for-adve:
Ortus Christi is a book of Advent meditations by Mother St Paul of Birmingham, issued in 1921. It belongs to a series of meditation books for the seasons, alongside her volumes for Lent, for Our Lady and for Ascension-tide. Twenty-eight meditations are provided, more than any single Advent needs.

The note explains the arithmetic: Advent lasts twenty-two to twenty-eight days, so the last eight meditations are kept for the days before Christmas. The subjects run from Our Lady's rest and the last judgment through five meditations on John the Baptist to the interior life of humility and oblation. A preface by the Jesuit censor praises Mother St Paul as a heart-searcher who presses self-reform even on souls who think they have little to amend.
39288-the-making-of-the-new-testament:
The Making of the New Testament, by Benjamin Bacon of Yale, belongs to the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge. That series put small learned books into common hands at a low price. Bacon held the chair of New Testament criticism and exegesis at Yale. The book first appeared in September 1912, by its imprint.

Bacon asks how the writings of the young church became a fixed canon. Letters, gospels, and acts were gathered, sifted, and bound over centuries. His study follows that slow making with a critic’s eye. The Home University Library aimed to give the lay reader real scholarship. Editors of fame stood behind the whole series of volumes. This one treats the most read book in the world as a made thing, with a history.
39313-rome-and-turkey-in-connexion-with-:
Rome and Turkey in Connexion with the Second Advent is a volume of sermons by the Rev E Hoare. Hatchards published it in London in 1876. Hoare was vicar of Trinity, Tunbridge Wells, and an honorary canon of Canterbury. His preface is dated Tunbridge Wells, January 1876. The three lectures on Turkey, he explains, were published at his parishioners' request. He added two on Rome, written in 1873.

Rome and Turkey, Hoare argues, are two great political witnesses. Their testimonies confirm each other's nearness to the glorious end. The contents divide accordingly. Rome receives The Outline and The Consumption. Turkey receives The Euphrates and The Frogs. A final sermon treats The Advent itself. The first lecture compares the promised return to a son welcomed home from India. His subject is the prophetic sketch of the world's history, read against the Ottoman Empire's position.
39614-ardours-and-endurances-also-a-faun:
Robert Nichols published Ardours and Endurances, with A Faun's Holiday and Poems and Phantasies, in New York. Nichols had already issued Invocation, a book of war poems. This volume, signed in 1917, gathers his verse in three books, and its first book follows the arc of a soldier's war from summons to aftermath.

The war poems move in sections: The Summons, Farewell to Place of Comfort, The Approach, Battle, The Dead, and The Aftermath. Battle pieces include a noon halt, a night bombardment, an eve of assault, and the last morning; The Dead gives a burial in Flanders and a plaint for friendship broken by death. Book two turns to a faun's holiday, and book three to phantasies: songs from The Prince of Ormuz, fragments of Orestes, black songs, and a mystery of Danae. Readers get a soldier-poet's war and the dream world he set against it.
39780-baltimore-hats-past-and-present:
Baltimore Hats Past and Present is a trade history by William Brigham. Its full title adds a sketch of the hat trade from its first days. The book was printed for free spread, not for sale in shops. Rights date the work to the year eighteen ninety.

Parts first ran as trade sheet tales across two years of issues. Old town books lent by a state past lore group fill its facts. Heads trace first days, war days, and the firms of the new age in turn. Thanks at the front name the men who lent rare lists for the work. The book stands as a keen town trade tale told by its own folk.
39785-tunnel-engineering-a-museum-treatm: Tunnel Engineering: A Museum Treatment is Paper 41 of the United States National Museum's Bulletin 240, issued by the Smithsonian Institution in Washington in 1966. The bulletin gathers Papers 34 to 44 under the heading On Science and Technology, from the Museum of History and Technology. The paper treats tunnel engineering as a museum subject: the history and practice of boring through rock and earth, set out with the museum's collections behind it. Engineers and museum readers get the Smithsonian's survey form, a single paper bound for separate use.
39822-tics-and-their-treatment:
Henry Meige and E Feindel's Tics and Their Treatment was published in New York by William Wood and Company in 1907, with a preface by Professor Brissaud. S A K Wilson translated and edited the work, adding a critical appendix; Wilson was resident medical officer at the National Hospital for the Paralysed and Epileptic, Queen Square, London.

The authors' preface gives a twofold object. They make known facts of clinical observation, and assign to the tics their due place among the motor affections that follow nervous or mental disease. They follow the doctrine of Charcot, taken up since by Brissaud. The word tic, they warn, has been defined and redefined since the eighteenth century until its limits have swollen and shrunk excessively, and loose use of it breeds confusion of ideas.
39928-man-s-place-in-the-universe-a-stud:
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote Man's Place in the Universe, published by Chapman and Hall in a third edition of 1904. Wallace, the co-discoverer of natural selection, turns to astronomy. His subtitle states the question: a study of scientific research in relation to the unity or plurality of worlds. Are other worlds inhabited, or is the earth alone?

Sixteen chapters build the answer. Wallace surveys early and modern ideas, the new astronomy, and the distribution and distances of the stars. He treats the unity of the star system and our relation to the Milky Way. Later chapters set out the physical conditions life requires, and judge the planets against them. His conclusion denies that the other planets are habitable and gives the earth a near-central importance. The book shows a Victorian scientist arguing, against the fashion, for the rarity of life.
39940-ashton-kirk-secret-agent:
John McIntyre sent his detective into spy work in this Ashton-Kirk tale. Penn printed Ashton-Kirk, Secret Agent at Philadelphia in 1912, with plates by Ralph Boyer. McIntyre gives the book to Helen Ray.

Some Peculiar Circumstances opens the case. Ashton-Kirk goes to Eastbury, and the affair turns out to reach across nations. The Taking Off of Dr Morse gives it a corpse. Okiu, a Japanese figure, comes and goes through the list. The Methylene Stain and the house on Fordham Road build the trail. Karkowsky gets some attention, old Nanon speaks, and Okiu writes a letter. The German Embassy Ball sets a grand scene near the close.
40031-nooks-and-corners-of-english-life-:
Nooks and Corners of English Life, Past and Present, by John Timbs, is a popular history of everyday England. The hosted copy is the second edition of 1867, from Griffith and Farran of London. The preface promises pictures of the home manners of our forefathers at the most attractive periods of English history.

Chapters gather homes from cave to castle, old furniture, dress, food, and housewifery, peasant customs, fairs, and festivals, with tales of battlefields and great houses. Timbs, a tireless compiler of curious facts, salts the book with quotes and prints, including Horselydown Fair in Queen Elizabeth's time. It is a warm window on how Victorians pictured their own past.
40076-atrocious-judges-lives-of-judges-i:
Richard Hildreth edited Atrocious Judges, lives of judges infamous as tools of tyrants and instruments of oppression, printed at New York in 1856. The text derives from Lord Campbell's Lives of the Chief Justices and Lives of the Chancellors, with small changes for American readers. An appendix adds the case of Passmore Williamson, the abolitionist prisoner.

Most biographers have been arrant flatterers, the advertisement argues, but Campbell holds that history has dignity only so far as it is true. Truth must be told at all hazards and without reserve about men who gained place by any means, the editor insists. A check on strivers for distinction is the book's grim purpose. Legal historians get Campbell's candour repackaged.
40079-the-philosophy-of-disenchantment:
Edgar Evertson Saltus wrote this essay in pessimism, copyrighted in 1885 and published at Boston in 1887 by the author of a study of Balzac. Its motto, from Schiller, says we are all born in Arcadia.

The contents open with the genesis of disenchantment, then enthrone the high priest of pessimism. The sphinx's riddle, the borderlands of happiness, and the great quietus follow, ending with the question: is life an affliction? Saltus opens by dividing mankind into those who accept life off-hand and those who look the gift in the mouth. The second view, he argues, is purely modern as a system, however old its stray expressions. A dictionary of pessimistic quotation, he says, could be compiled from the dust-bins of literature. Decadent readers get their philosophy stated elegantly.
40164-history-of-the-opera-from-its-orig:
History of the Opera is a two volume history by Sutherland Edwards. Allen published it in London in 1862. Its title promises the story from opera's origin in Italy to the present time. Anecdotes of celebrated composers and vocalists of Europe are added. Edwards also wrote Russians at Home. The first chapter treats preface, prelude, and prologue as its heads. It takes up the origin of opera in Italy and its spread to Germany. The second chapter brings opera into France and England.

A chapter compares opera's merits with other forms of drama. The introduction and progress of the ballet get a chapter. Italian opera in England and under Handel follow in the contents. A general view of opera in eighteenth century Europe comes next. Edwards writes a theatre history full of stage anecdote. The work is an early full history of opera in English.
40173-the-literature-of-the-old-testamen:
George Foot Moore's Literature of the Old Testament belongs to the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge. Williams and Norgate published it in London, with Holt in New York. Moore was a professor in Harvard University and editor of the Harvard Theological Review, and had written a commentary on Judges.

The chapters begin with the canon of the Old Testament and the Old Testament as a national literature. The Pentateuch takes several chapters, on its sources, their character and their age. Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles and Ezra and Nehemiah follow in order. Story books, the prophets from Isaiah to the minor prophets, Psalms, Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes complete the survey, with a bibliography and index.
40449-the-woman-with-one-hand-and-mr-ely:
Richard Marsh wrote The Woman with One Hand, printed with Mr Ely's Engagement in one volume in London in a second edition. Marsh had written Frivolities, Tom Ossington's Ghost, and The Beetle, a mystery. Stanley Wood drew the frontispiece, captioned with a line from the tale: this time I succeeded in warding him off. The publisher's pages before the title praise Marsh as a humorist who is genuinely funny.

Those pages quote the Scotsman that a reader does not merely smile at Marsh but laughs outright, and laughs all the time. The Daily Telegraph calls Frivolities brimful of fun. The title tale itself opens with a chapter named An Agony, beginning as the narrator spots something that catches his eye at once. Two tales of Marsh's making thus stand back to back in this volume, the woman with one hand first and Mr Ely's engagement second.
40505-scurvy-past-and-present: Scurvy, Past and Present is a medical work on the disease scurvy, its history, and its treatment. The surviving head of this copy is given over to the transcriber's notes. Those notes cover the book's scholarly apparatus and its German medical literature. They cite Barlow's disease, the infantile form of scurvy, under its many variant names. The notes explain that archaic spellings in quotations were left unchanged, while most other inconsistencies were regularised.
40887-on-the-trail-of-the-immigrant:
Edward Steiner's On the Trail of the Immigrant, issued by Revell at New York in 1906, follows newcomers from the gate of entry into American life. Steiner, a professor at Iowa College in Grinnell, had made immigration his study, and the book is one of his series of works on the subject.

He dedicates it to Robert Watchorn, the United States Commissioner of Immigration at the Port of New York, whom he calls the Man at the Gate. Watchorn, Steiner writes, dealt with men of every kindred and tongue humanely, justly and without prejudice. The frontispiece shows the immigrants themselves, tickets fastened to their coats and dresses, passing out through the gate to take up their new inheritance as fellow citizens.
40935-a-greek-english-lexicon-to-the-new:
Thomas Green compiled this Greek and English lexicon to the New Testament, revised and enlarged. Hastings published it at Boston in 1896, in its thirty-third thousand of copies. A preface by Hastings, editor of the Christian, stands at the front of the dictionary.

Wallace Stearns prepared a supplement under the supervision of Thayer of Harvard. It adds words and forms found in the Greek texts then in use, the title page explains. Lachmann, Tischendorf, Tregelles, Westcott and Hort and the Revisers of 1881 are named there, making a pocket tool for preachers and students reading the Greek Testament.
40952-mushroom-culture-its-extension-and:
Robinson wrote this guide to mushroom culture, its spread and improvement. Routledge printed it in New York in the Country Series run. Plates show the mouth of a mushroom cave near Paris. Robinson says culture is little practised here for the means at hand.

Materials abound in town and country across these islands, he writes. He holds tenfold growth of the culture both fit and likely. Every place with gardener and horses should grow mushrooms most of the year. Good growers know the usual craft, but no full simple account stood in print.
40986-the-oera-linda-book-from-a-manuscr:
The Oera Linda Book presents a claimed ancient Frisian chronicle in two languages. Sandbach made this English version. He worked from a Dutch translation by Ottema. Trubner published it in London in 1876. The manuscript was said to date from the thirteenth century. Its owner gave leave for the printing. Photographs of two pages are bound in.

A translator's preface admits the storm around the book. Dutch and German scholars dispute its authenticity hotly. Some find internal evidence of truth in it. Others declare it a forgery, though perhaps an old one. Sandbach prints the Frisian text opposite his translation. Any reader with the language may verify him. Early Frisians sail to the Mediterranean in its tales. A woman lawgiver appears at Athens.
40996-in-white-raiment:
In White Raiment, by William Le Queux, appeared in this London edition in 1919. A doctor tells the tale and hides his true name. In the prologue he calls himself Richard Colkirk, a nerve specialist in Harley Street. As Dick Colkirk, the narrator, he vows to be frank. A death has lately freed him to speak at last. He says every doctor keeps a skeleton in his cupboard.

He calls the facts as strange as any in a living man's history. Social London, he notes, holds daily incidents that read as incredible in print. His consulting room is full and his fees are heavy. Yet one fact must stay hid to guard his name. The prologue sets up a confession tale of secret guilt and search for truth.
41179-portage-paths-the-keys-of-the-cont:
Portage Paths, the keys of the continent, is a history by Archer Butler Hulbert, issued at Cleveland in 1903. It is volume seven of a series on the historic highways of America, with maps. The first part treats the nature and use of portages, then how portages evolved over time. A portage is a carrying place between waters, the subject in short.

The second part catalogues the portages of America by region. New England and Canadian portages come first, then New York portages, then paths to the Mississippi basin. Hulbert opens by asking the reader to walk in fancy along a backbone of America. That watershed runs from the northern Atlantic shore to the valley of the Mississippi. The old carrying paths across it, he argues, unlocked the continent.
41334-my-experiences-in-a-lunatic-asylum:
My Experiences in a Lunatic Asylum, by a Sane Patient, was published by Chatto and Windus in London in 1879. The writer tells how a sane man, worn down and at times delirious from exhaustion, was shut up as a lunatic. His charge against the system is plain: two doctors' certificates can condemn a person who needs rest and care to what he calls a death-in-life of false imprisonment.

The book mixes his own story inside the asylum with an argument for changing the law. He describes the helplessness of a patient whose protests only confirm the keepers in their verdict. Works of this kind fed the Victorian campaign over lunacy reform. His case rests on a simple fear: that the same papers, signed in the same way, could shut up almost anyone.
41490-the-decadent:
The Decadent, privately printed for the author in 1893, calls itself the gospel of inaction, set forth in romance form. The title page promises reflections on the curious traits of these ultimate years and their diverse causes. A long Latin dedication honors a dear friend and a band of chosen spirits across the world. The tale proper starts on a train.

The 3.20 train from Boston slows at a way station, and Malcolm McCann, grim and sullen from dirt, cinders, coal smoke, and crying babies, hurries out with a grunt of relief. He glares at the grimy brick walls and tarnished signs of the refreshment saloon. A fat businessman trips over a laborer's pick in the crowd. The novel paints 1890s ennui in thick, sardonic prose.
41565-consignment:
Allan Nourse wrote a science fiction story printed in a magazine dated December 1953, with art by Sussman. A line at the start asks what chance a tiger, king in the jungle, would have in city traffic at Times Square. The tale then opens at night in a prison, where three shots drop three guards.

A man named Krenner throws a rope to the top of a high rock wall and climbs as sirens wail and rifles fire. Glass cuts at the top, a shot hits his foot, and he dives into a dark river on the far side. Three miles down stream he hopes to find a man named Sherman and an open road.
41718-dave-dawson-on-the-russian-front:
Dave Dawson on the Russian Front is a boys' war novel by R Sidney Bowen, printed at Akron, Ohio, in 1943. Bowen also wrote Dave Dawson at Dunkirk, Dave Dawson in Libya, and Dave Dawson with the Commandos. The first chapter, Mystery Man, opens in an English hotel. Dave growls at his pal Freddy Farmer to let a guy get some sleep.

Freddy, fresh from a two-day jaunt over to France, is sounding off as though he had been away a million years. Dave calls him a pain in seventeen different places at the same time, and a bow-legged commando. The chapters run through Room 1200, Eagles for Moscow, and Nazi Lightning. High stakes, success or suicide, and Satan is gleeful mark the climb to the end. Aces don't wait, and headaches for Hitler close the book.
41726-narcissus-a-twelfe-night-merriment:
Narcissus, a Twelfe Night Merriment, is a college play of 1602, here first edited from a Bodleian manuscript. Margaret L Lee of St Hugh's Hall, Oxford, edited it. David Nutt published it in London in 1893 in the Tudor Library. Five hundred copies of the edition were printed. The play was performed by youths of the parish at the College of St John the Baptist in Oxford.

The interlocutors list the myth in person. Tyresias and Cephisus stand beside Narcissus himself. Dorastus, Clinias, Eccho, and Lyriope fill the cast. Florida, Clois, the Well, and a Porter complete it. Lee keeps the manuscript's irregular spelling throughout. She modernises only punctuation and capitals, and expands contractions. An appendix adds three speeches and a letter composed for Francis Clarke, the college porter. Her preface thanks Professor Ker, Professor Napier, and Mr Madan.
41755-greater-britain-a-record-of-travel:
Charles Wentworth Dilke records a trip round the English-speaking world in 1866 and 1867. J B Lippincott issued the book at Philadelphia in 1869. Macmillan handled it in London. He dedicates it to his father.

His preface states the guiding idea. Everywhere he went, he stood in lands ruled or spoken in English. Climate and mixing with other peoples changed the stock. Yet in essentials the race stayed one. America, he argues, runs all peoples into an English mould. Alfred's laws and Chaucer's tongue rule there whether men will it or not. The half of the globe once Elizabeth's now spreads far beyond Victoria's Britain. Dilke wrote young, and his bold claims made the book famous. It named an idea, Greater Britain, that shaped later debate.
41801-the-diary-of-a-saint:
Arlo Bates published 'The Diary of a Saint' with Houghton, Mifflin in 1902; the contents divide the diary by months, January to December. The diarist, Ruth Privet, makes her first entry on January 1, standing at a window over a beautiful world. The moon shines on white sheets of snow, low meadows lie far off and enchanted, and cedars stand almost green against the whiteness.

Last night was another year, she writes, and the new one begins in a better mood. She recalls her father's old saying for her as a little girl: a cheerful Ruth Privet, as right as a trivet. She never did know what being as right as a trivet is. The week behind her held drizzly, unseasonable weather, her mother's bad days of pain, and Kathie Thurston in one of her despairing fits. The diary promises a year of watching, worry, and determined cheerfulness.
41817-john-marvel-assistant:
Thomas Nelson Page wrote a novel published in October 1909, drawn by James Montgomery Flagg. The narrator begins by claiming leave to tell his story in his own rambling way. He warns that he will stop, rest, and stray from the path as he pleases. Chapter one is titled My First Failure.

John Marvel himself enters only in chapter twelve. Earlier chapters treat a fight, a flight, and the pitching of a tent. Eleanor Leigh and her father hold large places in the tale. Later chapters bring a riot, a walking delegate, and a flag of truce. Page mixes law, labor trouble, and church work in a long social novel.
41879-dick-merriwell-s-pranks-or-lively-:
Burt Standish sends his schoolboy hero abroad in Dick Merriwell's Pranks, or Lively Times in the Orient, from Street and Smith in New York with copyright in 1905. Standish is billed as author of the Merriwell stories, favourites of half a million American boys. Thirty chapters carry Dick from the Bosporus to a sunset from a citadel.

Chapter one crosses the Sea of Marmora into the Bosporus, Constantinople ahead, Asia on one shore and Europe on the other. Dick, unjustly expelled from Fardale Military Academy, tours with Professor Zenas Gunn and his Texas chum Bradley Buckhart. Brad gasps that the land of the unspeakable Turk beats his dreams, while Dick warns him to wait until they land. Later chapters bring Persia, Damascus, a desert, and a foe's fate.
41999-notes-and-queries-number-220-janua:
One weekly number of Notes and Queries, dated Saturday, January 14, 1854, forms the hosted text. The London paper called itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. It sold for fourpence, or fivepence in a stamped edition.

Notes in this number treat Griffin's Fidessa and Shakespeare's Passionate Pilgrim, caps at Cambridge, and newspaper folk lore. Queries ask after Captain Farre, a fourteenth-century marriage rite, and a manuscript catena, among many small puzzles. Replies take up the asteroids, the emblem meanings of precious stones, Milton's widow, and table-turning. A photographic correspondence column treats the calotype process. Readers get Victorian learned curiosity in its weekly working dress, question and answer side by side.
42001-notes-and-queries-number-221-janua:
Notes and Queries, number 221, is one weekly issue of a Victorian literary correspondence journal. It appeared on Saturday, January 21, 1854. The journal served literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto comes from Captain Cuttle. When found, make a note of, it runs. The stamped edition cost eleven pence.

The contents divide into set departments. Notes open with a plea for the city churches. Echo poetry and a carol of the kings follow. Queries ask about Buonaparte's abdication and death warnings. Replies treat the Hoby family and poetical tavern signs. Chronograms and oaths earn long answers. A photographic correspondence column discusses iodized paper. Books wanted and notices to correspondents close the issue.
42002-notes-and-queries-number-222-janua:
Notes and Queries, number 222 of Saturday, January 28, 1854, is one issue of the famed weekly for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, bids the finder make a note of it. The price was fourpence, or fiveness stamped. Contents lines show the week's mix of notes, folk lore, and questions.

Notes treat a prophet named Francis Dobbs, Scott quoting himself, and the poet Thomas Campbell. Folk lore brings legends of County Clare and a slow worm superstition. Queries ask whether Shakespeare came of landed stock, and whether a society exists for burning the dead. Minor queries pile up on Fleet Prison, paper watermarks, and muffins and crumpets. Readers answered each other across issues, building a shared store of learning. This single number shows the journal at work, a Victorian web of curiosity in print.
42012-paths-of-judgement:
Anne Douglas Sedgwick wrote Paths of Judgement, a novel printed at London in 1904. Sedgwick had written The Rescue and The Confounding of Camilia. The tale opens on a hot hill road above Trensome Hall.

Mrs Cuthbert Merrick drives her stout pony up the steep lane in a shining dogcart. She finds the wide view from the hilltop a grievance, since the meadows below look dull to her eye. A smart crack of the whip brings her to a small stone house in a flower filled garden. From this country start, the novel's web of judgment and feeling is spun.
42288-the-communion-and-communicant:
The Communion and Communicant is a devotional tract on the Lord's Supper by Edward Hoare. Hoare was incumbent of Christ Church, Ramsgate. Hatchard published it in London in 1847. David Price transcribed this copy from that edition. Ramsgate Library lent the volume for the work.

The tract opens with praise of the sacrament. It is a remembrance of a Redeemer's love. It is a means of grace and a foretaste of heaven. Yet not all approach it with joy. Some neglect it wholly. Some receive it in a careless, worldly spirit. Others fear it as an awful mystery. Hoare blames that awe on Paul's warning about unworthy eating. His tract studies five Bible passages to set the matter right.
42674-the-diary-of-a-hunter-from-the-pun:
The Diary of a Hunter is a sports mans log from the plains of India to the great snow range at its north. It came out at London and Norwich in the year cut in Roman marks on its title page. A note tells how its print form was set, with spell kept as first struck.

Its first words own the state of the book with care. It is, with some cuts and ends of lines made whole, the true copy of a log. That log was not writ with a view to print. It was a lone note of the chase, kept from time to time for the man him self. Its game runs from the small deer of the plains to the great goats and sheep of the high rocks.
42763-swords-reluctant:
Max Pemberton writes a novel of war, love, and a plan to federate Europe in a Dillingham volume from New York held under rights from 1912. London readers knew the tale as War and the Woman, while New York took the title Swords Reluctant. Pemberton gives the book to Andrew Carnegie with a Latin line on friends as the true guard of a realm.

Pemberton thanks Sir Max Waechter and Sir Francis Trippel for help with the book and its aim. Figures are all invented, he grants, yet the scheme for a Federation of Europe comes from Waechter and won favour at courts abroad. Four books of chapters move from Gabrielle Silvester and a man of destiny to a race for an emperor, burnt RANOVICA, and surrender at the close.
42783-notes-and-queries-number-168-janua:
Notes and Queries, number 168, for Saturday, January 15, 1853, bills itself as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto is Captain Cuttle's: when found, make a note of. The number, with index, cost tenpence. Contents open with notes: an inedited poem by Pope, Southey's Doctor, an Oxfordshire legend in stone, Lady Nevell's music-book, and a monastic kitchener's account.

Queries ask about Pope and the Marquis Maffei, the church catechism, and a Countess of Southampton, with minor queries from hardening steel bars to plum-pudding. Replies treat Canongate marriages, Lady Katherine Grey, and Chaucer. A photographic section, new in 1853, handles pyrogallic acid, stereoscopic pictures with one camera, and Crookes's wax-paper process. The Pope note prints verses from a 1765 letter of Warburton to Hurd, too late for the poet's edition.
42784-notes-and-queries-number-169-janua:
Notes and Queries was a weekly sheet for men of books, art, old things, and family lines. The copy here is Number 169, dated Saturday, January 22, 1853. A lone copy cost four pence, or five pence in its stamped form. A line from a Dickens tale serves as its creed: when found, make a note of it.

Notes in this issue deal with a foul word, with old calls of fire and plague in London, and with the essays of Bacon. Folk lore brings Irish charms for warts, the devil, and the sound of storms in cold months. One note asks if Malta was the grave place of Hannibal. Small notes touch on Waterloo, the dodo, and a king of France. Queries ask on a lost word, on Tennyson, and on frauds in books. A last set deals with new art by light, a fresh craft of that age.
42785-notes-and-queries-number-170-janua:
Notes and Queries, number 170, is a weekly paper dated Saturday, January 29, 1853. Its sub title calls it a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. The motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of.

Notes lead the issue. One treats an index of charters, one the name Cowper or Cooper, and one the origin of the word Yankee, by William Bell. A new ballad treats the doctors of Shakspeare. Folk lore gives cures for the hooping cough. Then come small notes, questions, and questions with answers. Readers ask on epitaphs, a meteoric stone, and the Orkneys in pawn.
42786-notes-and-queries-number-171-febru:
A weekly number of a literary miscellany fills this item: Notes and Queries, number 171, for Saturday, February 5, 1853, priced at fourpence. Its masthead calls it a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, and its motto is a captain's rule: when found, make a note of.

Contents sort the number's small change. Notes treat Jacob Grimm on the genius of English, the keeping of valuable papers from damp, the clergy in the seventeenth century, and General Wolfe. Folk lore gives a baptismal custom, underground bells, and a cough cure. Queries ask about heavy rainfall, a lost manuscript, and the bronze statue of Charles the First. Replies take up a bishop, church tones, a crux in Shakespeare, and the right way to say Niagara.
42828-sargent:
T Martin Wood wrote Sargent, a study of John S Sargent with eight reproductions in colour. T C and E C Jack in London issued the book. Frederick A Stokes Company in New York issued it as well. The book stands in Masterpieces in Colour, edited by T Leman Hare. A front plate shows Lord Ribblesdale, held one of the finest of Sargent works.

The series list names mate books on Velazquez, Reynolds, Turner, Rembrandt, and Raphael, among many more. Wood treats Sargent life, sitters, and bold brush work in clear prose for general readers. Colour plates let a reader judge the portraits at first hand, if in small scale. Art lovers of the age got a cheap, bright door into a famed portrait painter. The book shows how colour print spread art fame to home shelves.
43042-the-expert-maid-servant:
Christine Herrick wrote this guide to the expert maid servant at home. Harper printed it in New York and London in 1904. Chapter one treats engaging the maid through an intelligence office. Chapter two takes the maid arrival, three the mistress and maid.

Duties of the maid of all work take chapter four here. Duties of two or more servants and service problems follow next. General suggestions and a recapitulation of daily duties close it. Cheap offices may urge maids to change places for fees, she warns. Housekeeping Made Easy and What to Eat stand among her past books on the title.
43112-sweet-content:
Mrs Molesworth's Sweet Content, in an edition dated 1891 from E P Dutton and Company of New York, is told by the girl herself. Sweet Content, she explains, was her name when she was a very tiny child, and she uses it for her title. W Rainey drew the illustrations.

She has been an only child ever since she can remember, but she was not always one. When she was a baby of a few months, scarlet fever broke out badly in the town where the family lived, and among its first deaths were her brothers and sister. She writes the story for readers who never heard of her, trusting the other characters with the exactly how it was of everything.
4314-appendicitis-the-etiology-hygenic-a:
John H. Tilden, a physician, wrote this book on appendicitis from a drugless, hygienic standpoint. He treats the causes of the disease first, then its dietetic and hygienic care, arguing that faulty habits of eating and living prepare the ground for attacks. His aim is prevention and natural recovery rather than routine surgery.

Tilden's chapters set out his theory of disease as the result of enervation and toxic buildup, applied here to one organ. Modern readers should note that his advice reflects early twentieth-century alternative medicine, not current practice. The book remains a document of that movement, and of the debate over surgery for appendicitis.
43199-the-last-tenant:
The Last Tenant, a novel by Farjeon, was published in New York in 1893. Farjeon had written A Fair Jewess. The tale is told by a calm husband whose wife wants to move house. Chapter one is called My Wife Makes Up Her Mind to Move. She hints that he lacks social ambition. He waits, knowing her moods, for the plan to show itself.

Contents promise house hunting, an old friend, and curious facts about a house in Lamb's Terrace. The couple view the house and get a shock. Later heads name Barbara, Molly, and a doctor named Cooper. An inquest, a fire, and a trip to Paris follow. Farjeon mixes domestic comedy with a haunted house mystery and a search for truth.
43229-the-hawthorne-a-christmas-and-new-:
The Hawthorn, a Christmas and New Year's present for young readers, was published by Riker at 129 Fulton Street, New York, in 1845. Its frontispiece, The Mother's Joy, was engraved by Neagle, and Mirick printed the book at West Brookfield.

The preface explains the name: a blossom suits the young better than a gem, whose cold glitter has little in common with their freshness. Flowers run through the teaching of Jesus, who took children in his arms and bade men consider the lilies of the field. The contents mix tales and verse: Frederick Ormsby, The Mysterious Picture, and The Quilting from Eliza Leslie, and The Rustic Wreath, The Storm, and The Christmas Visit from Mrs Hughs. Mrs Child and Mrs Sigourney also contribute, and a French fable, Le Loup et L'Agneau, stands among the pieces.
43379-hands-up-or-thirty-five-years-of-d:
Hands Up gathers thirty-five years of detective life in the mountains and on the plains, from the reminiscences of Cook, chief of the Rocky Mountain Detective Association. His kinsman compiled the book, printed at Denver in 1897.

The contents call it a condensed criminal history of the far west: the Allison gang, Denver's last legal hanging, the Italian murderers, Musgrove and his gang, and a half-million-dollar robber. Illustrations show lynchings, arrests, and hangings in grim sequence. Later chapters treat road agents of the Black Hills, strikers, a Mexican bandit, and a race for life. The Robinson Printing Company of Denver produced the volume.
43531-the-vegetable-garden-what-when-and:
Vegetable Garden is a planting manual reprinted from a farmer's cyclopedia. Its subtitle asks what, when, and how to plant. The Garden City edition was issued in nineteen seventeen, from a copyright of nineteen twelve. Pictures show a good collection of home grown vegetables and lettuce in a cold frame. Contents open with the garden's importance, its location, and its plan.

Fertilizers, soil preparation, and time of planting follow. Sowing, tools, mulching, and irrigation take their turns. Thinning, transplanting, and protection of plants fill the middle. Canning and storing vegetables earn sections of their own. A long list of garden products then runs from anise and artichoke through beans and cabbage. Peas, peppers, potatoes, and pumpkins stand in the later letters.
43580-horses-past-and-present:
Walter Gilbey wrote Horses Past and Present, a brief history of the horse in England to the close of the nineteenth century, printed at London in 1900. Plates show a cart horse of the fifteenth century, saddle and pillion riders, the Darley Arabian, and famed hunters and sires.

Contents march reign by reign, from before the Norman Conquest through William the Conqueror and each king and queen to Victoria. Gilbey notes how much has changed since 1800: breeds improved, travel remade, and farm work, hunting, and racing all reshaped. Light horses and heavy horses close the book, with breed societies for each. He cites a count of more than four thousand books on the horse in all tongues by 1886 alone.
43673-poeta-de-tristibus-or-the-poet-s-c:
Poeta de Tristibus, or The Poet's Complaint, dates to 1682. The Augustan Reprint Society reissued it in 1971. Harold Love wrote its intro and notes. The Clark Memorial Library at Los Angeles issued it. It stands as Publication Number 149 of the line. A facsimile copy in that library served as source.

William E Conway and two partners edited the line. Richard Boys and James Clifford advised it as well. Scholars from Michigan to Iowa fill that board. The library call mark reads PR3291, P795. Old spelling and print stand as first made. Scholarly reprints like this put rare Stuart verse back in reach. A 1682 lament gains fresh readers three centuries on, with a modern scholar to vouch for its worth and guide its thorns.
44109-the-son-of-a-servant:
August Strindberg wrote The Son of a Servant, his autobiographical novel of childhood and youth, translated by Claud Field and published by Putnam in 1913. Henry Vacher-Burch introduces the book with a study of Strindberg as a novelist, covering the years from this book's first appearance to The Inferno.

The contents read like stations of a hard growing up: Fear and Hunger, Breaking-In, Away from Home. Then come lessons with the lower classes and contact with the upper classes. The School of the Cross, First Love, and The Spring Thaw follow. With Strangers and Character and Destiny close the volume. The introduction warns readers what they hold: Strindberg portrays his own Judgment Day. His candour in self-revelation is amazing, the essay says, and asks what attitude a reader should take to it. English readers met Sweden's great self-accuser at the start of his story.
44124-reminiscences-of-the-guilford-gray:
Reminiscences of the Guilford Grays is the war record of Company B of the 27th North Carolina Regiment, by John Sloan. It was printed at Washington in 1883. The first chapter tells how the Grays were raised, with their first officers, drill, and the gift of a banner. The second follows balls and visits before the war came.

Then the boom of war arrives, with secession and the call for troops. Sloan writes as a member of the company, from Greensboro, North Carolina. Regimental histories like this one were written by veterans to keep their unit's service on record. They preserve names, marches, and small events that official reports leave out.
44616-mary-of-plymouth-a-story-of-the-pi:
James Otis tells the Pilgrim settlement through a girl's eyes in Mary of Plymouth, copyrighted in 1910 by the American Book Company. Short chapters, more than a hundred of them, follow the leaking Speedwell, the search for a home, the finding of the corn and the building of houses. Daily life fills most of the book, from wash day and chimney building to grinding corn and dipping candles.

Squanto, Massasoit and the friendly Indians enter alongside Governor Carver's death and Bradford's election. The harvest festival, stoolball, the arrival of the Fortune and the Ann, Merrymount and the first school all appear before the closing journey to Salem.
44755-eighteen-months-imprisonment:
Eighteen Months' Imprisonment, with a remission, was published in London in eighteen eighty-three. George Routledge and Sons issued it, and Wallis Mackay supplied the illustrations. The author masks himself as D S, a late captain in a regiment. The title page crowd scenes set the tone of a firsthand prison memoir.

The chapters walk through his arrest at a solicitor's office and the House of Detention. Bow Street, Newgate, and its scaffold and private executions follow. Then come Coldbath Fields and the daily round inside. He reports on prison fare, oakum picking, the tread-wheel, and prison trades. The hospital dead-house, criminal lunatics, and titled convicts all get chapters. The record keeps a close, rueful eye from the first foggy November arrest to the end.
44770-daisy-s-work-the-third-commandment:
Joanna Mathews, author of the Bessie books, wrote Daisy's Work for Robert Carter and Brothers in New York in 1870. The tale forms the second volume in Flowerets, a series of stories on the commandments, each priced alike. Its subject is the third commandment, against taking God's name in vain.

Nine chapters follow Daisy from a little flower girl to a teacher, with one chapter pointedly called The Swearing Class. The opening finds Daisy beside her flower basket near a great railroad depot, a spot of brightness amid dust, heat, and noise. Porters and hackmen shout and swear around her as trains start every few minutes. Mathews dedicates the story to her little cousin Lulu Chauncey.
44838-time-and-its-measurement:
James Arthur wrote a brief book on time and how men have marked it. The piece first ran in Popular Mechanics Magazine in that age. Its rights date to 1909 from Chicago. Old splits of day and night lead his first part's list. Night watches of the Old Testament stand in that list in full.

New Testament hours and feast days share the old count ways. Sun time by shade and noon marks on walls come next. Old dials from Herculaneum and Pompeii show in its plates. New dials and the true sun fix fill the rest of the part. Clock past fans get a neat tale in brief form. Plates do much of the work.
45118-our-standard-bearer-or-the-life-of:
Our Standard-Bearer is a life of General Grant, told as seen and related by Captain Bernard Galligasken and written out by Oliver Optic. Lee and Shepard published it at Boston in 1868, with pictures by Thomas Nast. The dedication hails Grant as the only man with the mind, moral force, and military genius to crush the great rebellion, the mightiest the world ever saw.

The subtitle promises Grant's youth, manhood, campaigns, and great services in rebuilding the nation his sword redeemed. In the preface, Optic says his friend the captain tells the story in his own way, and that his own task was merely to write the book. He owns to a careful study of the general's character and a hearty sharing of the captain's praise.
45479-the-story-of-joan-of-arc-the-witch:
Mangasarian lectured on Joan of Arc as the witch-saint for the Independent Religious Society, and the lecture appeared in The Rationalist in October 1913. The pamphlet lists past numbers of the series, which show his pulpit's range.

Saint Francis is called the second Christ. Marcus Aurelius, Voltaire in Hades, and the Titanic all receive lectures. The high cost of living and the higher cost of superstition share the list with Christian Science and common sense. Mangasarian, an Armenian-born minister who had left orthodoxy for rationalism, preached in Chicago to a congregation of freethinkers. Joan, burned as a witch and canonized as a saint, is his perfect subject: the same woman, condemned and crowned by the same church, five centuries apart. His lecture argues the rationalist case from her file.
45583-scapa-and-a-camera-pictorial-impre:
C W Burrows spent five years at Scapa Flow, the Grand Fleet base in the Orkney Islands, and gathered his photos in Scapa and a Camera, first published in 1921. Vice-Admiral F S Miller wrote the opening note. The volume is dedicated to Earl Beatty and the men of the Grand Fleet.

Four parts trace the growth of the base, scenes around Scapa Flow, the navy at work, and the German ships held there. Plates show H.M.S Cyclops at Long Hope, sunken block ships, sports on Flotta, and harvest services. The German battle cruiser Derfflinger appears four minutes before she sank on June 21, 1919. A map of the islands faces the text.
45962-the-organism-as-a-whole-from-a-phy:
The Organism as a Whole is a biology treatise by Jacques Loeb, of the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research. Putnam printed it at New York and London in 1916, with fifty-one illustrations. Its subtitle states its program: the organism studied from a physicochemical viewpoint. Loeb was the great champion of a mechanical account of life.

The physical researches of the last ten years, he begins, have put the atomistic theory of matter and electricity on a definite, probably permanent basis. We know, he argues, the exact numbers that govern the small world. His book extends that certainty upward, to growth, heredity, and instinct, treating the living whole as a machine that chemistry can in principle explain. The treatise is a manifesto of the new experimental biology, written at the height of its author's fame.
46102-an-american-girl-in-munich-impress:
Mabel Daniels wrote letters from Munich as an American music student, printed in Boston in 1905. She gives the book to her Mutterchen, her German landlady or host mother. Her first letter to Cecilia is dated September 15, 1902. Here I am in my Mecca at last, she writes, after a calm sea and prosperous voyage.

She wishes Cecilia could share her pleasures and troubles, and see German customs with wide blue eyes. Her study is a box, she owns, yet the height of cosiness by German standards. She swears she keeps an American point of view as firm as on walks to Harvard Square. Teachers, concerts, and student life fill later letters.
46256-in-the-ypres-salient:
Beckles Willson wrote In the Ypres Salient, the story of a fortnight's Canadian fighting from the second to the sixteenth of June 1916. Simpkin Marshall printed it at London. A map key and a painting of the salient open the book.

Willson quotes The Times of June the twelfth: long after small gains are forgotten, men will recall how the Canadians fought against hopeless odds near Hooge. The mayor of Ypres adds thanks in French for the British army's stand. A note traces the salient's birth in October 1914, when a small British force checked the German drive to the sea. The book honors Major-General Mercer among the dead.
46430-the-camp-life-of-the-third-regimen:
Robert Kerlin, chaplain of the Third Missouri Volunteers, published his letters from camp at Kansas City in 1898. A portrait of the chaplain fronts the book. The dedication is to the brave, true, and generous-hearted boys, his comrades, who offered their lives for their country in the cause of humanity.

What is camp-life like, the preface asks: what did we do, how did we fare? Kerlin invites the reader into camp to watch the moving panorama of soldier life. There, he says, human nature shows itself unrestrained by the gloss of civil society. With two brief exceptions, the chapters are letters written in camp and printed in newspapers as the war went on.
46431-st-bernard-s-the-romance-of-a-medi:
St Bernard's, The Romance of a Medical Student, is a novel published under the pen name Aesculapius Scalpel. The hosted copy is a fourth edition, printed in London in eighteen eighty eight. A motto in Latin holds that art is long and life is short, a fit head for a doctor's tale. Shakespeare lines on uncertain life and sure death stand beside it.

Chapters open on the first of October and move to the school of anatomy. Students' lodgings, a first apprentice hand, and a theatre beadle follow in the contents. Hospital wards and dissecting rooms give the romance its grit. The book trades on inside knowledge of how Victorian doctors were made.
46475-the-green-hand-adventures-of-a-nav:
George Cupples wrote sea tales drawn from his own early life, and this volume pairs his story with a short life of the author. Cupples was born in 1822 at Legerwood in Scotland, the son of a strict minister who taught him at home for his first ten years. A four and a half mile walk each way took him to school at Earlston.

Love of novels fed a wish to go to sea, and at sixteen his father let him sign on as a ships boy in training. That sea start gave him the stuff of the tales here, told as the deeds of a young naval officer. His other sea book, The Two Frigates, is named on the title page.
46513-the-westward-movement:
The Westward Movement is a school book of the past of the United States, made from the best tales of two great sheets. Barstow saw the book through the press. It was put out in nineteen twelve. It is one of a set of such books for the high years of the gram school. Its mates treat the first ships, the war of the birth of the land, and the war of the states.

The list of parts is a roll of the west in its great age. The start of the west move and the seat of the west head it. The horse post, the first boats of steam, and two great path men come next. Those path men are told by a chief of the land him self.
46565-picturesque-sketches-of-london-pas:
Thomas Miller wrote sketches of London past and present, with many engraved views. The Office of the National Illustrated Library issued the book from 227 Strand. Miller had written a history of the Anglo-Saxons and a life of Lady Jane Grey. Churches, halls, streets, and old stones fill the plates.

Chapters roam from Roman and Saxon London to Cheapside, the Tower, and the docks. St Paul's, the Mansion House, Billingsgate, and the Guildhall each get close study. Tales of Whittington, Lady Jane Grey, and the Crown Jewels add color. Town fans gain a rich walk through layers of London life and stone.
46755-life-in-a-german-crack-regiment:
Baron von Schlicht, also Count von Baudissin, wrote Life in a German Crack Regiment for Dodd, Mead at New York. Eleven chapters follow one regiment from imperial command to farewell at last. The Yellow Butterflies, nicknamed for yellow epaulettes, keep their battle anniversary in chapter one. More than forty years back, the regiment lost a third of its men.

Over half its officers fell in that famous fight, the record proudly states. A wreath honors the fallen while a rich dinner cheers the living each year. New mess rooms open the same day, and the colonel must blend grief with pleasure. Cards, morals, an aristocratic household, and a marriage offer fill later chapters. German officer life shows its polish and its rot.
46926-the-virgin-in-judgment:
Eden Phillpotts wrote The Virgin in Judgment, published at New York in October 1908. Phillpotts had written The Portreeve, The Secret Woman, and Children of the Mist. Three books divide the novel, each with thirteen or more chapters.

Chapter one, Crepuscule, opens at sunset on Ringmoor Down, near the west quarter of Dartmoor Forest. Phillpotts renders the moor as an ocean of trough and mound, moulded by storm, flame, flood, and ice. Chapter titles promise Warren House, pixies' house, the dogs of war, a wedding, and a voice from the pool. Dartmoor weather and folk carry the tale.
46966-adam-hepburn-s-vow-a-tale-of-kirk-:
Annie Swan published Adam Hepburn's Vow, a tale of kirk and covenant, with Cassell in 1885, and this copy is the twenty-third thousand. Four illustrations accompany it. She dedicates it to a friend and to the dear ones gathered round her in her happy home.

The contents follow the Covenanters' tragedy: the travellers, a nation's testimony, forebodings of evil, the minister's children, and the first martyrs. A thorn in the flesh, a long farewell, and Duncan McLean lead to the vow itself, at chapter ten. Up in arms, Rullion Green, the new maid, and betrayed carry the rising to its end. Brave to the last and at Haughhead close the tale. Swan wrote hundreds of Scottish tales for the religious market. The killing times of the 1660s were her subject: households ground between a persecuting state and an unbreakable kirk.
46983-the-memoirs-of-a-white-elephant:
The Memoirs of a White Elephant is a children's story by Judith Gautier. S A B Harvey translated it from the French. Duffield and Company published it in New York, with pictures by L H Smith and S B Kite. The translator's letter, dated from Atlantic City in 1916, introduces the hero. He is Iravata, the good and wise elephant of the King and Queen of Golconda.

Iravata narrates his own life. He serves as a war-elephant in magnificent armour, carrying the King into battle. Captured, he finds a way to free his condemned master. Later he runs away from the palace and joins a circus. There he performs amusing feats as a comedian. Homesick at last, he returns to Golconda and lives happily. The little Princess Parvati runs through his adventures. Gautier, the translator notes, also wrote tales of Persia and Japan, and could write and speak Chinese.
47403-children-above-180-iq-stanford-bin:
Leta Hollingworth studied children who test past 180 on the Binet scale. Her book came out in print in 1942 with the World Book Company. Her mate at Barnard College set the book in this form. One part first ran in her 1926 book on gifted young. That part's name is the same ask in short form.

Such scores are so rare that each case is told in full. Birth, school, kin, and tests ground each child's tale. She asks what schools owe minds of such high reach. Plain classes waste them, her work in sum holds. Mind men and teachers share the worth of her store. Each case is a life, not a mere count.
47422-a-defence-of-virginia-and-through-:
A Defence of Virginia, and through her of the South, is a polemic by Robert Dabney, printed at New York in 1867. Dabney was a Virginia professor and a late officer of the Confederate army. His target is the sectional party of the North. The contents map a long argument over slavery.

Early chapters treat the African slave trade and the legal status of slavery. Then come two long scriptural arguments, from the Old Testament and the New. An ethical chapter follows, then one on slavery's effects on work and wealth. Written just after the war, the book states the pro-slavery case at full length, as its side wished it remembered.
47496-greece-painted-by-john-fulleylove-:
John Fulleylove painted the pictures for Greece, and J A McClymont wrote its text. A and C Black issued the book at London in 1906. McClymont held a doctor of divinity degree. Companion books treat the Holy Land, Oxford, and Edinburgh. The Holy Land volume holds ninety-two plates. Most plates there are in color.

A plate here shows the Parthenon from the Propylaea at dawn. Pale gold light strikes the architraves within, its note says. The rock at right bounds the precinct of Artemis Brauronia. A column drum marks the Propylæa's east porch. The pedestal held Pyrrhos's statue of Athene Hygieia. McClymont used a fresh visit to Greece for his text. Painted travel books like this let home readers walk old lands in color before cheap cameras came.
47723-the-island-of-enchantment:
Justus Miles Forman wrote The Island of Enchantment, with pictures by Howard Pyle, printed in New York and London in 1905. A front plate shows the Doge sitting alone in a great carved chair. Contents name the young Zuan Gradenigo first, and the woman of abomination second. The first part opens on the spread of bad news.

Bad tidings spread fast, the tale begins; you cannot bury them. News come in secret to Venice was known across the city in two hours. Young Zuan Gradenigo meets his friend the German captain men call the Wolf. Lewis of Hungary is on his way to a second onslaught, and the Dalmatian towns are given over to harm. It is the spring of 1355, and a servant in the Doge's colours calls Zuan to his uncle at the palace.
47737-from-the-australian-front:
From the Australian Front is a picture book of 1917 whose net profits went to the Australian Soldiers' Patriotic Fund. Official photographs come from Hurley, Brooks, Baldwin, and Wilkins, the official photographers named at the front. Will Dyson drew a cook for the title spread in his soldier cartoon style.

A winter snapshot shows General Birdwood and his chief of staff, the Leader, in the captions. The Abbey de Bertin at Saint Omer, the arrival in Flanders, and one of the earliest battalions to enter the trenches appear in photographs. A joke has Frozen Bill planning two years at the centre of Australia to thaw out after the French winter. Anzac readers got a souvenir.
47795-recollections-with-the-third-iowa-:
Recollections with the Third Iowa Regiment, by Lieutenant Thompson, was published for the author at Cincinnati in 1864. The book was entered for copyright that same year in Ohio. Its preface tells how the pages were made from a diary. Thompson kept that diary through most of his two years of service.

Comrades asked him to compile the record, and he names that request first. The diary was written amid the scenes it attempts to describe, he says. He aims to give a faithful account of the principal scenes of the war. Iowa men at Shiloh and down the Mississippi fill his march. Such regimental memoirs poured from the press during the war itself. This one speaks while the guns were still warm.
47880-the-philosophy-of-immanuel-kant:
Lindsay of Balliol College, Oxford, wrote The Philosophy of Immanuel Kant as a short guide. The Jack firm of London and Edinburgh published the book, with Dodge of New York. The foreword quotes Schopenhauer's warning to his lecture classes. No one should let another person tell them what Kant's Critique contains.

Lindsay promises no short cut to Kant. His aim is to stir interest and offer a few helpful hints. He treats only the three Critiques, where Kant's system lives. Chapters take up criticism itself and Kant's problem of synthetic judgments. Time, space, and the categories follow. The antinomies and the proofs of God's existence come next. Moral theory and the Critique of Judgment close the study. A short life sketch opens the book, quoting Heine on Kant's quiet, ordered days in Königsberg.
48433-kant-s-critique-of-judgement:
Kant Critique of Judgement is a thought book turned by Bernard, Bishop of Ossory. A Macmillan house brought out this second changed print in nineteen fourteen. First print of the turn came in eighteen ninety two in its run. Bernard once sat as a mate of Trinity group in Dublin in past years. A long front word by the turn hand heads the scheme of the book.

Heads split thought in two, bound its realm, and join its halves by this craft. Taste is of the fair, part one of the scheme holds at its head. Free joy with no gain stake marks taste calls in that scheme rank. The fair is what, sans thought forms, wins all men joy, it holds. Broad joy, form aim, and need fill the next scheme ranks there.
48614-women-s-suffrage-a-short-history-o:
Millicent Garrett Fawcett, president of the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, wrote a short history of the suffrage movement, published at London by Jack and in New York by Dodge. A sonnet on British freedom heads the title page. The flood of British freedom, it warns, must not perish in bogs and sands. We must be free or die, who speak the tongue Shakespeare spake, the poem insists.

Fawcett led the constitutional suffragists against the militants' violence. Her history runs from the first petitions to the eve of victory. The book served as the movement's own brief record. Jack's cheap edition put it in many hands before the 1918 franchise act.
48967-mythology-among-the-hebrews-and-it:
Ignaz Goldziher wrote this study of myth among the Hebrews in German. Russell Martineau, of the British Museum, put it in English dress, with adds by the author. It was printed at London in 1877. Goldziher was a man of the Academy of Sciences of Hungary. The book is sent forth to three men of the schools of the East: Fleischer, Max Müller, and a third man whose name is cut off.

The full head of the book adds a second theme to the first. It treats not just of the myths of the Hebrews, but of their growth in the course of time. That is a bold frame for its day.
49014-reminiscences-of-the-nineteenth-ma:
John Adams, a captain in the regiment, wrote these memories of the Nineteenth Massachusetts Regiment, printed in Boston in 1899. In his preface Adams says he waited thirty-four years for someone else to write the history. At last he sends out his own soldier's story, told from memory. The account of prison life rests on a diary kept while he was a prisoner of war.

Chapter heads trace the regiment through its great battles. They run from Ball's Bluff and Fair Oaks to Antietam, Fredericksburg, and Gettysburg, where Adams was wounded. Later heads cover the Wilderness, Cold Harbor, and long months in rebel prisons. The last heads tell of his escape, capture, and return.
4905-galusha-the-magnificent:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Galusha the Magnificent opens on a foggy October afternoon, as Horatio Pulcifer walks home between Wellmouth Centre and East Wellmouth through rain, puddles, and pitch-pine groves. The Cape Cod setting, wet and gray, frames a comedy of village life in which an unlikely hero earns his grand title.

Lincoln's humor rests on local character: plainspoken neighbors, small-town pride, and the gap between a man's reputation and his actual deeds. The novel moves at a village pace, with weather and gossip doing much of the work. Readers get a gentle, funny portrait of Cape life, told by a writer who knew its people from the inside.
49117-the-boy-scouts-and-the-prize-penna:
The Boy Scouts and the Prize Pennant is a scouting adventure by Robert Shaler, published by Hurst and Company at New York in 1914. Shaler wrote other volumes in the line, named at the front, on the signal corps, pioneer camp, and the life saving crew. The first chapter, The Value of Woodcraft, opens in the woods at night.

Billy hears what he takes for an owl's far hoot. Hugh, lately made assistant scout master, doubts that tenderfoot recruits of the new Owl patrol could be so deep in the woods, or that any owl's call runs so deep. Racing clouds overhead promise a storm. Twelve chapters carry the troop through a wrecked balloon, first aid, field tests, and a big count for the Wolf Patrol, to victory well won.
49281-seeing-the-elephant:
Seeing the Elephant is an amateur drama issued in Boston by the house of Baker. The play was entered for copyright in 1873. Its unnamed author had written a long shelf of similar pieces. Temperance titles like A Drop Too Much stand among his other works.

The cast list sets a farming household at the centre of the stage. Silas Somerby is a farmer with a weakness for the bottle. Harry Holden serves as his right-hand man on the farm. Bias Black the teamster and Pat Murphy the labourer fill the yard. Silas's wife Rachel, son Johnny, and daughter Sally complete the home. The printed costumes fix each figure at a glance for amateur players. A lathered face and towel mark Silas in a comic shaving scene. Baker's house made its name selling such plays to home and school stages.
49320-cadet-days-a-story-of-west-point:
Captain Charles King, U S A, tells of a plebe's hard road at West Point in a Harper tale held under rights from 1894. Plates show plebe drill, the awkward squad, guard duty, and a cadet borne down the road on comrades' shoulders. King gives the book to a mother who gave her only son to the army.

Ads list King's war tales at one dollar to one dollar and twenty-five cents in cloth. Plate captions trace arrest, court-room calls, and Saturday tramps in the area as punishment. A rifle brought in by a drum-boy orderly and a colonel who scans a polished weapon add period detail. The tale runs from trial to final triumph, as the dedication frames the mother's long wait.
49338-the-boy-scouts-for-city-improvemen:
Scout Master Robert Shaler wrote The Boy Scouts for City Improvement, in 1914. Hurst at New York holds the rights from that year. Shaler had written a shelf of Boy Scout books before this one. Contents open under a spreading oak, then a friend in need. A fire call, willing workers, and repairing damages follow in the list.

Hugh and Billy talk on a stone curbing in the shade of a great oak. The day feels like August dog-days, though September is ending. They rest, watch people go by, and talk of skating and tobogganing. On duty, an alarm, and mocking the mayor fill the middle chapters. An accusation and a turning point lead to thanks to the scouts. The two lads wear khaki uniforms of their home town troop. Shaler gives civic service as adventure for boys.
49566-canada-and-the-british-immigrant:
Emily Weaver wrote this guide for Britons thinking of a new life in Canada. The Religious Tract Society printed it in London in 1914. A front plate shows a fruit ranch at Nelson, in British Columbia, under sun.

Weaver offers herself as a guide in her opening note. She came out from England as a girl, one of a large family, to settle in Canada. Her father had no farm training when he began. She knows at first hand the trials and joys that wait for the newcomer. A line from the Marquis of Lorne heads the book: honest heat in summer, honest cold in winter, and men made strong by clear skies.
49668-ancient-monuments-of-the-mississip:
Ancient Monuments of the Mississippi Valley is an archaeological work by Squier and Davis. It was the first volume of Smithsonian Contributions to Knowledge. The Smithsonian Institution published it at Washington in 1848. An advertisement explains the series as original memoirs on branches of knowledge. James Smithson's bequest funded that plan for spreading knowledge. A plate of ancient works at Marietta, Ohio opens the volume. Its subject is the mound works of the great river valley.

The authors surveyed earthworks left by early peoples of the region. Their book records plans and measures of those monuments. It appeared just as American archaeology was taking form as a study. The Smithsonian chose it to launch its publication series. Readers meet a founding text of mound builder research.
49669-home-problems-from-a-new-standpoin:
Caroline Hunt wrote a book that treats the home as a part of the social whole. The book came out in Boston in 1908. Hunt frames her work with a thought from Hobson on the social problem. She also quotes Ruskin on the aim of a good life. That aim is the most hale and glad folk that can be.

Hunt says homes once stood apart from trade and work strife. That time has passed, she argues. What homes buy, eat, and pay now links to the wide world. She asks how home life can be run with care and sense. Reform minds get a calm, clear brief.
49727-ralph-sinclair-s-atonement:
Ralph Sinclair's Atonement is a novel by Antony Sargent. Melrose of London issued it in 1903. Thirty-three chapters carry Ralph across two continents. A bolt from the blue opens the tale. Broadstone, Antwerp, and Railton Hall set the home scenes. Visions of the Klondyke draw the hero west. The far west and Montreal follow in the list. A ranger's ranch and Manitoba fill the middle.

A dream of gold and a missing link stir the plot. A snake in the grass and a confession come late. Dead, but alive again, teases one chapter. Till death do us part closes the book. Sargent mixes English halls with Canadian wilds. Atonement, as the title says, is the hero's road.
49779-publicity-stunt:
Robert Moore Williams's Publicity Stunt appeared in Other Worlds in March 1953, illustrated by Tillotson. Its headnote gives the orders behind the voyage. The crew must build up Venus, making it sound like the gateway to Paradise for the average Earthman.

Fog-flies, flying snakes and tame Venusians are all part of the sales pitch. Instead, Molock defies the Venusian Shad Brisbee on his sacred dancing ground. Brisbee stands seven feet tall and has six eyes, and Molock, unarmed but for a needle pistol, invites him to start chewing. Captain Wilkerson, officially in charge, protests that they will all be killed. Rita Morgan alone keeps her composure as Molock refuses to move the ship.
50140-the-story-of-the-thirty-second-reg:
The Story of the Thirty-second Regiment, Massachusetts Infantry, published at Boston in 1880, was written by Francis Parker, the regiment's own colonel. Parker says plainly that the book is not a history of the Civil War. It tells only what one regiment of the Army of the Potomac saw and did. He wrote it so the men could hand their children true pictures of the service.

Comrades fed him incidents, in talk and in writing, above all for the months after his own resignation. Chapters move from garrison life to the Peninsula and campaigning under Pope. Parker takes all blame for faults of style on himself. The preface is dated April 30th, 1880.
50400-dave-dawson-flight-lieutenant:
Dave Dawson, Flight Lieutenant, by Bowen, is a boys air war novel. Saalfield issued it at Akron and New York, rights held in 1941. Dave Dawson flies with the Royal Air Force in the new war. Squadron Leader Markham of the Eighty Fourth opens chapter one at his desk.

Paper work bores Markham, who flew daily in the last war with Jerry. A strange memo, number six four two nine, puzzles his adjutant Phipps at once. Zone K-24 is said to be evacuated; photo plates are called obsolete there. Dawson with the RAF, at Dunkirk, and in Libya are prior books. Action, codes, and young airmen fill this wartime series entry.
50432-workhouse-nursing-the-story-of-a-s:
Workhouse Nursing, the story of a successful experiment, is a report printed at London in 1867. It tells how the Select Vestry of Liverpool brought trained nurses into the workhouse hospital wards under their control. The experiment was tried in the male wards of the Workhouse Infirmary. It succeeded so well that the Vestry extended the system to the rest of the infirmary.

The account rests on the report of Mr Carr, the governor, and of a sub-committee of the Vestry. Replies are printed to inquiries sent to institutions and persons linked with the training of nurses in London and Liverpool. Letters on the subject from Miss Nightingale are among its papers. The writer sets out the grounds on which the Vestry undertook the scheme. The book was meant to guide managers of workhouses elsewhere who faced the same need.
50499-the-vanishing-point:
The Vanishing Point is a novel by Coningsby Dawson, illustrated by James Montgomery Flagg. The Cosmopolitan Book Corporation published it in New York in 1922. Dawson had written The Kingdom Round the Corner. An epigraph from Varensky sets the theme. Railroad rails seem to join at a vanishing point in the distance. Life, he says, runs on parallel rails of possibility and desire. To overtake their merging means death.

The first chapter is The Disappearance of a Patriot. The liner Ryndam halts at Plymouth Harbor at midnight. She puts off English passengers and mail by tug. Philip Hindwood lands first, and Santa Gorlof follows in sables. The third passenger never appears. Stewards shout Prince Rogovich's name through staterooms and decks. The engines thud like a heart stifled with foreboding. Shore lights wink across the water, as if signalling that the Prince will not be found that night.
50656-the-conspiracy-of-gianluigi-fiesch:
The Conspiracy of Gianluigi Fieschi is a past of Genoa by Emanuele Celesia of Italy. David Wheeler turned it to English for a London house in eighteen sixty six. Its next name sets the tale in Genoa of the sixteenth century years. A front talk by Wheeler notes how scant English past of Italy has grown. New vault search in Italy has changed home views, but ours stand stale.
