This plot tale marks that new search growth in strong form, he holds. One plot in it paints the whole state of Italy in that age. Younger pens of the land are the first free pens it has borne. A free press bore their work as its first fruit in that land. Fieschi stands in plate as Saint George at the front of the book.
50690-the-remedy-for-unemployment:
Alfred Russel Wallace, the famed student of nature, wrote a penny pamphlet on the cure for joblessness, issued by the Clarion Press in London. Ads for other Clarion tracts fill the first leaves. The piece first ran in the Socialist Review and is here reprinted with small changes.

Wallace wrote, he says, because no member of Parliament, not even the open Socialists, would stand on the base rules of their creed for this great ill. He names two: that goods should be made for use and not for profit, and that the true wage of work is the whole product of that work. From those rules he builds a plan to end chronic want of work and the hunger that dogs it.
50700-the-story-teller-of-the-desert-bac:
Backsheesh, or Life and Adventures in the Orient, by Thomas Knox, was published at Hartford in 1885 under the fuller title The Story Teller of the Desert. Knox, a veteran travel writer, recounts a journey over the Atlantic, down the Danube, and through the Crimea. From there he travels on through Turkey, Greece, Asia Minor, Syria, Palestine, and Egypt, and up the Nile into Nubia and equatorial Africa. Nearly two hundred and fifty illustrations fill the book.

Knox writes descriptive and humorous sketches of sights and scenes, in the manner that made his subscription travel books sell door to door across America. His preface tells of a young traveler whose father counted eighteen thousand dollars spent in a year, answered by lots of fun for the money. The volume is popular geography of its day, generous and entertaining.
50755-the-most-bitter-foe-of-nations-and:
Andrew White gave a speech at Yale on the worst foe of all lands. The speech went to the Phi Beta Kappa Society on July 25, 1866. It came out in print at New Haven that same year. The board wrote to thank him and ask for a copy to print. White sent the text with a note from Albany in August.

He sets the foe out as a curse of long, sad years. He then maps a way to throw it down for good. The Civil War had just closed when he spoke those words. His hearers were men of books in a time of fresh graves. The speech asks what a land must change at its core.
50854-mary-of-burgundy-or-the-revolt-of-:
Mary of Burgundy; or, The Revolt of Ghent is a historical novel by James, here reprinted by George Routledge and Sons of London in 1903. Laurie Magnus wrote the introduction to this edition. The tale is set in the Burgundian Netherlands of Mary, heiress of Charles the Bold.

Magnus's introduction sketches a prodigious career. James, historiographer royal to William the Fourth, was born in London in 1799 and died at Venice in 1860. He was the reputed author of upwards of a hundred novels, and compiled or edited nearly half as many volumes of letters, memoirs and biographies. In his last ten years he served as British consul in Massachusetts, in Virginia and at Venice. Scott, on whose style he founded his own, encouraged him as a novelist. Thackeray burlesqued him twice, which Magnus counts a distinction.
50929-ethan-allen-the-robin-hood-of-verm:
Ethan Allen: The Robin Hood of Vermont, by Henry Hall, was published by D Appleton and Company at New York in 1892. Hall died in 1889, and the preface by Henrietta Hall Boardman explains that the manuscript of finished fragments and notes was left in his daughters' hands to complete.

The aim was a fuller life of Allen than had yet been written. It singles him out from the cluster of patriots in the New Hampshire Grants for younger readers. The contents run from Allen's family and early life through the Green Mountain Boys, his outlawry, and the capture of Ticonderoga. Benedict Arnold and the diary of Edward Mott appear among the chapters.
50931-stories-of-enchantment:
Jane Pentzer Myers wrote Stories of Enchantment, a book of fairy tales for children published in Chicago in 1901. Harriet Roosevelt Richards drew the pictures. Myers opens with a short address to a little girl, describing a world between the land of dreams and broad daylight, where good wishes come true.

Twelve stories follow. They include The Ghost Flower, The Little Yellow Moccasins, The Little Ghost Who Laughed, and Titania's Maid of Honor. Other tales tell of Bran the wolf dog, a corn fairy, and a mist lady. Fairies dwell under the trees in Myers's border land, and sorrowful folk find friends and castles there. The tales aim to charm young readers while blurring, on purpose, the line between the real and the unreal.
51115-transfer-point:
Anthony Boucher ends the world quietly in Transfer Point, from Galaxy Science Fiction in November 1950. The blurb turns on its hero: it was a nasty plot Vyrko was involved in, and the worst part was that he constructed it himself and did not get the end right. Three people remain in a retreat, safe from the deadly yellow bands.

The great Kirth-Labbery built the retreat for a strange reason — he itched — and stocked it against the poisonous element agnoton. Vyrko sits recording the destruction of mankind twice over, once as fact and once as an epic poem, while Lavra teases him.
51123-paddington-past-and-present:
Paddington: Past and Present, by William Robins, was transcribed from the eighteen fifty-three edition. Robins printed the book for himself in Camden Town and sold it through all booksellers. His motto, set on the title page, is Milton's plea for the liberty to know, to utter, and to argue freely.

The preface argues that history is valuable less for facts than for lessons. Paddington, Robins notes, had been transformed from a quiet rural village into a city of palaces. Most residents, he complains, had no clear notion of the forces behind that change. Nor did they know how the profits of the change had been distributed. His plates show the old church and the new church of seventeen ninety-one on Paddington Green. The book is parish history written as an argument about land and power.
51273-advance-agent:
Advance Agent, a science fiction story by Christopher Anvil, ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in February 1957, with art by Finlay. A spy named Dan Redman stands at the heart of the tale. He has the worst break a spy can draw, by the blurb. He is saddled with the face and guise of a famed man.

Dan stoops to look in a mirror before he meets his director. The face there has strong cheekbones, copper skin, and a high arched nose. It is not a bad face, but Dan is not used to it yet. His coat draws tight across a chest and shoulders not his own. The tale turns on that borrowed face and a systematised enigma. Anvil writes brisk, wry science fiction of spies and schemes.
51299-ibrahim-pasha-grand-vizir-of-sulei:
Ibrahim Pasha, Grand Vizir of Suleiman the Magnificent, is a historical study by Hester Donaldson Jenkins. Columbia University published it at New York in 1911 in its studies in history, economics, and public law. The volume is number forty six, part two, of that series in its heading. Jenkins had been professor of history in the American College for Girls at Constantinople.

Contents open with the origin of the Turks and their advance from Central Asia to Europe. The rise and fall of the Seljuk kingdom and the rise of the Ottoman power come after in order. Ibrahim, the Greek born favourite raised to the grand vizirate, is the subject of the study proper. Jenkins writes the life of the man who stood nearest the throne of Suleiman in the great decade of the empire, and fell by the sultana intrigue in her account.
51449-moral-equivalent:
Moral Equivalent is a science fiction story by Kris Neville, with plates by Dick Francis, taken from Galaxy magazine for January 1957. A blurb asks why a culture should not copy another to the last detail, and warns the last detail may be final.

The tale opens in deep space, as the planet Lanit the Second shrinks to a bright speck. Beliakoff holds the ship at Breakoff Point while Kelly sets dials for the jump into the Slot. Beliakoff cracks his bony knuckles and begs for a gentle entry, since the old ship resents being slammed. Kelly grins and twirls the last dial too fast. Beliakoff says he is out by two decimal points, enough to ionize them all. Space fans get nerve, craft, and alien ways.
51523-with-the-scottish-regiments-at-the:
E Charles Vivian wrote an account of the Scots corps at the front, printed at London in 1914 as one of a daily paper's war books sold for a shilling. The book walks through the great corps one by one, giving each its own chapter and its record of battle honours.

Chapters treat the Guards and the Greys, the Royal Scots, the Royal Scots Fusiliers, and the King's Own Scottish Borderers. Then come the Black Watch, the Gordon, Seaforth, Cameron and Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders, and at last the Highland Light Infantry and the Cameronians. Books of this kind told folk at home what their own corps had done and suffered.
51813-the-bee-keeper-s-manual-or-practic:
The Bee Keeper Manual, or practical hints on the management and complete preservation of the honey bee, by Henry Taylor, was printed in London by Groombridge and Sons in 1860. The book stands in a sixth edition, with additions, and many engravings. It adds a description of the most approved hives.

Chapters open with the queen or mother bee and the common or working bees. Swarming, or single hiving, and depriving systems follow. Common straw hives, straw depriving hives, hive covers, and floor boards fill the hive part. Wood box hives, wood bar boxes, bar glass hives, and straw bar hives come in turn. White collateral hive, Nutt collateral hive, and the nadir hive stand late in the list. Summer management, wax and combs, propolis, honey, and pollen close the run. Bee keepers of 1860 got a full apiary guide.
51964-a-georgian-pageant:
Frank Frankfort Moore wrote A Georgian Pageant, essays on famed folk of the late seventeen hundreds. Hutchinson and Company issued the book in London in nineteen hundred eight. Moore says a long talk with J Churton Collins sparked the set. Collins died the day proofs were to go to him.

Moore argues that stock views of that age are oft dead wrong. Oliver Goldsmith and Samuel Johnson get fresh looks here. James Boswell and Henry Thrale stand in the same new light. Fanny Burney at court and the Gunning sisters face his doubt. Sheridan’s flight with Elizabeth Linley gets retold too. The first sketch opens at Kew Gardens in February seventeen hundred eighty nine. A small, prim lady walks there in state.
52008-dante-rossetti-and-the-pre-raphael:
Esther Wood's study of Dante Rossetti and the Pre-Raphaelite movement came from Sampson Low at London in 1893. The frontispiece is The Day-Dream, from Rossetti's chalk drawing, printed by permission of Theodore Watts. Wood is candid about her limits: the pages add no material facts to what is known, and the authoritative biography of Rossetti is yet to be written. Rossetti himself wished that task for Watts, his closest friend of later years, or for his brother William.

Her aim is different. She presents the movement in its relation to the larger tendencies of the age, and to the moral principles behind nineteenth-century taste. She has avoided, she says, the proper domain of the art critic. The Pre-Raphaelite movement is treated here as an ethical rather than an aesthetic revolution. Hall Caine's Recollections of Rossetti supplies her with vivid side-lights on the dominant personality.
52151-inspiration-its-nature-and-extent:
Hoare, vicar of Trinity at Tunbridge Wells and honorary canon of Canterbury, argues for scriptural inspiration in a Hatchards book of 1877. This London printing is the second edition, and five short chapters structure the case. They treat the divine element, the human element, their combination, and the difficulties.

Hoare opens by saying the subject cannot be overrated, since trust in the Gospel's mysteries rests on it. Human intellect, he grants, achieves much, yet it cannot cross into the unseen kingdom or learn God's plan of salvation. Scripture, he holds, is God's own communication on those deep things. If the Bible fails as such a message, he warns, no other source can take its place.
52272-two-sermons-preached-in-the-parish: Two sermons were preached in the parish church of Nonington, Kent on January 17, 1864, the Sunday after the funeral of John Pemberton Plumptre of Fredville in the same parish. Herbert James, perpetual curate of Goodnestone, and Edward Hoare of Trinity Church, Tunbridge Wells, shared the preaching. Batcheller of Dover and Nisbet of London printed the pair. James takes his text from Hebrews thirteen, verse seven, on remembering those who spoke the word of God. He treats God's gifts as gifts with a purpose, never thrown at random.
52618-the-decameron-day-6-to-day-10-cont:
The Decameron, last five days, holds fifty of Boccaccio hundred pleasant novels. Isaac Jaggard printed this English text at London in 1620 for readers. Seven honourable ladies and three noble gentlemen tell the tales in turn. A dedication to Phillip Herbert, Earl of Montgomery, fronts the volume in state.

Day six, under Madame Eliza, rewards witty answers to taunts and traps. Speakers who turn a sudden reply escape loss, danger, and disgrace thereby. A preface compares books to gardens where weeds spring among flowers unsown. Errors in copy and press are owned with a plea for courtesy. Old spelling and courtly speech mark this first English dress.
52788-midnight-jack-or-the-road-agent:
Midnight Jack, or The Road-Agent, is number one of Jackson's Novels, sold for one penny from Fleet Street, London. It opens in a dark vale midway between Fort Sully and Deadwood, by the Cheyenne River. Timon Moss, a gin smuggler, has lost a linchpin and a wheel, and rigs a drag of timber in its place. His mules strain and stall; the load will not move ten feet at a pull. Thirty miles from gold, he is bust.

So he dumps the dead weight, as a ship's crew does at sea: the books go over, box by box, while ten kegs of whisky stay safe. He will blame the wreck on Midnight Jack or the Sioux, as suits. Dime fans get a sly, rough start to a road agent yarn.
52932-the-book-its-history-and-developme:
Cyril Davenport wrote a history of the book from first records to his own day, printed in London in 1907. A golden binding of the Gospels of Charlemagne, set with jewels and enamels, fronts the book. Davenport starts with rock inscriptions, marks on wood, quipus, and wampum. Palm leaf books and the birth of alphabets follow.

Later chapters cover rolls of papyrus and vellum, the sewing and binding of medieval books, and the making of paper. Printing gets its own chapter, from Chinese types to block books and presses. Bindings in leather, cloth, embroidery, and even tortoiseshell close the survey. Any reader who loves books as objects will find craft lore on every page.
53031-the-barton-experiment:
The Barton Experiment appeared at New York from Putnam's Sons in 1877, by the author of Helen's Babies. The preface denies that it is a finished romance in any sense. Its people, the author says, stand close to real men who made names as reformers, and its chapters pit reformers at white heat against business sense, wet blankets, and slow results.

The aim is practical rather than lofty, since readers are urged to see that money and steady effort decide whether reform lasts. The village of Barton fills with bells, closed shops, and tense crowds as the tale opens, and what follows tests zeal against cost, habit, and doubt. Anyone drawn to temperance era reform fiction will find its terms stated plainly and its lessons drawn from life.
53162-some-poems-of-roger-casement:
Some Poems of Roger Casement was printed at Dublin by the Talbot Press in 1918. The front art shows Casement's own face, and the set holds a first survey of his life and work. Love verse leads: The Heart's Verdict, Mio Salvatore, and Love's Horizon and Love's Cares. Then the range widens. The Peak of the Cameroons climbs in two parts, and Hamilcar Barca stands in old Carthage.

Verse sent from the Congo Free State pleads for the Elgin Marbles to go back to Greece. The Irish Language, Parnell, and Benburb sing the home cause, and Hugh O'Neill's triumph closes the roll. A Hugo piece in English dress stands at the end. Verse fans get the whole bent of a man famed far more for deeds than rhymes, in his own lines.
53172-stargazing-past-and-present:
Stargazing, Past and Present, by J Norman Lockyer, was printed in London by Macmillan in 1878. The book grew from shorthand notes of eight Royal Institution lectures given in 1870. G M Seabroke helped Lockyer ready the notes for print.

In his preface Lockyer says other work kept the lectures from print for five years. Seabroke took the burden off his shoulders in 1875 and helped with the final proofs. Lockyer found the eight hours had left out many points of interest, so the book grew past the talks. A plate shows R S Newall telescope, a twenty five inch refractor. The work treats the tools of astronomy, old and new, and what they show. Sky fans get a famed teacher on the craft of watching stars.
53597-narrative-of-travels-in-europe-asi:
Narrative of Travels in Europe, Asia, and Africa, in the seventeenth century, is the travel book of Evliya Efendi. Hammer translated the work from the Turkish for the Oriental Translation Fund. Parbury, Allen and Company sold the volume in London in 1834 for the fund. An advertisement at the front introduces the traveller to English readers of that year.

The narrative of an Asiatic traveller, enthusiastically fond of seeing foreign countries, is in itself so great a singularity, it says. No apology seems requisite for presenting Evliya in an English dress, the advertisement adds. Evliya, who travelled forty years through the Ottoman world and beyond, left the largest travel book of his century. This first English portion made his name in the West, where scholars still mine his pages for the life of the empire.
53673-the-mercer-boys-on-a-treasure-hunt:
The Mercer Boys on a Treasure Hunt is a boys quest tale by Capwell Wyckoff. A World Syndicate house brought it out in nineteen twenty nine. Don and Jim Mercer stand by a town ball lot in the first part. Home from Woodcrest war school for the warm months, they watch kids play. Don longs for one swing at that ball with his school train skill.

Part names chart the hunt from a sage note to a cairn end. Ghost ship tale, a royal bid, and a raid start the case scheme. A wreck fort, pit rope, and hid way fill mid part names. Bell toll, forced march, and past come back thick the plot more. Gain and guile, a tar cask, and a den close the scheme.
53728-asiatic-cholera-a-treatise-on-its-:
Asiatic Cholera is a med work on the great plague of that name. Two doctors named Whitney wrote it as a pair in New York. It came out in 1866, while the plague still stalked the world. The young writer gives the book to the chiefs who taught him.

He had spent three years at a med school in that town. Their ward rounds and their lore on sickness shaped his views. The book takes up where the plague springs from in the world. It then sets out how the ill body fails, step by step. Cures tried in the East and the West are weighed in its pages. The aim is a rule of care that a young hand can trust.
53900-historical-record-of-the-seventh-o:
An official record tells the service of the Seventh, the Queen's Own regiment of hussars. It belongs to a set of army records ordered by the king in 1836. The order came from the Horse Guards on the first day of that year. Every regiment in the British army was to have its service set in print.

Each account was to give the raising of the corps and the stations where it served. Battles, sieges and other deeds were to be named in full. So were the colours and prizes taken from the foe. Lists name the officers and men killed or wounded, and those marked out for brave conduct in the field.
53997-hills-of-han-a-romantic-incident:
Samuel Merwin wrote Hills of Han, a romantic incident, illustrated by Walt Louderback and published at Indianapolis in 1919. A poem stands as prologue. Hills of Han, slumber on, it begins, while sunlight lingers on terraced tops and a yellow stream breathes its lullaby.

Then the poem turns: what is this filament leaping pole to pole and hill to hill, these strips of metal creeping where the dead have lain so still? Smoke of mill and roar of steam arrive by temple wall. A note warns that the story's slight geographical confusion is deliberate, a reminder that the tale is imagination built on fact. Readers get a novel of old China meeting the wire and the railway.
54195-grit-or-the-young-boatman-of-pine-:
Grit, or The Young Boatman of Pine Point, is a boys’ story by Horatio Alger, issued at New York by Hurst and Company. Alger is billed on the title page as the author of forty nine other rattling good stories. The Medal Library published the tale for wide sale. Chapter one opens with a single word cried out, the title itself.

Well, mother, what is it, answers a sturdy boy of fifteen. He is thick set and short for his age, but strongly made. His eyes are clear and bright, and his face is attractive. That boy is Grit, the young boatman of the tale. Alger builds on grit of character as much as on the name. Work, pluck, and a good mother carry his hero through want and spite.
54255-narrative-of-travels-in-europe-asi:
Narrative of Travels in Europe, Asia, and Africa holds the tours of Evliya Efendi. Joseph von Hammer turned the Turkish text into English for this set. The hosted text is the second volume of that English set. It came out in London in the year eighteen fifty.

Town by town notes on Brussa lead this part of the long tour. Mosques, colleges, baths, and hot springs each earn their own short head. Springs of sulphur and famed bath houses draw long praise in the text. The traveller roamed three world parts in the seventeenth century of his age. His eye for rite, trade, and odd custom fills page after page.
54383-the-american-railway-its-construct:
The American Railway, published by Scribner in 1889, explains the building and running of rail roads in the United States. Twelve men of the field wrote its chapters, among them Clarke, Bogart, Forney, Prout, Porter, Hadley, James and Adams. Thomas Cooley, chairman of the Interstate Commerce Commission, wrote the introduction. More than two hundred illustrations fill the book.

The first chapter builds a railway from survey to finished track. It counts more than three thousand bridges and tells how foundations are laid under water. Later chapters take up feats of engineering, locomotives and cars. The Howe truss, the use of iron and the birth of the cantilever all get plain treatment for the general reader.
54557-rough-ways-made-smooth-a-series-of:
Rough Ways Made Smooth is a set of familiar essays on scientific subjects by Richard Proctor. Longmans, Green issued this new impression in London in 1903. Proctor had used the same plan in Light Science for Leisure Hours. His preface is dated from a ship in the Irish Sea in 1879.

The essays promise science in untechnical terms for general readers. Some titles, Proctor warns, look remote from science at first sight. All are treated in their scientific meaning, and in plain words. The sun's corona and his spots open the collection in two pieces. Sun-spots and commercial panics stand provocatively side by side. New planets near the sun and the British transit expeditions follow. The past history of the moon and a new crater in it come next. November meteors and cold winters round out the skyward survey.
54587-the-pope-the-kings-and-the-people-:
The Pope, the Kings, and the People is a polemical history by William Arthur, edited after his death by Blair Neatby and published by Hodder and Stoughton in 1903. Its full title calls it a history of the movement to make the Pope governor of the world. That movement is traced by a universal reconstruction of society, from the issue of the Syllabus to the close of the Vatican Council.

The motto comes from the coronation service of the pontiffs. Take the tiara adorned with the triple crown, it says, and know that you are the father of princes and kings. Neatby's preface explains his limits: by his own choice his care was confined to abridgment. There was no time to verify Arthur's multitude of references and quotations. A passage preserved in the preface notes that Arthur's forecasts have already been verified.
54694-international-language-and-science:
Couturat and co-authors argue for an international language in science. Constable printed their considerations in London in 1910. Donnan, a Liverpool professor, Englished the work for science men. His preface hopes readers judge only after quiet, fair study.

It is not a question of another language, he writes there. It is a final solution by science methods of one problem. The authors held chairs at Caen, Copenhagen, Zurich, Leipzig, and Graz. The book weighs how science might gain one shared tongue. Special letters and symbols of the proposed tongue fill a transcriber note in the text.
55162-enchantment:
Harold MacGrath wrote Enchantment, short stories of whimsical adventure, copyrighted in 1905. A series page places the book among The Pocket Books, designed to represent the three aspects of American romance: adventure, mystery, and humour. Companion volumes hold Anna Katharine Green's detective tales and MacGrath's own Princess Elopes.

MacGrath also wrote The Man on the Box and The Puppet Crown. His name in 1905 promised light romance told at speed, kings in disguise and hearts in peril. The tales here favour coincidence, disguise, and the sudden turn. Readers get a bestselling romancer's short pieces, issued in a pocket series built for railway reading and an evening's escape.
55261-nothing-of-importance-a-record-of-:
Bernard Adams wrote Nothing of Importance, a record of eight months at the front with a Welsh battalion. Methuen put it out at London, first in 1917, with a portrait and three maps. The months run from October 1915 to June 1916. A memoir of Adams stands at the front, marked in memoriam. He was born on November 15, 1890, at Beckenham in Kent, and won prizes at Malvern school.

At Cambridge, Adams won gold medals for a Greek epigram and a Latin ode. He took a first in the Classical Tripos and then read economics. The India Office made him warden of a hostel for Indian students in South Kensington. There his warmth won all who knew him, a friend writes.
55432-ameboid-movement:
Ameboid Movement, by Asa A Schaeffer, came out from the press of Princeton in 1920. Schaeffer taught the study of animals at the University of Tennessee. His book sums up past work on how the ameba moves, from the notes of Rosenhof down to his own tests.

Wallich showed that a new false foot forms when the outer skin breaks and the inner flow pours out. He showed that the two kinds of flesh in the cell trade places, each turning to the other. Later parts treat the skin layer as the true organ of motion. Tests probe that layer and its powers. A last part treats the wavy path of the ameba, and the spiral paths of kin forms. Cell students get a full, clear brief.
55622-red-wagon-stories-or-tales-told-un:
Wells Hawks gathered tales told by circus folk under the big tent between shows. I and M Ottenheimer issued the book at Baltimore, with rights held in 1904. Hawks gave the yarns to kids who once led spotted ponies to water at the lot. Seven old hands form the circle that talks each night.

A press agent, a bill poster, a candy butcher, and a boss canvasman all take turns. An old grafter mourns, a band master plays solo, and an elephant tale tops the set. Slang, sawdust, and road life fill each short piece. Readers gain a warm, rough view of circus work from the inside.
56195-the-boy-volunteers-on-the-belgian-:
The Boy Volunteers on the Belgian Front, by Kenneth Ward, was published in 1917, in a series of boys books on the European war. The series was cloth bound, fully illustrated, at fifty cents a volume. Its books relate the adventures of two American boys, and their experiences in battle and on air scout duty.

The Belgian Front volume describes two American boys who were in Europe when the great war commenced. Their enlistment with Belgian troops, and their remarkable experiences, are based on actual occurrences. Line drawings show fighting machines, airplanes, and maps of places where important battles took place. Later volumes put the boys with the French airmen, and with the British artillery. Readers gain, the adverts say, considerable knowledge of the different types of battle planes used by the warring nations. Readers get a boys war series written while the war still raged.
56198-the-abandoned-country-or-frank-rea:
The Abandoned Country ran as Frank Reade Junior's tale in 1904. Frank Tousey issued it as Number 84 of his weekly. The date is June 3, 1904 in New York. Five cents was the number's price. A year's subscription cost two dollars fifty. Noname signs as its author in the old style.

A Wonderful Tale opens the twelve chapters. Plans Are Made and In Southern Seas follow. Up the Fiord and The Ruined City come next. Across the Lake and Barney's adventures fill the middle. A geological phenomenon gets a chapter of its own. On an Island and A Startling Discovery build late. A Serious Accident fills chapter eleven. A front scene shows Frank and Randall hauling Barney up ice. Hard to kill an Irishman, Barney cries there. Dime novel science sent its boy inventor to a lost continent at a nickel a week.
56226-conrad-in-quest-of-his-youth-an-ex:
Leonard Merrick wrote this novel of a man who goes back to seek his youth. Mitchell Kennerley printed Conrad in Quest of His Youth at New York in 1911. Its subtitle calls the book an extravagance of temperament.

A song of young Prague opens the first chapter, all laughter and thin dinners. Hope was the wealth of beginners then, and the singers were all millionaires, the verse says. Merrick asks us to picture that singer's shade back in a grey, changed London. Conrad goes back to the Latin Quarter in Paris in much that state. The bright society he craved has turned cold to him now, and his sadness matches the song's ghost.
56310-the-undercurrent:
Robert Grant's Undercurrent came from Scribner's Sons in New York in 1904. Yohn supplied the illustrations, and Grant dedicated the novel to his wife. Emil Stuart and Constance Forbes are pronounced man and wife by the Reverend George Prentiss. Constance has doubted whether she should renounce her ambition to help in the great work of education. She brings a nest-egg of five thousand dollars, realized from the sale of the family homestead at Colton.

Emil was until lately only a clerk with Toler and Company, lumber merchants. He has just started in business on his own account. Constance came an orphan from Colton to Benham a year before the wedding. The frontispiece shows her lover beside her, suggesting he escort her home. Later captions darken the tone: church attendance missed, a cry of how could you, and a surrender.
56345-the-world-s-greatest-military-spie:
George Barton wrote tales of the great spies of war, and the Page Company of Boston copyrighted the book in 1917. A second run followed in July 1918. Barton gave the book to William Flynn, chief of the United States Secret Service, for his work in clearing the land of foreign spies in the world war. The frontispiece shows the capture of Major André.

Nineteen tales fill the book. The first treats Schulmeister, the Alsatian smuggler called the Prince of Spies, who helped Napoleon take an Austrian army. Others treat Belle Boyd, who saved Stonewall Jackson, and Lydia Darrah, who saved the army of Washington. The Chevalier d'Eon, Nathan Hale, and Emma Edmonds all appear. The last tale treats Carl Lody and the spies of the great war then still being fought. The book is popular history told for thrills.
56403-the-future-of-the-women-s-movement:
The Future of the Women Movement, by H M Swanwick, was printed in London by G Bell and Sons in 1913. Mrs Fawcett, president of the National Union of Women Suffrage Societies, wrote the opening. Swanwick gives the book to F T S.

The first chapter treats the causes of the women movement. Woman becomes articulate, and the movement has turned political in England. Women handicap, the need for focus, and two kinds of change, education and industrial work, fill the heads. The second chapter asks what the movement is, and what the world is losing by its lack. The third treats the subjection of women, the weight of motherhood, and training for it. Later chapters treat war, foreign policy, and democracy. Suffrage fans get a thoughtful leader case for the cause and its road ahead.
56439-old-clinkers-a-story-of-the-new-yo:
Harvey O'Higgins wrote a tale of the New York fire crews and their hard trade. The book came out in Boston in 1909. O'Higgins also wrote The Smoke Eaters on the same theme. Martin Justice drew the pictures. The book is given to the lost heroes of the city fire force.

Old hands and new men face smoke, gas tanks, and tall walls. A front plate shows a chief who cries that there is no time to waste. Keighley's men pick a path through a ship's hold in one drawn plan. Grit, team trust, and quick thought rule each call. Readers feel the heat of the work.
56637-natural-artificial-sewage-treatmen:
Alfred S Jones and H Alfred Roeckling wrote Natural and Artificial Sewage Treatment. E and F N Spon published it at London and New York in 1902. Jones was a lieutenant-colonel and a fellow of the Sanitary Institute. Both men had read papers on sewage purification before societies of professional men. The papers were well received, and the authors rewrote them wholly for this book. The subject is brought up to date.

The book addresses district councillors, sanitarians, and all who face the sewage question. Its preface sets out the authors' main claim. Natural treatment is one treatment only. Artificial work must be raised to the same standard by more stages. The effluent needs its nitrates removed, and its harmful germs removed as well. That makes three artificial treatments against one natural.
56676-the-buried-treasure-or-old-jordan-:
Harry Castlemon wrote this boys' adventure, first of his Boy Trapper series, copyrighted in 1877. The frontispiece shows Don and Bert Gordon with the circus horses, and the publisher's pages list Castlemon's many other series by the volume.

The story opens on Godfrey Evans, who builds air-castles and finds something. Dan's strategy, a shooting match, and the newcomers follow. Midway the boys reach Old Jordan's haunt, and Old Jordan shows himself and gets in trouble. Clarence finds something out, Don tries an experiment, and a joke turns out to be no joke. Castlemon, the most popular American boys' author of his day, keeps the woods, the treasure, and the traps moving. Young readers get a camp-and-hunt story.
5669-considerations-on-representative-go:
John Stuart Mill's treatise asks which form of government best serves a people, and answers that representative government, rightly built, fits a society ready to use it. Mill opens by treating forms of government as a matter of choice, not fate. He then sets a test for any good government. It must manage public business well, and it must improve the character of its citizens. Later chapters weigh the dangers of majority rule, the reach of the vote, and how voting should work.

The book stays practical even when it turns philosophical, since Mill keeps asking what institutions actually do to ordinary people. He defends broad participation while warning that unchecked majorities can crush minorities, and he treats education and open debate as guards against that harm. Modern readers will find here the classic case for elected rule, with its hopes and its cautions stated in full.
56777-the-evolution-of-naval-armament:
Frederick Leslie Robertson, an engineer commander in the Royal Navy, traces how warships and their guns changed from sail to steam in this 1921 Constable volume. Eight half-tone plates and many drawings support the text, from a sixty-gun ship of the late seventeenth century to the Warrior and the Monarch. He admits at the start that the full history of naval architecture still remains to be written.

The chapters move in order: the sailing ship, the smooth-bore gun, the steam engine, and new principles of gunnery. The carronade, the truck carriage, the shell gun, and the rifled gun follow. Propelling machinery and the ironclad close the story. Robertson points students to Charnock's Marine Architecture and Fincham's Naval Architecture as the great fields of inquiry, while offering his own book as the readable path through the subject.
57200-the-gyroscopic-compass-a-non-mathe:
T W Chalmers, on the staff of The Engineer, wrote this plain account of the gyroscopic compass, printed by Constable of London in 1920 in The Engineer Series. His aim stands in the subtitle: a treatment without mathematics. Chapters open with basic gyroscopic facts, then tie the gyroscope to the turning of the earth.

Damping the swings of the compass takes three chapters, one for each great system: the Anschütz compass of 1910, the Sperry, and the Brown. Errors get their own treatment: latitude error, the north steaming error, ballistic deflection, and the quadrantal error and its cure. Chalmers opens by granting that the flaws of the magnetic compass are too well known to need a word. The book teaches sailors and engineers a new instrument in plain prose.
5736-the-professional-aunt:
Mary Wemyss opens The Professional Aunt with a wry observation. Parents often choose a boy's profession for him. So the shrewd, business-like child may become a painter, while the artistic, unpractical one joins the Stock Exchange. The novel that follows turns that irony on family life, as an aunt takes up her calling with professional seriousness. Chapters follow households, children, and the adults who try to manage them.

Readers get light, observant comedy about English family life, where aunts, nephews, and nieces negotiate affection and duty. Wemyss writes with humor and warmth, letting character do the work of plot. The book suits readers who enjoy domestic novels of manners, and anyone who has known a relative whose real profession was holding a family together.
57424-german-barbarism-a-neutral-s-indic:
Léon Maccas, a doctor of law of the University of Athens, wrote this indictment, published at London in 1916. Paul Girard of the Institut de France supplies a preface to the neutral's case. Chapter one treats the German theory of war in Maccas's contents at the front.

German actions cannot be justified on the plea of reprisals, chapter two argues. The treatment of officials, outrages on enemy subjects and outrages on neutrals follow in the list. Prohibited weapons, treachery on the battlefield and bombardment of undefended towns build a lawyer's brief from Greece, a neutral land, against Germany's conduct in 1916.
57437-sydney-to-croydon-northern-queensl:
Sydney to Croydon is an account of a journey to the Gulf country of northern Queensland by a writer who signs as Saltbush. The trip was made with a member of Parliament. The pamphlet cost one shilling and was printed at Sydney in 1889.

An old mate on the Croydon goldfield wrote and wired Saltbush to come and judge the field for himself. The mate held it the grandest goldfield ever found in northern Queensland. Saltbush and a friend who had seen Normanton before Croydon was thought of set out on Monday, July 25. They went by New South Wales toward the capital of Queensland, keen to see the New England and Darling Downs country. Gold seekers of the day got a ground level report on a hot new field.
57609-the-bookbinder-in-eighteenth-centu:
The Bookbinder in Eighteenth-Century Williamsburg gives an account of a craftsman's life, times, and craft, issued by Colonial Williamsburg in 1990. The tale opens with the 1770 inventory of Governor Botetourt's library at the Palace in Williamsburg. More than three hundred volumes stood on the shelves at his death.

Colonial Williamsburg rebuilt that library using the inventory and other records of books in print. The true library was shipped back to England and lost at sea on the voyage home. Most volumes share traits: brown calfskin, ridged spines, and gold titles on small coloured panels. Craft and history readers get a close look at colonial bookbinding.
57699-the-young-scout-the-story-of-a-wes:
The Young Scout, the story of a West Point lieutenant, is a boys' adventure novel by Edward Ellis. Burt published the book in New York, with copyright in 1895. The frontispiece shows Lieutenant Decker holding out his hand to an astonished friend.

It opens at peace: boys from the Burkville School rest under trees on the road home, full of mischief. The contents then run west: Geronimo, Apache cunning, and compliments at long range. Mendez the scout, an eavesdropper, and a call and a reply fill the middle chapters. Troopers wait for daylight, a flight is cut short, and a ranchman's home gives shelter. Later heads promise what befell Maurice Freeman, a reality, a reminiscence, and a surprise indeed. One print oddity stands: the book as printed ran two chapters numbered seventeen and two numbered eighteen.
57726-the-quakers-past-and-present:
Dorothy Richardson's The Quakers Past and Present was published in New York by the Dodge Publishing Company, and is signed from London in 1914. Richardson thanks Norman Penney, librarian of the Friends' Reference Library, for revising her manuscript. A sentence from William James heads the book: the Quaker religion, he wrote, is something it is impossible to overpraise.

Seven chapters, a chronological table, and a bibliography make the survey. The birth of Quakerism, the Society of Friends, the Quaker church, and the retreat of Quakerism come first. Quakerism in America, Quakerism and women, and the present position follow. Chapter one opens about a hundred years after authority in theology broke apart, when the Bible, abroad among the people for the first time, loosened the hold of set beliefs.
57934-the-third-alarm-a-story-of-the-new:
James Ford set his 1893 tale inside the New York Fire Department and gave it to a real battalion chief, John Bresnan. Young Bruce stands at its heart. Plates show the chief explaining the fire box to him and Bruce in a fire library, deep in the lore of the trade.

The story rides with the horses to fires and lands Bruce in hospital, where Laura visits. A deaf woman, a botany lecture, and a reckless ride fill the turns. Ford wrote of city trades with a reporter's eye. For boys of its day, the book made fire work a hero's craft. The third alarm of the title is the big call.
57986-the-emigrant:
Dostoieffskaya sets a novel of exile in Rome, in an English version by Vera Margolies issued in New York in 1916. Stephen Graham adds an introduction to the tale. The heroine, Irene Mstinskaia, sits in the garden of the Monte Pincio with a book she cannot read.

Irene, left free and well off by her parents' death, finds Rome filling her thoughts with the ghosts of its past. She feels the city's dead, from early Christians to fighters for Italian unity, still ruling its streets. That presence brings her tired soul a peace like that of a convent. Readers get a moody story of a Russian woman abroad, weighing wealth, freedom, and an empty heart in a city heavy with history.
58318-the-blacksmith-in-eighteenth-centu:
The Blacksmith in Eighteenth-Century Williamsburg gives an account of his life, times, and craft, in the Williamsburg Craft Series issued by Colonial Williamsburg in 1978. A churchman named Glanvill is quoted: iron seemeth a simple metal, but in its nature are many mysteries. Longfellow, by contrast, made his village smith a plain emblem of simple virtue.

To primitive peoples the smith seemed supernatural: he tamed fire and turned ores into magic weapons or peaceful tools. Smith gods include Hephaestus, Vulcan, and Odin, with Cyclops and Nibelung races of demigod smiths, the essay notes with colour. Gold seekers and iron seekers open the craft history of colonial forges. Craft readers get depth.
58398-letters-and-discussions-on-the-for:
Alfred Green published Letters and Discussions on the Formation of Colored Regiments at Philadelphia in 1862, in the second year of the Civil War. His full title adds the duty of the colored people in regard to the great slaveholders' rebellion. Green, a Black abolitionist, argues that slavery was the mainspring of the revolt and that Black men must take their part in crushing it.

In his opening address Green says he sought the oracles of history for a precedent and has never since seen cause to change his mind. The pamphlet gathers his pieces from debate: he had argued the question in the Pine and Palm. He had faced the Church Anti-Slavery Society in September 1861 and drawn a vigorous exchange in the Anglo-African. He warns readers that the character of the freedom to come depends on their own exertions. Readers get a founding voice for Black enlistment.
58662-gloves-past-and-present:
Willard Smith wrote on gloves past and present in a book printed at New York in 1917. Why gloves opens the chapters, then the ancient history of gloves and the language of gloves. How gloves came to Grenoble and glovers in the eighteenth century follow. None other symbol, the cross excepted, has so entered into the feelings and affections of men, Beck is quoted.

No other sign has so ruled and bound in integrity the transactions of life as the glove, the quote runs. American women are connoisseurs of hand made laces from abroad, Smith notes, yet gloves get no such study. Gloves in many marts, from artist to artisan, Annonay and its industry, and the gloves we buy fill the middle. Gloves of the hour close a trade history with manners in it.
58680-the-land-of-content:
The Land of Content, a novel by Edith Barnard Delano, bears a copyright of 1913. The tale opens in earliest spring, at the close of a warm day on a mountain top. White petals from farmyard cherries drift down like late snow in the low sun.

Two roads meet at the top: a ridge-road worn by the needs of mountain folk, and an old turnpike. The pike was once an artery between North and South, strung with towns and farms. Coaches and motor cars pound along it now, and an army swung north on it a generation back. That army drifted south days later with only its pride left. The quiet road and the busy one frame a tale of fate and the folk who live along them.
5900-umboo-the-elephant:
Howard Garis introduces Baby Umboo, a young elephant, in a circus cage on a sweltering day. Chako, one of the monkeys, cries that it is too hot for anything. It is hotter under the tent than ever it was in the jungle. He hangs by his tail, swinging from a wooden bar. In the jungle, Chako recalls, they could find a pool of water, a comfort the tent denies.

Young readers follow Umboo through circus life and jungle memory, with animal friends who talk, tease, and help. Garis writes in short, friendly chapters suited to bedtime, favoring gentle adventure over fright. The book suits early readers who love elephants, and families who enjoy animal tales where a baby hero learns the world one hot afternoon at a time.
59023-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the Project Gutenberg works of Immanuel Kant. The file is a finding aid for readers of the philosopher in English. It lists the Gutenberg editions of Kant's works and then prints the table of contents of each. Eight works appear. The three Critiques lead in their English forms. The Prolegomena, Perpetual Peace, and shorter writings on morals complete the list.

The Critique of Pure Reason comes first, in Meiklejohn's translation. Its contents run from the prefaces of 1781 and 1787 into the transcendental aesthetic, with its sections on space and time. The Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals follows among the later entries. Kant's books are hard enough in any language. Widger's index lets a reader survey the whole Gutenberg shelf at once and find the right volume and chapter before opening the heavy texts themselves.
59055-the-heir-presumptive-and-the-heir-:
The Heir Presumptive and the Heir Apparent is a novel by Mrs Oliphant, issued in New York in an authorized edition. The copyright page dates that edition to eighteen ninety one. Oliphant's other tales, including For Love and Life, are named on the title page. The plot turns on who will inherit a title and estate.

Chapter one opens with Lord Frogmore, about sixty, and his step brother John Parke. Parke is his heir presumptive, the man who inherits only if no closer heir is born. Parke announces one day that he wishes to marry, and the family stakes rise at once. Inheritance, marriage, and rank drive a classic Oliphant family drama.
59224-they-were-different:
Neil Kenney wrote a short tale printed in Worlds of If in May 1955. A woman who served the gifted pair as secretary and nurse tells their story. She dug through news files to build their history. Clips tell of their strange birth, their schooling, and their rare gifts.

Their mind reading and far seeing powers truly worked, she insists. They were the only births of their kind to live to full age. She took down their last sendings in a short hand made for the school. The tale then turns to their own words, sent from a ditch under fire from friends. She ends by asking the reader to pray and hope for mankind.
59232-notes-on-diseases-of-cattle-cause-:
Charles Korinek, a trained horse and cattle doctor, wrote these notes on the diseases of cattle. The Veterinary Science Association of America printed the book in 1917. Korinek had served as state veterinarian for Oregon and led its board of examiners.

Cause, symptoms, and treatment form the plan for each disease, as the title states. A chart at the front names the parts of a dairy cow, from muzzle and poll to the last point. Sixteen years of hands-on work stand behind Korinek's name on the title page. Farmers and stockmen, far from a town doctor, got a plain guide to spot a sick beast's ill and treat it in time.
59262-the-underworld-of-oregon-caves-nat:
Roger Contor wrote The Underworld of Oregon Caves National Monument for the Crater Lake Natural History Association. Copyright rests in 1963, and the National Park Service cooperated in the work. Contor had served as management assistant at the monument from 1960 to early 1962. A tour map names the rooms, from the Ghost Room to Paradise Lost.

Chapters explain how the caves formed from sea laid rock over deep time. Underground erosion, decoration, cave age, and life in the caves follow in order. Human history, conservation, a glossary, and park rules close the guide in brief compass. The rock story starts 180 million years back in a shallow sea. Visitors get geology they can follow by lantern light underground.
59368-juvenile-delinquent:
Juvenile Delinquent is a science fiction story by Edward W Ludwig, taken from Worlds of If for October 1955. A blurb warns that when all is restricted or top secret, a Reader is a very bad security risk. The tale is set in the year 2056.

Ronnie, age eight, stands alone in his upstairs bedroom as a clock ticks below. His small body shakes, and sweat shines on his white forehead. To Ronnie the clock seems to say that Daddy is coming, over and over. September twilight seeps in, and Ronnie welcomes the dark as a place to hide. A flicker of hope makes him wish his father might have an accident, then he bites his lip and stops. Readers get a child fear tale set in a future of secrets and mind reading.
59437-a-son-at-the-front:
Edith Wharton wrote A Son at the Front, published by Scribner's at New York in 1923. Wharton gives the book to the memory of Ronald Simmons. A line from Walt Whitman stands as motto: something veiled and abstracted is often part of the manners of these beings.

John Campton, an American portrait painter, stands in his bare Montmartre studio on the thirtieth of July 1914. His son George has landed in England and will join him in Paris the next evening. Campton's fame rests on a portrait of George shown three years before. He tears the calendar leaf to bring the moment nearer, smiling at his own weakness.
59465-pugilistica-the-history-of-british:
Pugilistica is a past of the British prize ring by Henry Downes Miles in three books. This first book came out at Edinburgh in nineteen six, from the John Grant house. Miles wrote for the sport sheets of his day for more than forty years. Full fight tales from the news sheets of the time crowd its pages. True face plates and tales of ring lords stand with the fight lore.

The span runs from Fig and Broughton in seventeen nineteen to a last crown fight. That crown fight set King and Heenan in Kent in December of eighteen sixty three. One hundred forty four years of ring rise and fall make the scheme. Miles claims rare fit for the task from his long ring watch. The front plate shows Southwark Fair in the old prize age.
59725-pictures-from-english-history-a-fi:
Pictures from English History calls itself a fireside amusement, printed at Bath in 1846 with engravings. A front plate shows Queen Victoria raising Lord Rolle. A short preface argues that lessons land best when they do not feel like a task, and that light forms can fix facts in a child mind for good.

The first chapter sets the frame tale. Children at the top of the house have romped till tired and now moan that they must stop, unsure what to do next. Downstairs their mother and her sister, fresh from India, sit by a bright fire and wait for the master of the house. A game of history pictures gives the idle crew a way to play and learn at once, and the book grows from that parlour plan.
59780-love-and-the-philosopher-a-study-i:
Love and the Philosopher, a study in sentiment, is a novel by Marie Corelli, author of The Sorrows of Satan and Thelma. Doran published it in 1923, with the Ryerson Press at Toronto. The first chapter opens in a garden. You women are always so sentimental, says the Philosopher, leaning back in a comfortable chair and flicking ash from an excellent cigar.

You overdo the thing, he tells her: you carry every emotion to an extreme limit, and it shows a lamentable lack of judgment. She listens with the tiniest quiver of a smile and offers no reply. A thrush sings on a spray of emerald leaves, content to his own heart, and such trifles of a summer day please her. Corelli builds her tale as a duel of feeling and reason between the two.
59787-cactus-forest-drive-saguaro-nation:
Cactus Forest Drive is a Park Service guide to Saguaro National Monument, eighteen miles east of Tucson, Arizona, sold for fifteen cents. George Olin drew the cover picture of giant cactus. The monument is one of more than 175 park units run by the National Park Service.

The guide urges visitors to take only pictures and leave only footprints and goodwill. Trails lead photographers to fine groups of saguaros, best shot late in the day when long shadows set the cactus in bold relief. Rules bar woodcutting, hunting, grazing, mining, and flower picking in the preserve. Travellers get a compact, friendly intro to desert scenery and park care.
59965-a-thousand-years-ago-a-romance-of-:
A Thousand Years Ago is a play by Percy MacKaye, published in 1914 as a romance of the Orient. MacKaye, son of the actor-manager Steele MacKaye, was a Harvard graduate of 1897 who had joined the Cornish art colony in New Hampshire. His earlier plays include The Canterbury Pilgrims, Jeanne d'Arc and The Scarecrow.

The printed edition carries the apparatus of the professional stage. A copyright notice quotes the federal penalties for unlawful performance, a hundred dollars for the first and fifty for each one after. The dedication, to Hermann Hagedorn, praises him in the play's own idiom: singer of flashing swords, lover of olden songs, and romancer of amorous magic and improvised comedy. MacKaye's poetic drama belonged to the civic theatre movement, which hoped to restore pageantry and verse to the American stage.
59982-the-human-element:
Human Element is a science fiction tale by Leo Kelley. It ran in Worlds of If Science Fiction in June 1957. A headnote marvels at what science can do in the last century. Even the circus is far better now, the note says, or is it. Kevin, aged forty eight, talks with a sallow man about the show.

The Great Golden Ball is billed as really something at that circus. The stranger goes each year and praises the wonders science brings forth. Kevin brushes back a lock of gray hair and frets as he listens. His worried face makes him look older than his years in the scene. Doubt creeps in: is better gear the same as a better show.
60034-the-principles-of-ornament:
Principles of Ornament is a textbook by James Ward, in a new and enlarged edition of 1896. Scribner published the book at New York that year, printed in London and Bungay. Ward was head master of the Macclesfield School of Art in England. Aitchison, professor of architecture at the Royal Academy, edited the volume for its readers.

 Aitchison preface says he found no good English text book on the principles of ornament in his examining. The necessary information could only be picked up by extensive reading and independent observation, he adds. Such reading is not to be expected from young students, the preface argues for the book. Ward supplies the want: the elements of pattern, from Greek fret to Gothic leaf, analysed for art students. The book belongs to the South Kensington system of design teaching, which trained the craftsmen of the empire in state art schools.
60156-dictionary-of-battles-from-the-ear:
Harbottle made the Dictionary of Battles, from the earliest date to the present time. It stands as number ten in a line of Sonnenschein dictionaries of reference. Dalbiac, Wale, Swan, and Latham made its mate volumes on quotations and sayings. A preface owns that Harbottle died before the last editorial work was done. Correcting the proofs and preparing the index fell to other hands, it says.

Each entry gives a battle in brief compass: date, armies, leaders, and result. One sample tells of a fight on April 20, 1809, in the Napoleonic wars. French and Bavarians under Napoleon, about ninety thousand strong, met Austrians there. The Austrian host numbered eighty thousand men in that entry. Cross marks send the reader from one topic to its mate in the book. The dictionary gives the student of war a shelf of fights in one volume.
60193-vignettes-a-miniature-journal-of-w:
Hubert Crackanthorpe filled Vignettes with short prose sketches of place and mood. John Lane brought the book out in London and New York in 1896. Most pieces run a page or two and bear the name of a town or a scene. France holds the largest share, with Spain and Italy close behind.

Readers rest on a ruined church roof above Avignon and watch heat lie on the town. Other pieces pause at Arles, Pau, Paris, Naples, and Pompeii. A few turn home to Chelsea, Richmond Park, and the Strand in London. Each sketch fixes a brief hour of light, talk, or quiet in clear, calm words.
60332-disenchantment:
Disenchantment, by Charles Edward Montague, was printed in New York by Brentano in 1922. Montague gives the book to Aubrey Montague of Lautoka, Fiji. Sixteen chapters treat what the Great War did to the minds of those who fought it.

Montague opens with the vision that drew men to war, then a chapter of misgiving. At Agincourt and Ypres links old and new battlefields. Later heads name tedium, the duty of lying, and men who say you cannot believe a word. One chapter asks if there is any cure, and one gives fair warning. Montague says the ungifted young came home fed up, and the gifted now give the details. Readers get a sharp, sad brief on war shine worn off.
60359-oregon-the-picturesque-a-book-of-r:
A motor traveller rambles the Oregon country in a picture book issued by The Page Company at Boston in 1917. Front pages advertise the author's other motoring books at three dollars each, boxed.

British Highways and Byways from a Motor Car reached a third impression. Three Wonderlands of the American West sold at three dollars fifty. This volume promises sketches and pictures of Crater and Klamath Lakes. The Deschutes River Canyon and the new Columbia Highway follow. The Willamette and Rogue River valleys bring cities and towns. Northern California adds its little-known lakes, rivers, mountains, and vast forests. A trip to Yosemite, the Roosevelt Dam, and the Petrified Forest of Arizona closes the run, all by motor car. Bishop's Cap on the Columbia Highway fronts the pictures.
60401-puppet-government:
George Revelle wrote Puppet Government, a short tale first printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction in October 1957. Brandon, a maker of hand-carved puppets, keeps getting odd job offers from the government. Each year men come back with fresh posts for him, though he says no each time. The Secretary of Interior now urges him to head a department of his own.

Brandon is tired, behind on his desk work, and puzzled by the push. He notes that his puppets are now world famous, the fruit of reviving a near-lost art. He earns a fair living and sees no cause to change. The thin secretary toys with a small wood figure as he talks, and the clash of wills drives the tale.
60475-peggy-s-giant:
Peggy Giant is a child book by M D Hillyard, printed in London in 1920, with seven full page color plates drawn by Peggy herself. Hillyard gives the book to Peggy. A front note tells how Peggy drew the first adventure of the ring.

In her drawing Nurse has just sat down at the sight of the Giant and dropped Peggy brown frock. Peggy stands behind the Giant and wonders what to say. The round bits near his foot are a broken cup and saucer, and the black dots are currants in the cake. Chapters name what Peggy found, a daisy field, and a sleepy giant. Later heads bring sweets and fairies, a mayor outing, and pixie games. Young readers get a tale told half in a child own hand.
60479-1900-or-the-last-president:
Ingersoll Lockwood wrote a novel that asks what if Bryan won the vote of 1896. Lockwood was a member of the New York bar. The book came out in 1896 with the title 1900, or The Last President. A quote from Garret Hobart warns of a break-up of the land. The tale starts on vote night, November 3, 1896.

News that Bryan has won stuns rich New York at supper. Police ride out and tell folk to bar their doors. Mobs form on the East Side under red flags. Lockwood paints a land split by class hate. Readers get a stark what-if from that tense year.
60491-the-seventy-s-course-in-theology-f:
Roberts, of the First Council of the Seventy, wrote the fourth year of the Seventy's Course in Theology, on the Atonement. The course book was printed at Salt Lake City in 1911. A verse from John heads it: as Moses lifted up the serpent, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.

Front matter lists the Seventy's Indispensable Library: the Bible, the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants, and the Pearl of Great Price. Added works include Taylor on mediation and atonement, Talmage on the articles of faith, and Orson Pratt's writings. Earlier year books are cited often, so students are urged to own the full set.
60698-bargain-basement:
Charles L Fontenay springs a retail riddle in Bargain Basement, from Worlds of If Science Fiction in September 1959. The blurb asks how a store could give away such buys, and answers: very easy, by doing a business in pennies and a profit in billions. Jack Hanshaw is the sucker, or perhaps not.

Jack rages at his new television: no picture, no static, and yesterday no cord at all, not even a socket for one. The set cost two dollars. It is shiny and odd, six inches thick with a thirty-five-inch screen, a lettered channel dial, and an antenna of concentric circles. His roommate Ken smells a sucker game.
60793-bible-pictures-and-stories-in-larg:
Bible Pictures and Stories in Large Print retells scripture for young readers. Lothrop printed the book at Boston in 1898 with pictures. Adam and Eve open the set in a lovely planted garden. They ate the one fruit God said they must not touch.

Cain and Abel follow, farmer and shepherd with gifts to God. Cain killed his brother and wandered homeless, the tale says. The Flood comes next, with Noah warned to build an ark. Large print and bold pictures carry each short tale for children. Each tale is told in short plain lines a child can read aloud with ease.
60803-monument:
Monument is a science fiction story by Major, printed in Worlds of If in March 1960 and billed as the tale that wagged the Dog Star. Its hero is Doctor Charles King, known against his will as Side Effect Charlie, because his great discoveries keep arriving by accident while he aims at something else. He thought he had made metal surfaces perfectly slippery, and instead dissolved the bonds of metal itself, founding a new industry on the wreck of the old one.

A second discovery, crystals grown in a nutrient solution after a laboratory lunch went wrong, led to the special project King is finishing as the story opens. With reporters briefed, he is about to pull a switch meant to restore his good name. Major builds the comedy on a simple truth: in King's laboratory, the side effect is always the main event.
60840-the-woman-movement:
Ellen Key, the Swedish thinker, wrote this survey of the woman movement, translated by Mamah Bouton Borthwick and introduced by Havelock Ellis, published by Putnam in 1912. She begins with the external results of the movement.

The first chapter looks back at the struggle for equality in culture, professional education, and work, and in family and civil status. Those demands, she notes, were voiced as early as 1848 in the American Declaration of Sentiments. Later chapters treat the movement's inner results and its influence on single women, daughters, marriage, and motherhood. Key, author of Love and Marriage, writes as both advocate and critic. Readers get the movement measured by one of its leading voices.
60886-time-payment:
Time Payment is Sylvia Jacobs's science fiction story, printed in Worlds of If in July 1960. Slick Tennant, king of the local rackets, feels the federal men closing in. His plan is to hide where no court can reach him: in the future. For months his hired detective has shadowed Richard Porter, the psychiatrist who built the Metachronoscope.

One night Slick slips into the Porter home with a stolen key. He takes the small son Dickie, aged seven, as his hold over the father. He demands one trip in the machine he insists on calling a time machine. The tale turns the gangster's escape plan into a trap of its own logic.
60928-the-contact-point:
The Contact Point is a science fiction story by Jack Sharkey, first printed in Worlds of If in January nineteen sixty one. A teaser holds that somewhere on Mars there had to be a meeting of the minds. Lieutenant Lloyd spots the first alien in the ruins of a strange red Martian city. It is the second day of exploration when he sees it.

His first impulse is to call out to the other men, the tale says. Instead he fears his voice will startle the creature down the rubble strewn street. He unholsters his pistol in silence and creeps toward what he hopes is the alien's back. First contact as armed stalking sets the tension.
61135-out-of-death-s-shadow-or-a-case-wi:
Out of Death's Shadow, or A Case Without a Precedent is a Nick Carter detective novel by Nicholas Carter, published by Street and Smith in 1905. Nick Carter has built the case against a woman accused of killing her husband. The story opens on the veranda of a Southern house outside St Louis, on the eve of her trial.

Carter's friend fears the jury, but Carter answers that conviction is certain and the case was easy. The killing had no witness, so the prosecution rests on the chain of proof Carter assembled. His remark that murder is a secret too heavy to carry sets the book's theme. Street and Smith issued Carter tales in great numbers, and this one works the courtroom side of detection rather than the chase.
61177-the-red-glutton-with-the-german-ar:
The Red Glutton, with the German Army at the Front, is a war report by Irvin S Cobb, published in London, New York, and Toronto. Cobb went with German forces in the opening phase of the Great War. Chapter heads trace a route through Belgium and France, from a small village to the trenches before Rheims. One chapter is called To War in a Taxicab.

Other chapters cover being a guest of the Kaiser, a German wrecking crew, and viewing a battle from a balloon. Louvain and its fate close the contents list. Cobb writes as an American observer inside an army his readers knew mostly as the enemy. Vivid place reporting, not strategy, is his strength.
61254-transient:
William Harris's Transient ran in Worlds of If Science Fiction in September 1962. Its head note gives the hook: the computer's answers were remarkable, especially when nobody had asked a question. Henderson, a biologist, feeds the machine a card and gets back a scrap of astrology: Moon in fourteen degrees Pisces.

He tries again with real work: a test of his mouse trials, one hundred fifty mice shot with a compound against one hundred fifty controls. The machine hums, blinks, and returns a daily horoscope about solace with close friends and care with money. Henderson works the sum out by hand, finds his trial proves nothing, and notes that someone must come in the morning for his sick machine.
61370-a-fortnight-at-the-front:
H Russell Wakefield wrote A Fortnight at the Front. Longmans, Green and Company issued it in 1915. Wakefield served as Bishop of Birmingham. A front plate shows Albert's ruined church. Its Virgin and Child lean over the wreck. He calls the trip a cure for pessimism. Short study gives no right to dogma, he opens.

His view may be shallow yet wide, he admits. Ground thirty-five yards from German trenches starts it. Bases far south and west end the sweep. Headquarters let him see all in comfort and speed. He blessed men where speech had to stay low. Confirmations and talks to troops fill his days. Courtesy from all hands struck him first. A bishop's two weeks with the army gave home readers a calm, kind word from the trenches.
61394-life-incidents-in-connection-with-:
Elder James White published Life Incidents in Battle Creek, Michigan, in 1868 through the Seventh-day Adventist Publishing Association. Volume one ties his own story to the great Advent movement, read through the three angels of Revelation chapter fourteen and the prophecy of Daniel on the cleansing of the sanctuary.

White admits in his preface that the field is wide and that full justice would take many volumes. What he offers is a participant's account of a movement he helped lead. Readers get firsthand history of early Adventism from one of its founders, mixing personal incident with the prophetic reading that drove the movement forward.
61560-notes-on-diseases-of-the-horse-cau:
Charles Korinek, a horse doctor trained at the Ontario college of his craft, wrote notes on the ills of the horse, printed in 1917. He had served as state horse doctor for Oregon. Sixteen years of working practice stand behind the book. A chart at the front names the parts of the horse.

Mouth, nostrils, poll, withers, cannons and hocks take numbers on the drawing. The first lesson treats the heat glass for animals. The tool sits in the rectum for three minutes, since a horse might break glass held in the mouth. Each ill then takes its turn, with cause, signs, and cure set out in plain order for farm and stable hands.
61649-pugilistica-the-history-of-british:
Henry Downes Miles wrote Pugilistica, the history of British boxing, here in its second volume, printed at Edinburgh in 1906. Miles was editor of The Sportsman's Magazine. The title page promises lives of the most famed fighters of the ring. Full reports of their battles go with likenesses and personal tales. A plate shows the first fight of Spring and Langan at Worcester in 1824.

A preface to the second volume names its men. The first period gives the battles of Spring, John Langan, Ned Painter, Neat of Bristol, Thomas Hickman, and Dan Donnelly. The second gives Jem Ward, Peter Crawley, Tom Cannon, Young Dutch Sam, and Barney Aaron, among others. Miles dedicates the records to Grimston, a patron of manly sports. The third volume, he notes, will take up Bendigo and the decline and fall of the ring.
61660-early-voyages-and-travels-in-the-l:
Early Voyages and Travels in the Levant is a volume of the Hakluyt Society, the body that prints old records of travel. The hosted text opens with the society's report for 1892. That report lists the books sent to its members. Among them are the travels of Pietro della Valle in India and a translation of the journal of Columbus's first voyage.

The book itself holds the diary of Thomas Dallam and extracts from the diaries of Doctor John Covel. Dallam was the organ builder sent with an organ as a gift to the Sultan at Constantinople at the end of the sixteenth century. Covel was a chaplain who travelled in the Levant in the next century. The report also looks ahead to voyages to Hudson's Bay and to the letters of Amerigo Vespucci. The volume joins the society's long work of saving early travel records in print.
61773-sewerage-and-sewage-treatment:
Harold Babbitt wrote this textbook on sewerage and sewage treatment, printed in New York in 1922. Babbitt taught municipal and sanitary work at the University of Illinois. The front picture shows work on Peck's Run Sewer in Baltimore, Maryland. The contents lay out the full plan of the course, chapter by chapter.

Early chapters cover work before design, how towns pay for sewers, and how much sewage a town makes. Storm water gets its own long part, with rain rates and flow rules. Later heads turn to the flow of water in pipes, the design of sewer systems, and street inlets. The book serves students and town engineers who plan such systems.
61859-the-ultimate-salient:
The Ultimate Salient is a science fiction story by Nelson S Bond, first printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1940. Its frame opens in Roanoke in spring, where the narrator Eben Clinton suffers from spring fever. A neat, quiet man comes up the walk with a bulky folder under his arm. Clinton takes him for a census man and answers the door himself.

The visitor proves to be no census-snoop. He tells Clinton, a bit sadly, that a mere telling will not do: it will have to be written, for Clinton will not be here then. The story is addressed to Brian O'Shea, man of the future, a soldier yet unborn. Upon O'Shea, the heading warns, will one day rest the fate of all mankind. Clinton's own afterword owns the headaches of a story-teller, from whose cracks and crevices strange things creep.
62004-the-church-rate-a-dialogue-between:
The Church Rate, a dialogue between a churchman and a dissenter, is a penny tract reprinted from The Village Churchman. William Edward Painter of the Strand, London, sold it at a penny, or seven shillings the hundred. Its text is Saint Peter: submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake. This is a second and enlarged edition, with the local allusions cut out.

The preface states the aim: to expose, in familiar language, the absurd arguments by which political dissenters justify their deeds of hatred against the established church. The writer holds that church the bulwark of national Christianity and of civil and religious liberty. The dialogue opens with Mr Churchman catching his neighbour Spinwell beating up recruits for a vestry meeting. Their talk argues the church rate, the tax every parish raised for the church, wanted or not.
62227-bicycling-for-ladies-the-common-se:
Maria Ward wrote a guide to bicycling for ladies, printed at New York in 1896. Bicycling is a modern sport, offering endless variety and chance, she begins. As an exercise it is at present without equal, doing much with fairly little effort. As a relaxation it has many good features. Possibilities opens the chapters, then what the bicycle does.

On wheels in general and bicycles in particular, for beginners, and how to make progress follow. Hints as to the art of wheeling, advice to beginners, dress, care of the bicycle, mechanics, training, and exercise fill the title's promise. Wheeling from the peg, showing the lean of the wheel, stands among the pictures. In the great bicycle craze, Ward teaches women to ride with sense, safety, and independence.
62303-a-winter-of-content:
A Winter of Content is a memoir by Laura Lee Davidson, issued in 1922 and dedicated to Louise, called the lady of the island. A line from the Odyssey stands at the front, about a small rocky isle in the mid sea. Pictures show snow patches, a rabbit turning white, a house, and heavy wood sleds still travelling down frozen lakes.

The first chapter opens on a small rocky island in a lake, with a canoe paddling away across blue water. A woman stands on a narrow strip of beach, looking after it. The narrator is that woman, left on the shore, while the canoe holds her companion. From that parting the book settles into a season of island winter life. Its title promises content found in cold and quiet, not despite them.
62333-the-norwich-directory-or-gentlemen:
The Norwich Directory; or, Gentlemen and Tradesmen’s Assistant maps a whole town. W Chase and Company printed it at Norwich on March twenty second, seventeen hundred eighty three. One shilling and sixpence bought the fat town guide then. Each chief dweller stands listed with house, trade, and street.

Houses bear numbers in its pages, a new civic grace of the age. Streets, lanes, markets, churches, and gates take their own tables. Aldermen, sheriffs, and the common council fill the next lists. Bishop’s court, excise, stamp, and post offices stand in their rows. Bankers, doctors, surgeons, and lawyers shine in the trade lists. Coaches, waggons, inns, and carriers fill the road wise pages. Hospitals, charity schools, and Norfolk fairs close the wide roll. A short history of Norwich and hints for its mending end it.
62459-usury-or-interest-premium-and-disc:
Usury, or Interest, Premium and Discount is a printed lecture given by Crittenden to the students of his Philadelphia Commercial College and published in 1863. Crittenden, a lawyer and consulting accountant who ran the school, speaks to future bookkeepers about the money charges that pass through a merchant's ledger every day.

He defines interest, discount, and premium from the standard dictionaries, then shows how each belongs on the books and how they differ in law and in practice. The talk also weighs the use and fairness of lending at interest. It is a neat fossil of business schooling in Civil War era Philadelphia.
62516-agatha-s-aunt:
Agatha's Aunt is a novel by Harriet Lummis Smith, published at Indianapolis in 1920. Smith had earlier written Other People's Business.

The first chapter, Boarders Wanted, opens in a big, many-windowed room gone shabby with poverty. The paper is faded and stained from a leak, and the once fine carpet has shrunk to a threadbare rug.
