Yet the room, like its owner, keeps a plucky defiance. Later chapters bring a social secretary, complications, and company manners. A character named Hephzibah comes to life, turns the tables, and helps drive the plot. Rescues, confessions, and an embarrassment of riches follow. The tale ends with fellow travellers and an introduction, in a comedy of genteel poverty and new chances.
62609-locomotive-engine-running-and-mana:
Angus Sinclair's Locomotive Engine Running and Management reached a tenth edition from John Wiley and Sons in New York in 1888. The title page promises the performance of locomotives in running different kinds of trains with economy and dispatch, plus directions for their care, management, and repairs.

Sinclair's preface tells how his notes grew. As a working locomotive engineer he jotted down facts about his engine's odd behaviour on the road. He kept noting in charge of the round-house of the Burlington, Cedar Rapids, and Northern Railway in Iowa. Much of the later book, on repairs and maintenance, first appeared in the American Machinist.
62685-ducks-and-geese-standard-breeds-an:
George E Howard wrote Ducks and Geese, a farmers’ guide to breeds and care. The Department of Agriculture issued it as Farmers’ Bulletin Number Sixty Four. The Government Printing Office at Washington put it out in eighteen hundred ninety seven. D E Salmon of the Bureau of Animal Industry sent it up for print.

White Pekin, Aylesbury, Rouen, and Cayuga ducks lead the breed lists. Muscovy, Call, East Indian, and Crested White ducks follow them. Toulouse, Embden, African, and Chinese geese get their own pages. Wild and Egyptian geese close the roll of standard kinds. Plain rules then cover the plant, the houses, and the yards. Brooding, water, feed mix, and grit each take a full part. How to kill and dress birds for market ends the duck half. Set eggs by hen or by machine, the last pages advise.
62890-a-comedy-of-elopement:
Christian Reid wrote A Comedy of Elopement, printed at New York in 1893. Reid was the pen name of a Southern writer known for Valerie Aylmer, Morton House, and The Land of the Sky. The tale opens in Florida in December.

On the sea wall at St Augustine, two girls walk at sunset and talk in earnest. One, barely fifteen, has a face of rare grace and listens more than she speaks. The old Spanish houses, the fort, and the warm soft air set the scene. From this quiet start the comedy of a runaway match unfolds.
63202-margaret-maliphant:
Comyns Carr wrote Margaret Maliphant, a novel printed at New York in eighteen eighty-nine. The tale opens at twilight on a marsh in Sussex, with one lone homestead in a level plain. The narrator recalls a tall, dark figure who walked down through the trees ten years before and vanished. Then the past spreads out before her like the plain itself.

Margaret and her sister Joyce, twenty-one and nineteen, are the sole children of Farmer Maliphant of Knellestone Grange. The Maliphants have held land on the Udimore hills and the downs of Brede for more than three hundred years. Their old stone house looks over the Romney Marsh, on land once held by the old abbey. The tale traces the family, its pride, and the parting that haunts the opening scene.
63263-place-names-in-kent:
Canon Horsley, late vicar of Detling, wrote this book on the place names of Kent, printed at Maidstone in 1921. His introduction recalls a schoolboy start at Canterbury, where Trench on the study of words and Isaac Taylor's Words and Places first roused his interest. In 1920, he found, no book yet treated the names of Kent as twenty other counties had been treated.

Horsley read widely, including twenty-six volumes of the county's archaeological journal, and first wrote weekly pieces for a local paper. The index shows his method. It lists names of Celtic, Roman, and Teutonic origin, and Saxon endings and elements. Church names and names from persons follow. Warnings against absurd derivations come too, down to the tons, hams, and cold harbours of Kent.
63474-alien-equivalent:
Richard R Smith wrote Alien Equivalent, printed in Planet Stories for the summer of 1955. Chester Farrell has spent three years on Mars and wants home. Behind him stands the Martian city of strange sounds and acrid odors; before him, three spaceships point at the sky. He touches the money in his pocket: at last he has the fare for Earth. At home in Cleveland wait his wife Louise and his son Sammy.

The Mars Mining Corporation pays its men little, though its ores sell on Earth for great profits. The trip out cost a hundred dollars; the trip home is priced to keep colonists in place. Governments and the company together want men to stay and work the mines. The head note promises the Martian game of Duchal, where a frail, dying race can beat the master Earthmen.
63500-muse-and-mint:
Walter Percy wrote these poems, Muse and Mint, printed Boston 1914. Sherman, French issued the book, given to mother and wife. They best loved his muse, the gift page says with warmth. Their love was the mint that made it joy, he adds.

An opening poem muses on the strangeness of all things at dawn. A blind child on a corner sells sprigs of mint in it. Contents sort poems under nature, fireside, and sentiment heads. Fireflies, Bo-Peep, a snowflake, and sugaring off fill nature part. Mother, a lullaby, and the last song stand among the fireside poems in the list.
63544-the-red-saint:
Red Saint is a novel by Warwick Deeping, author of Sorrell and Son. The book is dedicated to Captain and Mrs Merrill, with all faith and affection. It was first published in April nineteen oh nine at London and abroad. Chapter one opens at a spring at the edge of a beech wood. Denise of the Hermitage goes down to draw water there at dusk.

Far away through the April gloom she sees the light of a fire. It flashes between the dark slopes of two high hills, almost on the horizon. Long flames move, shooting upward or bending toward the ground. All is still under the great beeches, so the distant fire seems strange and ghostly, the tale says. The little pool where she filled her pitcher is fed by a spring believed miraculous and holy.
63545-a-short-history-of-the-printing-pr:
A trade history fills this volume, printed and published for Robert Hoe at New York in 1902. Its full title runs from the time of Gutenberg up to the present day, tracing the improvements in printing machinery. A long list of illustrations is itself a history of the press in names.

The earliest form of press stands first, then the Blaew press, the Stanhope, and the Columbian. Hand presses give way to power presses, cylinder presses, and rotary machines of growing size, up to octuple presses built for great newspapers. The text opens near 1450, with Gutenberg printing his first book from movable types. His press, the book says, was two upright timbers stayed by cross pieces. A flat bed held the type, and a wooden screw pressed the sheet.
64002-the-great-accident:
Ben Ames Williams wrote The Great Accident, published in New York in 1920. Williams had written The Sea Bride and All the Brothers Were Valiant. He gives the novel to Mother. The book is told in six books. The first bears the novel's name and opens with Hardiston, Amos Caretall, and Wint Chase. A council of war, the rally, Hetty Morfee, the election, and the notification close it.

Muldoon and Joan open the second book, with the strategy of Amos and an alliance after. Into Harness, Line of Battle, Defeat, and Victory name the books that follow. The last heads give Hetty her day and Wint's rally, and end with seeing Joan home. The first chapter sorts people into two kinds: small-town folks, and others. The others, it says, think small-town people narrow. In fact, the mid-western towns hold the real wide-awake sort.
64111-pugilistica-the-history-of-british:
The third volume of Pugilistica, Henry Downes Miles's history of British boxing, covers the ring from 1835 to 1863. Miles records the leading fights of the bare-knuckle era year by year, with the names, stakes, and outcomes of each contest. Fighters such as Bendigo and Tom Sayers stand out in its pages, and the volume closes with the last championship fight of the old school, King against Heenan on December 10, 1863.

Miles wrote as a sporting chronicler, and his method is plain record rather than praise. Round-by-round detail, betting odds, and the crowds at the fights all get their due. For readers of boxing history, the volume is a ringside ledger of the sport's final bare-knuckle decades, printed at Edinburgh in 1906.
64237-old-age-deferred-the-causes-of-old:
Old Age Deferred, by Arnold Lorand, is a doctor's handbook on the causes of old age and how to postpone it. The hosted copy is the fifth edition, from the Davis company of Philadelphia, 1920. Lorand added this edition's new part on hardening of the arteries and high blood pressure after watching prominent people die young.

His preface is honest: no one can turn an old man young again. But youth, he argues, can be stretched by ten or twenty years with hygiene and treatment, so that ninety or a hundred replaces decline at fifty. The book sold steadily for a decade on that careful promise.
64285-reminiscences-of-a-private-company:
Bevens wrote Reminiscences of a Private, the record of Company G of the First Arkansas Regiment of infantry, from May 1861 to 1865. He served as a private in that Confederate company. Portraits show him in 1861 and again in 1912, beside comrades and officers of the company.

The book opens with the old home town of Jacksonport as his children find it on a visit. Streets are overgrown with weeds, cottages dilapidated, and the brick court house tumbled down. Only a few kept homes and a good store break the air of decay. Against that present ruin, Bevens sets his memories of the war years. Such veteran memoirs preserved the common soldier's war, company by company, long after the armies disbanded.
6435-the-principles-of-scientific-manage:
Frederick Winslow Taylor, in 1911, sets management's principal object as maximum prosperity for employer and for each employee together. Maximum prosperity means more than large dividends: it means every branch developed to highest excellence so prosperity lasts. For employees it means more than higher wages: it means each man developed to maximum efficiency, fitted to the highest grade of work his abilities allow, and given that work when possible.

President Roosevelt, Taylor recalls, called conservation of national resources only preliminary to the larger question of national efficiency. Taylor came to Midvale Steel's machine shop in 1878, after apprenticeship as pattern maker and machinist, in depression after the panic of 1873, when mechanics could hardly find trade work. His book argues that science, not rule of thumb, must govern the shop, for both sides' good.
64620-granada-and-the-alhambra-a-brief-d:
Albert Calvert's Granada and the Alhambra, from John Lane at London and New York in 1907, gives a brief account of the ancient city and a particular account of its Moorish palace. The volume holds 460 illustrations and belongs to the Spanish Series, which Calvert himself edited. He dedicates it, by her permission, to the Empress Eugénie.

Four parts divide the text: The City of the Moor, The Alhambra, The Generalife and Catholic Granada. The plates range over the Alhambra from every side, the Sierra Nevada behind it, the gypsy caves of the Sacromonte, the Cartuja sacristy and the Royal Chapel. Views of gates, markets and old houses fill out the picture of the city.
6464-shop-management:
Frederick Winslow Taylor's Shop Management, dated 1911, grows from years of changing shop methods in manufacturing and industrial establishments across many trades. Two facts strike him most. First, the great unevenness, even in best run works, in the development of management's several elements. Second, the lack of apparent relation between good shop management and the payment of dividends. Trusts may dominate the day, yet each component company was built largely through individual energies.

A mid passage warns that piece work, where price alone is specified without limiting time, can let output fall off largely without management noticing. Hence Taylor's first of four principles for the best type of management: a large daily task for each man, with adequate measures taken alongside. The book is a manager's field report, practical and insistent on system over habit.
64696-unwelcome-tenant:
Unwelcome Tenant, by Roger Dee, is a science fiction story taken from Planet Stories of summer 1950. A headnote poses its riddle: the first Earthman to hit deep space discovered what was so terribly wrong with the world he had left behind. Why could he not turn back?

Maynard flies toward Mars. He is at the end of his second day, halfway, his atomic jets cut off. Ahead lies the zero point, where the gravity fields of two planets meet and cancel out. He divides his care between the Meinz pendulum in its bubble and the two ports, Mars ruddy before him and Earth a green crescent behind. He is calm, and proud. Then, as the pendulum quivers with the release of Earth's pull, terror strikes. It is not his own fear. Something inside him, never suspected, shrieks in panic and fights to tear itself free of him.
64743-plain-sermons-preached-at-archbish:
Plain Sermons, published at London in 1859, gathers ten sermons by James Galloway Cowan, minister of Archbishop Tenison's Chapel in Regent Street. The volume appeared by request of his hearers. Each sermon takes a short Bible text and works it into plain counsel for daily life.

The subjects run from taking thought for food and dress to right thoughts of Christ. Cowan speaks on confession, forgiveness and offerings that should cost the giver something. He also treats the limits of human knowledge and the slow work of spiritual growth. The last sermon warns that deep things stay hidden from the natural man. The style stays direct throughout.
64800-buffalo-bill-s-still-hunt:
Colonel Prentiss Ingraham spins another Buffalo Bill tale for the Street and Smith list. The New York house holds the copyright of 1907. Before the tale, a tribute praises William F Cody himself.

The story crosses the Rio Grande at the start. Silk Lasso Sam, the outlaw, enters in chapter three. Bonnie Belle of Pocket City brings the romance. A fair plotter schemes at Pioneer Post. Hangman's Gulch and a border burial darken the middle. Buffalo Bill makes a mad ride near the close. Ingraham knew the scout's circle well. He had forgathered with Ned Buntline and Cody in a dingy Rose Street office, he recalls. His hundreds of dime tales built the Cody legend as much as the Wild West show did.
64883-the-black-man-his-antecedents-his-:
William Wells Brown wrote The Black Man: His Antecedents, His Genius, and His Achievements for James Redpath at Boston in 1863. He dedicates the volume to advocates and friends of Negro freedom and equality wherever found. A portrait of Geffrard, engraved from a photograph taken at Port au Prince, fronts the book.

Brown's preface, dated at Cambridgeport in 1863, aims to refute claims of natural inferiority made by enslavers and their echoes. He offers sketches of people who rose past slavery and prejudice by genius and learning, many printed here for the first time. Contents list Benjamin Banneker, Nat Turner, Toussaint L'Ouverture, Crispus Attucks, Alexandre Dumas, and Phillis Wheatley among the lives.
64925-cadet-life-at-west-point:
Cadet Life at West Point is a book on the military academy by Reed, here in its third edition. A letter printed at the front, dated 10 January 1911 from West Point, returns the proof sheets. The writer says he has read them at last, though his house is torn up before a move. He praises the book as very interesting in that letter of a fellow cadet.

 It is particularly useful to young men who contemplate entering the academy in his judgment. The book recalls many pleasant incidents of the cadet life of its author generation. Conditions, the letter adds, are very little changed from the days of that class. Such books served as guides for boys dreaming of the long grey line, and as souvenirs for the men who had marched in it at the academy on the Hudson.
64963-heir-apparent:
Heir Apparent is a science fiction story by Alan E Nourse. It first ran in Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy in October nineteen hundred fifty three. The tale asks what drives a man to risk his life in space. It also asks if love can keep such a man home.

The story opens with crowds watching a dead hero’s casket come down from a ship. The teller says he alone should feel the deepest guilt. The scene then jumps back to his days as a young hospital interne named Ben. His friend Bart bursts in with big news. Bart has passed a hard test. Love, duty, and space flight pull against each other from there.
65137-the-longsnozzle-event:
Hal Annas pairs a famed space sleuth with a strange gun in a short tale from Imagination for April 1951. A head note states the hook at once: Len Zitts, the greatest detective in the galaxy, can name the killer with ease. His true care is the weapon used in the crime, not the arrest itself.

Zitts rises from a couch that shapes itself into a chair at the press of his big toe. Robotic arms slip soft shoes on his feet, fix his collar and tie, and comb his thick chestnut hair. A fair guest stands in the door with her mouth open at the show. More arms light his cigarette and pass a tray to the guest as talk starts in a room run by buttons.
65161-the-forest-giant:
The Forest Giant is a tale turned from the French of Adrien Le Corbeau by Ross. It was first out in nineteen twenty-four. Its parts bear strange names, from a first trip tale to the snap of a shell and the wheel of life. A close part named for a cell ends the book.

The first part tells of a small round thing that rolled past years past count. It rolled past plains, deep grass, and dim woods, in heat and cold, sun and storm. Snow drifts hid it yet did it no harm. Floods and winds hurled it past the air, yet it met all with the same calm lack of care. It had crossed falls of light and floods of shade, and it waits its hour still. That long wait opens the tale of the seed that grows to a giant of the wood.
65613-ye-olde-mint-being-a-brief-descrip:
Frank H Stewart Electric Company issued Ye Olde Mint at Philadelphia in 1909 as a brief account of the first United States mint. Congress set up the mint in 1792 at Seventh Street and Sugar Alley, later Filbert Street. The firm's own works adjoined the old buildings.

Plates show the mint office at 37 and 39 North Seventh Street and the coinage building behind. The text calls the coinage house the first brick building raised by act of Congress for public use. Land values, the writer fears, will doom the old walls to fall. A bronze tablet may mark the site. Washington's early words to Congress on a uniform currency open the history proper.
65769-return-engagement:
Margaret St Clair wrote Return Engagement, a science fiction story printed in Imagination in January nineteen fifty two. A head note states the plot in one line. An Earthman broke a law on an alien world. He had to be chastised in a manner to suit the aliens. The tale opens with McBream brooding on the ingratitude of humans.

McBream says a Martian who borrows in a spot sends greeting cards for life. A man fished out of the water sends a bill for his suit, he complains. The narrator picks up a book from McBream's desk. It is printed on big silky sheets and bound in deep garnet. Its title is Farquarson's Enchiridion of Extra Terrestrial Cookery. Science fiction readers get a comic space tale built around an alien cookbook.
65819-the-purple-pennant:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote The Purple Pennant, published in New York and London by D Appleton and Company in nineteen sixteen. Norman P Rockwell drew the pictures. Twenty six chapters carry a school sports season.

Fudge Is Interrupted opens the book, with Fudge Shaw hunting rhymes for an ode to spring. The Try Out and The Shadow on the Curtain follow. Chapters mix track and baseball: the game with Norrisville, the squad at work, and out at the plate. Clearfield Concedes the Meet and Springdale Leads build the close. The Purple Pennant itself ends the contents. A false mustache, a borrowed roller, and a train robber warning add schoolboy plots along the way. Boys get a season of races, games, and pranks at a school where the pennant is the prize.
65889-america-in-the-war-each-cartoon-fa:
Louis Raemaekers, the Dutch cartoonist whose drawings had scourged Germany since 1914, published America in the War with the Century Company in 1918. Each cartoon faces a page of comment by a distinguished American, the text forming an anthology of patriotic opinion.

The list of cartoons runs from the Stars and Stripes in the service of humanity to the end of the Hindenburg line. The commentators include Myron Herrick, John Jay Chapman, Gertrude Atherton, Ralph Cram, and Poultney Bigelow. Raemaekers drew for a neutral Holland until the war drove him to London; by 1918 his cartoons were Allied propaganda of the first rank. The book is a coalition in print: Dutch pencil, American prose, one enemy.
65899-wupatki-ruins-trail-wupatki-nation:
Wupatki National Monument in Arizona holds more than 800 ruins of the Sinagua people, and this trail booklet walks the visitor through the largest of them. Wupatki Ruin held over 100 rooms and some 250 to 300 people at its peak in the 1100s; its people lived there from about 1120 to 1210. The trail points out the ballcourt and the open court the booklet calls an amphitheater, and explains the plants along the path, such as ephedra, the jointfir or Mormon tea.

The National Park Service issued the booklet, here in its twenty-first edition of 1976. It notes that the ruin was dug in the 1930s and later years, and that the Service now preserves rather than restores such sites. Short numbered stops make it a guide to carry on the walk itself.
659-paul-the-peddler-or-the-fortunes-of-:
Horatio Alger, Jr. writes a boys' tale of New York street life in this volume. Paul, a young peddler, works the streets among bootblacks, newsboys, and shopkeepers, learning honesty, thrift, and pluck. A biography fronts the book, tracing Alger from Revere birth and Harvard to a pastorate and then to writing for street boys.

Alger writes with plain, earnest prose, full of city scenes and moral lessons. His heroes rise by work and character, not luck alone. The book endures as a typical Alger story, where a street merchant's fortunes turn on industry and a clean heart.
65965-the-jade-story-book-stories-from-t:
Jade Story Book, stories from the Orient, is the eastern volume of the Jewel Series of story books. The series list at the front names its sister volumes in the same dress. The Diamond Story Book and the Ruby Story Book, tales of courage and heroism, stand there. The Sapphire Story Book holds tales of the sea for the same readers.

The Emerald volume holds stories of spring, nature, and Easter in the list. The Topaz holds stories and legends of autumn, Halloween, and Thanksgiving for the year round shelf. The Turquoise holds stories and legends of summer and nature in its turn. The Jade book takes the Orient for its field, in the manner of the set. Its tales are old stories retold for children in a handsome gift volume. The book is one jewel of a planned rainbow on the nursery shelf of the 1920s.
66019-a-child-of-the-orient:
A Child of the Orient, by Demetra Vaka, was published in London and New York in 1914. Vaka had written on the lives of Turkish women before. She gives the book to her editor and friend Trumbull White. The tale is her own childhood, told in the first person. On her fifth birthday her grand uncle gave her a small Greek flag. He told her to pray by it and to recall her race.

Chapters bear names such as Djimlah, Aunt Kalliroe, and Yilderim. One tells how she was sold to St George. Later chapters cross to America, then return to Turkey. In Real America and Back to Turkey mark that turn. The book mixes family scenes, folk figures, and a child's pride in Greece under alien rule.
6617-poems-of-sentiment:
Wilcox returns in Poems of Sentiment, a 1919 London reprint of a book first issued in 1909 and reprinted many times. Double Carnations, Never Mind, Two Women, and It All Will Come Out Right open a set that runs through love, time, will, regret, and Easter morn. A little white hearse and a yellow-covered almanac add a somber, homely note.

The verse is direct and musical, with feeling worn openly and morals drawn in plain words. Wilcox does not hide behind hard images; she speaks to the heart at once. Poems of Sentiment suits readers who want verse that comforts, cheers, and names what love and loss feel like.
66212-list-ye-landsmen-a-romance-of-inci:
List, Ye Landsmen is a sea romance by W Clark Russell, copyrighted in 1892 by Cassell of New York. Russell was the author of The Wreck of the Grosvenor and The Frozen Pirate. His narrator tells the tale in the first person, arriving in the Downs aboard the Royal Brunswicker.

The narrator was born at Folkestone and raised by his uncle, Captain Joseph Round, near Deal. The contents map a busy voyage: a gibbet, an escape from the press gang, and Captain Michael Greaves of the Black Watch. A fight with Van Laar ends by transhipping him, and a round robin brings a midnight scare. Dollars are transhipped at Greaves' island, where a ship waits hidden in a cave. A whaler, a sailor's will, a tragic shift of course, and Amsterdam Island fill the later chapters. A Quaker skipper and Mynheer Tulp close the list.
66244-blessed-event:
Charles Myers wrote this science fiction tale, Blessed Event, taken from a magazine of February 1954. A headnote gives its wild premise straight: he was the millionth quadrillionth baby to be born on Earth, and naturally the event had to be celebrated, and was, in a devastating manner. The opening scene, though, is a quiet kitchen quarrel about a schoolboy's report.

Ginny, wiping her hands on her apron, begs Lester not to yell at the boy. Lester explodes over the class paper: excellent, it says, and that is four excellents this month. The worst mark the boy has ever had was very good. Ginny answers that he was awfully proud, and that he owns himself weak in spelling. Not weak enough for comfort, says Lester: the little head is crammed with brains, and he finds himself wondering whether cutting down the child's food might slow him.
66302-the-church-of-sancta-sophia-consta:
The Church of Sancta Sophia, Constantinople is a study of Byzantine building by Lethaby and Harold Swainson. Macmillan published it in London and New York in 1894. Its subject is the great church of Hagia Sophia in the old imperial city. Old writers quoted at the front call it the fairest church in the world.

The preface makes a large claim for its subject. Sancta Sophia, the authors say, is the most interesting building on earth. Like Karnak and the Parthenon, it ranks among the four great peaks of building. Unlike them it is no ruin, but stands well preserved. The book's first task is to untangle the church's long history. Its second is to study the design and the craft of its making. Both authors visited the city and worked from the building itself.
66323-the-natural-history-of-the-gent:
The Natural History of the Gent is a satire by Albert Smith, printed at London in 1847. Its preface starts from a newspaper paragraph of May 1846. A man named James Dickenson was charged with being drunk in Park Road, and the constable called him a gent.

The magistrate, Rawlinson, refused the word. He held that a man called a gent was the greatest blackguard there is. The prisoner agreed, and paid his five shilling fine. Smith had spent three or four years trying to bring the race of gents into contempt. The magistrate's ruling from the bench was a gift to his campaign.
66379-birthday-present:
Birthday Present is a short story by Arnold Marmor, first printed in Imagination, Stories of Science and Fantasy, in July 1954. Diane's husband spends most of his time on Mars, and the narrator spends most of his with Diane. It is a nice arrangement, the narrator says, much too nice to last. Diane tells him it is tonight or never.

She is picking her husband up at the spaceway for dining and dancing on her thirtieth birthday. The narrator is twenty-four and in love, and wants to marry her. Her plan is cold: he will crouch low in the back of the racer and strike her husband with a wrench as they drive away. Then they will carry the body up to the apartment and drop it out of the window. It will be listed as a suicide, since the man has been sick a long time.
66468-the-vampire-of-the-continent:
Count Ernst zu Reventlow wrote a German attack on England Englished and printed at New York in 1916. George Chatterton Hill wrote the preface. The heroic age of the Britons in the sixteenth century opens the charge. The pious pirates of the seventeenth follow, then the campaign against the enemy of peace in the era of Louis the Fourteenth.

We have conquered Canada in Germany, a chapter cries of Frederic the Great and England. The protector of neutral countries and liberator of Europe, the great harvest of the Napoleonic wars, and England digesting her booty fill the middle. Anglo German friendship and estrangement after Bismarck, and Edward the Seventh preparing Germany's ruin, close the case. England is the vampire of the continent in his title. War time readers get the German brief at full strength.
66690-tiberius-the-tyrant:
J C Tarver wrote a life of the Roman emperor Tiberius, issued in London in 1902. Archibald Constable and Company brought out Tiberius the Tyrant at Westminster. Tarver had written a life and letters of Gustave Flaubert. A long survey of Rome's growth, people, senate, and slavery opens the book.

Chapters then run from the death of Augustus to retirement at Capreae. Mutinies in Pannonia and on the Rhine, the fall of Sejanus, and Tacitus as source all get study. Tarver warns that later terms warp how we judge those days. Readers gain a deep, grave life of a dark and complex ruler.
66713-selling-point:
Norman Arkawy wrote this short story, printed in Imagination in December 1955. Ira sells door to door for the U S Robot Company, long a leader in machines for shops and factories. The firm now brings out home servant robots, built to help the housewife at every task. The magazine's hook warns of a twist: the models are called perfected, but nobody had weighed the one defect.

Ira works his foot into a closing door with an old salesman's grace and keeps his smile. The woman of the house says they want nothing and tries to squeeze the door shut on his shoe. He presses on with his patter, sure the demonstration will win her. The comedy of the hard sell meets the robot age.
66733-the-obedient-servant:
Tenneshaw wrote a tale of a rich man who buys a most odd gift. The tale ran in Imagination in June 1956. John Gardner wants a gift his wife just can not resist. He asks a salesman to show him the one named in the title. The tale's name is The Obedient Servant.

Gardner and his wife fight at the first meal of the day. They fight oft, but this day a dread thought strikes him. She is the last friend his wealth and scorn have left him. He has driven all the rest off with scorn and abuse. Now fear, not love, drives his strange gift plan.
66990-narrative-of-a-private-soldier-in-:
Narrative of a Private Soldier is the own tale of Billany, a foot man of a famed Scots band of the line. A word at its front by a famed priest of Glasgow stands with it. This is its first form for America, put out at Philadelphia in the early eighteen twenties.

Its title page tells its span in full. It gives many facts of the rise in Ireland in the last years of the past age. It tells of the trip to Holland the next year, and of the trip to Egypt two years on. It gives as well a full tale of his faith life and its turns. Its first word is brief by plan, since long first words are scarce read through.
67036-plain-sermons-preached-at-archbish:
Plain Sermons is a set of talks by Cowan, the priest of a chapel in a famed street of London. This is its second run, put out at London in eighteen sixty. A first run by the same hand is named at its front, at a set price in cloth.

His first talk takes the words of a letter of Paul for its text. The Lord is at hand, it runs. Be full of care for naught. But in all things, by prayer and plea with thanks, let your asks be made known to God. His next talk asks where the God of judgment is, from an old prophets words. Trust in God, judgment here and in the life to come, and like plain themes fill the set.
67043-the-high-place-a-comedy-of-disench:
James Branch Cabell wrote The High Place, a comedy of disenchantment, issued at New York in 1923 in a first edition limited to two thousand numbered copies. Frank Papé drew the pictures and decorations. The title comes from an old charge to build a high place for Chemosh and kindred gods on the hills. Cabell's list at the front places the book among Jurgen, Figures of Earth, and Domnei.

Florian, a nobleman, is shown in the frontispiece feeling himself in company not quite suited to his rank. The first part is named The End of Long Wanting, and it opens with a child errant. Cabell writes his romance of France in a polished, ironic voice, where gallantry and disenchantment share the same bed.
67107-the-honey-bee-its-natural-history-:
Edward Bevan, a physician, wrote this treatise on the honey-bee, published at London in 1827. He dedicated it to a Herefordshire rector who studied bees in elegant retirement.

The advertisement owns the book's mixed arrangement: Bevan aimed at a popular view of apiarian knowledge, mingling history and physiology with practice where they explain it. The work grew beyond his first plan as the materials grew upon his hands. Verse mottoes from Bowring and Paley frame the title page, one calling a bee among spring flowers among the cheerfullest objects that can be looked upon. Bevan keeps his volume compressed so as to stay affordable. Beekeepers get an early English classic of the apiary.
67314-water-reptiles-of-the-past-and-pre:
Samuel Wendell Williston studies swimmers in Water Reptiles of the Past and Present, printed at Chicago in 1914. The University of Chicago Press made the book, published in October of that year. Williston was professor of paleontology in the University of Chicago.

An introduction leads to the classification of reptiles and the skeleton of reptiles. The age of reptiles follows, then the adaptation of land reptiles to life in the water. Orders fill the back span: the Sauropterygia, with the plesiosaurs and nothosaurs. The Anomodontia bring Lystrosaurus. The Ichthyosauria get a chapter of their own. Mesosaurus and Protorosaurus close the march of forms. Students of old life get the water orders set in order, bone by bone and age by age.
67342-the-marriage-of-william-durrant:
The Marriage of William Durrant is a story by Ray Cummings, told in the first person as a confession. Durrant begins bluntly: his marriage has been a failure. He is, he says, one of those unfortunate men with whom fate deals unjustly.

He worked the whole thing out carefully, he insists, knowing what was necessary for their happiness, and went after it sanely and unswervingly. He lacked neither ambition nor purpose and did not shirk hard work. Yet the woman he loved and trusted deceived him, and his honour was trampled under foot. Durrant was born in Philadelphia thirty two years before, into a prominent society family. He took a university education, then entered his father's wholesale neckwear business. Only after his mother's death did he learn the true state of his father's affairs. Cummings, better known for science fiction, here writes a domestic tale of a marriage wrecked.
67393-the-fourth-battalion-the-king-s-ow:
Wadham and Crossley wrote The Fourth Battalion, the King's Own, and the Great War, a unit history of a Lancashire force. The book opens in 1914, the year all recall as the most marked in the unit's past. On Sunday, August 2, the men went to camp at Kirkby Lonsdale for their yearly drill. They were part of the West Lancashire Brigade of the Territorial Force. Word of war filled the air, and trains were held in case the men must march home at once.

Chapters trace Festubert, Picardy, Arras, the Somme, Ypres, and Givenchy in turn. A close chapter on the third battle of Ypres and a final sum close the tale. Long appendices list men, deeds, and honors. The book gives a plain, proud record of one battalion through the Great War.
67539-around-the-circle-one-thousand-mil:
The passenger department of the Denver and Rio Grande Railroad issued a free guide in 1892 to a thousand-mile loop through the Rocky Mountains. Its cover claim is bold: the journey holds more noted and grand scenery than any other thousand miles of travel in the known world. Names and addresses of the road's agents fill the first pages.

The route takes in the Rio Grande Southern and the Rainbow Route, then the Black Cañon and Marshall Pass. Toltec Gorge, Animas Cañon, and the Royal Gorge follow. Tables give the heights of peaks, passes, lakes, and towns, and a list names seventy points of interest. Tourists in search of grand scenery were the guide's prey.
67586-martin-valliant:
Martin Valliant is a novel by Warwick Deeping, author of Sorrell and Son, printed at New York by McBride and Company in a first edition. The tale opens at night, in a house among apple trees in Orchard Valley, where Brother Geraint pulls his black cowl over his head and slips out into the porch.

A full moon stares over the thorn hedge as the door is barred behind him. Geraint licks his lips, listens to a dog baying down the valley, and grins at the moon before he starts down the path. Dew lies like silver on the grass, the Rondel river runs sleek toward the sea, and the bell tower of Paradise cuts the bright sky. Deeping builds a tale of old England in rich, moonlit prose.
6762-politics-a-treatise-on-government:
Aristotle's Politics, in William Ellis's translation, is the second part of a treatise whose first part is the Ethics. The introduction notes that Aristotle did not split statesman from moralist as modern readers tend to do. Ethics paints the character needed for a good life, lived in society, and its last chapters turn to the statesman's legislative work.

Politics itself asks what makes a city just, stable, and good, weighing constitutions, citizens, and laws. Ellis's Dent edition, first issued in 1912, keeps the prose clear and scholarly. Politics is a founding work of political thought, still argued over by readers today.
6764-army-life-in-a-black-regiment:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson records the First South Carolina Volunteers, the first slave regiment mustered into United States service in the Civil War. First published in 1869 and reprinted in 1900, the book runs from a camp diary up the St. Mary's, St. John's, and Edisto rivers to picket duty, a night in the water, and life at Camp Shaw. Negro spirituals get a chapter of their own.

Higginson, their white colonel, writes with respect for his Black soldiers, their courage, humor, and faith. An appendix lists officers, first Black soldiers, and the struggle for equal pay. Army Life in a Black Regiment is a classic, first-hand Civil War memoir, essential to American history.
67728-the-valley-of-content:
Valley of Content is a novel by Blanche Upright, copyrighted in 1922 by Watt. Front matter notes its screen life under the title Pleasure Mad with Norma Shearer. A still shows Elinor at a Bohemian party in the flat of Templeton Druid. The book is dedicated to Marjorie Rambeau as the author beloved inspirer.

Chapter one sets a small table in the Bentons tiny bungalow kitchen dining room. A paper shaded lamp glows over polished cutlery and a bowl of wild roses. Modest home order stands against the gay party world the still displays. That clash of plain content and pleasure hunting drives the story ahead.
67755-memorabilia-or-recollections-histo:
Memorabilia, or Recollections, Historical, Biographical, and Antiquarian is a miscellany compiled by James Savage and printed for him at Taunton in 1820. It was sold by Poole there and by Baldwin, Cradock, and Joy in London. Its advertisement, dated Taunton, May 31, 1820, says the pieces were gathered from various sources and extensive reading.

Savage states his method plainly: authorities are named in footnotes, borrowed writers are credited, facts are the chief object, and no opinions or conclusions are drawn from them. The contents range widely, from anecdotes of Kennicott, Charles the Twelfth of Sweden, British pearls, and clocks to the English slave trade, Shakespeare, university degrees, peacocks, and ancient libraries. He offers the volume to young persons as an hour of instruction and amusement that will not sully the purest mind.
67816-the-bee-preserver-or-practical-dir:
The Bee Preserver is a manual on the management and preservation of bee hives, translated from the French of Jonas de Gelieu. Anderson of Edinburgh and Simpkin and Marshall of London published the translation in 1829. Gelieu was a minister in the principality of Neuchatel and a member of the economic society of Berne.

The translator dedicates the work to the Highland Society of Scotland. The Society had that year turned its attention to encouraging apiaries among the peasantry. Gelieu's system, proven in his native mountains, is offered as plain and profitable for Scotland too. The rules come with discoveries about the history and economy of bees. Swiss honey, the text notes, is abundant and of high quality. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
67957-mr-keegan-s-elopement:
Winston Churchill tells Mr Keegan's Elopement in a Macmillan volume from New York in 1903, first copyrighted by the Century Company in 1896. Churchill, author of Richard Carvel and The Crisis, appears in a frontispiece portrait. The tale appears in a series called Little Novels by Favourite Authors.

Chapter one rides the warship Denver into an October sunrise off Madeira, seas breaking over her forecastle as Funchal whitens at the mountain island's base. Keegan, chief boatswain's mate, smokes with his friend Jimmy Legs, the master at arms, collars up against the northeast wind. Dennis Keegan has reddish hair, small blue eyes, and a cheek swollen by navy plug tobacco. The narrator warns that Keegan's real status and influence aboard defy definition, like the captain's duties themselves.
68241-the-profanity-of-paint:
The Profanity of Paint is a small book of short tries by William Kiddier. It is sworn to the men who love hue. It was put out at London in nineteen sixteen. Its list of parts names near a score of short pieces. My book is true heads that list. My friends the trees and the theme piece of the book's name come next.

The sad chase of lore, the gift of still ness, and the charm of words fill the first run. The own note, hue it self, waste, and the bond stand past them. Dire tale, the strong drink of gifts, the keen tongues, and the shut ear fill the mid run. The paint man's smoke leaf, the crowd's food house, and the mid class stand in the late run.
68261-the-partnership-of-paint:
Partnership of Paint is a trade booklet issued by a Brooklyn paint maker in nineteen twenty. Its pages on interiors were supplied by a New York decorator, the firm thanks her in front. Her wide professional experience makes her word the last word in taste, it says. The opening chapter is called Paint Our Partner.

Paint as our partner in all the affairs of life may be a new thought, the chapter says. But it is an old established fact all the same, it argues. Paint is woven into every turn of the wheel of life. Suppose paint in every form vanished from the world some morning, it asks. Trains, motors, boats, and houses would stand paintless and strange. Our partner stands ready to jump into any breach, it says.
68329-redevelopment:
Wesley Long wrote Redevelopment, a science fiction tale printed in the November 1944 issue of Astounding Science-Fiction, with pictures by Williams. John McBride works at Station 1 of the Plutonian Lens, far out at the edge of the sun's realm. A phone call leaves him dazed, and he walks to the landing platform by the great lock. There sits Sandra Drake on the edge of the space lock, swinging her feet and greeting him brightly.

Sandra has flown in through the station's charge field with a charge-compensator, barely sparking as she lit, though an attendant mutters that three hundred amperes is no small spark. She asks McBride for help on a big matter. He owns that the station owes her one for a past favor. Long sets up his tale as a bargain struck between old rivals in deep space.
68358-underground-movement:
Underground Movement is a tale by Allen Lang from Infinity magazine. Engle drew the pictures for the December 1956 printing of the story. A mangled corpse held them captive in a dark tunnel, the blurb says. That corpse taught them a lesson about what freedom really means. The tale opens as a hatch swings open in a capsule car.

A man of the Bupo, the state secret police, steps out first. His face shows the insolence the riders knew as that uniform. He walks the aisle like a suspecting machine, catching every detail. Folk lean toward the walls as children shrink from a big animal. Then the capsule slams into something in the Tube and stops dead. The Tube runs five thousand kilometres under the Andes and the pampas. Senses built into that metal gut halted the pumps just in time.
68654-canada-in-war-paint:
Canada in War-Paint is a book of the great war by Captain Ralph Bell. It was first put out in nineteen seventeen at London and at a town of the north land. Draw work by a named hand stands in it. The front plate shows the mules of the host, from such a draw. Its list of parts is a roll of short, gay heads on the life of the troops.

Can vas and mud heads the run. Tent song, a snake man, and the mules come next. The desk, our farm, and fly craft past the guns of the foe fill the first run. Stir times, the sick line, the men who wait on chiefs, and the food of the host stand past them.
69026-essays-on-the-latin-orient:
Essays on the Latin Orient, by William Miller, author of The Latins in the Levant, was published by Cambridge University Press in 1921. A Philostratus motto reminds readers that the campaigners against Troy were not the only heroes Greece produced.

The essays survey the Romans in Greece and Byzantine Greece, then Frankish and Venetian Greece: the Frankish conquest, Frankish society, the princes of the Peloponnese, and the dukes of Athens. Later essays treat Florentine Athens and its Turkish capture, the duchy of Naxos, Crete under the Venetians from 1204 to 1669, and the Ionian Islands under Venetian rule. The first essay sets the frame. From the Roman conquest of 146 BC, Greece lost her independence for nearly two thousand years and followed the fortunes of foreign rulers.
69085-women-in-white-raiment:
John Lemley wrote a book in praise of good women in white raiment. The first form came out in Albany, New York, in 1899. Lemley ran The Zion's Watchman and wrote The Christ Lifted Up. A verse from Revelation heads his book's front pages. It speaks of those who walk in white for their worth.

His first part holds that the Bible lifts women's state. He sets heathen lands gainst Bible lands on that point. God's thought of woman at the first and Christ's care come next. The Paradise home in Eden starts the main tale of grace. Lives of pure women fill the book as proof. Faith readers get warm praise in old dress.
69444-present-status-and-prospects-of-th:
Baroness Bertha von Süttner wrote this survey of the peace movement's present status and prospects as letters reached her desk in growing number. Some correspondents mocked: the South African war followed the Hague Peace Conference, and Asia glared with a coming world war. Others pitied her shattered illusion.

She answers that the peace effort is no feebly manned boat battling storm and surf. It is a rock, which waves may top with spume but cannot move. Setting metaphor aside, she replies to both groups from the advocates' point of view. Readers get the peace movement's most famous voice defending her cause in wartime's shadow.
69445-universal-peace-from-a-woman-s-sta:
Universal Peace, From a Woman's Standpoint is an essay by Baroness Bertha von Süttner, the Austrian peace campaigner. She wrote it at an editor's request for American readers. The subject, she says, occupies her thoughts and actions so completely that she complied most willingly, though she would have chosen another title.

Everything a woman writes, she grants, is written from a woman's standpoint. But she refuses to treat peace and war only, or even chiefly, in their bearing on the feelings and lives of women. Such relations exist, and women's associations do a service when they put peace and arbitration on their programmes. Yet reflecting women, she believes, will judge this universal concern of humanity from a general point of view. Women who cry that war must cease because they suffer from it stand, she argues, morally lower than those who oppose it on wider grounds.
69449-the-island-of-anarchy-a-fragment-o:
The Island of Anarchy: A Fragment of History in the 20th Century, by E W, was published by Miss Langley at Lovejoy's Library, Reading, in 1887. Its motto bids the reader bind himself with one cord. A long passage from Montaigne in Florio's translation stands at the head of chapter one.

The ending of the nineteenth century, the fragment begins, was a time of terrible and strange things. England, the refuge of banished men, saw social disorder climb high. The narrator blames the advanced age of office-holders: age trifles, tinkers, and studies life from a frivolous point of view.
69533-impressionist-painting-its-genesis:
Impressionist Painting: Its Genesis and Development, by Wynford Dewhurst, was published in London by George Newnes in 1904 and dedicated to Claude Monet. Dewhurst writes as an admirer within a few years of the movement's battles. His thirteen chapters run from the growth of the impressionist idea to the ground the school had won by the new century.

Early chapters treat Jongkind, Boudin, and Cezanne as forerunners, then Edouard Manet on his own. The group of 1870 to 1886 follows, with full chapters for Monet and for Pissarro, Renoir, and Sisley. Degas, Toulouse-Lautrec, and Raffaelli stand among the realists, and a chapter honors the women painters Morisot, Cassatt, Bracquemond, and Gonzales. Whistler leads the American pages, and Max Liebermann the German. Long lists of plates, a bibliography, and an index close an early English account of the school.
69573-the-light-an-educational-pageant:
Catherine Bryce, who helped lead the schools of Cleveland, Ohio, wrote The Light, a pageant play put out in Boston in 1920. It was made for the Cleveland meeting of the National Education Association held that same year. A boy called Any City talks with a girl figure named Education, who wears Greek robes and bears a lamp.

The play moves in steps called glimmers, from first lessons through custom, new tools, training, rules, and the book. Later scenes deal with force, training for self rule, a warning, and a dream of what schools could be. Songs and music notes are given in the text. Schools could stage it with a large cast.
69686-the-hand-book-of-the-law-of-legaci:
The Hand-Book of the Law of Legacies belongs to Tyas's Legal Hand-Books, published by Robert Tyas in London in 1841. The book states the nature of legacies and the accidents to which they are subject. It sets out the rights of legatees, and the causes and manner of the ademption, cumulation, and abatement of bequests.

The preface calls the book a cautious guide meant to acquaint men with their rights, not to replace a lawyer. Its author believed that more knowledge would mean less litigation and distrust. Early chapters define legacies and legatees, then treat the assets of an estate: real, personal, legal, and equitable. The handbook serves heirs and executors who need the rules of inheritance in plain, short form.
69877-the-fire-in-the-flint:
Walter White wrote a novel printed in New York in 1924. Its title comes from an old English proverb. The fire in the flint never shows until it is struck. The hero is Kenneth Harper, a doctor who has just set up his office and waits for patients to come.

Harper fits out his rooms with care, from a shining exam table to a fine microscope. Two weeks of hard work and delay stand behind his quiet pride. The novel then tests what lies hid in the man when life strikes him. Work, race, love, and strain in a small town press on him. White builds the tale round the gap between calm looks and hid fire.
69911-the-war-against-germany-and-italy-:
The War Against Germany and Italy: Mediterranean and Adjacent Areas is the pictorial record volume of the United States Army in World War II set. First printed in 1951, it was reissued in Washington in 1988 by the Center of Military History. Photographers of the Army, Air Force, Navy, Marine Corps, and Coast Guard shot the record on film.

The preface notes that thousands of their pictures rest in the photographic libraries of the armed services, little seen by the public. The official history set brings them out as evidence of what the war looked like. This volume covers the Mediterranean theater: North Africa, Sicily, Italy, and the waters and lands around them. Captions tie each image to units, places, and dates in the campaigns.
70056-historical-record-of-the-71st-regi:
Historical Record of the Seventy First Regiment is a Highland Light Infantry history. Lieutenant Hildyard of the regiment compiled the record for Harrison in eighteen seventy six. The regiment was formed in seventeen seventy seven as the Seventy Third. McLeod Highlanders was its first title before the Seventy First name came.

A succession of colonels opens the book, from Lord McLeod in seventeen seventy seven. Gordon, Cradock, Dundas, Drummond, and Halkett follow in the colonel list given. Wittingham, Reynell, Arbuthnot, Macdonell, and Napier carry the line onward. Grey, Law, and Cadogan close the list at eighteen seventy four in post. The record runs a full century of Highland service to eighteen seventy six.
70105-gilead-balm-knight-errant:
Gilead Balm, Knight Errant is a set of quests in search of the truth. Bernard Capes wrote the tales, set out in Toronto in 1911. Eight plates by Cyrus Cuneo dress the book for the eye. Its hero is a young man blessed in looks, mind, and heart.

Each quest starts from a small clue or a strange ask. A sleeping fair one, an bare house, and a lost dog start the run. A stone doll, a ring with a rose, and a wax hand come next. A red case, a sent pack, and a shade fill the mid quests. A veiled dame and a fat gent close the list of his tasks. Balm's flaw, if flaw it be, is to see two sides to a thing. His wit is the grace that saves him, the book holds.
70157-the-vinegar-saint:
The Vinegar Saint is a novel by Hughes Mearns, author of Richard Richard, published by the Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia in 1919. Ralph Boyer drew the illustrations. The dedication quotes the saint himself: someone must keep watch lest the heavens fall. A postscript, offered for all prefaces, explains the book's long delay.

The chronicle of the town of Gorgas and its sharp-tongued moralist was nearly done when war news came out of Germany. Mearns laid it aside and stood guard duty leagues from home. He finished it only after the collapse, arguing that good is good and evil is evil, with no compromise between them. That, he says, is what the Vinegar Saint had contended all along. The novel joins a home-front fable to a soldier's afterword.
70189-the-sensitive-plant:
Percy Bysshe Shelley's long poem The Sensitive Plant was printed in London in 1899 for the Guild of Women Binders. Only fifty copies on Japanese paper were made, and this is number thirty eight. Laurence Housman drew the illustrations, from death in the garden to the garden entombed. An essay tells how the poem came to be.

Shelley wrote it near the end of his poetry, in the days at Pisa from January 1820. The idea came from flowers Mrs Shelley kept round her in her room on the south side of the Arno. The poem sings of beauty and death in a garden. Something inexplicable remains in it, the essay owns, after all its circumstances are gathered.
70220-mary-derwent:
Ann Stephens set Mary Derwent in the Wyoming and Mohawk Valleys in seventeen seventy-eight, and the Wilkes-Barre edition came from Fowler, Dick and Walker at the Boston Store Book Shop. A front plate shows the heroine leaping onto a rock to shield a missionary from attack. A map of the early settlements of both valleys sits among the book's thirty-two chapters.

Those chapters move from the valley of Wyoming through a missionary's cabin, a marriage contract, and Walter Butler's capture to the jail at Albany. Queen Esther, a serpent bracelet, and a lake by starlight season the war story. The gathering storm breaks into a first skirmish, a battlefield, and a warning and flight before a double wedding closes the tale.
70313-american-nights-entertainment:
American Nights Entertainment is a book about books and authors by Grant Overton, published at New York in 1923. Four publishing houses joined to make it: Appleton, Doran, Doubleday Page, and Scribner's. Overton dedicated it to booksellers and bookreaders everywhere. The preface says the book exists because the habit of reading spread fast, bringing a wish to know the people who write.

Overton counts the growth of book stores and book sales among the hopeful signs of the young century. Alongside bare life facts, he tries to show each writer's self, so often kept back from the books. His account of Galsworthy is named as an example of the method. The result is a survey of the living literary world of its day.
7033-picturesque-quebec-a-sequel-to-queb:
J M Lemoine offers Picturesque Quebec as a sequel to his Quebec Past and Present of 1876, inscribed to the citizens of Quebec. The preface promises to complete the city's history with new details on the spot where Samuel de Champlain settled in 1608. A rapid glance covers incidents, sights, objects, edifices, city gates, and improvements ancient and modern, as an antiquarian's ramble round streets, squares, and promenades may disclose.

Lemoine hopes the book will serve as a copious store of historical, topographical, legendary, industrial, and antiquarian lore, gathered not without trouble. Monuments, public and private buildings, and old walls all find a place. The volume is a loving guide to a city proud of its French roots and its stone walls.
70835-shakespeare-s-environment:
Stopes digs in the records in Shakespeare's Environment, printed in London in 1914. She had writ books on Shakespeare's family and his Warwickshire peers, and on Burbage and the stage. Her theme is the world round the poet, told from deeds, suits, and parish books.

Heads treat the fortunes of Shakespeare and his aunts of Snitterfield. One gives a new detail of John Shakespeare's life from Asbies. One asks what arms Mary Arden bore. One calls Stratford a bookless neighbourhood, and one lists a Mr Shaxpere with one book in 1595. More heads treat the Stratford bust, Thames locks, and the friends in the sonnets.
70873-anthony-cragg-s-tenant:
Anthony Cragg's Tenant is a novel by Agnes Giberne, published in London by the Religious Tract Society with colored illustrations by Lancelot Speed. Giberne wrote improving fiction for family reading. This tale opens with the arrival of Mr Dale, a tall shabby stranger, at the shop door of the proud Mrs Cragg. She is a fine lady in a bright blue gown and a hat with a scarlet wing.

Chapters promise a rescue, an unauthorized search, a secret made known, a dire mistake, and a very narrow escape, with little Dot at the center of a catastrophe. The story works in the tract-society manner, where pride, charity, and hidden worth are tried in small-town life. It shows how Victorian religious publishers carried moral fiction into ordinary homes.
7090-the-little-immigrant:
The Little Immigrant, privately printed in 1921 and surviving in few copies, tells how the author's great grandmother's parents met, married, and began a family. The introduction, by a great grandson, explains most names are disguised, though thinly, and gives a table matching false names to real ones. Renestine Jewel stands for Ernestine Jacobowsky, Aldine Bilter for her married sister, and Jaffray Starr for Jacob Sterne.

Lola, Ena, Lester, Andrew, and Frank stand for Laura, Eva, Leopold, Alfred, and Fred Sterne, while Josiah the longtime family slave and his wife appear with their counterparts. General Buell, whom the Starrs housed during Reconstruction after Civil War violence, keeps his true name. The book is a family memoir of immigration, marriage, and the postwar South.
71034-tom-taylor-at-west-point:
Frank Webster wrote Tom Taylor at West Point, or the old army officer's secret, printed at New York in 1915. A plate shows Tom and his fellow riders raising sabers high and yelling at page 202. Webster's boys list includes Only a Farm Boy, Bob the Castaway, Airship Andy, and Darry the Life-Saver among many titles.

Contents open with wonderful news, the examination, anxious days, success, an attack, and off to West Point. Getting ready, a slide for life, Captain Hawkesbury, anticipation, a lark, Tom's refusal, across the river, and an explosion follow. Hard work, furlough, a quarrel, unhorsed, in the hospital, the clue, discovered, restitution, and graduation close the tale. Boys got academy adventure.
71284-the-house-of-egremont:
Molly Elliot Seawell wrote The House of Egremont, a novel printed at New York in 1900 with plates by Relyea. Roger Egremont makes his bow to the world in the first chapter. The next shows him in close talk with two forces that shape his life: the Devil and Miss Bess Lukens.

Heads promise an Easter masquerade on a terrace, good and ill fortune, and Princess Michelle, who is set on the path to the destiny she has long dreamed of. Roger rides for Orlamunde, serves as coachman with a duke as footman, and fights his last fight with the Devil. A friend life given for friends and a foe named Hugo Stein frame the close. Court dress, duels, and romance fill a lush tale of old Europe.
71372-tarzan-triumphant:
Tarzan Triumphant is a tale of the ape man by Edgar Rice Burroughs, first put out in hard boards in nineteen thirty two. The host text keeps that first form. A late cheap print house of New York gave it this dress. The plate art of the cheap form is by a hand named at the front. The book is set in the wild heart of the dark land of the tale world.

The back word of the book lines up a strange cast cast up by fate in a lost vale. A gun man flees the gang wars of Chicago in the train of folk who know naught of his past. A bright earth lore man seeks rocks and finds more than rocks. A girl who flies the air is lost in a hid vale.
71671-innocent:
Innocent, a tale of modern life, is a novel by Mrs Oliphant, in a fourth edition of 1874. Sampson Low and partners published the book in London from Fleet Street that year. The edition carries illustrations for the tale in this issue. Oliphant is named as author of The Chronicles of Carlingford on the title page.

Contents open with The Old House, The News and How It Was Received, and The Family in order. The Friends of the Family and Frederick Way follow in the list of chapters. Pisa and the Palazzo Scaramucci carry the scene to Italy in the middle chapters. The Cousins, At Home, The Arrival, and A Love Tale fill the chapters after that journey. Oliphant heroine, named for her quality, moves through a world of family money and marriage plots with that innocence as both her shield and her danger.
7168-introduction-to-the-old-testament:
John Edgar McFadyen wrote this introduction for students, ministers, and lay readers who want the modern view of the Old Testament as a whole. He warns at once that he offers nothing for specialists, since the details of full study are intricate, perplexing, and all but countless. His aim is the wood rather than the trees.

The book therefore maps the shape of the whole testament before it dwells on single parts, helping a busy reader grasp how scholars now read these old books. McFadyen, a professor at Knox College in Toronto, keeps his prose clear and direct, so that a reader without time for deep research can still follow the main lines of the argument.
71851-six-months-on-the-italian-front:
Six Months on the Italian Front is a war correspondent's book by Julius Price of the Illustrated London News, published by Dutton in New York in 1917. Price was the paper's war artist. His subtitle gives his ground: from the Stelvio to the Adriatic, 1915 to 1916. The frontispiece shows him at San Martino del Carso.

The first chapter follows his marching orders. He travels by Folkestone and Boulogne, notes the one and only cigarette of the train journey, and reaches Rome to find no excitement in the streets. On the day of Italy's declaration of war the Corso Umberto is unruffled and business goes on as usual; the mobilisation he calls a triumph of organisation. Then come credentials, censorship, Venice bombed from the air and spy fever. Price reports the Italian war as an artist: scenery, staff work and national stoicism in equal measure.
71950-the-red-plant:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey wrote a Sunday school tale, entered at Washington in 1872 and sold at Philadelphia. It stands in a set called the Round Spring Stories. Guernsey's other tales, Irish Amy and Twin Roses among them, are named on the title page. The front picture shows a girl bringing a fuchsia to make amends.

Five chapters carry the whole short tale. The red plant opens it, and making good follows. A little bird carries the matter on. The weight of a bad name and eating humble pie close the book. It opens with Florry gazing at house plants on a lawn. Her mother sent her to borrow a pattern, and the flowers hold her fast.
71993-the-danger-of-premature-interment:
Joseph Taylor gathered The Danger of Premature Interment from old records of folk thought dead. W Simpkin and R Marshall issued the book in London in eighteen hundred sixteen. A plate shows the corpse of Cicero’s girl found whole after ages in her tomb. Taylor’s aim is to stop one dire wrong.

Men have waked in coffins, he warns, and some were tombed alive. Haste and poor checks sent them there too soon. One spark of life may yet hide in a still form, his motto says. Old Egypt and its ways with the dead get a full part. Lamps that burn for ages in tombs add a strange note. Burial in tight church yards harms the live, he adds, and must end.
72040-dorothy-dale-s-engagement:
Margaret Penrose wrote this late Dorothy Dale tale for girls, and Cupples and Leon printed it at New York. Dorothy Dale's Engagement takes its heroine to the edge of marriage. A front plate shows her telling her father that she thinks she is in love.

No, Daddy, she says in the plate, her words broken with feeling. Page 165 holds that scene, deep in the book. Dorothy's line runs from A Girl of To-Day through school, chums, and the city. Penrose also wrote the Motor Girls tales. Long-time readers who had grown up with Dorothy now saw her grown in turn, and her heart's choice forms this book's whole stake.
72065-the-little-merchant:
Little Merchant is a story for little folks by Oliver Optic of Boston. Optic was William Adams, author of The Boat Club and All Aboard. Lee and Shepard issued it in the Riverdale Story Books in 1870. Entry at Boston dates the work to the year 1862 in law. A front plate shows David and the frog for young eyes.

Riverdale is a very pretty place, the first chapter tells its readers. The village stands on the banks of a river from far hills. That river gives the place its name, the narrator explains at once. He will not stop to describe it, since readers learn as they go. A small boy's trade and thrift drive this moral tale forward.
72450-scheherazade-a-london-night-s-ente:
Scheherazade, a London Night's Entertainment, is a novel by Florence Warden. Warden also wrote The House on the Marsh, her title page notes. The new edition was issued at London in eighteen eighty nine. Contents run to thirty two chapters, listed without heads. Chapter one opens on a fine night in London with three young officers deciding how to travel.

Shall we go three in a hansom, one asks. Hansom be hanged, another answers, it is a lovely night, let us walk. They had been dining in Fitzroy Square with an old soldier, the tale says. He had been a major in their regiment fifteen years before. Clarence Massey, a pale faced, bright witted Irishman, is one of the three. Dicky Wood, tall and sweet tempered, is another.
7262-the-country-housewife-and-lady-s-di:
R. Bradley's Country Housewife and Lady's Director teaches the management of a house and the delights and profits of a farm, month by month from the year's beginning to its end. Its instructions cover the brew-house and malt liquors in the cellar, wines of all sorts, and the dairy. Butter and cheese on the worst of soils, brawn, fish, fowl, herbs, and roots follow, in the most elegant manner for the table.

Distilling, ketchup, and many curious and durable sauces join practical observations on ordering a country seat. Bradley writes for a housewife who must be steward, cook, and farmer at once, and his tone is plain and thrifty. The book turns household work into a yearly craft, useful and, in its own way, elegant.
72706-transient:
Ward Moore's Transient ran as a complete book-length novel in Amazing Stories in February 1960, illustrated by Finlay. Governor Almon Lampley, a widower in his earliest fifties, parks his car by an Odd Fellows Hall in a shabby small town. He is serving out his predecessor's term and hopes for election in his own right. The town sign reads population 1,983, seventeen short of two thousand. Lampley reckons its voters, its two precincts, and its three screwballs with a politician's eye.

Thirty years before, he had swung down from a day coach here, bursting with enthusiasm, selling farm implements. The railroad is gone now, its tracks melted for scrap, and the town has fallen behind. His secretary Marvin shares a running joke about the GOV-001 license plate, hostility under the kidding. The Governor hides his dislike of Marvin under self-deprecation.
72811-a-winter-in-retirement:
Hannah Blaney Washburn wrote these leaves of a quiet winter by the sea. A Winter in Retirement, or Scattered Leaves, came out at New York in 1914 from the Frank Allaben Genealogical Company. A short verse on the ocean's shore heads chapter one.

No prospect is more lovely, she writes, to those born on its shores, than the ocean. In summer heat its breezes bring a coolness never forgot by the wanderer from home. Even the hollow murmur before a storm, and the wild roar when the tempest rides, are recalled with a strange pleasure. They were the lullaby of many a calm night's sleep. In sickness, far from his birth land, the exile dreams of its pure air.
72863-the-pennant:
The Pennant, a boys’ baseball story by Everett Tomlinson, was copyrighted in 1912. Barse and Hopkins of New York and Newark published the book. Tomlinson had written Carl Hall of Tait and Captain Dan Richards before it. On Six Town Pond is the title of the first chapter.

Dan’s project and Great Snakes fill the next chapters of the contents. The reward of patience and then preparation lead toward the game itself. A dispute, a record, and the studying of a boy follow in the list. School, a try out, and a new pitcher carry the season forward. Tomlinson wrote clean school and sport tales for boys. A pennant race gives this one its spine and its glory.
73314-the-celestial-blueprint:
The Celestial Blueprint is a science fiction story by Philip José Farmer, printed in Fantastic Universe for July 1954. An editor's note promises apocalyptic fancy handled with Farmer's gift of laughter. The great Vincelleo, it says, liked being an artist: it let him turn the universe topsy turvy.

The opening sends Revanche striding through the office of Bioid Electronic. He is a stout, porcupine figure with weasel eyes and a fat cigar. Nobody stops him, and he does not announce himself. His anti-espionage field stays switched on as he enters. An anti-gravity elevator whisks him fifty stories up to Bioid's headquarters. The office overlooks the free city of Messina. A gold-plated attendant waits at the top, in a suite of size.
73416-of-no-account:
Ruth Lamb wrote Of No Account, a tale of faith and working life put out in London by the Religious Tract Society. The lead is Adam Livesey, a poor working man who calls himself of no account and wants to be left alone. He lost his father young, went to work at once, and helped feed the younger ones at home on small wages.

Twenty three parts trace Adam's hard home, his job under a new manager, talks in the mission room, and slow change of heart. Friends and foes test him at work and at church. By the end, lines about grace, lessons, and hope show a man won over step by step.
73431-death-of-a-mutant:
Death of a Mutant, a science fiction story by Charles De Vet, was printed in Super Science Fiction in February 1957. Its headnote says the boy was born with strange and wonderful powers. The world was not yet ready to accept the good of those powers. The world kills what it does not understand.

The boy stands on a low hill at dawn, throat bared to the morning chill, in faded trousers and a work shirt. Below him a dog barks, yelps, and stops. A figure darts between patches of brush over red sand. A man with a day's growth of beard draws a pistol from a chest holster as he comes on. De Vet builds a tense tale of a hunted child and the fear his gifts inspire. It belongs to the fifties wave of stories about mutants among ordinary folk.
73497-peter-merton-s-private-mint:
Lee Archer wrote this tale of a mint of one man, first printed in a journal of such tales in October 1956. A note at its head gives the lure of the plot in the form of a call to the reader. Your name is Merton, it says. All you have to do to get coin is reach in your safe. The more you take, the more you find there when you look once more. And this comes just when Quiggs has cut your days to come down to naught.

Peter Merton sits at his desk past a call from the men of the chief of law of the district. His head is in his hands. He is still sat that way when Miss Irene Simmons, his girl of the desk, comes in with the rest of the post of the dawn.
73583-fairs-past-and-present:
Fairs, Past and Present: A Chapter in the History of Commerce, by Cornelius Walford, was printed by Elliot Stock at London in 1883. The author, a lawyer and vice head of the Royal Historical Society, notes a gap: so wide and loved a thing as the fair had found no scribe. Fairs grew, he says, from a blend of faith and trade, apt for old times and strange to ours. Their stuff lies deep, and he chose depth over breadth.

Two great fairs lead the book: Sturbridge by Cambridge, the vastest in England, and Saint Bartholomew at Smithfield in London. French fairs of Champagne and Brie stand for the lands abroad. Trade fans get the rise, bloom, and fade of the fair in tales of booths, tolls, and crowds.
73677-the-plumed-serpent:
The Plumed Serpent is D H Lawrence's novel of Mexico, first published by William Heinemann of London in January 1926 and reprinted many times since. This thin-paper collected edition of his works places it among Sons and Lovers, The Rainbow, and Women in Love. The novel bears the name of the old Aztec god whose return some of its figures await.

The book opens on the Sunday after Easter, at the last bull-fight of the season in Mexico City, with four special bulls brought over from Spain. Chapters carry the party to a tea-party in Tlacolula, a fortieth birthday, and a move down the lake. Don Ramón and Doña Carlota take center place as the tale turns toward the Lords of the Day and Night and the coming of the first rain.
73692-with-my-regiment:
An officer writing only as Platoon Commander tells the first months of the Great War in With My Regiment: From the Aisne to La Bassee, from William Heinemann of London in 1915. The book is dedicated to Pat, who was killed in front of La Bassee on October 21, 1914. Contents chapters run from taking out a draft through early days on the Aisne.

An attack at dawn, a night attack, a farm in the firing-line, and a night patrol mark the advance. The tale opens in a seaside hotel lounge, where Mulligan dashes in: the narrator must take a draft of 180 men out that night.
7370-second-treatise-of-government:
John Locke's Second Treatise, published in 1689, is one of the founding texts of liberal political thought. Locke wrote against the claim that kings rule by divine right, answering Sir Robert Filmer's defense of absolute monarchy. In its place he sets out a theory of government built on the consent of the governed, written while England was settling its own revolution against a king.

Locke argues that people are naturally free and equal, holding rights to life, liberty, and property before any government exists. Rulers hold power only as a trust, to protect those rights, and a government that turns tyrannical may be resisted. The argument later shaped the American and French revolutions, and it still frames debates about rights, consent, and the limits of state power.
73738-john-brent:
Theodore Winthrop wrote a western novel first printed in 1861, here in a New York edition from Dodd, Mead. The narrator writes in the first person but swears he shall not maunder about himself. He is in no sense the hero of this drama, he says. Call me Chorus, if you will, is his bid to the reader.

Roughs and brutes, as well as gentlemen, take their places in the drama. None of the characters have scruples or qualms, he warns. They act by their own laws and are scourged or crowned as those laws suit nature's or not. Gerrian's ranch, Don Fulano, a Mormon caravan, a gallop of three, an idyl of the Rockies, and a lost trail fill the contents. Gold hunger heads the first chapter in Latin.
73807-address-of-president-mckinley-at-t:
A president honours a general in the Address of President McKinley at the Dedication of the Grant Monument, printed at Washington in 1897. The speech was given at New York on April 27, 1897. A plate of the monument attends the text.

Fellow citizens, he begins: a great life, dedicated to the welfare of the nation, here finds its earthly coronation. Even if this day lacked the impressiveness of ceremony and pageantry, it would still be memorable, he holds. It is the anniversary of the birth of one of the most famous and best beloved of American soldiers. Architecture has paid high tribute to the leaders of mankind, he says. But never was a memorial more worthily bestowed, or more gratefully accepted by a free people, than the beautiful structure before which we are gathered. Almost twelve years have passed since the brave spirit of Grant took its flight.
74064-the-grateful-elephant:
Eugene Watson Burlingame turned tales from the Pali tongue into English, and Yale brought out a set of them in 1923 with art by Dorothy Lathrop.
