Twenty six tales were picked from his larger book of Buddhist parables, printed the year before. A front picture shows an elephant lifting the Future Buddha with its trunk.

Burlingame says his rendering stays close to the Pali text, with a few hard words softened and a few lines left out. He states plainly that he did not write the tales down for child readers. A note at the front teaches how to say Pali names and long and short vowel sounds.
74162-the-recalcitrant:
Evelyn Goldstein wrote The Recalcitrant for Fantastic Universe in September 1954. An editor's note praises the story's tender, heartbreaking suspense. Its head verses ask why men seek one creature's destruction. The creature was proud of his strength and his home in a bee-loud glade.

Jim Simson watches his garden from behind closed curtains. A great honeybee works the azaleas, iris, and rhododendron outside. He and Amelia once tended that garden in all weathers. Those hours of planting are done now. On the road beyond the pines a helicar is coming for him. Within the hour, he thinks, they will take and destroy what he is. Losing Amelia forever is the thing he cannot bear. The tale turns on what Simson truly is.
7428-the-consumer-viewpoint:
Mildred Maddocks directed the Good Housekeeping Institute's department of household engineering, and this book reports what that department learned from years of testing household devices. It covers vital phases of manufacturing and selling. How is a device designed? How will it actually be used in a home? How can the maker guard against misuse it never foresaw?

The viewpoint of the title is the buyer's. Maddocks argues that designers and factory managers must think past known conditions of use to the care and skill real households bring. The book speaks to manufacturers and dealers, but its lessons still read clearly: test things as people will use them, not as engineers wish they would. It is an early classic of consumer research.
74445-the-eton-college-hunt:
A C Crossley wrote The Eton College Hunt, a short history of beagling at Eton. Spottiswoode, Ballantyne and Company issued the book, first in March nineteen hundred twenty two. J Robertson drew the pictures. T C Gouldsmith, master in nineteen hundred twenty one, faces the title page.

Crossley built the tale from school work breaks in one fall term. The pack had run for sixty four years when he wrote. Oppidan beagles and the college hunt join in one past here. Rowland Hunt and his heirs lead a key part. A gold age runs from eighteen hundred ninety nine to the war. Part two gives hare lore from old hands. Kennel care and pack craft close the school boy hunt book.
74664-a-brief-history-of-the-3rd-battali:
Printed at Aldershot in 1927, this brief history tells the story of the third battalion of the first Punjab Regiment. The battalion had borne many names, among them the 76th Punjabis and the 16th Madras Infantry. The book is dedicated to the comrades of all ranks who fell in the Great War.

The chapters carry battle honors as their titles: Sholinghur and the Carnatic, Mysore and Seringapatam, Ava and Burma. The regiment was formed in December 1776 under threat of invasion. Its Great War service runs through Egypt, the fighting around Kut, and the retreat to that town. Later chapters cover the third Afghan war, Palestine, and Waziristan. Lists of decorations, mentions, and casualties close the record.
74886-rena-s-experiment:
Rena's Experiment is a domestic novel by Mary Holmes. The Dillingham Company published it in New York in 1904. Holmes held the copyrights of 1901 and 1904. Twenty-three chapters carry the story. A frontispiece shows a figure standing breathless behind a man. The Burdicks and McPhersons fill out the cast.

The first chapter is called Nannie's Well. A farm woman in a sun-bonnet calls her daughter to set the table. Summer boarders are expected, and a letter has come. Charlotte Ann Parks ignores the call. She stands on a stone at the old well with a mirror in hand. She is trying a charm over the water. Later chapters bring Rena's letter, a dinner-party, and a trained nurse. A sick-room and a second experiment close the tale.
75011-all-quiet-on-the-western-front:
Erich Maria Remarque wrote All Quiet on the Western Front, translated from the German by Wheen and printed at London in 1929. The German original appeared that January; the English edition followed in March. Reprintings piled up until ninety thousand copies stood in print by June.

Remarque's preface says the book is neither accusation nor confession, and least of all an adventure. It tells of a generation destroyed by the war even when its men escaped the shells. Chapter one rests five miles behind the front, where eighty men remain of a company of one hundred and fifty. A quartermaster's error gives them double rations and smokes.
75316-the-fulfilment: An anonymous novel shows an odd front door. Its first pages give press praise for the author's earlier tale, Jewel Sowers. The Week's Survey, the Onlooker, and the Manchester Guardian praise that book. They call it a parable on selfishness. They also praise work done for its own sake. Its scene is a world named Lucifram, where things run opposite to Earth. For The Fulfilment itself, the head gives only the title. Its plot cannot be told from the pages shown here.
75401-ponies-past-and-present:
Sir Walter Gilbey surveys the native pony breeds of Britain in a book issued by Vinton and Company at London in 1900. A shooting pony, painted by A Cooper, fronts the volume.

Gilbey opens with the New Forest pony, then the Welsh. Exmoor and Dartmoor share a chapter. Cumberland and Westmoreland follow. Ireland gives the Connemara, and Scotland the Shetland. Uses and characteristics of the pony come next. Breeding polo ponies closes the book. His introduction notes the new attention to pony breeding, especially for polo. Britain holds large supplies of small, strong, sound horses, he argues. They could be turned to far more valuable account than they had been. The Polo Pony Society had set the example. Princess Victoria in her pony phaeton appears among the plates.
75413-the-private-journal-of-judge-advoc:
The Private Journal of Judge-Advocate Larpent is a war diary from the headquarters of Lord Wellington in the Peninsular War. Larpent served as the army's judge advocate from 1812 to the close of the war. His son, Sir George Larpent, edited the journal. The third edition came out in London from Richard Bentley in 1854. Letters at the front show the diarist's later life in the civil service. Robert Peel wrote to the Duke of Wellington about his health and his retirement from the Audit Board.

The journal itself gives the war from inside the staff tent. Courts martial, marches, sieges, and the talk of headquarters fill its days. Larpent saw the army's discipline and its justice at close hand. His post made him a hearer of every scandal and crime in camp. The book is a prime source for Wellington's last campaigns in Spain and France.
7549-quotes-and-images-from-the-short-st:
Guy de Maupassant's short stories fill thirteen volumes and number some 180 tales. They are the foundation of the modern short story, and this volume gathers quotations and images from them. The first volume alone contains Boule de Suif, Two Friends, The Lancer's Wife, The Prisoners, Father Milon, and Mademoiselle Fifi, with a study by Pol Neveux.

Later volumes add The Colonel's Ideas, Mother Sauvage, Madame Baptiste, and The Blind Man. They add the famous Piece of String, with The Model, My Uncle Jules, The Orphan, The Beggar, and The Parrot among the contents. Maupassant's world is Norman peasants, Paris clerks, soldiers, and lovers, all caught in a twist of fate. The quotation volume is a map to that world, story by story.
75523-the-achievements-of-luther-trant:
Edwin Balmer and William MacHarg wrote these detective stories of Luther Trant, published in 1910 with illustrations by William Oberhardt. The contents open, oddly, at chapter nine, The Eleventh Hour, before returning to the first case.

Chapter one, The Man in the Room, opens on a frosty campus walk. Young Trant, a psychologist with mismated eyes, rails at his professor: after five thousand years of civilization, police work still judges suspects by whether they flush or stammer. He cites the morning's carnival of arrests and the fact that most murderers are never punished. The psychological laboratory, he insists, can do better. Balmer and MacHarg build the detective story on the new science of measured emotion. Readers get an early laboratory sleuth.
75557-merely-the-patient:
Merely the Patient is a hospital memoir by Henry Howard Harper, published in New York in 1930. The book is dedicated to the eight doctors and nine nurses who made it possible. They helped, Harper says, not in writing it, but in making it. The contents run like a case chart with jokes in the margins. A Pain Discovers Me opens the tale. Running the Gantlet and The Cystoscopic Trap follow. The Shocking Discovery and The Calamitous Verdict stand in the mid run.

Harper's case was no common one. His convalescence itself became a disease, and a near fatal one. Blood poisoning set in after his operation. Skill and untiring care pulled him through, his preface witness says. The Road to Recovery is a chapter earned the hard way. The book is the patient's side of the chart, told with wit.
7560-quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-c:
Anthony Hamilton's Memoirs of Count Grammont paints the court of Charles II, and this companion volume gathers short passages and pictures from it. Notes by Sir Walter Scott frame the memoirs for later readers. Grammont, a witty exile at the Restoration court, stands at the center of the scenes. Each passage can be traced back to its full scene, so a striking line never has to stand alone.

Read together, the passages sketch a court ruled by wit, memory, and manners. Ambition, grudges, flattery, and the art of holding favor recur across them, often in a single sharp turn. The pictures add faces and dress to the talk. It works as a short cut into a famous memoir: lively, gossipy, and sharp about how people rose or fell by what they said.
75668-the-strange-career-of-the-chevalie:
Captain Telfer wrote this strange career of the Chevalier d'Eon de Beaumont. Longmans printed it in London in 1885 with portraits, facsimile. A 1782 painting shows La Chevalière d'Eon as frontispiece art. D'Eon served as French minister to Great Britain in 1763.

The preface treats Louis the Fifteenth secret correspondence of 1750. It began to serve Prince Conti ambition for the Polish crown. Secret help to smaller powers against Austria and Russia followed there. The king mistrusted his own ministers and worked round them secretly. His Crimea and Transcaucasia book stands named among the captain past works in front.
75837-house-property-its-management:
House Property and Its Management gathers papers on the methods of housing management begun by Octavia Hill and fitted to modern conditions. George Allen and Unwin published the book in London in 1921.

The papers hold up self-management by tenants as the ideal, while granting that it needs a real money stake by the tenants in the property. On Hill's lines, a trained manager collects the rents weekly, knows the tenants, and keeps the houses in repair. There must be no air of patronage in the work. The manager needs hard training in the law of rents and of landlord and tenant. She must also learn the faults that arise in houses and their cheapest cures. Above all she needs firmness joined with tact and sympathy. The papers note the poor showing of the state-aided housing schemes of the day.
75840-the-trail-of-the-serpent:
The Trail of the Serpent is a tale by the hand of a famed tale of a maid's dark deed. The host print is one of a set of that hand's tales in a gilt cloth form. That set is list at the front of the book. It runs to six and fifty tales in all. The tale of this book stands ninth in that roll. A verse from a bard stands past its name.

Poor race of men, said the kind ghost in that verse. Dear ye pay for your first fall. Some blooms of the first gar den ye still hold, the verse goes on. But the trail of the snake is past them all. The set list gives the span of the hand's work at a glance. Her most famed tale heads the roll.
75890-the-magic-lantern-and-its-manageme:
Hepworth, once a lecturer on science at the Royal Polytechnic Institution in London, wrote this handbook on the magic lantern, published in London in 1885. Its full title promises practical directions for producing the lime light, making oxygen gas, and preparing lantern slides. Hepworth says many people held back from the lantern because they feared it was hard to master.

His preface links the lantern to the new dry-plate photography of his day. A photograph, he argues, shows to best effect when thrown large by a lantern. The contents move from the history of the lantern to the lime-light itself, then to dissolving views, the old method and the new, and the working of the dissolving tap.
75897-a-new-dictionary-of-the-terms-anci:
A New Dictionary of the Canting Crew is a word book of street slang. Its maker signs with two initials and the tag of gentleman. The book came out in London from three shops in the city. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

The word lists cover gypsies, beggars, thieves, and cheats in their own speech. Proverbs, phrases, and sly turns of talk are bound in with the words. The preface gives a short tale of beggar life and its old roots. The maker says the book can guard the purse and life of a stranger. Fun and use are both claimed for the odd word hoard inside.
75928-self-and-self-management:
Self and Self Management belongs to the self help books of Arnold Bennett, whose works list fills the front pages here. His novels stand first in that list, from A Man from the North to The Roll Call. The Old Wives’ Tale and Clayhanger are among the famous titles. His short stories and fantasias fill columns of their own.

Bennett also wrote guides to living well on little, in plain English. How to Live on Twenty Four Hours a Day is the famed one. The Human Machine and Mental Efficiency stand in the same line. Self and Self Management treats the governing of one’s own habits and mind. Bennett argues that a man can train himself like a business. His counsel is brisk, practical, and free of cant.
75931-my-adventures-as-a-german-secret-a:
Captain Horst von der Goltz wrote My Adventures as a German Secret Agent, issued in New York by Robert M McBride and Company in nineteen seventeen. Von der Goltz had been a major in the Mexican Constitutional Army and an aide to Captain von Papen. A front photo shows the Bridgeman H Taylor passport he used. A quote from Shuster Strangling of Persia heads the book.

He gives the book and his hopes to the United States of Germany, whenever they may come to be. Chapter one opens with an old letter of scandal that drew him into the Kaiser service. Chapter two tells how he impersonated a Russian prince and stole a treaty. Later chapters treat plots in America, arrest, and prison tales. Spy readers get a confessed agent own account of German secret work.
76015-peppermint:
Alice Henkel describes Peppermint in a Department of Agriculture bulletin, Bureau of Plant Industry number 90, part three, issued December 28, 1905. Henkel assisted in drug plant investigations, and the Washington printing office issued the pamphlet. Three figures show runners, leaves, and a still.

Contents run from description and countries of growth through cultivation in the United States, harvesting, distillation, oil and menthol, exports, and prices. The text calls peppermint oil one of the most important essential oils made in America. Three mints are grown for it: the American mint, the black mint, and the white mint, the last two varieties of the first. The plant spreads by long running roots, with square stems one to three feet high and purplish flowers in dense spikes.
76298-the-history-of-the-psychoanalytic-:
Sigmund Freud wrote The History of the Psychoanalytic Movement, in an approved English translation by Brill, printed at New York in 1917 as a nervous and mental disease monograph. The series list shows Jung's dementia praecox psychology, Bleuler on schizophrenic negativism, Kraepelin on general paresis, and Abraham on dreams and myths in the same series.

Freud tells how the movement grew from his own practice into a school with allies in many lands, and some who broke away. Brill lectured on psychoanalysis at New York University and had led the Columbia psychiatry clinic. Jelliffe and White edited the series for American doctors of the mind. Historians get Freud's own one-sided history.
77102-war-paint:
Robert Winchester wrote War Paint, a tale of sudden love and battle on the Texas border. The magazine blurb praises the author of My Deputy and No Flyer Ever Lost. Two lean Texas rangers watch a girl drive into Wirton in a high powered roadster.

Sam Earp wishes his mother could see this new kind of girl, powdering her nose at the curb. The girl, Elaine Norcross Webb of New York, hears every word. She walks straight up to Sam and Bud Yancey and asks when the rest of the circus comes to town. The rangers take up her gibe with grave good humor, and the sparring starts the tale.
77175-the-man-elephant:
The Man Elephant, a book of African fairy tales in the Altemus series, was edited by Hartwell James, who also wrote the introduction. Henry Altemus of Philadelphia published it with forty pictures by John Neill. Five tales make the set, and the title tale comes first.

Parle, a pretty girl living with her family in a hut by an African river, deserved a better husband than the Man Elephant, the editor warns. A spell of Ramil's, happily recalled, clears the trouble up. The other tales bring a master weaver, a flying lion with a secret in his wings, a King Mungo, and an Uncle Lion. Frogs, spiders, and hunters crowd the pages between.
77691-the-natural-history-of-aleppo-and-:
Alexander Russell, a doctor, wrote the natural history of Aleppo and parts near it. A Millar printed the work in London in the Roman year MDCCLVI. The book is given to Alexander Drummond, consul, and the British factory at Aleppo. Plates show dress, homes, birds, fishes, and plants of the place.

Russell first meant to treat the plague, which raged three years in his stay. Wide practice among all ranks taught him the people's manners and ways. Climate, crops, and disease fill the work with exact, first-hand fact. Students gain a classic early survey of a great Levant city and its life.
77797-ambulancing-on-the-french-front:
Edward Coyle wrote this account of ambulance work on the French front, printed in New York in 1918. A picture note calls him one of the first Americans to serve as an ambulance man there. He gives the book to his mother, whose parting gift and prayer open the volume. The first chapter tells how he came to go.

In his preface Coyle says friends at home pressed him for news of the great war. He makes no claim to be a writer, but says he knows what he saw. His aim is to give facts from the firing line, since rumour had passed for fact in America. Matters that might aid the foe are held back for later historians.
7782-the-last-tournament:
Alfred Tennyson's The Last Tournament, in the author's edition, sits between Pelleas and Guinevere in the Idylls of the King. It opens with Dagonet the fool, made mock-knight by Gawain, dancing like a withered leaf before the hall at Camelot, high above yellowing woods.

Tristram enters with harp in hand and a ruby carcanet, prize of yesterday's jousts, and asks why the fool skips so. Behind the jest lies a darker tale: Arthur and Lancelot once rescued a babe from an eagle's nest, and gave her to a queen who took her coldly. The poem marks Camelot's late decline.
78282-the-mordant:
Merab Eberle wrote The Mordant, a short tale of science fiction with pictures by Morey. An opening note asks what would follow if a man of science found how to keep life and youth without end. Such a gift, the note warns, may not be a boon.

MacDowell seeks the mordant in his quiet labs in the Black Hills. A mordant, in dye work, fixes colour fast; his find would fix the body against decay. He does not seek fame as a keeper of the dead. He wants to see what endless youth does to those who get it. The tale tests that wish.
78334-the-great-sea-serpent:
Oudemans, a Dutch doctor of zoology and head of the zoo at The Hague, wrote a full treatise on the great sea serpent, printed by his own hand in 1892. Eighty two art cuts back the text. He gathered the reports of 187 sightings, plus an added list, and set them in time order for close study.

For each report he weighs the word of ship men, men of science, and plain folk, and sorts true signs from false. He begs sailors with cameras to snap the beast, since a photo would sway men of science as no sketch can. He also tells how to kill and keep a specimen, with harpoons and strong gear, should one be met.
78371-the-knitting-teacher-s-assistant:
The Knitting Teacher's Assistant is a school handbook for the teaching of knitting. The book was designed for use in national girls' schools of its day. Hatchards of Piccadilly put out this new edition in the year 1881. It sold for sixpence and had reached its fifty-third thousand by then. The editor had writ whole series of lady's craft books before this.

Her preface notes the little work had held its place fifty years. That long life proved it answered a general want, she argues. A scale of measurements for finer wool and pins stands added here. Questions and answers carry the teaching through the small book's pages. Teachers often fail to put plain knitting steps into clear words. This assistant pairs those answers with practice at the needles themselves. Pins number fourteen and Berlin fingering wool suit the patterns given.
78524-jay-bird-s-judgement:
A western story by W C Tuttle, told in cowboy dialect. Chuck Warner opens it nursing a bruised hip. His bucking bronco scattered the Cross J mail through the sagebrush. He limps about gathering catalogues he calls Shepherd's Bibles. One letter, badly sealed, tempts his conscience conveniently. Reading it becomes, in his mind, a duty of resealing.

At the Paradise post office, talk turns to the ranch's cook problem. Old Jay Bird Whittaker cooks for the outfit himself. The men's stomachs suffer in the sere and yellow leaf, Chuck mourns. A wife for the old man is the joking prescription. Tuttle wrote hundreds of such tales for the western pulps. Hashknife Hartley was his best-known hero, but ranch humour fills this piece.
78540-a-visit-to-the-elephant:
A Visit to the Elephant was printed at London in 1825 by Baldwin, Cradock, and Joy, among others. Its author is named only as the author of Samboe and Twilight Hours Improved. A verse from the Psalms heads the title page: O Lord, how manifold are thy works.

Chapter one praises faithful servants as a link in the chain of family charities. On an autumn morning, the servant Alan brings his master, Elmer, a paper telling of wild beasts arrived at the next town. Alan hopes the children, Harry, Joanna, and little Ellen, may see the elephant. He recalls a fine beast at Calcutta, as sensible as any Christian.
78560-the-illustrated-horse-management:
The Illustrated Horse Management is a work on the care of steeds by Edward Mayhew. He was a heal man of steeds of rank, and the hand of a past steed cure book. More than four mint plates stand in this book, from first draws made for it a lone. Its full bill names its whole field. It was put out in eighteen sixty four at a great east town.

That bill names marks on the frame of the steed and on its cures. It names the shoe craft, the teeth, the food, and the vices of stets. It names the stables them selves as a theme. Past that it gives a plain count of the place, cast, and worth of the points of a steed. It treats grooms, deal men, breed men, break men, and train men as well.
78660-knight-errant:
Edna Lyall wrote this novel, printed by W L Allison of New York. Lyall had written Donovan, We Two, and In the Golden Days. She gives the book to Evangeline Jameson, with lines saying her heart holds only love and love's good-will for her. The happiest man in Naples opens the tale, crying his joy to Signor Pietro in the street and dragging his friend Enrico into the cheer.

A goodly heritage, Francesca, and a cloudless betrothal follow, then a threatening sky and a storm. Piale schemes, an olive garden, and a pilgrim fill the middle. Chapters move to the stage, to England, to Genoa, and to yachting, across thirty-nine chapters in all. A final choice and the words all goeth but God's will close the list.
78682-the-lily-of-mordaunt: The Lily of Mordaunt by Georgie Sheldon appears as number 222 of the Eagle Series, Street and Smith's ten cent novels from New York. Almost the whole text shown here is the series list itself, running from number 224 down past 176. Neighbours include Leola Dale's Fortune by Charles Garvice and Wedded Yet No Wife by May Agnes Fleming. Sheldon's own Geoffrey's Victory also appears. No chapter of the Mordaunt story itself is shown, so this entry rests on cover and catalogue evidence alone.
78725-incident:
Thomas J O'Hara wrote Incident, a prize-winning tale from a writers' workshop at the College of the City of New York. The tale ran in Fantastic Universe, in the May issue. A star-ship drifts like a floating coffin, with one man left alive. A plague took the crew one by one, with no warning of its coming.

The captain died first, after fever, sores, and a brief mindless spell. The second mate simply did not wake one morning. The engineer fell into the fission chambers and dissolved into glowing atoms in space. A fourth man killed himself before the sickness took him. Six men had set out in a sealed ship through endless night, toward a goal beyond charted stars.
78741-the-royal-mint:
The Royal Mint: Its Working, Conduct, and Operations, by George Frederick Ansell, was published in London in eighteen seventy-one by Effingham Wilson. This is the third edition, re-written, enlarged, and revised. Ansell was an analytical chemist, late of the Royal Mint, and formerly of the Royal College of Chemistry. Engravings illustrate his account.

An appendix prints his letter to Lord Kinnaird about his own case. Kinnaird's reply, dated March first, eighteen seventy-one, opens the front matter. It describes a malicious Treasury report that ruined Ansell's prospects in the Mint. Gladstone and the Chancellor of the Exchequer enter the correspondence. The book is thus two things at once: a practical guide to coinage and a wronged official's public defense. Few mint manuals carry a grievance so openly.
78776-the-monster-of-grammont:
The Monster of Grammont, by George Goodchild, was published by the Mystery League at New York in 1930, in a first edition. The contents promise ghosts, a delay, the monster itself, and a detective named Fouchard.

A crimson trail, a second victim, conspirators, and a night of terror follow. Chapter one puts a bronzed driver at the wheel of a Bentley on a white Route Nationale in France, the speedometer wavering between the sixties and seventies. His companion fights a large-scale road map while Wallace, named in later chapters, heads for escapes and a little luck.
78813-doctor-and-patient:
Francis Weld Peabody, a Harvard professor of medicine, left papers that Macmillan published in 1930. He had died in 1927. Three of the papers had already run in print. The Care of the Patient comes from a journal of the American medical body.

The papers treat the bond between the doctor and the sick man. The public and the general practitioner opens the set. A life list at the back gives Peabody's posts: intern in 1907, work in Berlin and Baltimore, service in China and in the war, and the Harvard chair from 1921. The papers plead that the sick man is a person first, and a case only after.
78852-the-undercurrent:
Fay Ehlert wrote this one act play, The Undercurrent, for the stage. Samuel French issued it in New York and London in 1929. The play first ran in The Drama Magazine, copyright 1928. A caution warns the play is fully copyright protected everywhere.

Royalty is owed for stage, radio, reading, and film use alike. Amateurs may use it in restricted territory only, French notes. Ehlert gives the play to Singer and Piazza with appreciation. Through them it found its way to the professional stage, it says. A press notice credits her with rekindling interest in the short play form itself.
78912-the-agent:
Milton Lesser, writing as Stephen Marlowe, told this tale of a broken crooner and a strange offer. Its tag sings the old line: there's no business like show business. One-night stands in one-horse towns, flea-bitten rooms, and sandwiches three times a day fill the singer's life.

All the while his eyes stay on a dream that keeps slipping over the horizon. Then the bookings end, and the dream looks lost for good. A dark little man steps in with a promise: he will make the singer a star without looking at him twice. Too good to be true, the blurb warns; it sounds out of this world. The singer himself admits he was no great crooner, but he could sing. Vera, an old stage hand, brings the first thread of hope.
78922-is-man-a-free-agent:
Santanelli wrote a book that asks if man is a free agent at all. The book came out in Lansing, Michigan, in 1902. Its main theme is the law of suggestion. Hypnosis sits at its core, with mind and heredity round it. A photo of Santanelli fronts the book.

He sets out what hypnosis is, why it works, and how to bring it on. Thought passed from mind to mind is his key tool. He ties it to law in nature as a whole. A front tale tells of his own ups and downs in life. Stage and cure crowds of that age read such books with zeal.
78964-lazy-robert-or-the-colonel-s-serva:
Lazy Robert, or The Colonel's Servant, is a children's story by Aunt Hattie, the pen name of Madeline Leslie. Young printed it at Boston, entered in 1871, as the third volume of the Happy Home Stories for boys. A text from Paul heads it: if any would not work, neither should he eat.

Chapter one opens on another failure. Robert's aunt, marking his lesson in a small blank book, asks sorrowfully what he was doing all the study time. The butcher's dog came, Robert explains, and tried to fight his own dog Major, and Major followed him into the house for a frolic in the library. The contents promise a pattern reform story: Robert's lesson, his deceit, his confession, his spelling, his letter, a runaway chapter, his mother, and at last his death.
8081-louisa-pallant:
Henry James set this short novel at Homburg, opening on the terrace of the Kursaal on a beautiful night toward the end of July. The narrator, waiting for his young nephew, meets Louisa Pallant, a woman he thought he knew completely, and receives a revelation about her character that startles and touches him. The story that follows revisits old acquaintance, a mother's hopes, and a young man's summer in Europe.

James's interest is in what people hide, even from friends of years, and how one confession can recast a whole past. The tale is brief and elegantly told, with the spa town as its stage. It is a fine small example of James's art of nuance, and a good starting point for readers new to his shorter fiction.
8095-awful-disclosures-of-the-hotel-dieu:
Maria Monk's Awful Disclosures, with a continuation of her narrative after her escape from the Hotel Dieu nunnery of Montreal, became one of the best-selling books of the nineteenth century. Monk claimed to expose secret crimes inside the convent, and her story fed fierce anti-Catholic feeling in America. A transcriber's note warns that some page scans were illegible, and that chapter fourteen was missing from both contents and book, presumably a printing error.

The book's claims were widely disputed at the time and later discredited, yet it remains historically important as propaganda. It shows how a sensational tale could move public opinion and sell by the hundred thousand. Readers should approach it as a document of prejudice and popular print, not as reliable history of convent life.
8150-a-street-of-paris-and-its-inhabitan:
Honoré de Balzac wrote this little Parisian silhouette in prose to open a new series of the Comédie Humaine, while the first series was still finishing. Translated by Henri Pene du Bois and illustrated by François Courboin, it appeared in a limited New York edition of 1900, with four hundred copies printed. Its subject is a single Paris street and the man who inhabits it, observed with Balzac's usual intensity.

The preface notes that Balzac was never tired, and that tired men are those who rest and try to work afterwards. The sketch shows his method in miniature: a place and a person, rendered until they stand for a whole social world. For Balzac readers, it is a small but revealing fragment, and a doorway into his vast human comedy.
8384-pauline-s-passion-and-punishment:
Louisa May Alcott wrote this sensation tale before Little Women made her famous, and it shows a very different Alcott. Pauline, a beautiful woman, paces her room in a storm of feeling in the opening chapter. The story that follows is one of passion, revenge, and punishment, in the lurid style of the story papers where Alcott first published such tales.

The novella belongs to Alcott's secret career as a writer of thrillers, signed with pseudonyms and kept quiet once she became a children's author. Readers meet a heroine who acts on desire and pays for it, in prose far hotter than March family life. It is short, intense, and a useful corrective to the image of Alcott as only a domestic novelist.
8455-the-saint:
Antonio Fogazzaro's novel The Saint reached English readers under a cloud, since the Congregation of the Index had condemned it. The publishers of the authorized translation explain, in justice to the author, Senator Fogazzaro, that he had made plain in letters his own position. The novel itself follows a saintly reformer seeking renewal within the Catholic Church.

Fogazzaro, Italy's leading Catholic novelist, wrote of faith and modern thought in tension, and the condemnation made the book famous. Readers get a religious novel of conscience, where holiness collides with authority. The Saint remains a key text for understanding Catholic modernism, and the price its writers paid.
8465-the-russian-revolution-the-jugo-sla:
This volume pairs two studies dated March 18, 1918: Russian Revolution, by Alexander Petrunkevitch, Samuel Northrup, Harper Frank, and Alfred Golder, and The Jugo-Slav Movement, by Robert Joseph Kerner. Petrunkevitch opens with the role of intellectuals in Russia's liberating movement, citing a November interview from Petrograd in the New York Times.

The book captures the revolutions as contemporaries saw them, while outcomes were still unknown. Readers get wartime scholarship on Russia's upheaval and the South Slavs' bid for unity, written before the Soviet state hardened. It is a primary source for how Americans in 1918 understood events that would shape the century.
8508-the-evolution-of-man-scientifically:
Reverend William A Williams argues, in fifty arguments, that the evolution of man is scientifically disproved. He designed the book as an up-to-date textbook, a companion to other textbooks on evolution, and an antidote to books in libraries teaching evolution, infidelity, and atheism. He also aimed it as an aid to students, parents, teachers, ministers, lawyers, doctors, and all other lovers of the truth.

Williams's book belongs to the 1920s anti-evolution movement, and it states its case as science, though modern science rejects it. Readers interested in the Scopes era and the history of creationism will find a clear, period example of the argument. It should be read as a document of its controversy, not as current science.
8566-the-origin-and-permanent-value-of-t:
Charles Foster Kent, Woolsey Professor of Biblical Literature at Yale, wrote The Origin and Permanent Value of the Old Testament. It opens with the motto that ye shall know the truth and the truth shall make you free. Contents move from the eclipse and rediscovery of the Old Testament, through its real nature and purpose, to the earliest chapters in its history.

Kent, a pioneer of modern biblical study in America, argues that the Old Testament's value lies not in literal history but in its religious and moral growth. Readers get early twentieth-century liberal scholarship, clear and confident, aimed at general readers and students. The book suits anyone tracing how biblical criticism reached American churches.
9156-life-and-remains-of-john-clare-the-:
J. L. Cherry edited this life and remains of John Clare, the Northamptonshire peasant poet. The volume gathers letters from friends, extracts from Clare's diary, prose fragments, and old ballads Clare himself collected. Illustrations by Birket Foster grace the book. A dedication note recalls Clare's wish from 1825.

In that year Clare feared a speedy entrance into the dark porch of eternity, yet he lived on. Cherry's book preserves the voice of a farm laborer turned poet, tender and close to nature. It remains the key source for Clare's life and for the songs of his county.
9193-the-angel-of-lonesome-hill-a-story-:
Frederick Landis wrote this tale of a remote country place, subtitled a story of a president, in 1910. A handful of simple folk live without a railroad, served only by a stage that creeps through gullies and runs late. Children come, young folk marry, old ones die, and Indian Creek floods the bottom land.

Years pass in slow rhythm, streaked now and then by tragedy, until a lamp by night guides passers-by. The president of the title links this small world to the nation. Landis writes with tender humor about a place time nearly forgot.
9502-the-room-in-the-dragon-volant:
J. Sheridan LeFanu, master of the Victorian ghost tale, wrote The Room in the Dragon Volant, a novella of mystery and dread. A prologue presents a curious case, told with pointed care, of a traveller caught in a strange French inn. LeFanu, famed for Carmilla and Uncle Silas, builds fear from hints, not shocks. The Dragon Volant, a coaching inn, hides the tale's dark heart.

The hero faces a room, a plot, and a fate that blend love and death in one snare. Monsieur Droqville and other shadowy figures deepen the trap. A reader gets a taut, eerie tale of suspense, where old France, romance, and horror meet in LeFanu's best manner.
9836-the-pawns-count:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote The Pawns Count in 1918, a wartime spy tale of London restaurants and warnings. Pamela Van Teyl, a beautiful American girl in high fashion, points her friends to a wall notice: beware, be silent, enemy ears listen. Captain Richard Holderness, fresh from France, calls such warnings rot, familiar from every station and inn. John Lute and others join the lunch crowd.

Oppenheim follows pawns and players through wartime London, where talk itself is a weapon. His prose favors brisk, fashionable suspense. A reader gets a lively Great War spy novel, where a lunch-hour notice opens a game of secrets.
a-backward-glance-at-eighty-recollection: Charles Albert Murdock looks back on eighty years of life in this memoir. He recalls New England, a hidden harbor, nine years in the north, and San Francisco in the sixties. Later chapters cover public service, business ventures, people he knew, outings, and occasional verse. The writer also recalls Bret Harte and the changing city around him, in a warm personal record of a long life lived across two coasts.
a-fair-penitent:
Wilkie Collins's story first appeared in Dickens's magazine Household Words on July 18, 1857, as the note before the text explains, and was published anonymously like everything in that magazine. The tale opens among the papers of Charles Pineau Duclos, the French writer who succeeded Voltaire as historiographer of France. Two manuscripts found after his death hold the story.

From those papers comes the history of a woman of beauty and a ruined past, and of the men who judge, forgive, or pursue her. Collins uses the found-manuscript frame to give his melodrama a grave, old-world air. The short piece shows his early skill at sympathy for a fallen heroine.
a-first-year-in-canterbury-settlement:
Samuel Butler records his first year as a sheep farmer in the Canterbury settlement of New Zealand. A young Englishman with capital and more wit than experience, he ships out to the young colony and takes up a run in the high country. Ten chapters follow the voyage, the land, and the learning of a trade he had never practiced.

Butler writes about fellow settlers, shepherds, swaggers, and the price of wool with the dry observation that later made Erewhon. The letters home on which the book rests are frank about loneliness, weather, and money. It is both a settler's handbook in disguise and the first showing of a singular literary mind.
a-lover-s-complaint:
William Shakespeare's narrative poem opens on a hillside, where the speaker hears a sad tale echoed from a nearby valley. Below sits a young woman, pale and furious, tearing papers and breaking rings at her sides. She tells how a charming young man won her love with tears, gifts, and fine words, then left her.

In stanza after stanza she recalls his beauty, his practiced sorrow, and the tokens he gave her, some of them won from other women before her. She knows he is false and knows his tricks. Yet her confession ends in a hard admission: his falsehood still has power over her heart.
a-mere-accident: George Moore tells of a mere accident in a Sussex setting. The novel opens on three hundred yards of smooth white road leading from Henfield, with lush grasses and tall hedges. Restless boys, quiet nursemaids, and a vagrant fill the scene. Moore writes of country life and the accidents that change it.
a-street-of-paris-and-its-inhabitant: Honore de Balzac sketches a street of Paris and its inhabitant in this little prose silhouette, translated by Henri Pene du Bois and illustrated by Francois Courboin. The preface explains that Balzac wrote it to open a new run of the Comedie Humaine. He then retouched it for Hetzel's Le Diable a Paris, which did not use it. The Meyer edition of 1900 printed four hundred copies, twenty-five on Japan paper.
action-front: Boyd Cable writes Action Front, published in 1916 and dedicated to Spender of the Westminster Gazette in recognition of hospitality. The contents run from In Enemy Hands and A Benevolent Neutral through Drill and a Night Patrol. As Others See It, The Fear of Fear, and Anti-Aircraft follow. A Fragment, An Open Town, Signalers, Conscript Courage, and A Smashing Counter-Attack close with A General Action at Last, opening on Private Jock Macalister in a German trench.
adventures-in-contentment: David Grayson writes about leaving city strain behind to rent, and then own, a small farm, where daily work brings a calmer and fuller life. Chapters on buying the farm, the joy of possession, and neighbours met along the road show how simple pleasures can replace hurry and ambition. The book reads as a quiet argument that contentment grows from useful work, close ties, and attention to the land.
an-outline-of-the-history-of-christian-t: Edward Caldwell Moore outlines the history of Christian thought since Kant, as Parkman Professor of Theology at Harvard, published by Scribner's in New York. The survey follows theology through idealism, criticism, and modern doubt, with Harnack among its guides. Moore's outline remains a clear map of two centuries of Christian thinking.
appendicitis-the-etiology-hygenic-and-di:
John H. Tilden, an American physician, argues in this medical book that appendicitis grows out of daily habits rather than sudden chance. Tilden blames overeating, rich mixed meals, and chronic constipation for poisoning the bowels. He calls the resulting state constitutional catarrh, meaning a body-wide irritation kept up by bad living. In his view the inflamed appendix is one local sign of that wider disorder.

Early chapters trace how fermentation, gas, and sluggish bowels strain the caecum, the pouch where the appendix opens. Tilden then sets out hygienic and dietetic treatment, meaning care through cleanliness, rest, and food rather than drugs. He discusses enemas, fasting, and simple meals as ways to calm the bowel. Readers meet an early challenge to routine surgery, built on the claim that removing causes matters more than removing organs.
army-life-in-a-black-regiment:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson records the First South Carolina Volunteers. His first chapter states their claim plainly. They were the first slave regiment mustered into the service of the United States in the Civil War. Originally published in 1869 and reprinted in 1900, as the title page notes, the book rests on his camp diary as their colonel.

Thirteen chapters follow expeditions up the St. Mary's, St. John's, and Edisto rivers, nights on picket, and life at Camp Shaw. A chapter collects the Negro spirituals his men sang, with their words. Appendices give the roster of officers, the struggle for equal pay, and his farewell address. Higginson writes with respect that his soldiers earned, and the book honors them.
arthour-and-merlin-kolbing-1890-fragment:
Arthour and Merlin is a Middle English romance kept in the Auchinleck manuscript, a famous book made in London around 1330. E. Kölbing edited the text in 1890. The romance survives incomplete, and this edition says so plainly on its face.

The tale tells how Arthur came to the throne as a boy and how Merlin guided him. Wizards, battles, and court intrigue fill its pages. Then the text breaks off, and the rest is lost for good. Even as a fragment, it shows how England first pictured its greatest king and the wise man at his side.
astoria-or-anecdotes-of-an-enterprise-be:
Washington Irving wrote Astoria from his acquaintance with the Montreal partners of the North West Company, whose open-house tables supplied the tales of traders from the interior. His subject is John Jacob Astor's Pacific Fur Company and its post at the Columbia's mouth. Overland and sea expeditions set out in 1810 to found it.

Birch-bark camps, ceremonial audiences with governors, and brisk traffic after speeches fill the narrative's documentary middle. The overland party shapes its course by the three snowy Tetons, landmarks of the Columbia. Irving never went west himself, yet his research and style made Astoria the standard popular account of Astor's failed empire and a founding text of Western Americana.
awful-disclosures-of-the-hotel-dieu-nunn:
Maria Monk published this narrative as an exposé of the Hotel Dieu nunnery in Montreal, adding a continuation with incidents never before printed. Her preface says the volume also tells what followed her escape, including a return to Montreal to demand a legal investigation of her charges. She claims to answer all testimony published against her.

Chapters describe convent discipline, secret passages, and crimes she lays on priests and nuns. One night scene leaves her sleepless in a safe house, begging an escort to the steamboat for fear of being seized and carried back. The book became a bestseller of anti-Catholic sensation writing. Investigations at the time found no proof for its tales, and it stands now as a famous literary hoax that still shows the prejudices of its market.
bardelys-the-magnificent:
Rafael Sabatini published this swashbuckling romance in 1905; the hosted copy is the Barnes and Noble edition of 2011. Marcel de Saint-Pol, Marquis de Bardelys, wagers at the court of Louis XIII that he can woo and win Roxane de Lavédan within a set time. The king's wishes, a portrait, and a maid seen in moonlight launch the strange wooing in Languedoc, in the year of the rebellion.

Wounded and sheltered by his enemies, Bardelys lives under the name of René de Lesperon, a dead rebel, and the borrowed identity nearly hangs him. A tribunal at Toulouse, an eleventh-hour rescue, and duels with Saint-Eustache's party fill the middle. One defiance shows his manner: whoever affronts him, be he the king's commissioner himself, renders satisfaction. Sabatini's first great success still runs on honour, disguise, and swordplay.
bart-stirling-s-road-to-success-or-the-y:
Allen Chapman wrote this boys' novel for Cupples and Leon of New York in 1908, in the Boys' Pocket Library at thirty-five cents a volume. Bart Stirling works as a young express agent, and the frontispiece shows him with a rope looped deftly about his arms. Trouble begins with express matter gone astray and customers ready to blame the boy.

A missing trunk drives the crisis. A formidable lady tells Darry that Bart got rid of it to spite her, after her trouble with his mother, and threatens arrest if it does not show up today. Bart shrugs, but he is consciously uneasy beneath the official dignity. Chapman keeps the series formula brisk: a plucky agent, false suspicion, crooks in the freight business, and success earned by nerve and honesty.
britannica-1911-abandonment:
Abandonment receives a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word names the giving up of an interest, claim, right, or possession, and its force shifts with the branch of law in play. French abandonnement and Low Latin bandum, a decree, stand behind the term.

Suits can be abandoned, though the Judicature Act of 1875 narrowed the right to start fresh. Marine insurance takes the word for handing a wrecked ship or cargo to the insurers after a total loss in effect. Domicile, easements, and railways each hold their own sense of the act. Wife and child cases point onward to Desertion. The entry works as a signpost, sorting one word's many legal lives for lay readers.
britannica-1911-abatement:
Abatement receives a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word, from French abattre, to beat down, names a lessening or doing away with a thing. Law takes it up in a row of set phrases, each with its own rules.

Nuisance abatement lets the injured party remove the harm without breach of the peace. Freehold abatement names a stranger's entry on lands before the heir can enter. Debts and legacies abate in share when an estate falls short, and suits once abated on a plea to form alone, now struck out by rule. False lights at sea and customs deductions close the list. Heraldry adds a badge of disgrace to the same word.
britannica-1911-acaulescent: Acaulescent is a botanical term for a plant that appears to have no stem. This short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica builds the word from Latin parts: a, meaning not, and caulis, a stem, giving becoming stemless. The dandelion serves as the familiar example. Its stem is not truly absent but almost suppressed, so the leaves and flower seem to rise straight from the ground. Gardeners and botanists use the term to describe that growth habit precisely, without claiming the stem is missing altogether.
britannica-1911-accent:
Accent begins as the Latin accentus, itself a translation of a Greek word used by early grammarians for the musical pitch of their language. The long 1911 Britannica entry warns that the word is used in two contrasted senses. Pitch accent marks differences in musical tone between sounds, while stress accent marks the greater breath energy thrown onto one syllable of a word.

Languages divide the two very differently. Sanskrit and Greek marked chief pitch accent with signs, and no language long keeps pitch and stress in a fixed relation. Foreign or vulgar accent, the everyday sense, mixes both with other habits of pronunciation. Authorities such as Sievers and Jespersen anchor a technical survey meant for serious students of phonetics.
britannica-1911-accident:
Accident, from a Latin word meaning to happen, usually means something unexpected. It is a happening out of the ordinary course of things. Law narrows that loose sense in several ways. In the law of tort, an accident is due neither to design nor to negligence. In criminal law, an effect is accidental when it was not intended. It must also not be so probable that a prudent person should have guarded against it.

Logic uses the word quite differently. An accident there is a quality that belongs to a subject. Yet it is not part of that subject's essence. A triangle's area is such a quality. Its angle sum, by contrast, follows from its nature. Growing knowledge can move a quality from one class to the other.
britannica-1911-accompaniment:
Accompaniment is the musical term for the part added to support and heighten a main vocal or instrumental line, whether supplied by other voices, single instruments, or a full orchestra. An accompaniment may be obbligato, an essential part of the work, or ad libitum, optional. The same word obbligato also names an independent instrumental solo woven around a vocal piece.

History explains much of the entry. Early composers wrote accompaniments in outline as figured bass, leaving performers to fill them in, so later musicians wrote additional accompaniments for Handel and Bach. In song, the accompaniment grew from a few vamped chords into an art of its own, sometimes rivalling the voice itself as a partner in a duet.
britannica-1911-account:
Account means counting or reckoning, especially of money paid and received, and hence a statement of such payments, or any narrative report of events. The 1911 Britannica entry follows the word onto the stock exchange, where it carries several technical senses. Chief among them is the periodical settlement at which speculative bargains are squared.

Settlement took three or four days. On contango day, buyers and sellers arranged to carry commitments over. On ticket day, the name of the ultimate buyer passed through intermediaries so stock could transfer directly. On account day, cheques settled the differences. The word also names the period between settlements, and the mass of open commitments in a stock, a bull account or a bear account.
britannica-1911-accoutrement:
Accoutrement is a French word for clothing or apparel, probably drawn from an old term for the keeper of church vestments. The 1911 Britannica entry is short, and its point is a narrowing of meaning. In general use the word can cover dress of any kind, but its settled use is narrower and usually plural.

Soldiers own the word now. Accoutrements are the military equipment of a soldier other than his arms and his clothing: the belts, pouches, packs, and kit he carries into service. Readers who meet the term in military writing should picture that carried equipment, the gear that completes a soldier's outfit without being either weapon or uniform.
britannica-1911-acknowledgment:
Acknowledgment is an admission that something was given or done. Law uses the term in several connexions. A debtor may acknowledge a debt in writing. His signed writing can revive that debt. Time would otherwise bar the claim under the limitation statutes. A testator may sign a will away from witnesses. He may later acknowledge the signature before two of them.

Married women's deeds get stern treatment. A wife conveying land faced a special rule. The land must not be her separate estate. She had to acknowledge the deed before a judge. A commissioner could also take the acknowledgment. He first examined her apart from her husband. He made sure she consented freely. In the United States, the word names an officer's certificate. It states that a deed was acknowledged before him.
britannica-1911-act-of-parliament:
Act of Parliament is a declaration of the legislature. It enforces rules of conduct on the people. It may also define rights and grant or withhold them. Together, such declarations form the statute-book. That book holds the written law of the British nation. The entry dates its clear opening to the thirteenth century. Parliamentary records grow distinct under Edward I. A valid act must express the whole legislature's will. King, Lords, and Commons must concur in it.

Forms developed slowly, the entry shows. Bills took the shape of finished acts under Henry VI. The enacting clause reached general use under Charles II. Lord Coke called the preamble a key to a statute's meaning. Acts were long cited as chapters of a session's statute. Short titles later made citation simpler for lawyers.
britannica-1911-adamant:
Adamant is the modern diamond, in old usage. The word comes from a Greek term meaning untameable. It also named any very hard substance. Homer uses the Greek word as a personal epithet. Hesiod applies it to hard metal in armour. Theophrastus applies it to the hardest crystal. Confusion with a Latin verb shifted its sense. Adamare means to have an attraction for something. That likeness tied adamant to the loadstone.

Diamonds displaced the term in ordinary use. Adamant survives only figuratively and poetically now. An adamant resolve borrows the stone's hardness. Poetry keeps the word for unyielding things. The entry traces a full circle of meaning. A word for the hardest matter became pure metaphor.
britannica-1911-adjutant:
Adjutant is an army article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an officer who aids a commander. The word comes from a Latin verb meaning to aid. In the British army the post is held by a captain or a lieutenant.

The article sets out the work of the post in detail. The adjutant serves as staff officer to the head of the corps. He passes on that officer's orders to the men. He runs the orderly room and the daily affairs of the unit. He also takes charge of musket training and the drilling of recruits. In the forces of the continent the term runs wider. There it takes in staff officers of the higher units as well. The piece ends with a note that a bird bears the name too.
britannica-1911-advent:
Advent is the holy season with which the Christian church year begins, kept as a time of preparation for Christmas. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article traces the season from its first clear mention at the Synod of Lerida in 524. In the Eastern church it runs from Saint Martin's Day on the 11th of November. Elsewhere it starts on the Sunday nearest Saint Andrew's Day and ends at Christmas.

Lessons for the four Sundays turn minds first to Christ coming as Saviour, then to his return as Judge. The season was once kept with fasting as strict as Lent, and Rome still treats it as a time of penitence with purple vestments and no dancing. The article closes with folk customs, such as English women carrying Advent images from door to door, and Norman children driving vermin from fields with torches.
britannica-1911-agent:
An agent is, in broad use, any man who acts for an other. The word comes from a Latin verb that means to act or to do. It most likely came into law speech from France, since Roman law had other words for the same role, the 1911 Britannica entry says.

In the late Roman realm, the men who took in grain in the provinces for the troops and the royal house bore a like name. Their work grew in time to take in posts of the state mail and of spies. In law of today, an agent is a man with leave, shown in words or by clear signs, to act for an other. That other is the principal, and is bound by the acts of his agent to the full span of the leave he gave.
britannica-1911-agnes-saint:
Saint Agnes was a virgin martyr of the Catholic Church, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells her legend. She was a Roman girl, born a Christian, who died at the age of thirteen under the emperor Diocletian, on the twenty-first of January 304. The prefect Sempronius wanted her to marry his son. On her refusal she was condemned to be shamed before her death, but her honour was kept by a wonder.

Led out to die and tied to a stake, she could not be burned, since the faggots would not catch. The officer in charge then drew his sword and struck off her head. Agnes is the patron saint of young girls. On her eve, girls in the country once used quaint magic to learn who their husbands would be.
britannica-1911-anno-saint:
Saint Anno, archbishop of Cologne, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born about ten ten into a Swabian family, he was educated at Bamberg. He became confessor to the emperor Henry the Third. That emperor made him archbishop of Cologne in ten fifty six.

He played a large part in ruling Germany while King Henry the Fourth was a child. He led the party that seized the young king in ten sixty two. That coup stripped the empress Agnes, the king's mother, of power. For a short time Anno held chief authority in the kingdom. He soon had to share it with a rival archbishop.
britannica-1911-ant:
The 1911 Britannica article on the ant opens with the history of the word. The old English name meant the biter off. The name has come down for a thousand years. Ants impressed the Hebrews and Greeks as they impressed the English. Their social habits and hard work have always drawn study.

The article then gives the marks of the family. Ants form a family of the order that holds bees and wasps. Their jaws are made for biting. Most kinds have two pairs of thin wings. The key mark is a narrow waist of one or two knots. The article explains the workers. They are wingless females with undeveloped ovaries. They form the great bulk of each ant community. All ants live in societies.
britannica-1911-anthony-of-padua-saint:
Saint Anthony of Padua is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Lisbon on the fifteenth of August 1195, he was the best known follower of Saint Francis of Assisi. He joined the Augustinian order at fifteen and moved to the Franciscans in 1220.

The article follows his work as a teacher and preacher in Italy. A storm drove his ship to Sicily when he sought work in North Africa. He taught at Bologna, Toulouse, Montpellier, and Padua. His preaching won crowds across Italy. He led the strict wing of his order against softer rules. He died near Padua in 1231 and was made a saint the next year.
britannica-1911-anthony-saint:
Saint Anthony was the first Christian monk, born in Egypt about the year 250. At the age of twenty he began a life of strict self-denial near his home place. After fifteen years of that life he withdrew to a hill by the Nile called Pispir. There he lived shut up in an old fort for twenty years.

In the early years of the fourth century Anthony came out of his retreat. He set himself to order the monastic life of the crowds of monks who had followed him. They had settled in caves round his fort. In time he sought fuller solitude once more and withdrew to a hill by the Red Sea. A monastery that bears his name stands there now. His Life says he went twice to Alexandria, once to hearten Christians under persecution and once to preach against Arianism.
britannica-1911-apportionment:
Apportionment means the sharing out of a thing in fair parts, and this 1911 Britannica entry sets out how the term works in law. The word comes through French and medieval Latin from a Latin root meaning a share. In loose use it can cover the sharing of a gain, such as salvage, damages, or a duty. In strict legal use it falls into two classes.

Those classes are apportionment in respect of estate and in respect of time. The first can arise from what the parties do or by force of law. If a tenant is turned out of part of the land he rents, he owes rent only for the part he keeps. If the owner of the future interest sells part of it, a matching share of the rent passes to the buyer.
britannica-1911-archangel-government:
Archangel is a government of European Russia. The White Sea bounds it north. The Arctic Ocean bounds it too. Finland and Olonets lie west. Vologda lies to the south. The Ural mountains close the east. Novaya-Zemlya and other islands belong to it. The Kola peninsula belongs to it too. Its area is 331,505 square miles.

Population was 349,943 in 1897. Arctic Circle lands are desolate and sterile. Sand and reindeer moss cover them. Winters are long and severe there. Soil stays frozen even in summer. Rivers freeze from September to July. Kola is hillier and more genial. Large lakes diversify that peninsula. South of the circle, forests dominate. Lakes and morasses intermingle with trees. Excellent pasturage occurs in places. Nomad Samoyedes, Zyryans, and Lapps inhabit the north.
britannica-1911-ardennes-department:
Ardennes is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a department of France. It sits on the north-east frontier and takes its name from the forest. It was formed in 1790 from parts of three old provinces. Belgium bounds it on the north and north-east sides.

The count for 1906 is 317,505, on 2,028 square miles of land. The Meuse is its longest river, with a winding course of 111 miles. It cuts deep gorges as it runs north through the land. The Aisne crosses the south part in a like northward flow. Wooded highlands in the north rise to 1,640 feet at most. The south-west has a milder air than the rainy north. Wheat and oats lead its crops.
britannica-1911-argument:
Argument, a word meaning proof or evidence, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It comes from the Latin argumentum, from a verb meaning to make clear. That verb rests on a root meaning bright, seen also in a Greek word for white. The English verb argue comes from the same Latin source.

From that first sense flow the many uses of the word today. An argument can be a chain of reasoning, or a fact given to back a claim. It can mean a debate over the reasons for or against a view. It also names a short outline of the contents of a book, novel, or play. In logic it serves for the middle term of a syllogism and for named fallacies. In mathematics and astronomy the term takes special senses tied to tables, angles, and the paths of planets.
britannica-1911-arnault-antoine-vincent:
Antoine Vincent Arnault (1766-1834), a French playwright, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paris, he made his name at once with his first play in 1791. A second tragedy in the republican vein followed a year later. He left France during the Terror and was arrested on his return, but friends in high places won his release.

The article lists his posts and his loyalty. Bonaparte charged him in 1797 with setting the Ionian Islands in order, and he gained a seat in the Institute and a high post in the university. He stood by his patron through his falls, and after the Hundred Days he stayed in exile until 1819. He was re-elected to the Academy in 1829. His tragedies are now less known, the entry says, than his fables, written in graceful verse.
britannica-1911-arnim-harry-karl-kurt-ed:
Harry Karl Kurt Eduard von Arnim was a German court man who lived from eighteen twenty-four to eighteen eighty-one. He came of a wide spread house of Prussian rank. He was raised by an uncle who had served as chief at Paris and as chief of state craft. Posts in that craft came to him in turn.

He served as chief at the court of Rome and gave a bold plan for state men at a great church meet. That plan was turned down by his chief. He then won praise for his work on the peace pact past a war. A post as chief at Paris came to him past that work, a post of great strain.
britannica-1911-arraignment:
Arraignment, a law term for calling a person to answer an indictment in due form, is defined in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. After a grand jury finds a true bill, the prisoner is called by name to the bar. The indictment is read to him, and he is asked whether he is guilty or not.

Old customs, such as holding up a hand to identify the prisoner, are now obsolete. If the prisoner refuses to plead, a plea of not guilty is entered for him. A plea of guilty can bring sentence at once, while a plea of not guilty sends the case to a jury of twelve. In Scots law the same step is called calling the diet.
britannica-1911-arrondissement:
Arrondissement, a unit of local rule in France, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a French verb that means to make round. The unit dates in name from 1800, though it was in truth a new form of the district of 1790. It holds cantons and communes within it, but it is only a unit of rule and not a full legal body in its own right.

The article lists what the unit does. It forms the voting district that sends one member to the chamber of deputies, unless its people pass 100,000 and it is split. It is also a court district with a court of first instance, and a sub-prefect runs it. France held 362 of them in 87 departments at the time.
britannica-1911-assessment: Assessment is a term for an official valuation of income or property for tax purposes, or for the sum that valuation fixes, says a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin verb meaning to sit beside, to judge. The term also covers the amount of damages set by a jury in a court of law. The entry further notes assessment committees, set up under acts of 1862 and 1880 to draw the valuation lists on which the poor-law rate rests.
britannica-1911-aude-department:
Aude is the subject of a department entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a coastal department of southern France, formed in seventeen ninety from part of Languedoc. Its area and its population in nineteen hundred six are both given. The Mediterranean Sea bounds it on the east.

Other departments bound it on the north, west, and south, and they are named in full. A mountain range of medium height runs along its western edge. That range links the Pyrenees with the Cevennes hills. The Montagne Noire fills its northern frontier. The Corbieres, a branch of the Pyrenees, cross the department from south west to north east.
britannica-1911-avonmore-barry-yelverton:
Avonmore, Barry Yelverton, 1st Viscount (1736-1805), was an Irish judge born the eldest son of Frank Yelverton of Blackwater, county Cork. Educated at Trinity College, Dublin, he taught for some years before a marriage to Mary Nugent, a lady of fortune, let him read for the bar.

Called in 1764, Yelverton rose fast, taking silk in eight years, and sat in the Irish parliament for Donegal and Carrickfergus. He became attorney-general in 1782 and chief baron of the exchequer in 1783, then Baron Avonmore in 1795 and viscount in 1800. Famous for eloquence and charm, he backed Grattan and the Whigs for most of his career. Late in life he joined the court party and voted for the union, his viscounty being read as its reward.
britannica-1911-bailment:
Bailment, from French bailler, to place in charge, is a delivery of goods in law. One person, the bailor, hands goods to another, the bailee, for a set purpose. A contract, stated or implied, governs the handover. When the purpose ends, the goods must be returned to the bailor. Or they must be dealt with as he directs. Or they are kept until he reclaims them.

Chief Justice Holt's sorting of bailments in a 1704 case still governs the entry's account. A deposit kept for free makes the keeper answerable only for gross carelessness. A free loan, by contrast, binds the borrower to great care, since the deal favors him alone. Hiring sits between: the hirer must show the care a prudent man gives his own goods. Cases on bankers holding securities and on borrowed horses work out where the lines fall.
britannica-1911-baku-government:
Baku is a government of Russian Transcaucasia. It stretches along the Caspian's west coast. Persia bounds it on the south. Elisavetpol and Daghestan lie westward. Its area covers 15,172 square miles. The Caucasus range ends within it.

Both Caucasus slopes are fertile there. Forests, rice fields, and gardens flourish. Kura steppes need artificial watering. Cotton especially demands that irrigation. Vines and mulberries grow extensively. The Apsheron peninsula is dry and bare. Its famous petroleum wells redeem it. Wells run 700 to 1,700 feet deep. Output grew hugely across forty years. It passed 9.8 million tons in 1904. A serious fire hurt business in 1905. Pipelines carry light oil to Batum. Tank cars carry the heavier oils westward.
britannica-1911-balassa-balint:
Bálint Balassa (1551–1594), baron of Kékkö and Gyarmat, was a Magyar lyric poet. Born at Kékkö, he was taught by the reformer Péter Bornemissza and by his mother, Anna Sulyok. His first work, printed while his father was in prison, was a translation meant to comfort him.

The 1911 Britannica entry follows a life split between court, camp, and love. Balassa served as a soldier at Eger, fell in love with Anna Losonczi, and lost her to another man. He was wounded and held prisoner for two years on a campaign in 1574. His verses to Anna form the heart of his fame.
britannica-1911-balbo-cesare-count:
Cesare Balbo, Count Balbo (1789–1853), was an Italian writer and statesman born at Turin. His father Prospero held high office at the Sardinian court. From 1808 to 1814 the young Balbo served under the Napoleonic empire at Florence, Rome, Paris, and in Illyria.

When Napoleon fell, Balbo entered Piedmontese service and went on missions to Paris and London. Suspected of sympathy with the revolt of 1821, which he in fact opposed, he was sent into exile and then barred from public work. The 1911 Britannica entry shows him turning to writing as his way to serve Italy, with freedom from foreign control as his great aim.
britannica-1911-barbara-saint:
Saint Barbara is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She is honoured as a virgin martyr in both the Roman Catholic and the Orthodox churches. Her feast day falls on the fourth of December. The article presents her story as legend rather than firm record.

In that legend her father shut her in a tower to keep her from marriage. A follower of Origen there brought her to the Christian faith. When her father learned of it, he cut off her head with his own hand. The place of her death is given in rival forms, among them Heliopolis and Nicomedia, around the year 235. She is the patron saint of armourers and gunsmiths. Her aid is sought above all against lightning.
britannica-1911-barrington-john-shute-1s:
John Shute Barrington, first Viscount Barrington (1678–1734), an English lawyer and religious writer, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Theobalds in Hertfordshire, son of a merchant named Benjamin Shute, he studied partly at Utrecht and then law at the Inner Temple. As a Protestant dissenter, he wrote pamphlets in 1701 defending the civil rights of dissenters, the group to which he himself belonged.

Public work and a fall fill the middle of the entry. Barrington helped persuade Scots Presbyterians to favour the union of England and Scotland. He inherited estates that brought him the Barrington name, sat for Berwick-upon-Tweed, and became an Irish viscount in 1720. His part in the Harburg lottery bubble led to expulsion from the Commons in 1723. His chief religious book, Miscellanea Sacra, appeared in 1725.
britannica-1911-barrington-william-wildm:
William Wildman Shute Barrington, second Viscount Barrington (1717–1793), an English office-holder born on 15 January 1717, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Eldest son of the first viscount, he succeeded to the title in 1734, travelled, and entered parliament for Berwick-upon-Tweed in 1740. He later sat for Plymouth and took his seat in the Irish House of Lords in 1745.

Offices came steadily after that. Barrington served as a lord commissioner of the admiralty, helped manage the impeachment of Lord Lovat, and became a privy councillor in 1755. He was secretary at war twice, chancellor of the exchequer in 1761, treasurer of the navy, and briefly joint postmaster-general in 1782. He married Mary Lovell in 1740, left no children, and died at Becket in February 1793.
britannica-1911-bartholomew-saint:
Saint Bartholomew, one of the twelve apostles, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica with care about how little is actually known. Nothing is recorded of his early life, unless he is the Nathanael of the Gospels, a widely held identification that would make Bartholomew a family name meaning son of Tolmai. A Syrian tradition instead says his first name was Jesus, dropped out of reverence for his Master's name.

Tradition fills the silence after the Ascension. Bartholomew is said to have travelled as a missionary to India, then a very loose name for eastern lands, leaving a copy of Matthew's gospel there. He was said to have been flayed alive and then crucified head downward in Armenia, or, in another account, in Cilicia. In art he appears with a large knife, or holding his own skin, as in Michelangelo's Last Judgment. His festival is 24 August.
britannica-1911-basement:
Basement is an architectural term defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the lowest storey of any building, placed wholly or partly below the level of the ground. A true basement, then, is the partly or fully underground floor at a building's foot. It is not simply whichever floor sits at street level when a passer-by looks at the front.

Misuse is the entry's main warning. The word is incorrectly applied, it says, to the ground storey of a building when that floor is not below ground at all. Somerset House in London is the example. Its ground floor is built of plain or rusticated masonry, heavy rough-faced stonework. Above it sits a decorated storey divided with columns or pilasters. Because that floor looks solid and low, people called it a basement, but by the strict definition the name does not fit.
britannica-1911-battlement:
Battlement is a term in building explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the parapet, the low wall atop a castle or town wall. Gaps are cut in it at set spaces, so men behind it can shoot arrows at attackers. The cut-out parts are crenels; the solid widths between them are merlons. The term likely comes from a lost French form tied to bastille, from words for towers and building.

Use of the battlement is traced across lands and ages. The oldest case, at Medinet-Abu in Egypt, is of the inverted form, said to come from Syrian forts. Battlements crowned walls in Assyria and appear at Mycenae and on Greek vases. At Pompeii spur walls inside gave the defender full cover. Later the form turned to show: Muslim and Spanish work kept it as a crown for walls, and English builders trimmed windows and roofs with it.
britannica-1911-bauffremont:
Bauffremont is the name of a French noble family set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The family takes its name from a village in the Vosges, spelled nowadays Beaufremont. By a marriage link with the house of Vergy, the Bauffremonts set themselves up in Burgundy and Franche-Comté, the lands of east France. In 1448 Pierre de Bauffremont, lord of Charny, wed Maríe, a legitimated daughter of Philip the Good, duke of Burgundy, a match that tied the family to ducal blood.

Parliament and rank mark the later line. Nicolas de Bauffremont, his son Claude, and his grandson Henri all played weighty parts in the states-general, the great assemblies of the realm, of 1576, 1588, and 1614.  Alexandre Emmanuel Louis de Bauffremont (1773–1833), a prince of the Holy Roman Empire, was made a peer of France in 1817 and duke in 1818. He had served with the exiled princes, then come back under the Empire.
britannica-1911-beardsley-aubrey-vincent:
