Aubrey Vincent Beardsley is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Beardsley was an English artist in black and white, born at Brighton in 1872. As a boy he appeared in public as an infant musical prodigy. He played at concerts alongside his sister.

The family settled in London in 1883, and art came later. He worked first in an architect's office, then for an insurance company. In 1891, advised by Burne-Jones and Puvis de Chavannes, he took up art as a career. He studied at the Westminster School of Art under Professor Brown. From 1893 until his death at Mentone in 1898, his drawings kept reaching the public. They stirred a storm of criticism and much hostile feeling. The entry marks the brief, blazing career of a draftsman who divided his age.
britannica-1911-benedetti-vincent:
Vincent Benedetti, Count (1817–1900), was a French diplomatist born at Bastia in Corsica. He joined the foreign office in 1840 and served under the marquis de la Valette at Cairo, becoming consul there in 1845. Posts at Palermo and Constantinople followed, and during the Crimean War he acted as chargé d’affaires for fifteen months.

Benedetti acted as secretary to the congress of Paris in 1855–1856 and was France’s first envoy to the new king of Italy in 1861. His great stage, though, was Berlin, where he served as ambassador to Prussia until war broke out in 1870. His talks with Bismarck, and the meeting at Ems over the French demands, lit the spark of that war.
britannica-1911-benedict-of-nursia-saint:
Saint Benedict of Nursia (about 480–544) is called the patriarch of Western monks. All that is known of his life comes from the second book of Saint Gregory’s Dialogues, drawn from four of Benedict’s own disciples. Born of good family at Nursia near Spoleto, he was sent to study at Rome and fled its loose living.

Benedict settled first at Subiaco in the Abruzzi hills, then at Monte Cassino, and monks who tried to poison him mark the early trials Gregory records. His lasting work is the Rule, a prologue and seventy-three chapters setting out the monk’s life. Its chapters on the abbot show his wisdom most clearly, and the Rule shaped Western monastic life for centuries.
britannica-1911-beni-department:
Bení, or El Bení, is a department of north-eastern Bolivia, bordered by Brazil to the north and east. Santa Cruz and Cochabamba lie south of it, and La Paz to the west. Its people were reckoned at 32,180 in 1900, including six thousand wild Indians, over an area put at 102,111 square miles.

The Llanos de Mojos fill the department’s east, famed for the flourishing Jesuit missions planted there in the 1600s and 1700s. Their native heirs still live there, raising cattle and farming in simple ways. Cattle and forest goods, rubber and coca among them, go out in small amounts. Trinidad, the capital on the Mamoré river, was itself once a Jesuit mission town.
britannica-1911-bent:
Bent is first the result of bending, any lean away from the straight, as in a hook or a bow. That sense lives on in the phrase “to follow one’s own bent,” to go one’s own way off the common line. From a bent bow comes the thought of strain or stretch, as when Hamlet speaks of being fooled “to the top of my bent,” to the utmost of his power.

A second, unrelated bent comes from an Old English word for a coarse, rushy grass of wet places. Several grasses carry the name in common speech, and it survives in the form “bent-grass.” Chaucer’s use of bent for a hollow in the land shows the first word at work in old poetry as well.
britannica-1911-beresford-william-carr-b:
William Carr Beresford, Viscount Beresford (1768–1854), was a British general and Portuguese marshal, natural son of the first marquess of Waterford. He joined the army in 1785 and lost the sight of one eye in a shooting accident in Nova Scotia the next year. Toulon in 1793 first showed his quality, and the 88th regiment, the Connaught Rangers, followed.

Beresford led the desert march to Egypt with Baird and took Cape Town. He captured Buenos Aires with two regiments. Three days of fighting forced him to surrender it, and he spent six months in prison. His great work was rebuilding Portugal’s army in the Peninsular War. Wellington thought so highly of his organising power that he named Beresford as his own successor if he fell.
britannica-1911-bestuzhev-ryumin-alexius:
Alexius Petrovich Bestuzhev-Ryumin (1693–1768) was grand chancellor of Russia. He was born at Moscow, second son of Count Peter Bestuzhev. He was educated abroad, at Copenhagen and Berlin, and excelled in languages. Peter the Great sent him to the Utrecht Congress in 1712 to learn diplomacy. He then served the elector of Hanover. George I brought him to London in 1714 as his envoy.

The 1911 Britannica entry stresses his love of intrigue. One rash letter to the tsarevich at Vienna nearly cost him his life. Back in Russia he rose through court service to the chancellorship. A fall from favour sent him to his Goretovo estate in 1759. Catherine II recalled him and made him a field marshal. He took no lead in affairs after that. He died in April 1768, the last of his race.
britannica-1911-bestuzhev-ryumin-mikhail:
Mikhail Petrovich Bestuzhev-Ryumin (1688–1760) was a Russian diplomat, elder brother of the grand chancellor Alexius. He was educated at Berlin. Peter the Great sent him to represent Russia at Copenhagen in 1705. In 1720 he became resident at London, where the court was hostile to Peter. He was dismissed at once for protesting the new Anglo-Swedish alliance. After the Peace of Nystad he went as ambassador to Stockholm.

There he signed a twelve-year defensive alliance in 1724, the 1911 Britannica entry notes. Posts at Warsaw and Berlin followed before he returned to Stockholm in 1732. The article weighs his part in the 1739 killing of the Swedish envoy Sinclair. It calls him the arch-plotter in Swedish accounts. His last great mission was to Versailles. He died at Paris in February 1760.
britannica-1911-betterment:
Betterment means making better, set against the coined word worsement in the entry. It is a term used most of all for land and its value in money. It names the rise in value given to real property by outside causes. The owner is not the cause of that rise in such cases. A tenant or the public may be the cause instead of him.

When a public work raises the value of a piece of private land, the owner gains. He gains through no merit of his own, which is the point at issue. Many thinkers have sought to tax that unearned gain away from him. A betterment tax would send the profit to the public purse instead. Trials of the idea in America and England raised much dispute. The whole question turns on tax burdens and land values.
britannica-1911-blanc-mont:
Mont Blanc is the highest summit in the Alps, rising 15,782 feet on the borders of France, Italy, and Switzerland. The top itself is wholly French. Chamonix valley lies to the north and the head of the Aosta valley to the east, with great glaciers, among them the Bossons and the Brenva, streaming down its sides.

Jacques Balmat and Dr Michel Paccard made the first climb in 1786, and Balmat went up again the next year. De Saussure's third ascent in 1787 is called memorable, and Colonel Beaufoy soon became the first Englishman on top. Most climbs still started from Chamonix. The entry warns that the view, though vast enough to reach Lyons, is often poor for the height.
britannica-1911-blasius-saint:
Saint Blasius, also called Blaise, was bishop of Sebaste in Asia Minor and was put to death under Diocletian on 3 February 316. His feast falls on 3 February in the Roman Church and 11 February in the Eastern Church. Tradition says his flesh was torn with woolcombers' irons before he was beheaded.

That detail made him the patron saint of woolcombers, who still marked his day in England with a procession and holiday. A story of a child cured of a throat trouble on the way to his execution made him the saint called on for diseases of the throat and lungs. In England his day was once so honoured that the council of Oxford in 1222 banned work on it. He is also one of the fourteen helper saints grouped together in Germany.
britannica-1911-boisguilbert-pierre-le-p:
Pierre le Pesant de Boisguilbert (1676–1714) was a French judge who became an early writer on economics. Born at Rouen to an old Norman noble family, he entered the magistracy and in 1690 became president of the bailliage of Rouen. Farming his own lands and talking with Rouen merchants taught him local trade at first hand.

That study showed him how taxes crushed the poor, and in 1695 he published Le Détail de la France, picturing the ruin of all classes under a bad tax regime. Against Colbert, he held that wealth lies in what a country makes and trades, not in its stock of money. His cure was fairer, more even taxes, so the poor could buy more and output could rise. Later finance schemes borrowed his ideas with poor results.
britannica-1911-bolingbroke-henry-st-joh:
Henry St John, Viscount Bolingbroke (1678–1751), was an English Tory statesman and political writer of brilliant, reckless gifts. Baptized in October 1678 and schooled at Eton, he travelled in 1698–99 and learned French to a rare standard. His youth was wildly dissolute, with weeks of riot and drinking that shocked even his own circle.

Swift, his close friend, said he wished to be the Alcibiades or Petronius of his age. He entered parliament in 1701 for Wootton Bassett and rose fast under Harley. The long entry follows his years as a leading minister, his fall and flight on the Hanoverian succession, his years abroad, and his return to lead the opposition in print. His letters and political writings close the account.
britannica-1911-bonaventura-saint:
Saint Bonaventura (1221–1274), born John of Fidanza at Bagnarea in Tuscany, was a Franciscan theologian ranked among the great schoolmen. A childhood cure was credited to St Francis himself, from whom his name Bonaventura is said to come. He joined the Franciscans in 1243 and studied at Paris.

He took the Paris chair in 1253 and a doctorate in 1255, and in 1256 he was elected general of his order. The entry notes hard acts of rule, such as barring Roger Bacon from lecturing at Oxford. He helped win the papal election of Gregory X, who made him cardinal and bishop of Albano. He died at the council of Lyons in 1274. His contemporaries called him Doctor Seraphicus, and Dante gave him a high place, the closing lines recall.
britannica-1911-boniface-saint:
Saint Boniface (680–754), born Wynfrith in Devon, was the English monk who carried Christianity to Germany and is called its apostle. Born at Crediton of a good Saxon family, he became a monk young and studied at Exeter and Nutcell under Abbot Winberht. He soon stood out as scholar and preacher.

In 716 he sailed as a missionary to Frisia but was driven back by King Radbod's hostility. Pope Gregory II commissioned him in 719 to evangelise Germany and check the Irish monks' influence there. He worked in Bavaria, Thuringia, and Hesse, won chiefs over, and baptised great numbers. The long entry follows his rise as archbishop, his reforms of the Frankish church, and his death as a martyr in Frisia in 754.
britannica-1911-bridget-of-sweden-saint:
Bridget of Sweden (about 1302–1373), also called Brigitta or Birgitta, ranks as the most famed saint of the northern kingdoms. Her father, Birger Persson, was governor and provincial judge of Uppland and one of the richest landowners in the country. Married in 1316 to Ulf Gudmarson, lord of Nericia, she bore eight children, one later honoured as St Catherine of Sweden.

A pilgrimage with her husband to St James of Compostella in 1341-1343 preceded his death at Alvastra in 1344, after which she gave herself wholly to religion. Visions she had known since childhood grew more frequent, and her written revelations, turned into Latin by helpers, spread widely across Europe. She founded the order of St Saviour, the Bridgittines, with its head house at Vadstena, went to Rome about 1350, and won papal backing for the rule from Urban V in 1370.
britannica-1911-bridget-saint:
Saint Bridget, more rightly Brigid (about 452–523), stands among the patron saints of Ireland. Born at Faughart in county Louth to a father who was a prince of Ulster, she refused marriage and chose a lone religious life. Her cell, the first in Ireland, sat under a great oak tree, and the spot took the name Kil-dara, the church of the oak, from which Kildare is said to grow.

Her death is generally placed in 523. Buried first at Kildare, her remains were later moved to Downpatrick and laid beside St Patrick and St Columba. Her feast falls on 1 February. A large store of wonder tales gathered round her name, and as St Bride she won a wide following in England, with many churches named for her in Scotland as well.
britannica-1911-bridport-alexander-hood-:
Alexander Hood, Viscount Bridport (1727–1814), was a British admiral, younger brother of Samuel, Lord Hood. He entered the navy in January 1741 and became a lieutenant six years later, serving ten years in that rank in various ships. Posted next to the Prince, flagship of Rear-Admiral Saunders, he served in the Mediterranean before coming home to command the frigate Minerva.

In Minerva he fought at Hawke's great victory in Quiberon Bay on 20 November 1759, and in 1761 his ship retook the Warwick after a long fight against equal force. Service in the Africa in the Mediterranean, at Ushant in 1778 in the Robust, and a part in the court-martial of Admiral Keppel followed. Two years after Ushant he rose to rear-admiral of the white and served as one of Howe's flag officers, the start of the senior career the entry traces.
britannica-1911-bruno-of-querfurt-saint:
Bruno of Querfurt, Saint (about 975–1009), was a German missionary bishop and martyr from the family of the lords of Querfurt in Saxony. Educated at the famous cathedral school at Magdeburg, he was attached at twenty to the clerical household of the emperor Otto III. In 996 he accompanied the emperor to Rome and there gave up his post to enter the monastery of SS. Alexius and Bonifacius on the Aventine, taking the name Bonifacius in religion.

When news reached Rome of the martyrdom of Adalbert, bishop of Prague, in 997, Bruno resolved to take his place. Consecrated by the pope in 1004 as archbishop of the eastern heathen, he sought the emperor Henry II's aid, but war with Boleslaus of Poland blocked it. He went instead to St Stephen of Hungary, then to Grand Prince Vladimir at Kiev. Making no effort to win Vladimir to Roman obedience.
britannica-1911-bruno-saint:
Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, was born in Cologne about 1030 and educated there and afterwards at Reims and Tours, where he studied under Berengar. Ordained at Cologne, he was recalled to Reims in 1057 to become scholasticus, head of the cathedral school and overseer of the diocese's schools. He was also made canon and diocesan chancellor, a teacher-administrator of the first rank.

Protesting against a new archbishop's misdoings cost him all his offices and forced him to flee for safety in 1076. When that archbishop was deposed in 1080, Bruno was presented to the pope for the see, but Philip I of France blocked the appointment. Bruno then left Reims and withdrew with six companions to a desert among the mountains near Grenoble, where in 1084 he founded the Carthusian order. Called to Rome by Urban II after six years and offered the archbishopric of Reggio.
britannica-1911-burlington-vermont:
Burlington, a city in Vermont, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It is a port of entry and the seat of Chittenden county, on the east shore of Lake Champlain. It lies ninety miles south east of Montreal and three hundred miles north of New York. Burlington is the largest city in the state.

Its population rose from 11,365 in 1880 to 20,468 in the census of 1910. The city is served by two railways and by steamboats on the lake. It is built on a strip of land along the shore, rising from the water to a height of two hundred seventy five feet. That site and its cool summer air have made it a famed summer resort. It is also a centre for yachting and canoeing, and in winter for ice boat races.
britannica-1911-burton-upon-trent:
Burton-upon-Trent, a market town in Staffordshire and Derbyshire in England, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town lies mainly on the left bank of the Trent, which can be sailed from a point near it. Its people numbered 46,047 in 1891 and 50,386 in 1901. Four rail lines served it, and it stood 127 miles north-west of London.

The article calls the town purely a place of work, with no grand buildings, though the land along the river is pleasant. It notes the church of St Mary and St Modwen, parts of an old abbey, and a half-timbered house of the fifteenth century. A free grammar school dated from 1525, and Lord Burton gave the town a fine bridge and its town buildings.
britannica-1911-cagliostro-alessandro-co:
Alessandro Cagliostro is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Cagliostro was an Italian alchemist and impostor who lived from 1743 to 1793. His real name was Giuseppe Balsamo, and he was born at Palermo. He was schooled at a monastery in Sicily, then expelled for misconduct and disowned by his kin. A wild life of forgery and crime followed.

The article tells how trouble forced him to flee Sicily. He travelled through Greece, Egypt, Arabia, and Persia, learning alchemy on the way. In Malta he presented himself as Count Cagliostro to the grand master of the order there. Letters from that patron opened great houses in Rome and Naples to him. He then travelled Europe under shifting names with his wife. He sold love potions, elixirs of youth, and powders of alchemy at large profit.
britannica-1911-canterbury-charles-manne:
Charles Manners-Sutton, first Viscount Canterbury, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born on the twenty ninth of January 1780, he was the elder son of an archbishop of Canterbury. He was schooled at Eton and at Trinity College, Cambridge, and took his degree in 1802.

The article centres on his long run as speaker of the House of Commons. He entered the house in 1806 for Scarborough and trained as a lawyer. In 1817 he was chosen speaker, and he held the chair through seven votes. He gave up a home office post to keep the chair in 1827. His Tory leanings drew sharp attacks from the Whig side. In 1835 he lost the chair and was raised to the peerage.
britannica-1911-capital-punishment:
Capital punishment means putting a criminal to death by law. The sentence must come from a properly set authority. This long 1911 Britannica article traces the practice through history. It sets legal execution apart from private vengeance. In early society, the victim's kin took blood revenge themselves. Cities of refuge and church sanctuary softened that system.

The article then follows the law country by country. In Babylon, Hammurabi's code named death for many offences. Roman law counted loss of citizen status as a capital penalty too. England once made death the price of almost every felony. Reformers such as Bentham and Romilly attacked that code. By the article's time, only four crimes stayed capital in England. They were treason, murder, piracy with violence, and firing dockyards. Scotland, Ireland, India and the colonies get their own accounts. Modes of execution are also covered.
britannica-1911-caprivi-de-caprera-de-mo:
Georg Leo von Caprivi (1831–1899) was a German soldier and statesman. He was a count, and later chancellor of Germany. This 1911 Britannica entry traces his career. He was born at Charlottenburg on 24 February 1831. His family came from Carniola, as the Kopriva. Caprivi was educated in Berlin and entered the army in 1849.

He served on staff work in the war of 1866. In 1870 he was chief of staff to the 10th army corps. That corps formed part of the 2nd army in France. He distinguished himself around Metz and Orleans. At Vionville his advice shaped a delicate change of direction. At Beaune-la-Rolande his corps bore the brunt of the fight. After the peace he held high military offices. In 1883 he became chief of the admiralty. He had to command the fleet and defend the department in the Reichstag. He resigned that post in 1888.
britannica-1911-carpenter-lant:
Lant Carpenter (1780–1840) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English Unitarian minister born at Kidderminster, the son of a carpet manufacturer. He studied at a nonconformist academy at Northampton and at Glasgow University before joining the ministry. In 1802 he became librarian at the Liverpool Athenaeum, and in 1805 he took a church at Exeter, moving to Bristol in 1817.

At both cities Carpenter also taught school, and Harriet and James Martineau were among his Bristol pupils. The entry credits him with broadening the spirit of English Unitarianism. He dropped baptism, which he saw as a superstition, and used a form of infant dedication instead. Constant work ruined his health, and doctors ordered him to travel. He drowned on the night of 5 April 1840, washed overboard from a steamer sailing from Leghorn to Marseilles.
britannica-1911-catherine-saint:
Six saints share one name in a church entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Rome's roll of saints holds six Catherines in its long list. First stands Catherine of Alexandria, virgin and martyr of old tale. Her feast falls on the twenty-fifth day of November each year. Catherine of Sweden, Bridget's child, comes next in the list there.

Siena's Catherine, who lived from 1347 to 1380, stands third. Bologna's Catherine was a visionary abbess of the Poor Clares. Genoa's Catherine gave her life and wealth to the sick poor. She nursed plague folk in the scourge years of that port. Ricci's Catherine of Florence was a nun famed for trances. In trance she felt the pains of the Passion each week.
britannica-1911-cecilia-saint:
Saint Cecilia is honoured in the Catholic Church as patron saint of music and of the blind, with her feast on the 22nd of November. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica weighs the rival tales of her death. Long telling made her a noble Roman lady martyred with her husband about the year 230.

Newer study backs an older voice, Fortunatus, who placed her death in Sicily under Marcus Aurelius, between 176 and 180. A church in her honour stood in Rome from about the 300s and was rebuilt in splendour about 820. Her link with music rests on one passing line in her legend, that she praised God with instruments as well as voice. Yet that line inspired works by Raphael, Rubens, and Domenichino, and poems by Chaucer and Dryden.
britannica-1911-cement:
Cement is a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on binding materials, from the Latin caementum, rough pieces of stone. The word first named a mix of broken stone and tiles with a binder. It then spread to any material that can unite fragments into one mass. In engineering, used without qualification, it means Portland cement and its kin. These are hydraulic cements. Once set, they resist water and can even set under water.

The entry explains the classes of hydraulic cement. Builders have always known that some limes resist water when set. Ordinary lime can gain the same property from added siliceous matter, such as pozzuolana. Pure lime, burned from chalk or limestone, slakes fiercely with water. Mixed with sand it makes common mortar. That mortar sets only by drying and hardens only at the surface. So fat lime mortar serves only above water level.
britannica-1911-charlet-nicolas-toussain:
Nicolas Toussaint Charlet was a French artist who lived from seventeen ninety-two to eighteen forty-five. He was born in Paris, the son of a horse trooper who died in the ranks. His mother, a staunch fan of the great chief, schooled him as best she could. He first worked at a town hall, where he logged new troops.

Loss of that post for his views freed him to draw full time. He made near two thousand prints, most of all of troops and war. One print of a guard who would not yield became famed all through France. He also drew town and farm life with wit.
britannica-1911-chateaubriant:
Châteaubriant is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of western France, in the department of Loire Inférieure. It stands on the left bank of the Chère, 40 miles north north east of Nantes by rail. Its population in 1906 was 5969. The town takes its name from a castle founded in the eleventh century by Brient, count of Penthièvre. A square donjon and four towers of it remain.

Beside it stands a second castle, built in the first half of the sixteenth century by Jean de Laval. It is famed as the home of Françoise de Foix, mistress of Francis I. Its finest feature is a colonnade linking the main building to a pavilion. The town is a railway centre with trade in farm products. Leather and preserved angelica are made there. In 1551 Henry II signed an edict against the reformed religion at Châteaubriant.
britannica-1911-chernigov-government:
Chernigov is a government of Little Russia on the left bank of the Dnieper, bounded by Mogilev, Smolensk, Orel, Kursk, Poltava, Kiev and Minsk. Its area is 20,233 square miles, an undulating plain cut by ravines and river valleys. Forest covers about a third of the north, and marshes line the rivers. South of the Desna the dry soil slowly takes on the character of steppe.

The Dnieper forms the western border for 180 miles, and its tributary the Desna runs through the government for nearly 350 miles. People numbered 2,316,818 in 1897 and an estimated 2,746,300 in 1906, mostly Little Russians. Farming leads, with beet, tobacco and hemp widely grown. Timber work, cattle breeding, bee keeping, quarrying, sugar works, distilleries and cloth mills are also described.
britannica-1911-cheshunt:
Cheshunt is an urban district in Hertfordshire, England, on the Lea, 14 miles north of London by the Great Eastern railway. Its people rose from 9,620 in 1891 to 12,292 in 1901, and the church of St Mary is Perpendicular. Nursery and market gardening under glass, brick making and saw mills lead its industries. Roman coins and other remains point to a Romano-British village or small town on the site.

Cheshunt College, founded in 1768 to train young men for the ministry, moved here in 1792 from Wales. A plan to join it with Hackney College failed, and in 1905 the board chose to reorganise it and remove it to Cambridge. Nearby mansions add history, above all Theobalds Park, where James I died in 1625. The old Temple Bar from Fleet Street stands at one entrance to that park.
britannica-1911-chimkent:
Chimkent is a town of Asiatic Russia in the province of Syr-darya, 70 miles by rail north-north-east of Tashkent, holding 10,756 people in 1897. Most of its people are Sarts, the entry says. It occupies a key position at the west end of the valley between the Alexander range and the Ala-tau. Trade routes meet there from Siberia, from the Aral Sea and Orenburg side, and from Ferghana and Bokhara to the south.

A citadel on high ground above the town was stormed by the Russians in 1864 and now stands in ruins. Rail reached the town from Orenburg in 1905, strengthening the route meeting place role the entry describes. Consumptive patients visit Chimkent to try the koumiss cure, a course of fermented mare's milk. Cotton mills and soap works give the town its industry beyond trade and the cure traffic.
britannica-1911-christopher-saint:
Saint Christopher is honoured in the Roman Catholic and Orthodox Eastern churches, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives him an entry that weighs fact against legend. He is the patron of ferrymen. Nothing that is authentic is known about him, the entry says plainly. He seems to have been a pagan born in Syria, baptized by Babylas of Antioch.

Christopher is said to have preached with much success in Lycia and to have been martyred about 250, under the emperor Decius. Round that small nucleus, a vast mass of legend gradually collected. All accounts agree that he was of great stature and singularly handsome, and that this helped him in his work. One later tale made him at first a hideous, man eating ogre with a dog's face, who gained human form only at baptism. Other marvels tell of a staff that sprouted into a date palm and converted thousands.
britannica-1911-claremont:
Claremont is a city of Sullivan county, New Hampshire, in the west of the state, bordering on the Connecticut river. Its people numbered 6,498 in 1900 and 7,529 in 1910, over an area of six square miles. Two branches of the Boston and Maine railway serve it, and it holds the Fiske free library and a richly endowed high school. Sugar river flows through the city into the Connecticut, falling 223 feet within the limits and furnishing good water power.

Woollen and cotton goods, paper, mining and quarrying machinery, rubber goods, linens, shoes, wood trim and pearl buttons are among its manufactures. Several villages lie within the city, Claremont, Claremont Junction and West Claremont the principal ones. First settlement came in 1762 and a township was organised in 1764, though city charter waited until 1908. The name came from Claremont, Lord Clive's country place, the entry adds.
britannica-1911-clotilda-saint:
Clotilda, Saint (d. 544) was the daughter of the Burgundian king Chilperic and wife of Clovis, king of the Franks. Her father was slain by his brother Gundobald, by Gregory of Tours's account, and Clotilda was exiled while her sister took the veil. A Lyons epitaph of a Burgundian queen who died in 506 probably names her mother instead, the entry cautions. Brought up in the orthodox faith, she married Clovis about 493, after he had conquered northern Gaul.

Clotilda did not rest until her husband had abjured paganism and embraced the orthodox Christian faith in 496. With him she built at Paris the church of the Holy Apostles, later Sainte Geneviève. After Clovis died in 511 she retired to the abbey of Saint Martin at Tours. She incited her sons against Gundobald in 523, yet failed to protect her grandsons' rights or to prevent civil discord among her children.
britannica-1911-co-respondent:
Co-respondent, in law, is generally a person made respondent to, or called upon to answer, along with another or others, a petition or other proceeding. The general sense covers anyone joined as an answering party beside the main respondent. A more particular sense has grown up since one statute, and that sense dominates the entry. Readers are sent on to the article on Divorce for the working detail of suits of this kind.

Since the Matrimonial Causes Act 1857 the term applies particularly to the person charged by a husband in his petition for dissolution of his marriage. The charge is misconduct with the husband's wife, adultery in the ground of the suit. That person is made, jointly with the wife, a respondent to the suit itself. General legal joining and this specific divorce use are the two layers the short entry sets out.
britannica-1911-cochabamba-department:
Cochabamba is a central department of Bolivia occupying the eastern angle of the great Bolivian plateau, with an area of 23,328 square miles. Its people numbered 328,163 in 1900, chiefly of Indian and mestizo types. Average elevation runs between 8,000 and 10,000 feet, and mean temperature ranges from 50 to 60 degrees. That height and temperature make it one of the best climatic regions in South America, the entry judges.

The department is essentially agricultural, though gold, silver and copper deposits are also found in its ground. Wheat, Indian corn, barley and potatoes and most temperate fruits and vegetables grow in its climate. Coca, cacao, tobacco and tropical fruits are also produced, and forest products include rubber and cinchona. Lack of transport facilities has blocked development of any industry beyond local needs, except cinchona and rubber. Sheep and cattle thrive, and a silkworm experiment gave highly successful results.
britannica-1911-colchester-vermont:
Colchester is a township of Chittenden county, Vermont, on Lake Champlain. It lies just north-east of Burlington, split from it by the Winooski river. Its people rose from 5,352 in 1900 to 6,450 in 1910. The Central Vermont railway serves it. Land rolls gently for the most part. River banks, lake shore and valleys give it fine views.

Mallett's Bay, an arm of the lake, hosts summer schools. Soil varies, with much good meadow and land fit for grain and fruit. Two villages share the town. Colchester Centre is small and quiet. Winooski, on the river, is the larger place. Water power drives its mills there. Cotton and wool goods, lumber and carriages lead its output. Fort Ethan Allen, a United States post, stands within the township. Ira Allen founded the village in 1772.
britannica-1911-colman-saint:
Saint Colman (died 676) was bishop of Lindisfarne, most likely an Irish monk of Iona at first. He came south and took the see in 661. King Oswio of Northumbria held him as a close friend. At the synod of Whitby in 664 the great clash of Roman and Celtic church ways came to a head. Colman spoke for the Celtic side.

The king ruled against him, and his cause fell. Colman then left with some monks for Iona and then Ireland. He settled on the island of Inishbofin. There he built a monastery and died on 8 August 676. The entry takes care to part him from two namesakes. One is Saint Colman of Cloyne and the other Saint Colman Ela. The name itself comes from the Latin word for a dove. The Book of Leinster lists 209 saints of that name.
britannica-1911-columba-saint:
Saint Columba, in Irish Colum, was an Irish saint, and this 1911 Britannica entry begins with his birth and teachers. He was born on the seventh of December 521, most likely at Gartan in County Donegal. His father belonged to the reigning family of Ireland, tied closely to the house of Dalriada in Argyll. His mother came of a famed Leinster royal line.

To those strong ties, as much as to his piety and ability, the entry credits the vast influence he held. In his youth the Irish Church was being reformed, and monasteries sprang up that made Ireland a centre of learning. Columba studied under two of the most noted Irishmen of the day, both named Finian, and in due course he took up the monastic life himself.
britannica-1911-combermere-stapleton-cot:
British field marshal Stapleton Cotton, first Viscount Combermere, born in seventeen seventy three, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second son of a Cheshire baronet. He was schooled at Westminster. At only sixteen he got a junior officer post in a Welsh regiment.

A few years later he bought a captain's post in a dragoon guard regiment. He served in Flanders under the Duke of York. Still in his twentieth year he joined a light dragoon regiment as a senior officer. While with that regiment near the king at Weymouth, he became a great favourite of George the Third. In seventeen ninety six he went with his regiment to India. He served on the way in Cape Colony and in the war against Tippoo Sahib.
britannica-1911-commitment:
Commitment, in English law, is a written order to hold a person in custody, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. A court or a judge issues the order, and in cases of treason the privy council or a secretary of state may do so. The order names the person or describes him well enough to be known. It tells officers to convey him to a prison or other lawful place.

He is to be held there for a set time, or until he has done a set act named in the order. Payment of a fine laid on him at conviction is given as a case in point. To make the sense clear, the text prints a form in use under statute. That form runs from a county court to its constables and to the governor of the prison, and states the conviction and the command.
britannica-1911-confalonieri-federico-co:
Federico Confalonieri, Count Confalonieri (1785–1846), was an Italian revolutionary born at Milan of a noble Lombard family. In 1806 he wed Teresa Casati. In the Napoleonic years he stood among the foes of French rule in Italy. Men saw him as a leader of the Italiani puri, the Italian national party. The Milan riots of 1814 stained his name by error.

The minister Prina was killed in those riots, and Confalonieri was charged with a share in the deed without just cause. After Napoleon's fall he went to Paris with other Lombard men. They pled for a free Lombard state under its own prince. Austria took Lombardy all the same, and London gave him no more hope. He then joined the Freemasons and other secret societies of the day. The entry turns next to Austria's close and secret process against him.
britannica-1911-convent:
Convent is a brief entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica that pins down a word used for religious houses. The article takes the term from the Latin conventus, from a verb that means to come together. A convent is a group of people set apart from the world and given to a religious life, and by extension the building where they live.

The piece notes that the word points most often to a nunnery, though it can cover a monastery as well. It also deals with the smaller form conventicle, used in a slighting way for the meetings or meeting places of dissenting groups, with a hint of secrecy or law-breaking. For such a short entry, it does useful work: it sorts the kind sense of the word from the hostile one and shows how tone can shift a term's meaning.
britannica-1911-coquelin-benoit-constant:
Benoit Constant Coquelin was a French actor who lived from eighteen forty-one to nineteen nine. He was born at Boulogne and was meant to be a baker like his father. A love of the stage led him to train in Paris instead. He won a first prize for comic roles within a year.

The entry follows his long run at the chief Paris stage, where he made many new parts. A row over tours led him to quit, tour far, and then return. He later ran his own stage and won great fame as Cyrano. He died while at work on a new Rostand play.
britannica-1911-cormorant:
Cormorant is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica from a Latin name that means sea crow. The name came through French, where a form of it still lives in street speech. It is a large sea fowl of a set kind. That kind heads a clan of kin fowl that feed in the sea.

The bird of the entry haunts most of the sea coast of Europe. It breeds in groups at posts on the coast. Steep cliffs are its most wide choice, with rock isles and trees in use at times as well. Its nest is a large mass of sea weed. The ground round the nest looks as if splashed with white wash from the dung of the bird. The bird lives on fish and on fish alone.
britannica-1911-corporal-punishment:
Corporal punishment is chastisement laid by one person on the body of another. By the common law of England, Scotland, and Ireland, such punishment is unlawful in most cases. It is allowed in self defence or in defence of others under attack. It is also allowed for persons who hold set power to punish. A court of justice with due power may also order it in law.

Force used in defence must be fairly needed to guard the person attacked. Parents and guardians stand first among those with power to punish a child. Teachers hold like powers by a charge handed from the parents in trust. Those powers reach acts done on the way to and from school. They also cover acts done in what may fairly count as school hours. English law of nineteen o four owned those rights in plain terms.
britannica-1911-corti-lodovico-count:
Count Lodovico Corti is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Corti was an Italian diplomat, born at Gambarano in 1823. As a young man he joined plots against Austrian rule and was exiled to Turin. There he entered the Piedmontese foreign office and began his career.

The article follows his rise through post after post. He served as secretary in London, then as minister in several capitals. In 1875 he became ambassador to Constantinople. Called home in 1878, he led foreign affairs and sat at the Congress of Berlin. There he backed Greek independence but refused a British offer of alliance. He came home, in the phrase of the day, with clean hands, and his countrymen were angry. The entry shows a skilled servant caught by the hard choices of a young nation.
britannica-1911-crescent:
Crescent, from a Latin term for the act of growth, first named the new moon as it waxes. From that it came to name that moons form in its first part. In shield lore the form stands with horns up. Turned to one side or the next, it takes set names that mark its pose.

A crescent marks the next son of a house in shield lore. Orders that bear the name were set up in Naples and past a sultan in late days. The form is the war and faith sign of the Turks. A tale ties it to a moon that rose past a siege and woke the town dogs.
britannica-1911-crown-point:
Crown Point is a village in Essex County, New York, on Lake Champlain. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it north of Ticonderoga on the west shore. Rail and canal links served the small settlement in that day. Lumber, wooden goods, graphite, and spar came from the township round it.

Champlain fought Native forces near the site in 1609. That clash began long enmity between the French and the Five Nations. The French built Fort Frédéric there in 1731 for its key lake route. British forces took the point at last in 1759. Green Mountain Boys seized its fort again in May 1775.
britannica-1911-cuthbert-saint:
Saint Cuthbert, bishop of Lindisfarne, who died in 687, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was probably a Northumbrian by birth. The old Lives say a vision led him to take monastic vows. The vision came at the death of bishop Aidan. He entered the house at Melrose in 651.

Eata was abbot there, and Boisel was his teacher. Cuthbert succeeded Boisel as prior about 661. He had spent some time at Ripon with Eata before that. Bede paints his missionary zeal at Melrose in glowing terms. In 664 he was moved to act as prior at Lindisfarne. In 676 he became a hermit on the island of Farne. Miracles were said of his years there. In 684 a council at Twyford chose him for higher office. The life traces a monk drawn, step by step, to a bishop's seat.
britannica-1911-cyprian-saint:
Saint Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He lived from about the year 200 to 258. The text calls him one of the most famed bishops of the early church. It also counts him among its most notable early martyrs.

He was most likely born at Carthage, of a patrician family. He was wealthy and highly educated. For a time he taught rhetoric at Carthage. He had a fierce temper and a love of fine letters. While still a pagan, he seems to have sought debate with converts to the new faith. He set out, the text says, to vanquish them in argument. Instead, he was himself vanquished by the new religious force. The article traces how a proud teacher became a leader of the church he had opposed.
britannica-1911-dahlberg-erik-johansen-c:
Dahlberg, Erik Johansen, Count is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Swedish soldier and engineer. As an engineer officer he served in the last years of the Thirty Years War and in Poland. He had a great share in the crossing of the frozen Belts.

The article tells why fame came late. Despite such services he stayed an obscure lieutenant colonel for years. In 1676 he at last became director general of fortifications. His repair of Sweden's fortresses earned him the title of the Vauban of Sweden. He founded the Swedish engineer corps and retired as field marshal in 1702. The article also credits him with the great collection of drawings of Swedish places, Suecia antiqua et hodierna.
britannica-1911-dandolo-vincenzo-count:
Vincenzo Dandolo, count Dandolo (1758–1819), was an Italian chemist and agriculturist born at Venice. He was of good family, though not of the doges' house, and began as a physician. He opposed the oligarch party as Napoleon approached and went as an envoy to seek French protection. When Venice fell to Austria instead, he moved to Milan and joined its great council. In 1799 he retired to Paris and published a treatise on national renewal.

Back near Milan, Dandolo gave himself to scientific farming. Napoleon made him governor of Dalmatia in 1805, where he drained pestilential marshes and spread better farming. When Dalmatia returned to the Illyrian provinces in 1809 he went home to Venice. The emperor had made him a count for his service. His Italian treatises cover farming, vines, cattle and sheep, and silk-worms. He died at Venice on 13 December 1819.
britannica-1911-daphne-plant:
Daphne in botany is a genus of shrubs of the order Thymelaeaceae, with about forty species native to Europe and temperate Asia. The spurge laurel is a small evergreen with green flowers and ovoid black berries that are very poisonous, found in England in copses and on hedge-banks in stiff soils. Mezereon grows two to four feet high, with leaves that fall and fragrant pink flowers in early spring.

The whole mezereon plant is acrid and poisonous, its bright red berries are cathartic, and its bark serves in medicine. Several more species earn garden places: cneorum trails with sweet pink flowers, pontica spreads with greenish-yellow blooms, and indica and japonica grow as greenhouse evergreens. The entry names each kind with its homeland and flower colour.
britannica-1911-defendant: Defendant is a term from law for a person against whom a case is brought. Such a person is called on to answer a claim in court. This short 1911 Britannica entry defines the word. It once had a narrower sense, the entry says, covering only a person sued in a personal action. In a real action the matching term was tenant. By 1911 that split was all but dropped, apart from a few states in the United States.
britannica-1911-deferent: Deferent, in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, is a term of ancient astronomy, from a Latin word meaning bearing down. It names the mean orbit of a planet in the old system of the heavens. That orbit carried the smaller circle, the epicycle, in which the planet was thought to revolve. The entry adds a modern note: what the old writers called the deferent is now known to match the true orbit of the planet round the sun.
britannica-1911-dominic-saint:
Saint Dominic (1170-1221), founder of the Dominican Order of Preaching Friars, was born in 1170 at Calaroga in Old Castile. He studied theology at Palencia for ten or twelve years and was ordained about 1195. As a canon of Osma cathedral he followed the Rule of Saint Augustine and rose to prior of the community. In 1203 he travelled with his bishop on a royal embassy, and at Rome Innocent III charged them to preach to the Albigensian heretics.

For ten years, 1205 to 1215, that mission in Languedoc was the work of Dominic's life. The article sets out the Albigensian creed in detail: two gods, matter as evil, and sins counted even in marriage and meat-eating. Such teaching, the article argues, threatened civil society itself, not Catholicism alone.
britannica-1911-element:
Element is a word article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a term for the basic parts of a thing. The Latin elementum renders a Greek word that meant that which stands in a row. Its own root is obscure. One guess ties it to a Latin verb for nourish, making it kin to the word for food.

Another guess sees in it the letters L, M, N, the first three of the second part of the alphabet, like our ABC. Apart from chemistry, the word names the rudiments of any science. Euclid's Elements of Geometry is the classic case, and Saint Paul speaks of beggarly elements. In mathematics it can mean a basic concept at work in a problem. In electricity it names the cell of a battery.
britannica-1911-elephant:
Elephant is the name for the two living kinds of the Proboscidea, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. The name is also stretched to cover their near extinct kin in the same line. Full traits of the group and of the genus Elephas are given in a linked piece, so this text picks out how the two living kinds differ. 

The more specialised of the two is the Indian or Asiatic elephant, Elephas maximus. It is marked by the deep complexity of its molar teeth, the text says. Those teeth are built of a great number of tall, thin plates of enamel and dentine. The gaps between the plates are filled with cement in each tooth. Its ears are of moderate size, and the tip of its trunk bears a distinct finger like growth.
britannica-1911-elisavetpol-government:
Elisavetpol was a government of Russia in Transcaucasia, bordered by Tiflis and Daghestan to the north, Baku to the east, Erivan to the west, and Persia to the south. The hosted file holds several articles together; this entry is the government article within it. Its area is given as 16,721 square miles. The land ranges from snowy Caucasus peaks to dry steppes beside the Kura river.

The country falls into three zones: high Caucasus slopes, arid Kura steppes needing irrigation, and the Armenian plateau cut by tributaries of the Aras. Nearly one-fifth of the surface is forest. The population was 885,379 in 1897 and was estimated at 953,300 in 1906. Tatars form 56 percent and Armenians 33 percent, with Kurds, Russians, and smaller groups besides. Wheat, maize, barley, oats, rye, and rice are grown, and cotton planting has begun.
britannica-1911-embankment:
Embankment, in engineering, is a mound of earth or stone, usually narrow beside its length, raised by art above the general level of the ground. Such mounds serve two main classes of purpose. They keep railways, canals, and roads level where a valley or low ground must be crossed. They also hold back or limit water, forming the walls of reservoirs or shielding low land from river floods and the sea.

The word has also come to mean the mass of material, faced with a stone wall and guarded by a parapet, set along a river bank in a city. The Thames Embankment in London is the standing example, carrying a broad road with the Underground railway beneath it. The entry sets an embankment apart from a quay. A quay is confined to places where ships are loaded and unloaded, though the building method may be the same.
britannica-1911-embezzlement:
Embezzlement, from the Anglo-French embesilement, to destroy, is in English law a special form of theft. It differs from common theft in two points. The crime is committed by a person standing as clerk or servant to the owner of the property. Also, the property, when taken, is already in that clerk's or servant's hands.

The special crime arose because larceny required goods to be taken out of the owner's possession, so servants could steal goods trusted to them and escape the law. A statute of Henry VIII in 1529 made it a felony for servants to convert caskets, jewels, money, or goods given into their keeping. A gap shown by a case in 1799, over a clerk and a cheque, brought a new act that same year. The law in force is the Larceny Act of 1861, whose section 68 the entry quotes.
britannica-1911-epiphanius-saint:
Epiphanius, Saint (about 315–402), was a celebrated Church Father, born early in the 4th century at Bezanduca, a village of Palestine near Eleutheropolis. He is said to have been of Jewish stock. In his youth he lived in Egypt and took up an ascetic life. 

In 367 Epiphanius became bishop of Constantia, once Salamis, the chief city of Cyprus, and held that see until his death in 402. Zealous for truth but passionate and bigoted, he gave himself to spreading monasticism and to fighting heresy, above all Origen and his followers. His chief work is the Panarion, a “medicine chest” of remedies for eighty kinds of heretical belief. Its accounts of the older errors, where it keeps large pieces of Irenaeus in the original Greek, are more trustworthy than its reports on the heresies of its own day.
britannica-1911-equivalent: Equivalent, in chemistry, is the share of an element that joins with one unit weight of hydrogen. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica adds that it can also replace that unit weight. Multiplied by the valency, it gives the atomic weight. The finding of such weights is left to the article on stoichiometry. In a wider sense, the word marks amounts of stuffs that cancel each other out. Caustic soda and acids are given as cases of that wider use.
britannica-1911-esher-william-baliol-bre:
William Baliol Brett, later Lord Esher, is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English lawyer and judge who rose to the post of master of the rolls. Born in eighteen seventeen, he studied at Westminster and at Cambridge. He was called to the bar in eighteen forty.

The entry tracks his odd path into parliament and his work as a law officer. It notes his part in a noted trial after a bomb attack in London. It then covers his years as a judge and his push to cut delay and cost in court. He left the bench in eighteen ninety seven and was made a viscount.
britannica-1911-establishment:
Establishment, in the sense treated here, means a special link between the state and a church, and this 1911 Britannica entry works out what the word covers. The term comes through French from a Latin root meaning to make stable, and in plain speech it can mean the act of setting something up or the thing set up. The entry sets that loose sense aside and deals only with the church and state case.

Its best short account is that establishment means a clear, distinct tie between the state and one religious body that other bodies of the same kind do not share. Every group, the entry notes, stands under the state's rule in the same basic ways, through law and through duties over property and members. Establishment is none of that. It is the extra tie, the special rights or standing granted on top.
britannica-1911-exelmans-rene-joseph-isi:
René Joseph Isidore Exelmans, count and marshal of France (1775–1852), was born at Bar-le-Duc on 13 November 1775. He volunteered in 1791, made lieutenant in 1797, and served as aide to Generals Éblé and Broussier. In Italy in April 1799 he won a captaincy of dragoons. He followed Murat through the campaigns of 1805, 1806 and 1807. Valour at Austerlitz made him colonel, and his conduct at Eylau made him general of brigade in 1807.

Taken prisoner in Spain in 1808, he was held in England until 1811. Murat then made him grand-master of horse at Naples. He rejoined France for the Russian campaign and won divisional rank at Borodino. Tried in January 1815 for treasonable dealings with Murat, he was acquitted. Napoleon made him a peer and gave him the second cavalry corps for Waterloo. He later called Ney's execution an abominable assassination and lived years in exile.
britannica-1911-fabian-saint:
Saint Fabian was pope at Rome and died as a martyr in the year 250, as a 1911 Britannica entry relates. He was chosen in January 236 to follow Pope Anteros in the post. One old account says a dove lit on his head as the church met to choose. He was a stranger in the city, yet the sign marked him out at once.

He died in the harsh purge under the emperor Decius on January the twentieth. His body was laid in the catacomb of Calixtus, where a stone marks the place. The entry credits him with better order in the Rome church and care for martyr records. It also notes high praise from Cyprian of Carthage.
britannica-1911-falkland-lucius-cary-2nd:
Lucius Cary, second Viscount Falkland, who lived from about 1610 to 1643, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Sir Henry Cary, lord deputy of Ireland, and of Elizabeth Tanfield. He was educated at Trinity College in Dublin. In 1625 he inherited the manors of Great Tew and Burford in Oxfordshire from his grandfather.

At about twenty one Falkland wed Lettice Morrison. A quarrel with his father led him to leave England for service in the Dutch army, though he soon came back. On his father's death in 1633 he became Viscount Falkland. His mother had turned to the Roman Catholic faith, and some sought to draw him the same way. His studies, under the sway of Chillingworth, led him to settle questions by reason rather than by tradition. At Great Tew he gathered a circle of gifted and learned men round him.
britannica-1911-false-point:
False Point, a snug harbour of Bengal, is placed in a port entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits in the Cuttack district of India on that coast. Famine men in 1867 called it the best harbour on that shore. Its name came from ships that mistook it for Point Palmyras. That true point lies one degree of coast to the north.

The berth is safe, roomy, and shut in by land on all sides. Big ships must still lie out in an open roadstead. No one used the port till it was opened in 1860. The Orissa canals then built up its trade at speed. Rice and oil seeds flow out to far ports from its quays.
britannica-1911-fiacre-saint:
Saint Fiacre was a hermit of the seventh century who came from a noble Irish line. Little is known of his life in Ireland. Old tales say he left home and went to France with friends. There he sought the bishop of Meaux and asked to live alone in the woods.

The bishop gave him land at Breuil in Brie, where he built a small priory and a guest house. He won fame for wonders and drew guests such as Saint Killian. His bones were later moved to Meaux. He is still honoured as patron of Brie and of those who tend gardens.
britannica-1911-fillan-saint:
Saint Fillan is a 1911 Britannica article on two Scottish saints of one name. Fillan is also spelled Faelan. Both saints were of Irish origin. Their lives are of a purely legendary character, the text says.

The Fillan whose feast falls on the twentieth of June had churches in his honour. One stood at Ballyheyland, in Queen's county, Ireland. Another stood at Loch Earn, in Perthshire. The other saint is commemorated on the ninth of January. He was specially venerated at Cluain Mavscua, in County Westmeath. By the eighth or ninth century he was honoured at Strathfillan, in Perthshire. An ancient monastery there bore his name. Like most houses of early times, it was afterwards secularized. Its lay-abbot held high rank in the Scottish kingdom. That was in the reign of William the Lion. Church readers get two lives folded into one short entry.
britannica-1911-florian-saint:
Florian is a saint and martyr honoured in Upper Austria, as the 1911 Britannica entry recounts. In the eighth century Puoche was named as the place of his tomb. On that site rose the famed house of canons regular that bears his name, and it stands to this day. His written life is old, but of no worth as history. Its tale is borrowed from the life of Saint Irenaeus of Sirmium.

The cult reached Poland when his relics were brought there in 1183. Casimir of Poland built him a church at Cracow. He is shown as a warrior with a vessel, pouring out water on flames. His aid is sought against fire, and his feast day falls on the fourth of May.
britannica-1911-font:
Font, from Latin fons, a fountain or spring, is the vessel used in churches to hold the water for Christian baptism. In the apostolic age baptism was given at rivers or natural springs, and its first form was immersion in the water. Pouring water on the head, called infusion, came early into use in the west and north of Europe. Immersion was awkward there and sometimes dangerous, while the eastern churches never accepted the change. Sprinkling was also allowed as valid, though early examples are rare.

These ways of baptizing shaped the vessels. After persecution ended, special buildings arose for the rite, with a large basin where candidates could be immersed. The long article then follows the font through the ages of church building. It describes Norman, Early English, Decorated and Perpendicular fonts, their stems, steps, panelling and heraldic carving, with named examples in English churches.
britannica-1911-francais-antoine-count:
Antoine Francais, count Francais of Nantes (1756-1836), was a French politician and author born at Beaurepaire in Isere. In 1791 Loire Inferieure elected him to the Legislative Assembly. There he won note for violent attacks on the farmers-general, the pope and the priests. He was not re-elected to the Convention. During the Terror, having belonged to the Girondin party, he had to hide in the mountains to save his life from the men then ruling Paris and the provinces.

In 1798 Isere sent Francais to the Council of Five Hundred, where he became a secretary. The next year he voted against the Directory. Under the Consulate he served as prefect of Charente Inferieure and rose to the council of state. In 1804 he gained the great post of director-general of the indirect taxes. His services were rewarded with titles.
britannica-1911-francois-de-neufchateau-:
Nicolas Louis François de Neufchâteau (1750-1828), French statesman and poet, was born at Saffais in Lorraine on 17 April 1750, the son of a schoolteacher. A book of verse printed when he was fourteen won praise from Rousseau and Voltaire, and the town of Neufchâteau gave him its name. He later served as procureur-général at Santo Domingo and sat in the revolutionary assemblies.

As minister of the interior from 1797, he gave France its system of inland navigation, helped open the Louvre museum, and promoted the first great show of industrial products. He presided over the Senate from 1804 to 1806 and asked Napoleon to take the title of emperor. Made a count in 1808, he retired in 1814 to study farming, and also left editions of Pascal and Gil Blas.
britannica-1911-giant:
Giant is a word for beings like men but huge in size and strength. Its word entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word came through French from Latin gigas and Greek gigas roots. In classic myth such beings stand apart from plain wonder tale beasts.

Hesiod sings in the Theogony of Giants born from Heaven and Earth. Such titans could heap mountains high to scale the sky in war. Old Greek lore held giants to be earth born native races of old. That root link is in doubt, yet the thought was well known then. The Bible tells of tall races in Palestine, such as the Anakim.
britannica-1911-gilbert-nicolas-joseph-l:
Nicolas Joseph Laurent Gilbert (1751-1780) was a French poet, born at Fontenay-le-Chateau in Lorraine in 1751. The 1911 Britannica entry has him educated at the college of Dole, then living a half-scholarly life at Nancy. In 1774 he found his way to Paris.

As an opponent of the Encyclopaedists and a praiser of Louis XV, he won considerable pensions. The entry credits the satire of pieces such as Mon Apologie of 1778 and Le Dix-huitieme Siecle of 1775 with preserving his name. Later writers, Alfred de Vigny among them, cast him as a victim of his philosophic opponents' spite. His best-known verses are the Ode imitee de plusieurs psaumes, usually called Adieux a la vie. He died in Paris on 12 November 1780, after a fall from his horse.
britannica-1911-gillingham-kent:
Gillingham is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a borough of Kent, England, on the Medway river just east of Chatham. The entry gives population counts for eighteen ninety one and nineteen hundred one. That count grew fast in those ten years.

Most people in the town worked with their hands, the entry says. Many were employed in the Chatham dockyards nearby. Cement and brick works in the area gave more jobs. The church of Saint Mary Magdalene holds work from several periods and some early brasses. A great battle between Edmund Ironside and Canute is placed at Gillingham by tradition.
britannica-1911-giraud-giovanni-count:
Giovanni Giraud (1776-1834), count and Italian dramatist of French origin, was born at Rome. The 1911 Britannica entry says he showed an early passion for the theatre. His first play, L'Onesta non si vince, was produced with success in 1798, when he was twenty-two.

He took part in politics as an active supporter of Pius VI, but plays were his main work. In 1809 he became director-general of the Italian theatres. The entry judges his comedies bright and amusing on the stage, but of no particular literary quality. The best of them are named as Gelosie per equivoco of 1807 and L'Ajo nell' imbarazzo of 1824. His collected comedies appeared in 1823, and his Teatro domestico in 1825. He died at Naples in 1834.
britannica-1911-gough-hugh-gough-viscoun:
Hugh Gough, Viscount Gough, a British field marshal, opens a long war life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Limerick in seventeen seventy nine, he took a post in the army as a teen. He served at the Cape of Good Hope and in the West Indies. At Porto Rico, Surinam, and Saint Lucia he saw hard fight in his youth. In eighteen oh nine he was called to the war in Spain.

At Talavera he was hit hard and his horse was shot dead. Wellington backed a rare field rise in rank for his work there. His men took a French eagle at Barrosa in a proud feat. At Vitoria his unit took the baton of a French marshal. Wounds and Spain knighthood from the king close the Spain years. India and China posts came in his late years.
britannica-1911-gozzi-carlo-count:
Carlo Gozzi, a count from an old family in Venice, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. Born in Venice in March 1722, he joined the army in Dalmatia at age sixteen. Three years later he came back to Venice. There he won fame as a wit in a club that worked to keep Tuscan writing pure.

Gozzi fought the new French style plays of Chiari and Goldoni. His poem Tartana came out in 1757, and his fairy tale play about three oranges came out in 1761. The play mocked both men and used the Sacchi troupe. Its magic scenes pleased crowds so much that Gozzi wrote more fairy tale plays.
britannica-1911-ground-rent:
Ground rent was a Roman law payment called the solarium. The lessee of a building plot paid it yearly. The lease was a perpetual one. In English law the term has a settled meaning. It is the rent at which land is let for building. The charge falls on the land alone. It does not cover the buildings placed on it. So it normally sits lower than a rack rent.

The landlord keeps a reversionary interest in those buildings. That security made ground rents a favoured investment. Trustees could invest in freehold ground rents within set limits. The discussion works through cases on meaning and devise. It covers distress and apportionment too. It then turns to the Scots ground-annual. That payment fills the same place in Scots law. Irish and American practice close the account. Pennsylvania banned new irredeemable ground rents in 1850.
britannica-1911-guibert-of-nogent:
Guibert of Nogent (1053–1124) was a historian and theologian. He was born of noble parents at Clermont-en-Beauvoisis. His parents dedicated him from infancy to the church. He studied at the Benedictine abbey of St Germer. At first he loved the secular poets. Anselm of Bec later turned him toward theology. In 1104 he became head of Notre Dame de Nogent.

His autobiography, De vita sua, came late in his life. It gives vivid glimpses of his times and customs. His account of the commune of Laon is a first-order document. His history of the First Crusade appeared about 1110. Much of it paraphrases the anonymous Gesta Francorum. Where that source ends, his book thins into notes and anecdotes. His works also include Moralia on Genesis. He wrote sharply against abuses in relic worship.
britannica-1911-halfway-covenant: Halfway Covenant was an expedient taken up in the Congregational churches of New England between 1657 and 1662, as a short 1911 Britannica entry explains. Under its terms, baptized persons of moral life and orthodox belief could gain baptism for their children and other church benefits. That standing stopped short of the full membership that admitted a person to the communion of the Lord Supper. Readers who want the wider story are sent on to the main entry on Congregationalism in America.
britannica-1911-hampden-henry-bouverie-w:
Henry Bouverie William Brand, 1st Viscount Hampden (1812–1892), was speaker of the House of Commons. He was the second son of the 21st Baron Dacre. He descended from John Hampden in the female line. He entered Parliament as a Liberal in 1852. For some time he served as his party's chief whip. In 1872 the Commons elected him speaker. He kept the chair until February 1884.

His speakership faced systematic Irish Nationalist obstruction. On 2 February 1881 he refused further debate on Forster's Coercion Bill. That step led directly to the closure in parliamentary procedure. He was created Viscount Hampden in 1884. The Dacre barony devolved on him in 1890. He died on 14 March 1892. His son succeeded him as second viscount. That son governed New South Wales from 1895 to 1899.
britannica-1911-hatchment:
Hatchment is a heraldry article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Properly it means a shield granted for some act of note, or achievement. The word is a worn form of achievement, traced through several old spellings. Achievement itself comes from a French word tied to bringing a thing to a head, or conclusion.

In the entry's day the term was mostly used for funeral shields, it says. Such a shield sits in a black diamond shaped frame on the wall of a dead person's house. It is placed over the entrance at the level of the second floor. It stays for six to twelve months, then moves to the parish church. The custom was falling out of use, though still not rare. The entry then sets out how the shield differs for a bachelor or a single woman.
britannica-1911-hennebont:
Hennebont is a town of western France, in the department of Morbihan, 6 m. N.E. of Lorient by road, with 7,250 people in 1906. It stands about 10 m. from the mouth of the Blavet, which splits it in three: the walled Ville Close, the Ville Neuve on the left bank, and the Vieille Ville, older than either, on the right.

Ramparts and a gateway with towers guard the Ville Close, whose streets hold houses of the 16th and 17th centuries. The chief church is Notre-Dame de Paradis, of the 16th century, with a carved stone spire. A small river port takes ships of 200 to 300 tons, and a big foundry makes tin-plate for sardine boxes. Boat-building, tanning, distilling and granite work also go on. The town is famed for its stand in 1342, when the widow of Jean de Montfort held it against Philip of Valois and Charles of Blois.
britannica-1911-henry-ii-the-saint:
Henry II (973–1024), called the Saint, was Roman emperor, son of Henry the Quarrelsome, duke of Bavaria, and great-grandson of Henry I the Fowler. Born on the 6th of May 973, he was first meant for holy orders and schooled at Hildesheim and Regensburg. That plan was dropped, but he kept a strong care for church affairs and monastic reform. He became duke of Bavaria in 995.

When Otto III died childless in 1002, Henry seized the imperial insignia and pressed his claim. On the 7th of June 1002 the Franks and Bavarians chose him king at Mainz, and he won over Swabia, Thuringia, Saxony and Lorraine. War with Boleslaus I of Poland over Bohemia, Meissen and Lusatia ran through the reign. In May 1004 he was crowned king of the Lombards at Pavia. He and his wife Kunigunde were said to have taken vows of chastity. Pope Eugenius III canonized him in 1146.
britannica-1911-hill-rowland-hill-1st-vi:
Rowland Hill, 1st Viscount Hill (1772–1842), was a British general, born near Hawkstone, Shropshire, in 1772, a nephew of the preacher Rowland Hill. Gazetted in 1790, he served as a staff officer at Toulon and was wounded at Alexandria in 1801. By 1803 he was a brigadier-general.

In 1808 Hill took a brigade to Portugal, and from Vimeira to Vittoria he was Wellington's ablest helper. He led a brigade at Vimeira, Corunna and Oporto, and a division at Talavera. In 1811 he destroyed Girard's detachment at Arroyo-dos-Molinos. Early in 1812, now a lieutenant-general, he stormed the works of Almaraz on the Tagus, then led Wellington's right wing.
britannica-1911-howe-william-howe-5th-vi:
William Howe, 5th Viscount Howe (1729–1814), was a British general, younger brother of the admiral Earl Howe. He entered the cavalry in 1746 and became lieutenant a year later. After his regiment was disbanded in 1749 he became captain in Lord Bury's 20th regiment, where Wolfe was then a field officer. He was major in 1756 and lieutenant-colonel of the 58th in 1757.

Howe commanded the 58th at the capture of Louisburg. In Wolfe's Quebec expedition he led a composite light battalion, headed the landing at Wolfe's Cove, and fought on the Plains of Abraham. He then held his regiment in the defence of Quebec through 1759–1760 and led a brigade in the advance on Montreal. The long life follows him into the American war, where he held the chief command against the colonists, and through the criticism that followed his conduct of it.
britannica-1911-hubner-joseph-alexander-:
Joseph Alexander Hübner, who lived from 1811 to 1892, was an Austrian diplomat. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth in Vienna. His birth name was Hafenbredl, later changed to Hübner. He began state work in 1833 under Metternich. That chief trusted him fast and sent him to Paris in 1837. Posts at Lisbon and Leipzig followed. In 1848 he was sent to Milan on court business.

The revolt that year seized him as a hostage for some months. Back home, he compiled the papers of the emperor's abdication. His journal of that year came out in 1891, in French and German. It is prized as a key to the plots of the time. In 1849 he became envoy to France. His sway helped keep Austria friendly with the allies in the Crimean war. He spoke for Austria at the Paris congress of 1856.
britannica-1911-ignatiev-nicholas-pavlov:
Nicholas Pavlovich Ignatiev, Count Ignatiev, a Russian diplomat who lived from 1832 to 1908, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Saint Petersburg in January 1832. His father had won the tsar's favour by his loyalty during a military plot in 1825. At seventeen Ignatiev became an officer of the Guards.

His career in diplomacy began at the congress of Paris after the Crimean War. In 1858 he was sent on a risky mission to Khiva and Bokhara, and eluded a plan to hold him hostage. He came home with a treaty of friendship from Bokhara. Next he served as envoy to the court of Peking. There, in 1860, he played on Chinese fears of the Anglo French advance. Russia gained not only the left bank of the Amur but a large tract of land and coast south of it.
britannica-1911-implement:
Implement comes from the Latin implementum, a filling up, from implere, to fill. In common use it means a tool, and in the plural the set of tools needed for a trade or for one piece of work. It is also the broadest term for the weapons and tools that survive from early human life.

In later Latin, implementa covered all the things needed to stock a house or farm. The word was used for house furniture, for the robes and sacred vessels of a church, and for items of clothing. In Scots law it keeps the old sense of filling up, meaning full performance of a contract or agreement, so to implement a contract is to carry it out.
britannica-1911-infant:
Infant is the subject of a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes through French from a Latin word for one who cannot speak. In common use it means a very young child. In law it means a person under full age. Such a person bears legal limits that adults do not.

The text notes that the age of full age varies widely across legal systems. In Roman law, puberty was fixed at fourteen for boys and twelve for girls. Below that age a child stood under a guardian called a tutor. After puberty a lesser infancy lasted to age twenty five. In that stage a young person's acts could be undone, and a curator managed the estate. The tutor cared for the person, the curator for the property.
britannica-1911-irkutsk-government:
Irkutsk is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a vast province of Asiatic Russia in east Siberia. Lake Baikal and wild lands bound it on three of its sides. A belt of plains forms the most peopled part of the province.

The entry tells how a great road, now a rail line, runs that plain belt. High ranges of the Sayan chain fill the south west of the land. Snow caps crown the top peak of that chain all year long. Side chains strike off to the north east at a high reach. Deep wear by wind and water shaped the jumbled hills over long ages.
britannica-1911-jacini-stefano-count:
Stefano Jacini, an Italian statesman and writer on farm and land questions who lived from 1827 to 1891, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came from an old, rich Lombard family and studied in Switzerland, Milan, and German schools. In the years of Austrian rule he turned to books and to land studies.

His work on landed property in Lombardy, printed in 1856, won a prize in Milan. A later study laid bare the harms of Austrian rule in the Valtellina. Jacini served as minister of public works under Cavour and later prime ministers. He backed the St Gotthard tunnel plan and the pact with Prussia for the war of 1866. From 1881 to 1886 he led a large inquiry into farm life in Italy.
britannica-1911-joseph-new-testament:
Joseph, in the New Testament, is the husband of Mary, the mother of Jesus. He is shown as a descendant of the house of David in the text. His family line appears in two forms that differ, in Matthew and in Luke. The form in Luke is most likely the fuller and truer in detail. The form in Matthew is clearly built in a set pattern of generations.

Of Joseph's own life the Bible records almost nothing at all, the entry says. Three facts are shared by both birth accounts in the Gospels. He was of David's line, Mary was betrothed to him, and he lived at Nazareth. Each account handles those facts in a different way and order. In Matthew, Joseph stands in the front of the tale. In Luke he is set wholly in the background of events.
britannica-1911-joseph-old-testament:
Joseph in the Old Testament is treated in a long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is the son of the patriarch Jacob by Rachel. The name also covers a tribe of Israel descended from him. The article first weighs what the name itself may mean in Hebrew.

Unlike the other sons of Jacob, Joseph counts as two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh. With Benjamin close beside them, these formed the sons of Rachel in the tribal scheme. The house of Joseph held the centre of Palestine, from Esdraelon to the hills of Benjamin. In practice the name came to stand for the northern kingdom as a whole. The piece then recalls the famed story told in Genesis. The envied younger son was seized by his brothers at Dothan and sold to traders. Carried down to Egypt, he won the king's favour by reading a dream aright.
britannica-1911-jourdan-jean-baptiste-co:
Jean Baptiste Jourdan, a marshal of France who lived from 1762 to 1833, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Limoges in April 1762, he was apprenticed as a boy to a silk merchant of Lyons. In 1776 he enlisted to serve in the American War of Independence. Invalided out in 1784, he married and set up in trade at Limoges.
