When the revolutionary wars began, Jourdan volunteered and rose fast. By 1793 he was a general of division in command of the Army of the North. In October 1793 he won the key victory of Wattignies. His moderate views then made him a suspect, and he went back to trade for a time. Restored in 1794, he took command of the Army of Sambre-et-Meuse. The article follows his hard fights to force a crossing of the Sambre.
britannica-1911-kalnoky-gustav-siegmund-:
Count Gustav Siegmund Kalnóky (1832–1898) was an Austro Hungarian statesman. He was born at Lettowitz in Moravia on the 29th of December 1832, of an old Transylvanian family. After some years in a hussar regiment he entered the diplomatic service in 1854. He kept his link with the army and reached the rank of general in 1879.

He was secretary at London from 1860 to 1870, served at Rome and Copenhagen, and in 1880 became ambassador at St Petersburg. His success in Russia won him, on Baron Haymerle's death in 1881, the post of foreign minister for Austria Hungary. He held it for fourteen years, taking little part in the inner quarrels of the Dual Monarchy. He kept firm the alliance with Germany made by those before him, and worked with Bismarck in the steps that brought Italy into the alliance.
britannica-1911-kaluga-government:
Kaluga is a government of middle Russia, ringed by the governments of Moscow, Smolensk, Orel, and Tula, with an area of 11,942 square miles. Its surface is a rolling plain, reaching 800 to 900 feet in the southwest, and cut deep by watercourses in the northeast. The Oka, a main feeder of the Volga, and its streams the Zhizdra and Ugra drain all but a western strip, which the Bolva carries to the Dnieper.

The land is built chiefly of coal bearing beds, with patches of soft Jurassic clays and limestones. Boulder clay covers the north, with ridges of boulders brought in the glacial age from Finland. The mean yearly temperature is 41 degrees. Iron ores are the chief mineral wealth, and nearly 40,000 people work in mining. Coal beds occur in several places and some are worked, and fireclay, china clay, and chalk add to the yield.
britannica-1911-kazan-government:
Kazan is a government of middle Russia, ringed by the governments of Vyatka, Ufa, Samara, Simbirsk, Nizhniy Novgorod, and Kostroma. Its area is 24,601 square miles. It belongs to the basins of the Volga and its feeder the Kama, and those streams split it into three regions.

The first region, right of the main river, is cut by deep ravines and two ranges of hills, one of them skirting the Volga. The second, between the left banks of the Volga and the Kama, is open steppe. The third matches the first in its eastern part and is forest covered in the west. Marls, limestones, and sandstones of Permian or Triassic age are the chief rocks. Jurassic beds show in a small part of the south, and Tertiary rocks run along the left bank of the Volga. The survey goes on through climate, farms, and peoples in the usual full order.
britannica-1911-keith-george-keith-elphi:
George Keith Elphinstone, Viscount Keith (1746–1823), was a British admiral. He was the fifth son of the 10th Lord Elphinstone and was born in Elphinstone Tower, near Stirling, on the 7th of January 1746. Two of his brothers went to sea, and he followed them into the navy in 1761, in the Gosport, then commanded by Captain Jervis, the later Earl St Vincent.

In 1767 he sailed to the East Indies in the Company's service. He put £2000 lent by an uncle to such good use in a private trading venture that he laid the base of a handsome fortune. He became lieutenant in 1770, commander in 1772, and post captain in 1775. In the American war he served against the privateers and at the taking of Charleston. In January 1781, in command of the Warwick, he captured a Dutch ship of equal force that had beaten off an English vessel days before.
britannica-1911-kenmure-william-gordon-6:
William Gordon, 6th Viscount Kenmure (d. 1716), was a Jacobite leader, son of Alexander, the 5th viscount. He was descended from the stock of Sir John Gordon of Lochinvar, whose grandson was made Viscount Kenmure in 1633. The family had in general held to the Presbyterian cause, though the 5th viscount had in time joined the court of the exiled Stuarts.

The 6th viscount's siding with the Pretender in 1715 is said to have owed much to his wife Mary Dalzell, sister of the earl of Carnwath. He raised the royal standard of Scotland at Lochmaben on the 12th of October 1715. About two hundred gentlemen joined him there, Carnwath, Nithsdale, and Winton among them. The entry follows the rising to its failure and to his fate as a captured rebel lord.
britannica-1911-keppel-augustus-keppel-v:
Augustus Keppel, Viscount Keppel (1725–1786), was a British admiral, second son of the second earl of Albemarle. He was born on the 25th of April 1725 and went to sea at the age of ten. He already had five years of service when he was posted to the Centurion and sent with Anson round the world in 1740.

He had a narrow escape from death at the taking of Paita in November 1741, and he was named acting lieutenant in 1742. In 1744 he rose to commander and post captain, and he was actively employed until the peace of 1748. In 1747 he ran his ship the Maidstone ashore near Belleisle while chasing a French vessel. A court martial cleared him with honour, and he was given a new command. After the peace he was sent into the Mediterranean against the corsairs of Algiers.
britannica-1911-kovno-government:
Kovno, in Lithuanian Kauna, is a government of north-western Russia. It is bounded by Courland and Vitebsk to the north, Vilna to the south-east, and Suwalki and East Prussia to the south. Its area is 15,687 square miles. The land is mostly level, broken only by two low ridges that never pass 800 feet. Many lakes and marshes lie in the flat hollows, and forests cover about a quarter of the surface. The Niemen, Windau, Courland Aa and Dvina drain it.

The people numbered 1,553,244 in 1897 and an estimated 1,683,600 in 1906. Lithuanians and Zhmuds together form 74 per cent, Jews 14 per cent and Poles 9 per cent. Farming is the work, with 63 per cent of the land under crops. Grain and potatoes are exported, flax is grown, and dairying thrives. Each year 18,000 to 24,000 men must leave to find work. The factories are chiefly distilleries, tobacco works, steam flour-mills and hardware shops.
britannica-1911-kursk-government:
Kursk is a government of middle Russia, bounded by Orel to the north, Voronezh to the east, Kharkov to the south and Chernigov to the west. Its area is 17,932 square miles. It takes up the southern slope of the central plateau, 700 to 1100 feet high and cut deep by ravines. Chalk, iron-stone, potters' clay and phosphates are dug here. Some four hundred streams cross it, but none serves as a waterway.

A coat of rich loess covers the land, and Kursk belongs almost wholly to the black-earth region. Near Byelgorod lies a noted magnetic anomaly, an oval patch 20 miles long and 12 miles wide. The people numbered 2,391,091 in 1897, with an estimated 2,797,000 in 1906. They are thoroughly Russian, three-quarters Great Russians and one-quarter Little Russians, and 94 per cent are peasants, who own over 59 per cent of the land and live mostly in large villages.
britannica-1911-kutais-government:
Kutais is a government of Russian Transcaucasia, lying between the Caucasus range on the north and the Black Sea on the west, with Tiflis on the east and Kars on the south. Its area is 14,313 square miles. It takes in the districts of Guria, Mingrelia, Imeretia, Abkhasia and Svanetia. The land falls into four parts: the lowlands of the Rion river, the south slopes of the Caucasus, the west slopes of the Suram mountains, and the slopes of the Armenian highlands.

The lowlands run to over 2400 square miles. They are barren near the shore but very fertile higher up the Rion. The climate is moist and warm, and the lowlands often pass a winter with no frost at all. Rain, driven in by west winds, ranges from 50 to 120 inches a year. Spurs of the Pontic range rise to 11,240 feet, cut by deep gorges.
britannica-1911-landlord-and-tenant:
Landlord and tenant is a branch of law on the renting of land. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with Roman law. There the bond grew from the contract of letting and hiring. Long leases and holding at will had their own forms. The entry then turns to the law of England. Scotland and Ireland match it on the main point.

English law knows no full private ownership of land. The crown is the last owner of all land. Even a fee simple estate is, in form, a tenancy. The article sticks to holdings made by lease and hire. A lease, a pact for a lease, or transfer can create the bond. Most kinds of land and rights may be let. Some things may not, such as church livings and posts of trust. A lease made by or to a child can be undone at his choice.
britannica-1911-lasalle-antoine-chevalie:
Antoine Lasalle was a French soldier of noble birth in Lorraine who lived into the early eighteen hundreds. The 1911 Britannica entry says he joined the army at age eleven and had risen to a junior rank when the revolt broke out. Stripped of his post as a noble, he joined the ranks as a plain man.

The entry then races through a bold career won back by nerve and command. He leapt a horse over a bridge wall to shun capture, saved a fellow chief in Egypt, and broke blade after blade in one fight. At the head of light horse he scared a strong fort town into yield with a small force and no guns, a feat the entry calls rare.
britannica-1911-lauzun-antonin-nompar-de:
Antonin Nompar de Caumont, duc de Lauzun, was a French courtier and soldier born in sixteen thirty two. He was the son of the comte de Lauzun and a daughter of the duc de La Force. He was brought up with the children of a kinsman, a great marshal. One of those children became the one passion of Lauzun's life. He entered the army and served under Turenne, also a kinsman.

In sixteen fifty five Lauzun took his father's post over the king's household troops. He rose fast in the favour of Louis the Fourteenth at court. He became colonel of the royal dragoons and a field marshal in rank. His rough wit and skill at practical jokes pleased the king greatly. But his jealousy and violence were the causes of his undoing. He blocked a meeting the king sought and backed a rival at court.
britannica-1911-law-merchant:
Law Merchant, the body of rules that governed trade deals, is explained in a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Merchants laid down those rules themselves to govern their own dealings. The rules grew from customs shared by traders across Europe. Local twists changed them a little from place to place.

The law merchant arose because the civil law was too slow for the needs of growing trade. Long distance traders wanted courts that acted fast and knew their ways. Guild courts in Italy and fair courts in France and Germany heard such cases. In England the story falls into three stages in the entry. At first it stood apart in its own courts. Then common law courts took it as custom to be proved case by case. Under Lord Mansfield it was moulded into the mercantile law of today.
britannica-1911-leber-jean-michel-consta:
French historian Jean Michel Constant Leber, born at Orleans in seventeen eighty, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was also a keen book collector. His first work was a poem on Joan of Arc in eighteen oh four. A grammar work of the same time drew official notice.

A senior official found him a small post that left time for study. Leber went to Italy with that official, but left soon. He held that attacks on church lands were wrong. Back in Paris he wrote light stage works while he gathered rare old tracts. He kept his post under the restored kings. Later he wrote a close study of the crowning rites of French kings.
britannica-1911-lent: Only a fragment of the Lent entry is held here, a few lines cut from the middle of a longer piece. The scrap opens mid-thought on wheat flour. It states that simnel cakes are still common in Gloucestershire. It adds that the custom of mothering is still kept with care at Usk in Monmouth. Nothing more of the entry survives in the hosted text, so no wider account of its subject can be drawn from what is present.
britannica-1911-letters-patent:
Letters patent are open grants made by the sovereign, and this 1911 Britannica entry explains the form and its uses in English law. Law and good policy alike, it begins, demand that royal grants of land, rights, and freedoms be made with care and in a form the public can reach. Letters patent are that form. The entry sets aside patents for inventions, which are treated under their own heading.

The letters speak in the sovereign's name to all who shall see them and set out a grant of rank, office, monopoly, or other rights. They are left open, not sealed shut, which is what the word patent means here, and they are kept on the Patent Rolls where any subject may read them. The entry goes on to the many uses of the form.
britannica-1911-lizard-point: Lizard Point, the farthest south point of Great Britain, is described in a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in Cornwall, and ships bound up the Channel most often sight it first. Two lighthouses stand there. Grand cliffs, small bays, and caves draw many visitors. Coloured veins in the serpentine rock are a noted trait. A reef called the Stags runs south and is a danger to ships.
britannica-1911-llantrisant:
Llantrisant is the subject of a town entry in the 1911 Britannica. The town lies in Glamorganshire in Wales. It sits in a pass with a fine view south over the vale. The text gives the parish count in 1901 as just over ten thousand souls. Two rail lines served the town and linked it with Cardiff and London. A ruined fort stood above the town on a steep hill.

The past of the town fills the rest of the entry. The fort was once held to rank next to Cardiff in strength. King Edward the Second was seized near the town in 1327. Charters from the 1300s and 1400s are listed in full. The old town body was wound up in 1883. Welsh was still the main tongue when the entry was made.
britannica-1911-mallow-plant:
Mallow, known to botanists as Malva, is the type genus of the mallow order, with about sixteen kinds of annual and lasting herbs. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article sets out the marks of the group and its best known kinds. The flowers are white or pinkish, never yellow, and the leaves are veined like rays and often lobed.

Three kinds grow wild in Britain: the musk mallow, the creeping dwarf mallow, and the common mallow with reddish purple blooms. The common kind is rich in mucilage, a slimy juice that made it a home remedy for colds and sore throats. The dye called mauve takes its name from this plant's colour. A last part treats the marsh mallow, a plant of salt marshes whose root yields the substance asparagin.
britannica-1911-marot-clement:
Clément Marot, a French poet of kings, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Cahors in the winter of 1496 to 1497. His father Jean was a Norman poet of fair note himself. Jean held a court post as poet and annal writer to Anne. The boy was brought into France, his own phrase, in 1506.

At Paris the young Marot learned law and the craft of verse. His father took great pains to teach him that craft well. The reigning mode was stiff, showy, and full of old figures. Ballade and rondeau forms bound that verse in tight rules. Marot drilled in that mode with care in his youth. He would do more than any man to cast it down.
britannica-1911-melbourne-william-lamb-2:
William Lamb, second Viscount Melbourne, an English statesman who lived from 1779 to 1848, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second son of the first viscount, whose father had made a large fortune from the law. After Trinity College at Cambridge, William read law at Glasgow and was called to the bar in 1804.

In 1805 Lamb wed Lady Caroline Ponsonby, who won some fame as a novelist with Glenarvon, though the pair parted in 1825. He entered Parliament in 1806 and joined the opposition under Fox, whom he greatly admired. His liberal leanings were never firm, the entry notes, and he often backed Lord Liverpool in his long tenure. In the short ministry of Canning in 1827 he served as chief secretary, a step on the road to the top of British politics.
britannica-1911-merchant: Merchant is a word explained in a brief note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It comes through French from Latin words for trade and for goods. It names a trader, one who buys and sells goods for gain. In the usage of the day the word is most often kept for a dealer who sells in bulk. It serves as well for a man who trades on a large scale with lands abroad. That is the whole of the note.
britannica-1911-mercury-element:
Mercury, the metal element, is the subject of a chemistry entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives its symbol and atomic weight at the start. It stands out from all other metals by being liquid at common temperatures. That trait gave it the English name quicksilver and a Greek Latin name meaning water silver.

The text traces how far back knowledge of the metal goes. It was not known to the ancient Jews, nor named by the earliest Greek writers. Theophrastus, about three hundred years before Christ, mentions it as made from cinnabar. Copper and vinegar were used in that early process, the entry explains.
britannica-1911-meuse-department:
Meuse, a department of north eastern France, is the subject of a regional entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was formed out of part of Lorraine and part of Champagne. The entry gives it 280,220 people in 1906 and an area of 2,409 square miles. Belgium and the Ardennes bound it on the north, and the Vosges and other departments on the south.

About half the department drains to the river Meuse, shut in west by the wooded Argonne and east by the Cotes de Meuse hills. The other half sends its waters to the Seine by streams that rise within it. The highest ground, at 1,388 feet, lies to the south west on the ridge between the two basins. Heights sink gradually from south to north, yet seldom fall below a thousand feet.
britannica-1911-milner-alfred-milner-vis:
Alfred Milner, Viscount Milner (born 1854), was a British statesman and colonial administrator, born at Bonn, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. He was educated at Tübingen, at King's College, London, and at Balliol College, Oxford, where he won scholarship after scholarship. He graduated with a first in classics in 1877 and was elected a fellow of New College.

Milner was called to the bar in 1881 and joined the staff of the Pall Mall Gazette, rising to assistant editor. He left the press in 1885, stood for parliament and lost, and served as private secretary to Goschen. In 1889 he became under-secretary of finance in Egypt, staying four years through the first great reforms there. Back in England in 1892, he was made chairman of the Board of Inland Revenue.
britannica-1911-molesworth-robert-molesw:
Robert Molesworth, first Viscount Molesworth, who lived from 1656 to 1725, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came of an old Northamptonshire family. His father Robert was a Cromwellian who made a fortune in Dublin. The son backed William of Orange in his turn.

In 1695 he became a leading member of the Irish privy council. A viscount title came to him in 1716. Two sons held the title after him in turn. Richard, the third viscount, saved the life of Marlborough at Ramillies and rose to field marshal. The entry traces the title down the line. It also notes a great grandson who was a famed High Church writer and his sons of note.
britannica-1911-orpiment:
Orpiment is a yellow mineral form of arsenic trisulphide, and a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains it. It occurs in small amounts in nature, in lands such as Bohemia and Peru. Its crystals form in the rhombic system and show a bright golden yellow colour. The old Latin name was auripigmentum, and it is also called yellow realgar.

For trade use, an artificial kind is made by heating sulphur with arsenic trioxide. The product ranges from yellow to red, by the mix of the two parts. All such products are strong poisons, the entry warns. Under the name king’s yellow, orpiment once saw wide use as a pigment. By 1911 safer colours had largely taken its place in paint.
britannica-1911-pageant:
Pageant is a word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a show word with tangled roots. In broad use a pageant is a show or grand sight. Its deeper senses tie it to the old mystery plays of the church.

The article works through the forms of the word from the 1300s on. The core root seems to mean a frame made fast, a stage of wood. From that base the word could name the stage itself. It could also name the scene played on that stage. When the plays took to the streets, each guild had its own wheeled stage. On those high carts, with rooms above and below, the plays rolled from stop to stop. Later shows kept the wheeled floats but dropped the plays.
britannica-1911-pajol-claude-pierre-coun:
Claude Pierre Pajol, Count Pajol (1772-1844), was a French cavalry general, born at Besançon, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. The son of an advocate, he was meant to follow his father's calling. The events of his youth turned his mind another way, and he joined the battalion of Besançon.

In 1791 Pajol went to the army of the Upper Rhine with a volunteer battalion. He fought in the campaign of 1792 and was one of the stormers at Hochheim in 1793. From Custine's staff he passed to that of Kleber, fighting on the Sambre and the Rhine in the years that followed. He later served under Hoche and Massena in Germany and Switzerland. As a colonel in the short peace he was sent as envoy to the Batavian Republic and was a delegate at Napoleon's coronation.
britannica-1911-palmerston-henry-john-te:
Henry John Temple, third Viscount Palmerston, an English statesman born in seventeen eighty four, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Broadlands near Romsey, he came of the Irish branch of the Temple house. That branch stood far off in blood from the great English house of the name. It had its own marks of rank all the same.

In the reign of Elizabeth that Irish line gave a desk aide to two great men of state. That aide rose to lead a famed college in Dublin. His son held the top rolls post in Ireland. That son in turn was the sire of one of the most able envoys of the age. The statesman of the entry came down from a cadet son of that house, a speaker of the Irish lower house.
britannica-1911-parchment:
Parchment, skins of set animals prepared by set methods, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Such skins gave the world a writing stuff for long ages. Books of centuries rest on this tough and lasting skin. It could be had with ease in fair amounts in most places.

Proof of its use runs back to very old times, and true pieces of it still live. Tales tie skin writing in Egypt to the days of the Pharaohs of the fourth dynasty. Skin rolls from about 1500 years before Christ rest in the British Museum and elsewhere. Egypt made and sold papyrus in vast amounts, so it had small need of skins. Skin rolls there were thus rare at all times. In western Asia, by contrast, skins served widely as a writing base.
britannica-1911-parlement:
Parlement, in old French any meeting for discussion, took a special sense in France, and this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article traces that change. From the late thirteenth century the word named the sessions of the royal court. When the Parlement of Paris became a permanent court of justice, it kept the name. It held supreme authority in cases before it, above all in appeals.

The article goes back to the early Capetian kings. They summoned their chief vassals and prelates to court at the great festivals of the year. There the nobles advised the king on political matters, and the king gave judgment in cases brought before him. Such cases were few early on. Yet the king always held that his right to judge was general and without limit.
britannica-1911-parsifal-bell-instrument:
Parsifal Bell-Instrument, a stringed device made to stand in for church bells, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was built by Schweisgut of Carlsruhe, from a design by Mottl, for use in Wagner's opera Parsifal. Its frame is broad and flat, much like a grand piano or a billiard table.

The device has five notes, each with six strings tuned in two sets an octave apart. Large hammers, padded with cotton wool, strike the strings when the player hits them hard with the fist. The entry explains why such a device was needed at all. Modern stage music asks for the deep, grave sound of real church bells. In a scene of high religious weight, no weak substitute would serve.
britannica-1911-paulinus-saint:
Paulinus, Saint is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Roman consul who became a monk and bishop. Born at Bordeaux in 353, the son of a rich prefect of Gaul, he was taught by Ausonius. In 378 he was raised to the rank of consul. At a festival of Saint Felix of Nola he began his lifelong devotion to that saint.

The death of their only child in infancy deepened the couple's weariness of the world. Received into the church about 389, he withdrew with his wife to Spain. He settled at Nola beside the tomb of Saint Felix, spent his fortune on poor pilgrims, debtors and public works, and built basilicas and an aqueduct. Not later than 409 he became bishop of Nola, holding the see until his death in 431.
britannica-1911-peel-arthur-wellesley-pe:
Arthur Wellesley Peel, first Viscount Peel, an English statesman born in 1829, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. The youngest son of the great Sir Robert Peel, he was schooled at Eton and Balliol College, Oxford. He entered parliament for Warwick in 1865 in the Liberal interest. A string of junior posts followed, from the poor law board to the home department.

In 1884 Peel was chosen Speaker of the Commons. He was thrice re-elected and held the chair till ill health forced him out in 1895, ranked among the greatest Speakers for fairness and quick judgment. He was made a viscount with a pension of 4,000 pounds. From 1896 he chaired the royal commission on the licensing laws. His draft report split the commission, and his own plan called for a sharp cut in licensed houses.
britannica-1911-pendant:
Pendant is a word for any thing that hangs down in place. The 1911 Britannica entry brings it through French from a Latin verb to hang. In dress it names a jewel that hangs from a brooch or chain. It also names the loose end of a knight's belt past the buckle. That loose end most often ends in an ornamental tip of metal.

In building the word takes on more than one set sense. It names a long boss that hangs from the crossing of roof ribs. Such bosses shine most in fan tracery and in hammer beam roofs. Long corbels under wall pieces have borne the name at times as well. Pendant posts are timbers carried down a wall to take the braces.
britannica-1911-pendleton-george-hunt:
George Hunt Pendleton, American lawyer and lawmaker, was born in Cincinnati in Ohio on 25 July 1825 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied at Heidelberg, read law, and began work at the bar in Cincinnati. He sat in the Ohio Senate in 1854 and 1855. From 1857 to 1865 he served as a Democrat in the national House.

In the House he fought the war policy of Lincoln. He ran as the Democrat choice for vice president in 1864. After Congress he backed the Ohio idea with force. That plan held that the state should pay its bond principal in greenback paper, not in coin. Farm folk in the West saw relief in it and made him their leader.
britannica-1911-penza-government:
Penza is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a province of eastern Russia. The province is bounded by four other provinces named in the text. Its area is just under fifteen thousand square miles. The count given for 1906 puts its people near 1,699,000. The land rolls in hills with deep valleys and ravines. No part of it rises above nine hundred feet.

The rocks are chalk, sandstone, sands, and marls in the main. Chalk, potter's clay, peat, and iron are the chief minerals. The soil is a black earth mixed with clay and sand. Thick woods cover the north of the province. The south shows the open grassland of the steppe. Three rivers drain it, the Moksha, the Sura, and the Khoper. Timber is floated down those streams.
britannica-1911-peppermint:
Peppermint is a perennial herb of the mint family, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes the plant and its rise to notice. Its Latin name is Mentha piperita, and it stands out from other mints by its stalked leaves and its oblong heads of flowers. It grows wild near streams and in wet ground in parts of England and across Europe. It is also grown widely for its oil in England, Europe, and the United States.

Oddly, it was picked out as a species of its own only late in the seventeenth century. Dr Eales found it in Hertfordshire and showed it to Ray, who printed it in 1696. Its healing powers were soon seen, and it entered the London list of medicines in 1721. Growers know two forms of it, the white mint and the black mint.
britannica-1911-perm-government:
Perm is a province article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a government of eastern Russia. It is bounded by the governments of Orenburg, Ufa, Vyatka, Vologda, and Tobolsk. Its area is 128,173 square miles. In law it belongs wholly to Russia in Europe, yet its eastern part, some 57,000 square miles, lies in Siberia.

The Ural Mountains cross it from north to south, thick with forest and cut deep by rivers. The range is thirty to forty-five miles wide. Its highest peaks pass five thousand feet in the central stretch, with Denezhkin at 5,360 feet. Southward the chain sinks fast and barely reaches three thousand feet. Where the great Siberian road crosses, the highest point is only 1,400 feet. Rivers of three great systems drain the province well: the Pechora, the Tobol, and the Kama.
britannica-1911-pheasant:
The pheasant is the subject of a bird entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its names in English, German, and French all come from a Latin word for the bird. That Latin name points to the river Phasis in Colchis, where the bird was common. Legend said the Argonauts brought it into Europe from there.

The entry weighs whether the common pheasant was in fact native to parts of Europe. Old remains of kindred birds in Greece and France are cited as a clue. If it was brought into England, that move must have come very early. The text then turns to the bird itself and its place in the wild and in sport.
britannica-1911-pica-rodent:
Pica, a small rodent also called the tailless hare or piping hare, is the subject of a science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Picas form a family with a single genus, Ochotona. They differ from true hares and rabbits in their short round ears and lack of a tail. Their hind limbs are also shorter, and their collar bones are complete.

The soles of their feet are hairy, and their fur is soft and thick. Picas live in cold and desert regions, in rock cracks or in burrows. One Himalayan kind haunts pine forests instead. They are quick and active, and most kinds utter a piping or whistling cry. In Siberia they stack grass in small heaps to store food for winter. Central Asia is their stronghold, though a few kinds reach Arctic America and the Rocky Mountains.
britannica-1911-piedmont:
Piedmont is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a part of northern Italy. Switzerland bounds it north, France west, and Lombardy east. In plain terms it is the upper basin and vale of the Po. Alps ring it on all sides save toward the Lombard plain.

In 1859 it was split into four provinces for its rule. They were Alessandria, Cuneo, Novara, and Torino in that time. The whole area comes to 11,340 square miles of land. Its folk work the land in the main for their bread. Wheat, maize, rice, chestnuts, wine, and hemp are its chief crops. Silk work and the making of cotton and wool cloth count too.
britannica-1911-pint: Pint is a liquid measure of capacity, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains in brief. It is one eighth of a gallon in the scale of measures. The imperial British pint is 0.57 of a litre, or 34.66 cubic inches in volume. The United States standard pint is less, at 0.47 of a litre. The word is thought to come through Spanish from a Latin word for a painted or marked vessel. It appears in French as pinte for a liquid measure as early as the 1200s.
britannica-1911-piper-carl-count:
Count Carl Piper is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Piper was a Swedish statesman, born at Stockholm in 1647. After study at Upsala he entered the foreign office. A mission to Russia in 1673 and service in the Scanian War brought him to the king's notice.

The article follows his steady climb. He was ennobled in 1679 and made a secretary of state ten years later. Charles the Eleventh, dying, commended him to his son and heir. Under Charles the Twelfth, Piper became the most trusted of ministers. He was made a senator, then a count, then chancellor of Upsala University. During the Great Northern War he ran the king's travelling chancellery. In effect, the entry says, he was prime minister to a warrior king.
britannica-1911-plock-government:
Plock, or Plotsk, a government of Russian Poland on the right bank of the Vistula, is surveyed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Prussia lies to its north, and the Polish governments of Lomza and Warsaw to its east and south. Its area is a little over four thousand square miles, and its surface is flat.

The land stands a few hundred feet above the sea and rises gently to the north, toward the Baltic lake district. A few hills reach six hundred feet, while the broad valley of the Vistula lies far lower. In the west, wide terraces with forests, small lakes and poor growth step down toward the plains. Marshes fill parts of the centre and north, and peat bogs there are used for fuel. The high plains bear rich clays and a kind of black earth, so the entry sets out a farming land of mixed worth.
britannica-1911-poltava-government:
Poltava is a government, or province, in the south west of Russia. The 1911 Britannica entry bounds it by Chernigov in the north. Kharkov lies to the east, and Kiev lies to the west of it. Ekaterinoslav and Kherson bound it on the south side in turn. Its area is 19,260 square miles of land in all.

The land is a rolling plain some 500 feet above the sea. A few heights in the north reach up to 670 feet high. To the south west the plain eases down to 300 feet or so. Deep cut river banks give parts the look of hill country. Low flat plains stretch off to the left of those rivers.
britannica-1911-potosi-department:
Potosi is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a department of Bolivia. It fills the south-west angle of that land, the entry says. Chile bounds it on the west and Argentina on the south. The count for 1900 is 325,615 folk, most of them Indians. Its area is given as 48,801 square miles.

The east is crossed north to south by a branch of the Andes. Spurs and broken ranges jut east from that main chain. Streams there feed the Pilcomayo and Guapay rivers on their long runs. The west is part of the high Bolivian plain by Lake Titicaca. That west is a barren salt waste, near unfit for man to live in.
britannica-1911-pozzo-di-borgo-carlo-and:
Carlo Andrea Pozzo di Borgo, count and Russian diplomat, was born at Alata near Ajaccio on 8 March 1764 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came of a noble Corsican family. Schooling at Pisa shaped his early years. In youth he stood close to Napoleon and Joseph Bonaparte, since the two houses were then firm allies in politics.

Pozzo was one of two men sent to Paris to ask that Corsica join France in full. He then sat as a Corsican deputy on the benches of the right till August 1792. Home again, Paoli gave him a warm welcome in Corsica. By then he stood against the Bonaparte brothers, who had swung to the Jacobin side. He rose to head the civil rule of the island while Paoli led the army.
britannica-1911-present:
Present is a word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English word with a crowd of senses. At its base it means what is at hand, or before a person, in place or in time. The word serves as an adjective, an adverb, a noun, and a verb.

The article sorts the senses by their roots. The time and place senses come from a Latin word for being at hand. From a verb of that stock came the sense of bringing a thing before a person. That path led to the noun sense of a gift. In law the phrase these presents names the deed at hand. In church use, to present means to name a man for a vacant post. A near word for a dark foreboding has a root of its own.
britannica-1911-president:
President is a title whose long history the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces from Latin roots. The word comes from a Latin term for one who sits in front, who presides. In classical Latin, the like word praeses was given to all governors of provinces, and in Diocletian's time it shrank to the men who governed the smaller provinces for the emperor.

The sense lived on through the middle ages. Counts, royal seneschals and other crown officers bore the style in the records of Charlemagne and later. In England the word long meant the king's lieutenant in a province or post, as in President of Wales, of York or of Berwick. In some British colonies in North America, a president of the council led the government. When Pennsylvania and New Hampshire became states, one member of the ruling council still bore the name.
britannica-1911-regent:
A regent is one who rules in the place of a king. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica draws the word from the Latin for to rule. The post fills a gap when a king is a child or unfit. In strict English law, though, the idea has no firm place. Coke held that a king in law can never be a minor. Need has still forced regencies in England and Scotland often.

Who may name a regent was long in dispute. Coke urged that the choice rest with parliament. In later times an act of parliament has always made the post. Scotland named regents by council or by statute from early on. In 1315 Robert the First named the earl of Moray in council. Acts later set regents for Mary and for the line after Queen Anne.
britannica-1911-regiment:
Regiment, as a word for a body of troops, is traced from a rule word in a 1911 Britannica army entry. The Latin root means rule or the post of a ruler. In that sense the word was in wide use in the fifteen hundreds. John Knox used it in the title of his famed blast at rule by women. Its army sense dates from the French host of that same age.

At first the word meant a command, with no set size or form. As hosts grew more set in form, each such command took a like shape. In time it came to mean the command of a colonel as a set unit. British foot regiments hold a mixed count of small groups. Horse regiments form a true field unit of four troops, the text says.
britannica-1911-remiremont:
Remiremont is a town of eastern France in the department of Vosges, set on the Moselle a mile below its meeting with the Moselotte. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the commune 10,548 people and notes Fort Parmont guarding it among wooded hills. Its abbey church, consecrated in 1051, keeps an 11th century crypt with tombs of the abbesses.

The town takes its name from Saint Romaric, who founded a monastery and convent on the hills in the 7th century. The nuns settled in the town in the 11th century and grew rich and strong under gifts from dukes and kings. Their abbess was a princess of the empire, and her fifty canonesses had to prove noble birth. In time the ladies gave up their vows, took the title of countess, and married. Both houses were shut in the Revolution.
britannica-1911-riccati-jacopo-francesco:
Count Jacopo Francesco Riccati lived from 1676 to 1754 and was an Italian man of math. The 1911 Britannica life gives Venice as his birth place in May 1676. He studied at the university of Padua and took his degree in 1696. Science was his chief love through a long and calm life. The senate of Venice sought his word on hard tasks of use.

He wrote to the great minds of Europe in his day. Much of his work came out in a famed Leipzig journal of learning. He refused the head post of the academy at St Petersburg. Life in Italy, free and quiet, suited him far more. His name lives on in the math problem called Riccati's equation.
britannica-1911-rochester-kent:
Rochester is the subject of a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Rochester is a city in Kent in England, on the river Medway. It lies east of London by rail, next to Chatham and Strood. By 1901 its people numbered over thirty thousand. Bridges link it to Strood across the river.

The article gives most space to the cathedral church of Saint Andrew. Augustine founded a church there in the year 604. Danish raids hurt it, and Norman bishops rebuilt it in stone. Later work added a long choir, side chapels, and a low central tower with a spire. A shrine to a murdered pilgrim drew crowds and wealth to the monks. Though small, the church shows many styles of building. Readers get a close guide to its growth over eight hundred years.
britannica-1911-rossi-pellegrino-luigi-e:
Pellegrino Luigi Edoardo Rossi, Count Rossi (1787-1848), was an Italian economist and statesman, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his wanderings. He was born at Carrara and educated at Pavia and Bologna, where he became professor of law in 1812. In 1815 he backed Joachim Murat, and after Murat's fall he fled to France and then to Geneva.

At Geneva he lectured on law applied to Roman law, and his success won him the rare honour of citizenship of the city. He sat in the cantonal council and drew up a revised constitution, the Pacte Rossi. The diet rejected it, a blow that turned his thoughts toward France. In 1833 he took the chair of political economy at the Collège de France, left open by the death of Say.
britannica-1911-ryazan-government:
Ryazan is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a government, or province, of central Russia. It is bounded by the governments of Moscow, Tula, Vladimir, and Tambov. Its area is 16,250 square miles. Ryazan forms a link between the central Great Russian provinces and the steppe lands to the south east. The wide, deep valley of the Oka river is the natural line between them.

North of the Oka the surface is often sand, marsh, and forest, the entry says. South of it the rich black earth prairies begin. The whole province is a plateau about seven hundred feet above the sea, cut deep by river valleys and ravines. Its worked riches include iron ore, limestone, clay, peat beds, and coal. The north belongs to the forest region still.
britannica-1911-sackville-george-1st-vis:
Sackville, George, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a British lord. He is most often recalled as Lord George Sackville or Lord George Germain. Born on the 26th of January 1716, he was third son of a duke. He was schooled at Westminster and at Trinity College in Dublin.

In 1737 he was made captain in a horse regiment at once. Three years later he moved to a foot regiment as a senior officer. The regiment sailed at once for war service on the Rhine. At Fontenoy he was wounded in a charge and taken to the French king. Louis the Fifteenth had his wound dressed in his own tent. Freed, he was sent home to serve against the Pretender.
britannica-1911-sacrament:
Sacrament, in the 1911 Britannica, is treated as a rite known by its Latin name and its long past. The Anglican catechism calls a sacrament an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace. The Latin word first meant any thing or act given a solemn sense it did not hold on its own.

In old Rome the term named the cash each side in a suit left with a priest, lost by the loser. Livy used it for the oath soldiers swore not to desert. Pliny used it for the oath of the Christians of Bithynia at their meetings. The entry then tracks Tertullian, who used the word in both senses. He spoke of baptism and the Eucharist, and of water, oil, and bread, as a law term became a core church word.
britannica-1911-saint:
Saint, from a Latin word that means holy, was at first a term for all believers, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. That use is seen in the New Testament and in the most ancient records of Christian thought. Some modern sects that base their rule on the Bible alone still use it that way.

In ancient carved records the word often means souls in bliss, or the martyrs. People were buried near the saints, as the records put it. For a long time the term was also an official title, held above all for bishops. Only near the sixth century did it become a title of honour for the dead whose cult was marked in the churches. Honour went first to the martyrs, with a yearly feast of their death.
britannica-1911-scent: Scent, an odour or smell, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In particular it names a fragrant liquid distilled from flowers, used as a perfume. The word should properly be spelled sent, the entry argues. It comes from a Middle English verb meaning to perceive by the sense of smell, from French and Latin roots. The added letter c crept in during the seventeenth century, as it also did in the word scythe.
britannica-1911-sea-serpent:
Sea-serpent is the subject of this 1911 Britannica entry, which collects the old reports of huge serpents in the sea. Belief in giant serpents, on land and in the water, goes back to very early times. Pliny tells of a land serpent 120 feet long that a Roman army besieged with engines as if it were a city. The fullest accounts, though, come from the early Norse writers.

For them the sea-serpent was a theme of prose and verse alike. Olaus Magnus pictured it as 200 feet long and 20 feet round. He said it ate calves, sheep, and swine and could rear up like a mast beside a ship and snatch men from the deck. Pontoppidan, writing later, held that sailors and fishermen of his day widely believed in the creature, and gave the means they used to escape it.
britannica-1911-sextant:
Sextant is a tool entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains a device for measuring angles between far points in the sky. Its name comes from an arc that spans a sixth part of a full circle. Old forms used plain sights set on fixed and moving arms.

The entry tells how weak old tools drove men to seek a better way. Mirrors let a user see two points at once in one glass. Two schemes from one great thinker each used that mirror trick. One scheme used a single mirror and a scope aimed at one mark. The next used twin mirrors and twin scopes for a surer read.
britannica-1911-shuvalov-peter-andreivic:
Peter Andreivich Shuvalov is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a Russian envoy who lived from 1827 to 1889. He came of an old house that rose to fame in the 1700s. One kin member founded a famed school in Moscow. As a youth the count showed no drive to match them.

He studied just enough to earn a place in the army. For near twenty years he lived as a Guards officer. In 1864 court favour made him head of the Baltic lands. He showed such skill and tact in that post that he rose fast. In 1866 he was put at the head of the police. That choice came when revolt fears ran high in Russia. He was also trusted with secret tasks by the emperor. One such task took him to London in 1873.
britannica-1911-sidmouth-henry-addington:
Henry Addington, first viscount Sidmouth, an English statesman who lived from 1757 to 1844, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a doctor and was schooled at Winchester and Oxford. His close friendship with William Pitt turned him to affairs of state. In 1784 he won a seat in parliament for Devizes.

His grasp of the rules of the House won him the Speaker's chair in 1789. King George the Third trusted him as well. When Pitt quit office in 1801 over relief for Catholics, Addington was pressed to form a state. He took the lead and made the peace of Amiens with France in 1802. That peace soon showed cracks, and Pitt withdrew his backing from his old friend.
britannica-1911-siger-de-brabant:
Siger de Brabant is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French thinker of the thirteenth century who taught at the University of Paris. Little is known for sure about his early life. By twelve sixty six he held a post in the arts school there.

The entry follows his part in sharp fights over how to read the Greek thinker Aristotle. Church leaders charged him with false teaching more than once. He fled to Italy, and the facts of his death stay unclear. The entry notes the odd honour paid to him by the poet Dante. Dante placed him in heaven next to the very men who had fought his views.
britannica-1911-smolensk-government:
Smolensk is a government, or province, of middle Russia, and this 1911 Britannica entry surveys its land and rocks. It belongs partly to Great Russia and partly to White Russia. Moscow and Kaluga bound it on the east, Orel and Chernigov on the south, and Pskov and Tver on the north. It covers 21,632 square miles in the west of the great central plateau.

The rivers cut deep into the plateau, so the west is hilly, while the land slopes away to broad plains in the east and south. Coal-bearing limestone fills the east and is quarried for building stone. Chalk shows in the far south, and sands, marls, and iron-bearing clays cover the west. A thick sheet of boulder clay lies over all. The soil is mostly clay, in general poor, and stony or sandy in several districts.
britannica-1911-souham-joseph-count:
Joseph Souham (1760-1837) was a French general who rose from the ranks. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his start as a private soldier before the Revolution. By 1793 he had reached general of division rank. He served under Pichegru in Holland and under Moreau on the Danube.

Falls from favor marked his middle years more than once. He returned in 1809 and won a count title for his work at Vich in Spain. In 1812 he drove Wellington back from Burgos with skill. Wounded at Leipzig, he later backed the restored king and retired in 1832.
britannica-1911-squint: Squint is a short word article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In its main sense the word means oblique vision, in particular the eye condition called strabismus. In building, a squint is a slit beside the chancel arch giving a view of the altar. In that sense it is also called a hagioscope. The head adds a guess at the word's origin in Swedish and Old English terms for flinching or avoiding.
britannica-1911-st-aldwyn-michael-edward:
Michael Edward Hicks Beach, first Viscount St Aldwyn, born in 1837, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as an English statesman. He was the son of a baronet, whom he succeeded in 1854. He studied at Eton and at Christ Church, Oxford. In 1864 he entered parliament as a Conservative for East Gloucestershire.

Beach rose through posts on poor law and home affairs to chief secretary for Ireland in 1874. He joined the cabinet in 1877 and ran the colonies office from 1878 to 1880. In 1885 he became chancellor of the exchequer and leader of the House of Commons. Eye trouble forced him to resign in 1887, but he came back at the Board of Trade. In 1895 he took the exchequer again and held it through the South African war. He insisted that war loans be paired with fresh taxes each year.
britannica-1911-stair-james-dalrymple-1s:
James Dalrymple, Viscount Stair, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Stair was a Scottish lawyer and statesman who lived from 1619 to 1695. He was born in Ayrshire, on a small family estate. His father died while he was an infant. His mother, praised for her fine spirit, saw that he was well schooled. He went to Glasgow university in 1633 and graduated in arts in 1637.

The article tells how war drew him into army service for a time. In 1641 he was called back to teach at Glasgow. His subjects were maths, logic, ethics, and politics. Students praised his zeal, and colleagues praised his skill in college business. After near seven years he resigned and moved to Edinburgh. He was called to the bar in 1648. His talents lay in learning and business more than in speech in court.
britannica-1911-standards-department:
Standards Department is an office article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a branch of the English Board of Trade. The office keeps the master weights and measures of the realm. Against those masters, all other weights and measures in the land are judged.

The article traces the keeping of the standards back through past offices. For long years they lay at the exchequer, under its chamberlains. That post ended in 1826, but the care of the standards stayed at the exchequer. A law of 1866 set up a named department at the Board of Trade. Its head bore the title Warden of the Standards. The work took in checks of local and makers' standards, and of gas meters and oil testing gear.
britannica-1911-stavropol-government:
Stavropol, a government of northern Caucasia in Russia, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It covers 26,492 square miles. Astrakhan and the land of the Don Cossacks bound it on the north, Kuban on the west, and Terek on the south and east. It holds the eastern part of the broad steppes that stretch north from the foot of the Caucasus chain.

The article describes the ground in layers. In the west a broad swell of land rises to 1,500 or 2,000 feet. South of it stands a group of sixteen mountains, among them Beshtau. North and east of the heights lie wide steppes, only 200 to 400 feet above the sea. They slope gently toward a lowland in the north and toward the dry shores of the Caspian in the east. The river Kuma and its branches drain most of the land.
britannica-1911-stony-point:
Stony Point is a township in Rockland county, New York, on the west bank of the Hudson river. The 1911 Britannica article puts its chief village thirty-five miles north of New York City. The township count fell from 4,614 in 1890 to 3,651 in 1910. Its land is rough, with Dunderberg and Bear Mountain as the high points. Good farm land lies only along the river edge.

The township takes its name from a rocky point that juts into the river and rises steep on all sides. A lighthouse stands on part of it. The state bought the rest in 1897 as a battlefield park. Brick making is the chief trade in the villages, with stone crushing and gravel at other spots. In the war for independence the point guarded the King's Ferry crossing, a key link between New England and the middle states.
britannica-1911-strangford-viscount:
Viscount Strangford was an Irish title held by the family of Smythe, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It was conferred in 1625 on Sir Thomas Smythe of Ostenhanger and Ashford in Kent. It became extinct in 1869 on the death of its last holder. From Sir Thomas the title passed down to Percy Clinton Sydney Smythe in the line.

Percy Smythe succeeded his father as sixth viscount in 1801 in that descent. He entered the diplomatic service in 1802 and represented his country at Lisbon, in Brazil, at Stockholm, at Constantinople, and at Saint Petersburg. In 1825 he was created a peer of the United Kingdom as Baron Penshurst in his own right. He had literary tastes and in 1803 published poems from the Portuguese of Camoens with notes. Byron at that time called him Hibernian Strangford in his verse, a tag the text preserves.
britannica-1911-stratford-de-redcliffe-s:
Stratford Canning, Viscount Stratford de Redcliffe, opens a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London in 1786, he was a merchant's son left fatherless young. His mother raised him at Wanstead after his father's early death. Eton and a brief stay at King's College, Cambridge, schooled him. In 1807 his cousin George Canning set him to foreign office work.

That year Canning went as secretary on a mission to Copenhagen. In 1808 he rose to first secretary at Constantinople in Turkey. When his chief moved to Vienna, Canning stayed in sole charge. Britain then fought Napoleon with all its might and main. Canning was left to his own judgment on the spot there. In 1812 he brokered peace between Turkey and Russia at Bucharest.
britannica-1911-superintendent:
Superintendent names an officer in charge, but its weight in history is church based. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica focuses on Reformed churches of the Lutheran type. At the Reformation the ordering of new churches was a pressing need. Priests were in poor repute and nobles were seizing church lands.

Luther would have kept bishops if they had joined the reform. When they refused, new officers had to be named instead. Superintendents took on much of the old bishop work in new form. In Scotland they oversaw wide districts and reported each year. The entry traces how state power and church order fit in this plan.
britannica-1911-sycophant:
Sycophant is a word study in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. In ancient Greece the word meant a public informer, like the Roman delator. Old writers linked the term to figs and to bans on fig exports. They also linked it to theft of fruit from sacred fig trees.

The entry weighs rival roots for the term and finds fault with some. One view ties the word to a rude hand sign called showing the fig. That sign could insult a person and hint at a false charge. A third view links its form to words like hierophant. Readers get a careful look at how a word for an informer took shape.
britannica-1911-szechenyi-istvan-count:
Szechenyi, Istvan, Count is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Hungarian statesman who gave his fortune and energy to raising his country. Born at Vienna on the twenty-first of September 1791, the son of Count Ferencz Szechenyi, he entered the army at seventeen and fought with honour at Raab in 1809. His famed ride through the enemy lines on the night before Leipzig in 1813 carried the orders of two emperors to Blucher and Bernadotte.

At the Diet of 1825 he gave a whole year's income, 60,000 florins, to found a Hungarian academy for the mother tongue, and other magnates followed his lead. He pushed the opening of the Danube from Buda to the Black Sea and started steamboats on three waters. In Stadium of 1833 he laid out a broad plan of reforms his country badly needed.
britannica-1911-talent: Talent is a short word entry in the 1911 Britannica. The word names an old Greek unit of weight. It was the heaviest unit in use in that age. It served for coin and for goods by weight alike. The weight itself came at first from Babylon. Kin forms were in use in Palestine, Syria, and Egypt. In later Latin the word took a bent sense of will. Its common sense of gifts and skill comes from a tale. That tale is the parable of the talents in Matthew.
britannica-1911-tashkent:
Tashkent is one of the largest and most key cities of Russian Central Asia, and the seat of rule for Russian Turkestan. It sits in the vale of a river some miles above its join with a great stream. Rail lines link it to a Caspian port and to a Russian city far to the north.

The city was once ringed by walls, now in ruin, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Rich gardens ring it now, and its houses hide among fruit trees by the water runs. Homes are low, of stone and sun dried brick, for quakes shake the land in oft turns. The old native city grew fast in folk in a short run of years. The new Russian city by its side has clean broad streets lined with poplar trees and garden homes.
britannica-1911-tenement:
Tenement is a term of law from a Latin word for to hold. The 1911 Britannica entry quotes Coke on its wide legal sense. It covers all heritable lands and rights that a man may hold. In broad legal use it means real property, not goods or cash. In plain speech it means a house or a place to dwell.

In great cities the word took on a more grim cast. Tenement houses hold many families under one roof in cramped rooms. Those families share the hall, the stairs, and the yards in common. Many such houses were built with no thought for joint use at all. Their foul, unfit state drew public care only in late years.
britannica-1911-toreno-queipo-de-llano-y:
Queipo de Llano y Gayoso de, Count de Toreno (1840–1890), was a Spanish politician born in Madrid. He studied at the Madrid Institute and University. In 1864 he entered parliament as a Moderado and sat in all the Cortes of Queen Isabella's reign. He held the seat for Asturias, his family's home province. He stayed loyal to the Bourbons through the revolution, yet still sat in the Cortes of 1871 to 1873.

In 1873 Toreno founded an Alphonsist paper, El Tiempo. When the Restoration came, he was made mayor of Madrid and then, in 1875, minister of public works. In that post he raised the state of public libraries, museums, academies, and archives. He also had key works printed, among them the Cartas de Indias. He later served as foreign minister and twice as president of the House of Deputies.
britannica-1911-torrington-george-byng-v:
George Byng, Viscount Torrington, an English admiral who lived from 1663 to 1733, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Wrotham in Kent. His father, ruined by money losses, had to sell his property. The boy entered the navy in 1678 as a king's letter boy.

Byng left the sea for a garrison regiment for a time, then returned as a lieutenant. In 1688 he helped bring the fleet over to the prince of Orange. That act made his fortune when the revolution succeeded. He fought at the taking and burning of the French fleet at Vigo. In 1704 he helped reduce Gibraltar and fought at Malaga, winning a knighthood. In 1708 his squadron foiled the Old Pretender's attempt to land in Scotland. Ten years later he beat the Spanish fleet off Cape Passaro. That win forced Spain to give up its invasion of Sicily.
britannica-1911-tournament:
Tournament, or tourney, was the name given in the middle ages to a kind of mock fight, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a long history entry. The word comes from a French verb for turning, from the rapid turning of the horses. One medieval writer defined them as exercises held not in enmity, but for practice and display of prowess.

Men who carry weapons have always played at war in times of peace. Yet the tournament proper does not appear in Europe before the ten hundreds, in spite of later books that gave it laws from Henry the Fowler's day. More than one chronicler records the violent death in 1066 of a French baron said by his fellows to have invented tournaments. In England the sport was counted a French fashion. By the eleven hundreds it had grown so popular that Henry the Second had to forbid it.
britannica-1911-townshend-charles-townsh:
Charles Townshend, second Viscount Townshend, an English statesman who lived from 1674 to 1738, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of Sir Horatio Townshend, a zealous supporter of Charles the Second. His father was made Baron Townshend in 1661 and Viscount Townshend in 1682. The old Norfolk family is traced back to a legal adviser of the Paston family.

Charles succeeded to the peerage in December 1687 on the death of his father. He was educated at Eton and at King College, Cambridge, in his youth. He had Tory sympathies when he took his seat in the House of Lords. His views changed in time, and he began to take an active part in politics as a Whig. The long account that follows traces his rise in that party and his years in office at the head of affairs.
britannica-1911-trident:
Trident, a Latin word for a three toothed fork, is explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The tool is a fork or spear with three prongs. From the earliest times it has been the stock tool for spearing fish. In Scotland such a spear goes by the name leister.

That sea link made the trident the badge of Poseidon, the Greek god of the sea. Homer arms Poseidon with it in both of his great poems. The trident as a sign of rule over the sea shows as early as Archilochus, at about 700 before Christ. Britannia holds it in art as mistress of the sea in later ages. In the arena shows of old Rome, one class of fighter bore a trident as his weapon of choice.
britannica-1911-troyon-constant:
Constant Troyon is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born on the twenty eighth of August 1810 at Sevres, near Paris, he was a French painter. His father worked at the famed china works of that town.

The article tells of a slow start and a late bloom. Troyon began as a painter of fine china ware and spent years at that small scale work. He roamed the country painting scenes of land as funds allowed. When funds ran out he went back to china work to save again. In 1846 a trip to Holland changed his path. A famed Dutch bull painting showed him his true gift. From then on he painted beasts of the field with fast growing skill. His works won fame in Britain and America as well as in France.
britannica-1911-tula-government:
Tula is a government of central Russia. Moscow bounds it on the north, Ryazan on the east, Tambov and Orel on the south, and Kaluga on the west. It covers 11,950 square miles. Its people were put at 1,662,600 in 1906. A low plateau, 950 to 1,020 feet high, crosses it from south-west to north-east. That ridge splits the drainage of the Oka from that of the Don.

The government is split into twelve districts, with Tula as chief town. Just 2.4 per cent of the land is held unfit for farm work. Farm work is the chief trade of the people. Small trades and home crafts have always done well there, such as the making of tea urns, brass wares, and harmoniums. The main factory works make machines and hardware goods.
britannica-1911-tver-government:
Tver, a government of central Russia on the upper Volga, is surveyed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is bounded by Pskov and Novgorod, by Yaroslavl and Vladimir, and by Moscow and Smolensk, and it covers near twenty five thousand square miles. The land lies on the south slope of the Valdai plateau.

Though cut by deep valleys, the region is in truth a plateau of eight hundred to a thousand feet. Its high west is where the Volga, the Southern Dvina and the Msta rise in marshes and lakes. The rock is chiefly limestone of two ages, over older beds that show only in low valley cuts. A thick sheet of boulder clay covers the whole, left by the great ice sheet. Ochre, brick clay and building stone are dug, and there are iron bearing springs. The soil is mostly clay and, as a rule, not rich.
britannica-1911-united-states-the-consti:
Government of the United States is set out in a long section of the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The part opens with a clear plan in three parts. First come the states and their governments. Second comes the federal system and how the states stand to the whole nation. Third comes the build of the federal government itself.

The text gives a plain reason for that order. The states are older than the federal government. In many ways the federal plan was shaped on the scheme the thirteen first states had in use. So the account starts with the states and then moves to the national frame. That frame is more tangled and needs fuller treatment. Readers who want the base rules of rule in the United States will find a firm start here.
britannica-1911-ushant:
Ushant, the far west isle off the coast of France, gets a short place note in the 1911 Britannica. It lies off Finistere as part of that same district. Its folk count for nineteen oh six was two thousand seven hundred sixty one. Granite forms near all of the isle, some three thousand eight hundred fifty acres. Steep rough shores can be reached at few points, and fog adds to the risk.

Small black sheep feed on its grass lands at large. Half the land grows grain or potatoes for its folk. Men work as pilots and fishers at sea. Women work the fields at home in their place. Past notes tell of an English raid in thirteen eighty eight. A sea fight off the isle in seventeen seventy eight had no clear win.
britannica-1911-valentia-sir-francis-ann:
Sir Francis Annesley, Viscount Valentia, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1585, he was an Anglo-Irish statesman who settled in Ireland young. Land grants and posts came his way through the favour of King James the First.

The article follows his rise and his hard fall. He sat in the Irish parliament from 1614 and became secretary for Ireland in 1618. A rare grant gave him the right to a viscount's title on a kinsman's death. He fought the lord deputy's line and helped force his recall in 1629. The next deputy, Wentworth, struck back with force. At a dinner in 1635 Annesley used hot words against him. A court martial condemned him to death, though the sentence was not carried out. Parliament later ruled the sentence unjust.
britannica-1911-vermont:
Vermont is a state of the United States in the New England group, on the north Atlantic side. The 1911 Britannica article gives its total area as 9,564 square miles, of which 440 are water. Quebec bounds it on the north. The Connecticut river parts it from New Hampshire in the east. Massachusetts lies south, and New York and Lake Champlain west. The state forms part of the upland of New England.

Its mean height above the sea is about one thousand feet. The crest runs from 106 feet at Lake Champlain to 4,364 feet on Mount Mansfield. The Green Mountains form the spine of the state, running north and south a bit west of the mid-line. Four more peaks top four thousand feet, among them Killington and Camel's Hump. West of the Greens, the Taconic range runs in a near line with them.
britannica-1911-warrant:
Warrant, in English law, is defined in a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In chief use it means a written order that gives a person power to do an act or hold an office. The word is found in very old state papers, though not at first in its modern sense. Its root sense was closer to a pledge or a guarantee.

That root still colours the term, since a warrant backs the man who acts on it. Warrants come in three broad kinds. Some are for state and office work, some are for court work, and some are for money and trade. Royal warrants once drove much state action on the kings own word. By modern practice a minister must sign them as well. Rules for warrants that fix the great seal are also set out.
britannica-1911-warrenpoint:
Warrenpoint is a seaport and resort town in the north of Ireland, at the end of a branch rail line south west of Belfast. It lies on the north shore of a fine lough, with a range of hills at its back. Across the water rise a second range of hills.

Those hills shield the town from harsh winds, the 1911 Britannica entry says. They give it and its sister resorts on the lough a mild air that draws guests in winter as much as in summer. A quay there can take large ships, and farm goods ship out from it. The shores of the lough are set thick with the country seats of the rich, on wooded slopes. A short tram run east leads to one of the most famed resorts in Ireland.
britannica-1911-wolseley-garnet-joseph-w:
Wolseley, Garnet Joseph Wolseley, Viscount is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a British field marshal. Born at Golden Bridge near Dublin on the fourth of June 1833, he was commissioned in 1852. He served in the second Burmese War and was badly wounded at Donabyu in 1853.

The article follows his Crimean and Indian service. He landed at Balaklava in December 1854 and served as an assistant engineer in the trenches before Sevastopol. After the fall of the city he helped embark the troops and was among the last to leave in July 1856. Bound for China in 1857, his transport was wrecked; diverted to India, he made his name at Lucknow.
britannica-1911-x-ray-treatment:
X Ray Treatment is the subject of a medical entry in the 1911 Britannica. The entry says X rays were then in wide use to treat disease. They helped most with skin ills of a long term kind. They also helped with growths of the glands. Swellings of the spleen and of the throat gland are named. For some forms of cancer they eased pain and slowed growth. No firm cure of cancer by rays had yet been shown.

One skin ill, rodent ulcer, did seem to yield to the rays. The use grew from harm seen when rays were used to view the body. Skin burns and loss of hair first showed the power of the rays. A worker in Vienna tried them for cure in 1896. Soft rays that soak into tissue were held best for cure.
britannica-1911-yaroslavl-government:
Yaroslavl, a government of central Russia, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is one of the smallest governments of Great Russia, at 13,747 square miles, yet among the most peopled and busy. The Volga flows through a broad, shallow lowland at its heart, some 230 to 260 feet above the sea. Hills around it rise to 700 or 800 feet.

The article notes many marshes and ponds in the west, between two rivers, and low wet tracts in the south. Old clay and sandstone beds cover near the whole ground. Thick layers of clay full of boulders, left by the great ice sheet of the ice age, hide them almost everywhere. Older red marl beds lie beneath. The entry gives a clear picture of a flat river land built by ice and water.
britannica-1911-yeniseisk-government:
Yeniseisk is the subject of a province entry in the 1911 Britannica. The province lies in east Siberia in Russia. It runs from the Chinese border to the Arctic shore. Its area is given as near one million square miles. Four provinces bound it on west, east, and south sides. Its south tip and its north cape span a huge range. That range gives it many kinds of land and weather.

Alpine tracts lie in the south of the province. Cold tundra wastes lie on its Arctic shore. A high ridge bounds it on the south side. Slopes below that ridge hold thick wild woods. A few Tungus families live by hunting in those woods. Gold rich deposits lie in vales of the south tracts. Gold washing camps line streams in the wild taiga. A low range splits dry steppes from a terrace of plains.
bruin-the-grand-bear-hunt:
Mayne Reid wrote a bear-hunting tale for boys, in an edition dated 1861. Chapter one sets the stage at the Palace Grodonoff, on the Neva near St Petersburg. A Russian noble of that name owns the house. His crest, cut in granite over the gate, shows a bear with a knife in its breast, haft in a human hand.

Two live bears, chestnut-brown and big as buffalo, guard the yard. Chains alone keep guests safe from their rush. Bear crests mark door after door of the court. Hunt talk and bear lore form the book's stock, as its title vows. Reid, styled Captain on the title page, made his name on wild tales of hunt and war for young readers. The grand hunt of the title grows from this housed pair and the house's bear pride.
castle-rackrent:
Maria Edgeworth published Castle Rackrent in 1800, the first true regional novel in English, narrated by Thady Quirk, faithful steward to four generations of Rackrent heirs. This 1895 Macmillan edition adds Anne Thackeray Ritchie's introduction and Edgeworth's own glossary explaining Irish terms like tester, a sixpence, for English readers. Sir Patrick drinks, Sir Murtagh litigates, Sir Kit locks up his wife, and Sir Condy gambles the estate away.

Thady reports ruin as loyalty, praising masters whose improvidence he documents guinea by guinea. A wager over filling a punch bowl brimful shows the household's style. Edgeworth invented a form Scott and Turgenev learned from: the unreliable family chronicler through whom a whole society condemns itself politely.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abandonment: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on abandonment, more properly self-abandonment, treats a term of ascetical and mystical writers for the first stage of the soul's union with God through conformity to his will. It is the prelude to the unitive way of approaching God by contemplation, involving passive purification through trials, desolation in giving up prized consolations, and aridity in prayer. Some writers equate it with the obscure night of St. John of the Cross, while the entry warns against a quietist misuse of the term.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-mell:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Mellifont describes the first Cistercian monastery in Ireland, three miles from Drogheda in County Louth. St. Malachy, travelling to Rome in 1140, visited St. Bernard at Clairvaux and resolved to found a similar house in his diocese of Armagh.

Malachy left companions at Clairvaux for their novitiate, and in 1142 they came back and raised Mellifont with Christian O'Conarchy as first abbot. A French monk, Father Robert, built the monastery to Clairvaux's plans, and the church's consecration in 1157 drew great celebrations. So many postulants came that six daughter houses arose within ten years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acanthus-plan:
Acanthus is a plant native to middle Europe whose leaf has ornamented every age. Two varieties exist: one wild and thorny, one with soft, spineless branches. The acanthus first appears in ancient Greek art. It was chosen for decoration because of its leaves' beauty and its abundance in Greek soil.

At first sculptors copied it directly from nature, and Greek sculpture rendered it truthfully, whether soft or spiky, showing the character, texture, and modelling of the leaf. During the fifth century BC the acanthus ornament took an important place in architecture and became the Corinthian capital's principal ornament. From Alexander's conquest in the East, its transformation in later Eastern art can be traced.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accident:
In philosophy, accident means what merely happens to be in a subject: any chance, side attribute. The entry starts from plainly dividing things into stable and unstable, self-standing and dependent. Thinkers split two ways on the problem: some denied objectivity to substance and gave it to the mind, while others made the accidental element mind-side and gave substance alone real standing.

Aristotle and his medieval followers take a middle course, holding both substance and accident real, while admitting a mind-side factor in sensing. Accident thus names a contingent relation between an attribute and its subject, one of the five predicables, beside genus, difference, species, and property. A later part applies the doctrine to the Eucharist, where the theory demands, the entry notes, needlessly many miracles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achille-desur:
Achille Desurmont was an ascetical writer born at Tourcoing, France, on 23 December 1828, who died on 23 July 1898. He attended the Jesuit college at Brugelette in Belgium and Cambrai's theological college.
