Drawn to the religious state, he entered the Redemptorist congregation in 1850, professed the next year, and was ordained priest on 24 September 1853. His talent won him posts as prefect of students and professor of theology.

In 1865 he became superior of the French province, remarkably energetic and an excellent organiser, whose kindness won his subjects' affection and confidence. Under him foundations multiplied, spreading into Spain again and into Peru, Ecuador, Chile, and Colombia. Forced to move his religious from France to Holland, he kept every one faithful through the troubles. He founded the ascetical review La Sainte Famille in 1875 and wrote much and well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-admont:
Admont, a Benedictine abbey in Styria, Austro-Hungary, stands by the Enns, about fifty miles south of Linz. Its foundress counts as St. Hemma, Countess of Friesach and Zeltschach, since, entering Gurk's convent, she left her lands for a monastery near Hall's salt works. The foundation began only in 1072, more than a quarter century after her death, and two years later Gebhard of Salzburg consecrated the abbey church to St. Blasius.

Gebhard also brought twelve Benedictines from Salzburg as the new community's nucleus. Admont rose to prominence in its first century, notably under Abbots Wolfhold and Gottfried, then declined amid war and rapine after the mid-thirteenth century. Restoration came under Henry VII and Engelbert, though Turks, social unrest, and the Reformation later troubled it. Burnt in 1865, abbey and church were soon rebuilt, and Admont remained an important factor in Styrian history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-advent:
Advent, from Latin advenio, to come to, is by present usage a period beginning with the Sunday nearest St. Andrew's feast on 30 November, embracing four Sundays. The first Sunday may fall as early as 27 November, giving Advent twenty-eight days, or only twenty-one when the first Sunday falls as late as 3 December. With Advent the Western churches' ecclesiastical year begins.

During this season the faithful are urged to prepare worthily for the anniversary of the Lord's coming as incarnate God of love. They are to make their souls fit abodes for the Redeemer in Holy Communion and grace. They are also to ready themselves for his final coming in judgment, at death and the world's end. The liturgy serves that aim, with Isaias's prophecies calling ministers to adore the coming Lord the King. The entry also traces Advent's history as fast and liturgy across rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-august:
Albert Auguste de Lapparent was a French geologist born at Bourges in 1839 and dead at Paris in 1908. Geology is the study of rocks and the earth's structure. He graduated first in his class at the École Polytechnique and then studied at the School of Mines. Appointed a mining engineer in 1864, he joined the team drawing the geological map of France and wrote on geology for the Annales des Mines from 1866 to 1880.

Lapparent's Treatise on Geology, published at Paris in 1884, won praise for a style as striking as its substance. It treated the earth's history through bold ideas about its forces and changes rather than bare lists of fossils. His Course in Mineralogy of 1885 brought him the presidency of the French Society of Mineralogy. His Lessons in Physical Geography of 1896 was the first treatment of that subject in France. He entered the Academy of Sciences in 1897 and became its secretary in 1907.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfred-von-re:
Alfred von Reumont, statesman and historian born at Aachen on 15 August 1808, died there on 27 April 1887. Set to medicine at Bonn and Heidelberg by his father's wishes, he left it on his father's 1828 death and tutored at Florence. Within a year he served as the Prussian ambassador's private secretary there, graduating Doctor of Philosophy at Erlangen in 1833. He served Berlin's Foreign Office, Florence and Rome legations, and as Frederick William IV's private secretary, ennobled in 1846. He then served as Rome legation counsel in 1847 and Tuscany ambassador in 1851.

Annexation put him on half pay, unwillingness to appoint a Catholic blocking his intended Rome embassy, and he turned to letters at Rome, Aachen, and Bonn. His many Italian works include Andrea del Sarto of 1835 and southern travel sketches. Despite severe bodily sufferings he kept lively personal relations to the end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosian-cha:
Ambrosian chant, chant composed by St. Ambrose, has long been a research subject among historians and archaeologists. When Ambrose became Milan's bishop in 374, he found a liturgy tradition links to St. Barnabas, brought from Greece and Syria. It joined celebrant song to spoken word and liturgical action.

Scholars such as Dreves, Gevaert, and Riemann have tried to show how melodies fit the authentic Ambrosian texts. The hymn Splendor paternae gloriae survives in many forms, and Nunc Sanctae nobis Spiritus in five variants, one from the Bibliotheca Trivulziana. The Hic est dies verus Dei melody interests because the Pentecost hymn Veni Creator Spiritus uses it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ark-of-the-co:
The Ark of the Covenant, Hebrew aron, was not a great construction like Noah's ark but a chest. Scripture calls it the Ark of the Testimony, the Ark of the Testament, and the Ark of God, with Ark of the Covenant the most familiar in English. It measured two and a half cubits long and one and a half cubits broad and high, made of incorruptible acacia wood called setim.

Overlaid inside and out with purest gold, it carried a golden crown or rim, and four golden rings at its corners, likely toward the top, through which carrying poles passed. The long article describes the chest, its mercy seat and cherubim, its place in tabernacle and temple worship, and its journeys and loss in Israel's story. Readers get both the object's making and its meaning as the throne of God's presence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baptismal-fon:
A baptismal font is the basin holding water for baptism, in which the candidate is immersed or over which he is washed. Today it is usually a decorative stone basin, though metal or wood serve, set on a pedestal at a handy height. Its form marks the end of a development that mirrors the history of baptism's modes. In Apostolic times there were no special fonts: baptism happened at the seaside or in streams and pools.

Tertullian tells of Peter baptizing in the Tiber, and missionaries like Paulinus baptized in rivers. Indoor baptism, for privacy and solemnity, became the rule, and reverence for water brought a special basin. In the East the font took the form of a deep pool or cistern, fit for total immersion, called kalymbethra. At the water's blessing, the priest pours in the oil of catechumens, then chrism, and finally both oils together.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benediction-o:
Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament, a popular Catholic evening devotion, receives a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. In France it is called Salut, and in Germany Segen. It centres on the consecrated host. Catholics believe this bread becomes Christ's body. It is shown on the altar in a monstrance, a sun-shaped vessel, amid lights.

Hymns, litanies, and canticles fill the service, which often closes Vespers, Compline, or the Stations of the Cross. At the end the priest, shoulders covered by a humeral veil, lifts the monstrance and traces the sign of the cross in silence over the kneeling people. The entry then traces the rite's history, forms, and rules.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-alexa:
Blessed Alexander Briant, an English Jesuit martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Somerset about 1556 to a yeoman family, he was executed at Tyburn in 1581. At Hert Hall, Oxford, his beauty and purity won him the name the beautiful youth, and teaching by Robert Persons, with Richard Holtby's friendship, brought his conversion.

Ordained at Reims in 1578, he laboured on the English mission with exemplary zeal until arrest. Rack and trial for priesthood and treason followed, and he died with Edmund Campion's companions. The entry presents a young priest whose face and faith alike drew notice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesar-clemen:
Caesar Clement, great-nephew of Sir Thomas More's friend Doctor John Clement, died at Brussels on 28 August 1626. He studied at Douai, moved with the college to Reims in 1578, and entered the English College at Rome in 1579, where he was ordained priest in 1585. Though meant for the English mission, he never crossed to England.

Instead he became Dean of Saint Gudule's in Brussels, and vicar-general to the King of Spain's army in Flanders. English exiles received his generous help, above all the Augustinian canonesses of Louvain. In 1612 he and Robert Chambers were sent from Rome to visit Douai College and end discontent with its rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canon-of-the-:
The Catholic New Testament, as fixed by Trent, matches in contents the New Testament of all Christian bodies today. It holds seven formerly disputed books: Hebrews, James, Second Peter, Second and Third John, Jude, and the Apocalypse. It also holds three disputed passages: the ending of Mark, Luke's bloody sweat, and the woman taken in adultery. Since Trent no Catholic may question the inspiration of these passages.

A complete canon from apostolic times has no basis in history. The canon grew between about 100 and 220, pushed by disputes with doubters inside and outside the Church and slowed by honest hesitation, reaching its final term only at Trent. Writings with an apostolic stamp were prized from the first, and the New Testament itself shows Paul's letters and the Synoptic Gospels already in circulation among the churches.

Canon as applied to Scripture means the authoritative list of writings composed under divine inspiration for the good of the Church, from Israel's beginnings to the Catholic Church's full growth. The Greek kanon first meant a reed or measuring rod, then a rule or standard, and Athanasius in the fourth century first applied it to the Scriptures. The passive sense, a regulated and defined collection, has ruled ever since.

Protocanonical books are those always received without dispute, matching the Hebrew Bible and the Protestant Old Testament. Deuterocanonical books, contested in some quarters but long secure in the Catholic Bible, are Tobias, Judith, Baruch, Ecclesiasticus, Wisdom, First and Second Maccabees, with additions to Esther and Daniel. The two terms are modern, unused before the sixteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-franc:
Charles-Francois Houbigant was born at Paris in 1686 and died there in 1783. He entered the Congregation of the Oratory in 1704 and taught the classics at Juilly, rhetoric at Marseilles, and philosophy at Soissons. Back at Paris, he headed the Conference of Church Antiquities and Discipline of St-Magloire from 1722. Overwork brought a severe sickness that took his hearing in a peculiar way.

The infirmity turned him to Biblical study under a scholarship founded by L. de Carrières. His first work, in 1732, was a vocabulary of Hebrew roots modelled on Lancelot's garden of Greek roots. In 1746 he published prolegomena to Scripture with a Latin Psalms translation, followed in 1748 by a critical Hebrew Psalter, forerunners of his great Hebrew Bible with notes. Later works include a 1770 dialogue among a Jew, a Protestant, and a Sorbonne doctor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-lalem:
An entry on Charles Lalemant, the Jesuit priest who became Canada's first Jesuit mission superior. Born in Paris in 1587, he reached Quebec in the 1620s. His letter to his brother of August 1626 opened the Relations, the long series of reports on missionary work in New France. Blocked by the Quebec trading company, he sailed home to protest, only to be captured, shipwrecked twice, and delayed for years.

Lalemant finally returned in 1632, after Quebec passed back to France, and became friend and confessor to Champlain, the explorer who founded the colony, staying with him as he died. Later, back in France, he served as procurator, or business manager, of the Canadian missions and helped secure the island of Montreal for a new colony. He also wrote a little-known spiritual work on the hidden life of Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-lenor:
A biographical entry on Charles Lenormant, a French archaeologist, a scholar of ancient remains, who was born in Paris in 1802. He began in law, but an 1822 Italian and Sicilian visit made him an enthusiast for antiquity. He later travelled with Champollion, the decipherer of Egyptian hieroglyphs, to Egypt. He worked on the scientific commission in the Morea and rose through posts at the Royal Library and the Cabinet of Medals.

Lenormant lectured at the Sorbonne chiefly on ancient history and the origins of Greek civilisation, and in 1849 he won the chair of archaeology at the Collège de France. Study of Christian civilisation in its sources made him a convinced Catholic, and his writings defended freedom of teaching against state control. Student protest forced him from his Sorbonne chair in 1846, but he edited the Correspondant and directed the commission on historic monuments until his death at Athens in 1859.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clermont:
Clermont, or Clermont-Ferrand, comprises the whole department of Puy-de-Dome and is suffragan to Bourges. Once very extensive, it lost Haute-Auvergne in 1317 to Saint Flour and the Bourbonnais in 1822 to Moulins. Its first bishop was Saint Austremonius. Local tradition makes him one of the seventy-two disciples, a Jew by birth who came with Saint Peter from Palestine to Rome. He became Apostle of Auvergne, Berry, Nivernais, and Limousin.

Clermont tradition says he converted Senator Cassius and the pagan priest Victorinus and was beheaded in 92. That tradition rests on a tenth-century life written at Mozat, where his body rested from 761. Gregory of Tours, born in Auvergne in 544, instead counts Austremonius among seven envoys who evangelised Gaul about 250. Clermont's bishops include many saints, from Urbicus about 312 and Illidius, who cured the emperor Maximus's daughter at Trier, to Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop from 470 to 479.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-compagnie-du-:
Georges Goyau's entry follows the Compagnie du Saint-Sacrement, a seventeenth-century Catholic secret society. It drew many Catholic celebrities of the age. Henri de Levis, Duc de Ventadour, founded it in March 1630 at the Capuchin convent in the Faubourg Saint-Honore. With him stood Henri de Pichery of Louis XIII's household, Jacques Adhemar de Monteil de Grignan, a future bishop, and Philippe d'Angoumois, a Capuchin. Soon Pere Suffren, Jesuit confessor to Louis XIII and Marie de' Medici, joined, with Coligny kin.

In 1631 it took the name Company of the Most Blessed Sacrament. A board of nine, changed quarterly, ruled it under a superior. Absolutely secret, it still won praise for admirable charities, even from critics of its secrecy. Those critics attacked its dealings with Protestants. Decline came in 1660, and action nearly ceased in 1665, after Tartuffe's banning. The General Hospital and the Seminary of Foreign Missions outlived it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Francesca Steele's entry follows an enclosed Dominican reform devoted to perpetual adoration of the Blessed Sacrament. Father Anthony Le Quieu, French Dominican born at Paris in 1601, founded it against opposition. He joined the Friars Preachers in 1622, served as novice master at home and Avignon, and began foundations there in 1639. Twenty years later the first house opened at Marseilles for three Avignon ladies. Marseilles' bishop gave the habit, approved rule, and erected a simple congregation.

Only after the founder's death did Innocent XII approve constitutions in 1693, authorizing vows and enclosure. First for perpetual adoration, it is not austere, yet sets a very high perfection. Revolution suppressed Marseilles' mother-house, reopened 1816. Bollene suffered worse: thirteen nuns died martyrs under the Commune, their beatification cause pending, while survivors resumed adoration in 1802. Bollene sent sisters to Cannington in 1863, later moved to Taunton, with houses at Oxford, Newport, and Hal. None stand in America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-contingent:
Francis Siegfried's entry treats the contingent, Latin contingere, to happen. Aside from secondary, obvious senses, such as qualifying the predicable accident or a class of modal claims, its main technical use names one great division of being. That division is contingent being, set against necessary being. Meaning can be viewed from outside, and the idea's birth from inside. Viewed from outside, the contingent appears first in the ideal order, as the note between which and actual existence no clash stands, admitting though not demanding actual life.

Thus it matches possible being and bears the name contingent outright. Further distinctions follow. The argument from contingent to necessary being is not, as Kant held, the familiar ontological argument. From inside, the contingency concept derives from outer and inner experience. An objection: experience reaches no further than sense phenomena, challenging derivation beyond that field. Balmes, Driscoll, Aveling, Eisler, Blanc, and Urraburu anchor sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-convent:
George Cyprian Alston's entry traces convent, Latin conventus, originally a provincial assembly of Roman citizens for administration and justice. Monastic history gives the word two meanings. First, a religious community of either sex corporately. Eastern laura hermits, in separate cells around their common superior's, were collectively called a conventus when eremitical life joined cenobitical life. Western monasticism used the term from the beginning, and abbas et conventus still means an establishment's entire community.

Second, the buildings housing a community, more properly a strictly monastic order's home. Educational work spans schools and teacher training. Base charges against the conventual system need no refutation beyond general reference. Canon law covers convents' establishment and government at length. In most older contemplative orders choir nuns keep the whole Divine Office. Most orders divide choir sisters from lay sisters. Poverty and other causes often place convents in ordinary houses, ill-suited to ideal adaptation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-tr:
The Council of Trent, the nineteenth ecumenical council, opened on 13 December 1545 and closed on 4 December 1563. Its main object was fixing church doctrine against Protestant teaching, joined to thorough reform of abuses within church life. Luther's 1518 appeal to a council and German diets' demands had pressed the issue for decades before Paul III summoned the fathers.

Across three periods, at Trent and briefly Bologna, the council defined Scripture and tradition as joint standards of revelation, then justification, the sacraments, and reform of bishops and benefices. Sessions debated, decreed, and disciplined in turn, laying a firm foundation, the entry concludes, for overthrowing heresy and carrying out genuine internal reform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-counterpoint:
A music entry explains counterpoint, the art of sounding two or more independent melodies together, from its name to its practice. The term comes from the Latin for point against point, since a note was once called a point. It arose in the fourteenth century for an art already centuries old.

Early harmony appeared as organum, the singing of a second voice against the chant. It grew through French discant, English gymel or twin song, and false bass into full polyphony, many voices woven together. The entry follows the art through its golden age, its decline, and its modern revival, when composers returned to its original principles. Readers get both the history and the technical terms, each glossed as it appears.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-of-dina:
A philosophy entry examines David of Dinant, a pantheistic thinker of the early thirteenth century about whom very little is known. His birthplace is uncertain: Dinant in Belgium or Dinan in Brittany. He spent a period at Innocent III's Roman court and taught, perhaps at Paris, where his Quaternuli, or little notebooks, were condemned by a provincial council in 1210.

Condemnation was confirmed in 1215 by Cardinal Robert Courcon, and David fled France to escape punishment. When and where he died remains unknown, except that it was after 1215. Since the council ordered his writings burned, his doctrines survive only through opponents, chiefly Albert the Great and Saint Thomas. They report that he identified God with prime matter and reduced all reality to bodies, minds, and eternal separate substances.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divine-judgme:
Divine judgment is treated here under two heads, its meaning in itself and the beliefs of peoples before Christ about judgment after death. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry defines it as God's retributive justice at work, fixing the fate of rational creatures by their merits and faults. It covers God's grasp of the moral worth of free acts, his decree of their due outcome, and the execution of that verdict in reward and punishment.

Separate articles handle the particular judgment of each soul and the general judgment of all. The second part surveys pre-Christian faiths, including the Samaritans, whose hopes of resurrection and a day of vengeance were first set in order by their great theologian Marka in the fourth century. The entry thus joins doctrine to the history of belief.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doctrine-of-t:
Atonement stands nearly alone as a theological term born in English, and its history is a curious one. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces atone from the phrase at one, first meaning to reconcile, then the act by which reconcilement is made. In Catholic teaching the Atonement is the satisfaction of Christ, by which God and the world are made at one. Saint Paul's words run that God, in Christ, was reconciling the world to himself.

The Council of Trent set out the doctrine in its sixth session, showing the weakness of nature and of the Mosaic Law. The entry follows Trent's teaching to its close, where Christ, by laying down his life in perfect love, paid the debt to justice. It ends with peace made through the blood of his cross, the heart of the doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmond-freder:
Edmond-Frederic Le Blant was a French scholar of early Christian remains, born in 1818 and dead at Paris in 1897. Trained in law, he took a safe post in the customs in 1843, which left him free to study. A trip to Italy in 1847 and talks with Giovanni Battista de Rossi turned him to the same task in France: gathering the first Christian writings cut in stone in Gaul.

His great collection of those inscriptions came out in volumes in 1856, 1865, and 1892, and won him a seat in the Academy of Inscriptions. He went on to study carved stone coffins, above all those of Arles, and wrote on early Christian art, belief, and daily life. The piece shows a patient worker building French Christian archaeology stone by stone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-endowment:
An endowment is property, a fund, or a revenue set aside for good. It supports a person, institution, or object, such as a student, a professor, a school, or a hospital. The word most often marks charitable corporations founded by private gift. In church circles it also means a conditional donation or legacy in a will. It is meant to secure some spiritual benefit for a long time.

Early Christians gave lavishly, handing their goods to the Church. Justinian made church builders endow their churches, and church law soon required maintenance for any cleric ordained to a church. A man who wanted a parish church on his estate had to endow its clergy with land. A bishop might not consecrate a church until its endowment was secured. In the fifth century, lands poured into the Church in Germanic countries, only to be lost in the upheavals of the migrations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugenie-de-gr:
Eugenie de Gramont was a French nun of the Sacred Heart order who led its first school in Paris. She was born at Versailles in 1788 to a court family. The fall of the French monarchy drove her kin into exile, and she lived for a time in England. Back in France, she joined the new society at Amiens in 1806, and her mother later joined under her own daughter.

In 1815, despite her youth and a slight physical deformity, Mother de Gramont took charge of the society's first Paris school. It stood first in the Rue des Postes and then in the Rue de Varenne. Apart from a break during the revolution of 1830, she governed it until her death in 1846. The entry praises her keen mind and firm hand. It is also frank about her grave error in 1839, when she opposed the foundress, a step she mourned for life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exposition-of:
Exposition is a way of honoring the Holy Eucharist by showing it with due solemnity to the faithful, so they may pray before it. The practice followed the Elevation of the Host in Mass, first heard of about 1200. Elevation likely began as protest against teachers who held the bread unconsecrated until words were spoken over bread and wine alike. Paris made it a synodal rule before 1200.

Soon gazing on the Host became a prime devotion, with fanciful promises of safety from sudden death. Devices such as a black curtain behind the altar and torches held behind the priest helped the sight. The feast of Corpus Christi, born of Saint Juliana's visions, seems an effect of this longing rather than its cause. By the fourteenth century exposition stood firm in Germany. Synods at Breslau in 1416 and Cologne in 1452 curbed informal showings, and carved Sacrament houses with lattice doors became the compromise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fear-from-a-m:
Fear, viewed morally, is unrest of soul at the approach of some present or future danger. Theologians divide it into grave fear and trifling fear. Grave fear moves a steadfast man; trifling fear springs from slight harm. Reverential fear, dreading to offend parents or superiors, may grow grave.

Acts done in fear remain voluntary unless fear has dethroned reason. Grave fear can excuse failure under positive law, but not natural law. A vow extorted by unjust fear is invalid, while one from natural fear stands. Contracts under duress are voidable at the injured party's choice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-firmament:
The firmament is the vault of heaven in Genesis, set to divide the upper waters from the lower. The Hebrew word means something beaten or hammered out and then spread wide. Ancient peoples pictured the sky as a solid dome: the Egyptians as an iron ceiling, the Babylonians as forged metal. Greeks and Romans saw a vault of crystal bearing the fixed stars.

The Bible speaks of the heavens as strong, as if of molten brass, and of floodgates opened at the deluge. Other passages stress stretching out, as God spreads the heavens like a tent. Genesis sets the stars in the firmament and places birds beneath it, in the air. The article notes that Scripture here reflects the common cosmology of its time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-nugen:
Francis Nugent, born in 1569 near Armagh or in County Meath and dead at Charleville in France in 1635. He was a Capuchin Franciscan who founded the Irish and Rhenish provinces of his order. Son of Sir Thomas Nugent of Moyrath and Lady Mary Devlin, he was sent young to France, where the penal laws denied him schooling at home. Before twenty he held doctorates from Paris and Louvain and taught in both cities, fluent in Greek, Hebrew, and several European tongues.

In 1589 he joined the Capuchin Flandro-Belgian province as Francis, was professed and ordained. From 1594 he guided the forming French provinces, founding communities at Metz and Charleville while lecturing in Paris. As custos-general of France he attended the general chapter at Rome in 1596, became commissary general at Venice, and in 1599 defended a thesis before Clement VIII himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-clem:
Francois Clement, born at Beze in Cote-d'Or in 1714 and dead at Paris on 29 March 1793, was a Maurist Benedictine and historian of prodigious industry. Educated at the Jesuit college at Dijon, he professed in 1731 and was sent to the Blancs-Manteaux monastery at Paris to share the congregation's learned labours.

He prepared volumes eleven and twelve of the Literary History of France, covering 1141 to 1167. He then edited with Dom Brial volumes twelve and thirteen of Bouquet's Collection of Historians of Gaul and France, published in 1786. It contains 439 original documents with exhaustive introductions and acute critical notes. His chief work was a wholly recast edition of the Art of Verifying Dates, published at Paris in 1770. It is a tool for fixing the chronology of historical facts that scholars used for generations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-feua:
Francois Feuardent, born at Coutances in Normandy in 1539 and dead at Paris on 1 January 1610, was a Franciscan theologian and preacher of the Catholic League. After humanities at Bayeux he joined the Friars Minor, studied at Paris, took his doctorate in theology in 1576, and taught at the university with great success. He threw himself into the political and religious troubles of France. With John Boucher and Bishop Rose of Senlis he became a foremost preacher of the League. As Roennus notes, there was scarcely a church in Paris where he had not preached.

 His works fall into three classes, scriptural, patristic, and controversial. They are headed by a new edition of Nicholas of Lyra's Bible with the ordinary gloss, published at Paris in 1590 in six folio volumes, with commentaries on books of Scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-leno:
Francois Lenormant, son of Charles Lenormant, was born at Paris on 17 January 1837 and died there on 9 December 1883, an archaeologist of precocious and wide-ranging scholarship. His father supervised his education and shaped his studies, and at fourteen he published in the Revue archeologique on Greek tablets found at Memphis. In 1857 he won the Academy of Inscriptions' numismatic prize for an essay on the classification of Lagid coins and took a law licentiate the same year. He visited Italy in 1858 and accompanied his father east in 1859.

His father died on that journey, and Francois returned with the body, then set out again for Greece, excavating at Eleusis and publishing his archaeological researches there in 1862. Made sub-librarian of the Institut de France in 1862, he travelled east again in 1865 and 1866. His later books covered ancient coinage, Apulia and Lucania, and a Hebrew-based translation of Genesis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-vach:
Francois Vachon de Belmont, born at Grenoble in 1645 and dead in 1732, was the fifth superior of the Sulpicians at Montreal. He came to Canada in 1680 as a missionary among the Indians of La Montagne, serving there until 1700, when he succeeded Dollier de Casson as superior of the order. At his own expense he built Fort de La Montagne on the site of the present Grand Seminary and raised the old seminary still standing in Notre Dame street. He began the Lachine canal.

His writings include a History of Canada, printed in the Quebec Historical Society's collection of memoirs on ancient Canada, and a History of Brandy in Canada in the same collection. They also include a funeral oration for Mother Bourgeoys quoted in Faillon's life of her, praises of persons who died in the odour of sanctity at Montreal, and a number of manuscripts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-lalem:
Gabriel Lalemant, a Jesuit missionary born at Paris in 1610, died a martyr's death in the Huron country in 1649. Nephew of Charles and Jerome Lalemant, he joined the Society at Paris in 1630 and reached Canada in September 1646. After two years at Quebec he was sent to the Huron missions as assistant to Jean de Brébeuf.

He had scarcely been a month among the Hurons when the Iroquois burned Saint Ignatius and fell on Saint Louis. The raiders seized both priests, dragged them back to Saint Ignatius, and tied them to stakes. Lalemant watched his companion die in the afternoon, then bore his own torture from six in the evening until nine the next morning. Their bodies were later buried at Saint Mary's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-general-judgm:
The General Judgment, or Last Judgment, is the doctrine that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead. Prophets call it the Day of the Lord, and the New Testament repeats it under the names Parusia, Epiphany, and Apocalypse, with Christ himself painting its scene in Matthew. Apostles made it a pillar of preaching and letters alike.

All ancient creeds confess it, from the Apostles' words on judging living and dead to the Athanasian demand that all rise with their bodies and answer for deeds. Early Fathers who dreamed of a thousand-year reign still held the universal judgment firm. The Roman Catechism gives its reason: since the dead's good and bad influence runs on through followers until the world's end, justice wants one final reckoning of all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ghent:
The Diocese of Ghent covers East Flanders in Belgium, with more than a million inhabitants and 362 parishes. Paul IV erected the see in 1559 at Philip II's request, taking its ground from Tournai. Pius VII re-established it in 1801 after the French Revolution, and its present bounds were fixed in 1834. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces its bishops, clergy, and churches across those centuries.

Its first bishop, Cornelius Jansenius, had served as Philip's representative at the Council of Trent. The seventh bishop, Antoine Triest, gave Saint-Bavon much of its art and founded a loan fund for the poor. In 1813 Ghent seminarians refused Napoleon's imposed bishop and chose army service over schism. Later bishops sent priests to a new seminary at Troy, New York, and launched Peter's Pence in 1859. Canon Pierre-Joseph Triest's Sisters and Brothers of Charity spread care for the sick, the insane, and children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grandmont:
Grandmont is an abbey and order in Haute-Vienne, France, whose foundation date is very uncertain. The traditional story rests on a bull of Gregory VII now shown to be a forgery, and its founder Saint Stephen is said to have settled at Muret near Limoges in 1076. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows an order of extreme austerity that claimed to be distinct.

Stephen's maxim was that there is no rule save the Gospel of Christ. His followers observed poverty most strictly, forbidding lands, cattle, revenue, or impropriate churches. Begging was allowed only when no food stood in the house, and then the bishop was first informed. After Stephen's death in 1124 his disciples moved to the rocky desert of Grandmont, and by 1170 the order numbered sixty monasteries, mostly in Aquitaine, Anjou, and Normandy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregorian-cha:
Gregorian Chant is an article on plain chant, often taken to include early church music and later compositions in a similar style down to the sixteenth century and even modern times. In a stricter sense it means the Roman form of early plain chant, as distinct from the Ambrosian, Gallican, and Mozarabic chants. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows its gradual supplanting of the rivals.

The Ambrosian chant, which survives at Milan, has two complete manuscripts of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Many more belong to the fifteenth and sixteenth, with an incomplete twelfth-century manuscript now in the British Museum. Its Office chants are antiphons and responses, as in the Roman books, while its Mass chants include Ingressa, Psalmellus, Cantus, Offertory, and Transitorium. Its syllabic pieces are often simpler, its ornate pieces more extended, than the Gregorian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-hya:
Breton Jesuit Guillaume-Hyacinthe Bougeant, born at Quimper in 1690, taught classics at Caen and Nevers and spent his later years writing in Paris. His playful 1737 essay on the language of beasts annoyed his superiors enough to earn him a brief exile, yet English, Italian, and German versions followed.

His histories of the Thirty Years' War and the Peace of Westphalia rank among the best Jesuit histories of their day and also reached German readers. He wrote a treatise on the form of consecration and a three-part catechism still in use after many editions. He also wrote three comedies mocking the Jansenists, the first of which ran through twenty-five editions within months.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hebrew-poetry:
Hebrew poetry fills the Old Testament's Psalms, Prophets, Job, and Proverbs, and this entry defends reading Scripture as literature without denying its inspiration. God speaks, as medieval Jewish commentators said, in the tongue of ordinary people. The Massoretic editors themselves laid out Psalms, Proverbs, and Job in verse lines and half-lines.

Bishop Lowth's lectures of 1753 founded modern study by naming parallelism as Hebrew verse's engine: statement answering statement in synonymous, antithetic, or synthetic pairs, built on the mashal or likeness. Poetry here is tribal and lyrical rather than individual, an outcry of praise, blame, curse, or blessing driven by feeling. Its echo-rhythm, seen in Deborah's chant, fixes and heightens each object it names.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-ghen:
Henry of Ghent, known as the Doctor Solemnis, was a thirteenth-century scholastic philosopher and theologian. Born at Ghent, he lived at Tournai as secular priest and canon and became Archdeacon of Bruges and then of Tournai. He taught for long periods at Paris, taking his doctorate in theology in 1277. In 1282 Martin IV chose him to arbitrate the dispute over mendicant privileges in hearing confessions, where he defended bishops' rights against the regulars. He died at Paris or Tournai in 1293.

Ranking just below Aquinas, Bonaventure, and Scotus, Henry treated the school questions with originality in his Quodlibeta and incomplete Summa Theologica, as psychologist and metaphysician. Where he differed from Aquinas, on individuation or prime matter, his views are seldom as sound, though his criticisms are vigorous. A follower of Aristotle supplemented by Plato through Augustine, he passed the Augustinian element of scholasticism to Scotus and his successors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hubert-andre-:
Hubert-André Dumont was a Belgian geologist, born at Liège in 1809 and dead there in 1857. At only twenty he won the Brussels Academy's gold medal for his geological description of Liège province, a memoir marking an important advance in stratigraphical geology. In 1835 he took a doctorate in mathematical and physical science and became professor of geology and mineralogy at Liège.

Dumont held that chair until his death, serving a time as university rector, and his native city raised a statue to him. A devout Catholic, he saw one son enter the Society of Jesus. His chief achievement was his geological map of Belgium, first issued in 1849 and later completed in larger editions. With Gosselet's work on Belgian palaeozoic rocks, it founded later research in the region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-of-remir:
Hugh of Remiremont, called Candidus or Blancus, was a cardinal of noble birth, probably from Lorraine, dead soon after 1098. He became a Benedictine at Remiremont, and Leo IX called him to Rome and made him cardinal-priest of San Clemente in 1049. A shrewd envoy, he stayed loyal to the pope only while it served his gain.

After Nicholas II died in 1061, Hugh backed the antipope Cadalous, then submitted to Alexander II in 1067. As legate to Spain he made priests stay unwed and set the Roman rite in place of the local rite, but simony charges called him home. Further simony as legate to France led Gregory VII, whose election he had shaped, to depose him, and from then on he stood as Gregory's bitter foe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irish-college:
When Elizabethan and Jacobean persecution shut Ireland's monastic schools, Irish clergy had to train abroad, and this entry maps the colleges that took them in. Rome's Irish houses get separate articles, so this survey covers Spain, Portugal, Belgium, and France in turn, country by country. Its most famous Spanish case is Salamanca, founded at Father Thomas White's petition by Philip III's decree of 1592 and opened in 1593.

Styled the Royal College of Noble Irishmen, Salamanca set the pattern for houses that fed priests back into a persecuted homeland. The entry follows foundations, patrons, student support, and fates across the Continent. It shows a whole exile education system. That system was built because schooling at home had become a crime. Readers get the network, not just one college's tale.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob-van-mae:
Jacob van Maerlant was the greatest Flemish poet of the Middle Ages. He was born about 1235 and died after 1291. Little is known of his life. His name likely came from Maerlant on Voorne island. There he worked for a time as a sexton, hence his surname de Coster. Later he lived at Damme near Bruges. Tradition says he served as town clerk there.

His earliest works were chivalric romances in courtly fashion, adapted from French or Latin sources. They included Alexanders Geesten, Historie van den Grale, Merlijns Boeck, Roman van Torec, and Historie van Troyen. But courtly romance little suited his taste. He leaned toward the didactic and useful. So he turned to instructive works that taught history, nature, and morals. The entry traces a poet who chose teaching over romance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-phili:
Jacques Philippe Lallemant, a French Jesuit, was born at St-Valéry-sur-Somme around 1660 and died in Paris in 1748, and outside his books little is known of him. The debate over Chinese rites pulled him into print. His Journal historique, covering Sorbonne meetings called to condemn Lecomte's Mémoires de la Chine, came out in 1700 and stood up for his fellow Jesuit Lecomte against Jacques Lefèvre of the Sorbonne.

His Histoire des Contestations sur la Diplomatique, dated 1708, backed the Jesuits Hardouin and Papebroch in their quarrel with the Benedictine Mabillon. Yet his chief books struck at the Jansenists. They followed hard on one another: Le Père Quesnel séditieux in 1704, Jansénius condamné in 1705, and Le véritable esprit across 1706 to 1707. He likewise issued Les Hexaples, a work in six columns dealing with the constitution Unigenitus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-nugent:
Philanthropist, temperance advocate, and social reformer James Nugent was born at Liverpool on 3 March 1822. He died at Formby near Liverpool on 27 June 1905. He was educated at Ushaw from 1838 to 1843 and at the English College, Rome, from 1843 to 1846. He was ordained at St Nicholas, Liverpool, on 30 August 1846. After posts at Blackburn and Wigan, he was sent to Liverpool on 1 January 1849.

In 1851 he brought the Sisters of Notre Dame to Liverpool. They now run an English Catholic teacher training college at Mount Pleasant. In 1853 he opened the Catholic Institute, where Newman lectured on the Turks in October 1853. In 1863 he became chaplain of Walton Prison and held the post twenty-two years. In 1865 he founded a Refuge for Homeless Boys, which trained 2,000 boys by 1905. In 1867 he founded the Northern Press, later the Catholic Times. In 1872 he organized temperance work. The entry presents a priest of Victorian social reform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jan-baptista-:
Jan Baptista van Helmont, a scientist, was born at Brussels in 1577 and died near Vilvorde on 30 December 1644. He stands high in chemistry's early annals and came from a good Flemish family. Raised by his uncle, he studied humanities at Louvain. He refused a Master of Arts degree as a source of pride. The Jesuit order drew him, but he did not join it, and he investigated Stoic philosophy.

A wish for evangelical poverty moved him to hand all his property to his sister, and a wish to relieve human suffering moved him to medicine and to Louvain's surgery chair. Scabies sickness broke off his studies, and Galenist doctors, treating him with purgatives and missing its parasitic nature, disgusted him with Galenists. Travel through England, France, Switzerland, and Italy in search of new medical knowledge followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-antoine-: Jean-Antoine d'Aubermont, a theologian of Bois-le-Duc who died in 1686, joined the Dominicans in 1633 and taught philosophy and theology in houses of his order. He took his doctorate at Louvain in 1652 and headed the local Dominican college the next year. Most of his writings defend papal infallibility and answer Gallican teaching, and near his death he upheld Aquinas as author of the Corpus Christi Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Léonce Élie de Beaumont, a French geologist born near Caen in 1798 and dead there in 1874, mapped France's rocks and shaped his science at home. After the École Polytechnique and the School of Mines, he toured English mines in 1822 with Dufrénoy under their teacher Brochant de Villiers.

From 1825 the pair spent eighteen years building a geological map of France, a work whose release counted as a landmark for French geology and made both men famous. Élie de Beaumont taught geology at the School of Mines and the Collège de France, rose to chief engineer and inspector-general of mines. He kept directing the national survey until his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-paul-alb:
Jean-Paul-Alban Villeneuve-Bargemont, a French economist and deputy born in 1784 and dead in Paris in 1850. He served the Empire and Restoration in prefectural posts, became councillor of state in 1828, and refused the oath to Louis-Philippe in 1830. He sat as a Legitimist deputy in the 1830s and 1840s.

A visit to Lille, where nearly half the people lived as paupers, fixed Villeneuve-Bargemont on the social question. As deputy he helped write the 1841 law limiting child labour, the first French law protecting workers, and eased marriage costs for the poor. Against Smith and Say, he held that economics should weigh distribution and well-being, not production alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-lalema:
Jérôme Lalemant, a French Jesuit missionary born in Paris in 1593 and dead at Quebec in 1665. He entered the order in 1610 and reached Canada in June 1638, going straight to lead the Huron missions. There he conducted the first regular census of Indigenous peoples.

Lalemant organised the donnés, lay helpers of missionaries, reshuffled mission posts around the new central house of Sainte-Marie on the Wye, and returned to Quebec as general superior in 1645. Recalled to France in 1656, he led La Flèche college briefly before Laval brought him back as vicar-general in 1659. He wrote many Relations and most of the surviving Jesuit Journal volume.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-von-la:
Johann von Lamont was a Scottish-born astronomer and physicist who directed the observatory at Bogenhausen near Munich. Born at Braemar in 1805, he lost his father in 1816. A monk of the Scots monastery at Ratisbon took him to Germany. There he took up mathematics and science. He joined the new Bogenhausen observatory as assistant in 1827 and became its director in 1835.

Lamont's work fell into three fields: astronomy, surveying, and earth physics. He studied nebulae and star clusters, calculated the mass of Uranus from its moons, and catalogued eighty thousand faint stars. In surveying he extended the Bavarian survey. He fixed longitudes for Vienna, Munich, Geneva, and Strasburg. In earth physics he organized a meteorological society across Germany. He built his own registering instruments, including a portable theodolite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-clement:
John Clement was a physician and scholar who tutored the children of St. Thomas More. Born in Yorkshire about 1500 and educated at St. Paul's School and Oxford, he entered More's household to help educate his children and assist his linguistic studies. In 1519 Wolsey made him Rhetoric Reader at Oxford, and he later became professor of Greek there.

Turning to medicine, he became a Fellow of the College of Physicians in 1528. He attended the dying Wolsey at Esher in 1529 at Henry VIII's request. He served as president of the college in 1544 and censor in 1555. Under Edward VI he retired to Louvain, so obnoxious to the Protestant authorities that the general pardon exempted him. He returned under Mary, practiced in Essex, fled again under Elizabeth, and died in exile at Mechlin in 1572.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-delavau-:
John Delavau Bryant was an American physician, poet, and editor who converted from Episcopalianism to Catholicism. Born in Philadelphia in 1811, son of an Episcopal minister, he took degrees from the University of Pennsylvania. He entered the Episcopal seminary in New York in 1839, left after a year to travel in Europe, and was received into the Catholic Church at Philadelphia in 1842.

Graduating in medicine in 1848, he volunteered during the yellow fever epidemic at Portsmouth and Norfolk in 1855 and stayed until it subsided. He edited the Catholic Herald in the early 1860s and wrote the controversial novel Pauline Seward, which ran through ten editions. He published an exposition of the newly defined Immaculate Conception in 1855. His chief work, the epic poem The Redemption of 1859, founded on the Bible and Catholic tradition, won favorable reviews before falling out of print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-sergeant:
John Sergeant was an English controversialist who wrote over fifty works against Anglicans and fellow Catholics alike. Born at Barrow-upon-Humber in 1623, son of a yeoman, St. John's College, Cambridge, educated him as an Anglican, and he graduated in 1643. As secretary to Bishop Morton of Durham, his patristic researches converted him, and he studied theology at Lisbon, where he was ordained in 1650.

Teaching humanities and philosophy at Lisbon, he became canon and secretary of the chapter in 1655. He then spent twenty years on the English mission in controversy with Stillingfleet, Tillotson, and other Anglicans, and with Catholics who opposed Thomas Blacklow's views. During the Oates Plot his dealings with the Privy Council scandalized Catholics, and he dodged arrest as a physician under false names. His difficult temper worsened with age, but his chief works, from Schism Disarmed to Sure-Footing in Christianity, made him a formidable disputant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-the-sile:
John the Silent was a fifth-century bishop of Armenia who gave up his see for perpetual silence in the desert. Born at Nicopolis in 452 to wealthy, honored, and Christian parents, he inherited on their death in 471. He distributed most of it among relatives, and built a church and monastery with the remainder, living there with ten companions in mortification and self-denial.

Drawn from solitude by the Bishop of Sebaste, he was made Bishop of Colonia in 481 despite his struggles against promotion, keeping his monastic spirit in office. When his brother-in-law Pasinius burdened the Church, John appealed to Emperor Zeno, then left his see for St. Sabas's Laura near Jerusalem, serving in silence and menial labor without revealing his rank. Permitted at last to live in a rock hut in the desert, he passed his remaining days in seclusion and unbroken silence, whence his surname, dying in 558.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-climent:
Jose Climent was a Spanish bishop distinguished for charity, education, eloquence, and an exemplary life. Born at Castellon de la Plana in 1706, he studied and taught theology at Valencia and served years as a parish priest. He was consecrated Bishop of Barcelona in 1766, resigning his see in 1775.

His episcopate founded hospitals, established free schools, and spread knowledge through low-priced publications, including his Spanish translation of Fleury's Manners of the Israelites and Christians. His pastoral instruction of 1769 on renewing ecclesiastical studies brought denunciation at Charles III's court for praising the Church of Utrecht. A commission of archbishops, bishops, and religious superiors cleared him. His sway over his people showed when he quelled a dangerous Barcelona rising against conscription, and he refused promotion to wealthy Malaga on conscientious grounds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lavant:
Lavant is an Austrian bishopric in southern Styria, suffragan of Salzburg, first seated in Carinthia's Lavant valley. Archbishop Eberhard II of Salzburg set up a collegiate chapter at St. Andra on 20 August 1212, and, finding the place remote, won leave to found a bishopric there, deeded on 10 May 1228 with the chair secured to Salzburg's archbishops forever.

Court chaplain Ulrich became first bishop, and a 1280 deed counts seventeen parishes in Carinthia and Styria, a small diocese whose bishops also served as Salzburg's vicars-general and deputies at Friesach. Dietrich Wolfhauer, tenth bishop, is the first called prince-bishop, and from Theobald Schweinbeck in 1446 the title ran unbroken. Humanist Johann von Rott, Counter-Reformation promoter Georg Stobaus, and financier Maximilian Gandolph von Kienburg stand out among later bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lawrence-arth:
Lawrence Arthur Faunt (1554-1590 or 1591) was a Jesuit theologian, born Arthur Faunt. He spent two years at Merton College, Oxford, under the philosopher John Potts. He then took his bachelor's degree at the Jesuit college in Louvain.

After time in Paris he proceeded master of arts at Munich under Duke William of Bavaria's patronage. When he entered the Society of Jesus is disputed: some date it 1570, others 1575, the year he went to Rome's English College for theology and added Lawrence to his baptismal name. Professor of divinity there, he won Gregory XIII's favour. He became rector of the new Jesuit college at Posen in 1581, teaching Greek, moral theology, and controversy in high repute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lent:
Lent, a Teutonic word first meaning simply spring, has from Anglo-Saxon times translated Latin quadragesima, the forty days or fortieth day. That Latin term itself imitated Greek tessarakoste, formed like Pentecost. That etymology matters for the early Easter fast's development.

Some fifth-century Fathers, like Leo, Jerome, and Socrates, called the forty days' fast an apostolic institution, but modern scholars near-unanimously reject the claim. The first three centuries show wide diversity of practice and gradual growth in duration. Irenaeus, writing Pope Victor in the Easter controversy and quoted by Eusebius, reports varied practice. Some fasted one day, others two or several, others forty hours of day and night. He calls this variety ancient, which rules out any apostolic tradition on the matter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-ch:
Liturgical chant means music fit for public worship, judged by whether its style and performance serve the rite. In its strict sense it is melody sung by the human voice alone, plain or harmonized. The entry also counts voice joined by organ and instruments, and even instruments alone when they carry the rite.

Four strands make up sacred music here: plain chant, harmonized chant, either of these with organ and instruments, and organ and instruments alone. The entry weighs how each strand ranks against the others. Voice keeps first place even when instruments join, a rule rooted in the voice as the first and finest instrument.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-lallema:
Louis Lallemant was a French Jesuit master of the spiritual life, born at Chalons in 1588 and dead at Bourges in 1635. He joined the Society in 1605, taught philosophy and theology, and served four years as master of novices.

Made director of fathers in third probation, the order's final training stage, he set heroic ideals and demanded that others match his own uncompromising pursuit of them. Ill health cut him short after three years, and he died at Bourges within months. His Doctrine Spirituelle, gathered by his pupil Rigoleuc, fixed much of French Jesuit spirituality, as Alvarez had fixed Spain's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-sebasti:
Louis Sebastien Le Nain de Tillemont was a French historian and priest, born at Paris in 1637 and dead there in 1698. Schooled at Port-Royal's little schools under Nicole, he caught a passion for history from reading Baronius and resolved to return to that writer's sources.

From eighteen he gathered notes and extracts for life, spent years at Beauvais, and was ordained late, subdeacon in 1672 and priest in 1676. After Port-Royal scattered in 1679, he withdrew to his estate at Tillemont, working in piety and study until death. His histories of the first six Christian centuries' emperors and church, dry yet exact, remain models of source-based scholarship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-margaret-of-t:
Margaret of the Blessed Sacrament was a Carmelite nun, born in Paris on 6 March 1590 and dead there on 24 May 1660. She was second daughter of Madame Acarie, Blessed Marie de l'Incarnation, who brought Reformed Carmelites into France. She took the habit at the first Carmelite convent in Rue St Jacques on 15 September 1605.

She made private vows in 1606 and solemn vows in 1607 under Mother Anne de Saint-Barthelemi. In 1615 she became sub-prioress, and in 1618 prioress at Tours. Her skill sent her to Bordeaux in 1620 to restore harmony, then to Saintes for eighteen months. Recalled to Paris in 1624, she replaced Mother Madeleine de Saint-Joseph as prioress in Rue Chapon. She served there several times as prioress, edifying sisters by a zeal for bodily mortification her superiors sometimes had to temper. Dropsy at last killed her, her heart going to Pontoise, where her mother lay buried.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-testament:
The New Testament entry opens with its name, description, origin, transmission and contents. Testament renders testamentum, the Latin writers' translation of Greek diatheke. With profane authors diatheke almost always means a man's legal disposition of goods after death. Yet the Septuagint translators early used it for Hebrew berith, a pact or alliance, above all Yahweh's alliance with Israel.

In 1 Corinthians 11:25, Jesus uses new testament for the alliance He established between God and the world, called new against Moses's mediation. Later the name passed to the collection of sacred texts holding the two alliances' history and doctrine. Old Testament first appears in Melito of Sardis about 170. The entry then treats each book's origin, the text's transmission, and the New Testament's history and doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-old-testament:
The Old Testament, from Hebrew berith and Greek diatheke for covenant, names both God's old covenant with Israel and the scriptures that record it. Prophets foresaw a new covenant to replace Sinai's, Christ spoke at supper of blood of the new testament, and Paul called himself a minister of that new covenant.

Early Christians then applied the name to the whole revelation in Israel's history, and Melito and Clement already call the books scriptures of the Old Testament. The entry traces canon, text, versions, and interpretation across Jewish and Christian ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oliver-legipo:
Benedictine bibliographer Oliver Legipont, born at Soiron in 1698, spent his life traveling to libraries to examine and order them. Schooled by Franciscans at Verviers and formed at Great Saint Martin's in Cologne, he was ordained in 1723 and took his licentiate in 1728.

Though eager for ministry and teaching, Legipont found his calling in books, helping found a Benedictine college at Heidelberg. Most writings stay unedited, but his edition of Ziegelbauer's Benedictine literary history and his philological and bibliographical dissertations keep lasting value. He died at Trier in 1758. His Itinerarium of a noble pilgrimage appeared at Augsburg in 1751 and in Spanish in 1759.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-the-:
The Order of the Incarnate Word and Blessed Sacrament, founded by Jeanne Chézard de Matel in the early seventeenth century, teaches youth above all. Born at Roanne in 1596 and dead at Lyons in 1670, Jeanne saw her rule approved by Urban VIII in 1633 and confirmed by Innocent X in 1644.

First housed at Lyons, the order spread through Avignon and Paris, was driven out in the Revolution, and revived at Azerables. In 1852 Bishop Odin brought Mother Saint Claire's band to Brownsville, Texas, founding the first American house amid hardship and frontier want.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-mint:
The papal mint is treated here through the coinage struck by popes once they held temporal power, since coining is a sovereign right. Yet true coins of Zacharias, Gregory III, and possibly Gregory II survive from before full independence. Two are silver, and their stamp matches Byzantine and Merovingian pieces of the seventh and eighth centuries, with a square shape also found on Byzantine coins.

Pieces reading Gregorii Papae, Sancti Petri cannot belong to Gregory IV, given their minting style. Hartmann explains them as imperial Byzantine pieces bearing the name of Rome's first civil magistrate, since eighth-century popes acted as prefects of the city. No coins survive from Stephen III or Paul I, and later pages follow the mint through medieval and modern issues, types, and legends.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-particular-ju:
Particular judgment is the Catholic doctrine that each soul's eternal fate is settled at once after death, by God's just judgment. No formal definition states it outright. Eugene IV's Union Decree of 1439 implies it, however. Graced souls needing cleansing go to Purgatory. Pure souls enter the beatific vision at once. Souls dying in mortal or original sin alone face eternal punishment, graded to their sin.

The same teaching appears in Michael Palaeologus's profession of 1274, Benedict XII's Benedictus Deus of 1336, and professions of Gregory XIII and Benedict XIV. Scripture proofs are indirect, since texts like Ecclesiastes and Hebrews speak of judgment after death without clearly marking a judgment distinct from the world's end. Later pages argue the case from parables, Fathers, and reason, and answer objections.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perpetual-ado:
The Perpetual Adorers, or Sacramentines, were orders given wholly to adoration of the Blessed Sacrament. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry weighs a question of priority between two seventeenth-century founders. Père Antoine, a Paris-born Dominican, began the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament about 1639, though their house at Marseilles was firmly set up only in 1659 and 1660 under Sister Anne Negrel.

Their rivals were Mother Mechtilde's Benedictine Adoratrices, whose perpetual adoration began in 1654, five years before the Sacramentines gained the right to reserve the Host. The entry argues for Père Antoine's priority, since his order aimed solely at eucharistic worship from the start, while Mechtilde's adapted to that end later. Migne's dictionary names his order and the 1848 Adoration Réparatrice as the only ones wholly devoted to the cult.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-marchan:
Peter Marchant was a Flemish Franciscan theologian, born at Couvin in the principality of Liège in 1585. He joined the Franciscans in 1601, lived austerely, mastered scholastic philosophy and theology, and taught in his order's schools for years. In 1625 Rome's general chapter elected him definitor general, and in 1639 he became commissary general over Germany, Belgium, Holland, Britain, and Ireland.

Irish politics entangled him during the Confederation of Kilkenny, when false reports led him to back the Ormondists against the papal nuncio Rinuccini. Called to justify himself, he addressed the 1661 general chapter with his Relatio veridica, a rare book the chapter condemned and ordered destroyed. His chief work, the three-volume Tribunal Sacramentale of 1642, set out moral theology plainly for confessors. He died at Ghent in 1661.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philosophy-of:
Immanuel Kant was the Königsberg philosopher whose critical system remade modern thought, born in 1724. He studied at his native university under Knutzen, learning Wolff's philosophy and Newton's physics, spent nine years tutoring after his father's death in 1746, and returned to Königsberg in 1755. Privatdozent until 1770, he held the philosophy chair until 1797 and died in 1804.

His pre-critical writings defended Wolff, but the Critique of Pure Reason of 1781 opened the critical period. It argues that mind shapes experience through its own forms, while soul, world, and God lie beyond proof as ideas of reason. The Critique of Practical Reason, the Critique of Judgment, and Religion within the Limits of Mere Reason followed, making morality, not dogma, religion's core. The entry judges the system agnostic in theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piedmont:
Piedmont was a region of northern Italy, its name from pedes montium, feet of the mountains, enclosed on three sides by the Alps. It holds the upper Po plain and Alpine valleys descending from the Pennine, Graian, Cottian, and Maritime ranges, bounded by Switzerland, France, Liguria, and Lombardy. Today it forms the provinces of Turin, Novara, Alessandria, and Cuneo.

Its passes to Gaul made it important from antiquity. Christianity, slow until the fourth century, spread fast in the fourth and fifth among a Romanized people, with early sees at Turin, Asti, and Aosta. Feudal marquessates of Ivrea, Susa, Saluzzo, and Montferrat divided it until Savoy's counts rose: Humbert I held Aosta, and his son Otto's marriage to Adelaide of Turin founded the later Piedmont. The survey follows Savoy to modern Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-charle:
Pierre Charles L'Enfant was the French-born engineer who planned Washington, born in France in August 1755. Trained as an engineer, he joined Lafayette as a volunteer for the revolted colonists in 1777. He became captain of engineers in 1778 and brevet major in 1783, serving valiantly through the Revolutionary War. Afterwards he remodelled New York's old City Hall for the First Congress.

When the federal city's site was chosen, he spent much of 1791 on his Plan of the City, intended for the Permanent Seat of Government on the Potomac. A quick temper and overbearing disposition brought quarrels with superiors, and Washington dismissed him on 1 March 1792 before his plan was carried out. He refused payment for the Capitol plan and a West Point professorship, built Washington fortifications in 1812, quarrelled again, and sought recompense from Congress in vain. He died near Bladensburg in 1825, poor and forgotten.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-cousta:
Pierre Coustant was a learned Maurist Benedictine, born at Compiègne on 30 April 1654. Schooled by Jesuits there, he entered Saint-Rémi at Reims at seventeen, took vows in 1672, and studied under François Lamy at Soissons. In 1681 his superiors sent him to Saint-Germain-des-Prés to help edit St. Augustine, separating genuine writings from spurious ones.

His learning won him the new edition of St. Hilary of Poitiers, replacing Erasmus's defective 1523 text, and work on the Maurist Breviary and Augustine's general index. Immediately after Augustine's works appeared in 1700, he undertook a complete collection of papal letters from Clement I to Innocent III, sifting authentic from false and restoring texts chronologically. After more than twenty years he published the first volume in 1721, covering 67 to 440, with a 150-page preface on papal primacy. He died that same year at Saint-Germain-des-Prés.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-olivai:
Pierre Olivaint was a French Jesuit priest whose path from unbelief to faith made him a symbol of Catholic revival in France. He was born in Paris in 1816 to parents without religion. He absorbed Voltaire's ideas at school, yet by 1837, moved by Lacordaire's preaching, he professed the faith to Father Ravignan.

At the Normal School he gathered a circle of Catholic students known for prayer and charity. He taught history and in 1845 entered the Jesuit novitiate at Laval on the very day of a parliamentary attack on the order. He worked with the Conferences of Saint Vincent de Paul. In 1871, during the Paris Commune, he was seized and shot with fellow prisoners in the Rue Haxo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plain-chant:
Plain chant is the unaccompanied church music of the early Middle Ages, the Church's own music before polyphony, singing in many parts, appeared. Growing up gradually in worship, it remained the sole music of the Church until the ninth century. It then held a place of honour beside the new music and served as the foundation on which polyphony was built.

The name cantus planus, plain song, arose among theorists of the twelfth or thirteenth century to set it against measured music, with notes of strict relative length. Also called Gregorian chant after Saint Gregory I and Roman chant for its Roman form, it faded in esteem after the sixteenth century. Yet the Church always kept it as her proper music, and the entry traces its revival in modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-postulant:
Postulancy is the trial stage ere the novitiate, in place since monastic life began. In the East, the would-be monk met many rebuffs, to test whether his call was true. The custom passed to the West. Benedict's rule bids the house not take a newcomer too lightly, but try the spirits. If, after he repeats his plea, he bears rebuffs and blocks for four or five days and still holds on, the door opens to him.

In varied orders the trial ran from three to ten days. Then came a novitiate of one, two, or three years, once seen as training, not as its first stage. After taking him in, houses of old sent the man back to the world on open leave, free to come back when he chose. The Customs of St Victor notes the practice as common to many houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-principality-:
Waldeck-Pyrmont was a former state of the German Empire, covering 433 square miles. It held two parts. South Waldeck, ringed by Prussian Hesse-Nassau and Westphalia, held 407 square miles and 49,965 folk in 1905. North Pyrmont, ringed by Lippe, Brunswick, and Hanover, held 26 square miles and 9,162 folk. In 1905 it counted 56,341 Protestants, 1,890 Catholics, and 629 Jews. The land takes its name from Waldeck castle on the Eider, a west Fulda branch.

About 1150 Widukind V of Schwalenberg seized the castle and styled himself Count of Waldeck. Waldeck stood as a Hessian fief from 1438, a tie ended in 1846. In 1631, when Gleichen's counts died out, Waldeck gained Pyrmont. In the war of 1866 Waldeck backed Prussia and joined the North German Confederation. Prussia took over the administration by the Treaty of Accession of 1867.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-redemption-in:
Redemption means either strict deliverance for a price or ransom paid, or simple deliverance by power from oppression, violence or captivity. This encyclopedia entry traces the idea in Hebrew through the verbs ga'al and padah, with kopher, ransom, closely related. Ga'al serves technically in the Mosaic Law for redeeming an inheritance, a vowed thing or tithes by price. Padah serves for redeeming the first-born of children or animals.

Outside the Law, and in relation to Israel's God, both verbs mean simple salvation or deliverance by power. The New Testament narrows redemption to man's rescue from sin by Christ's death, expressed by lutroumai, from lutron, a ransom, and its derivatives. The entry thus moves from law-court prices in ancient Israel to the theological heart of the New Testament, with Schurér, Nowack and Schwalm among its scholarly sources on Jewish life and law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-remiremont:
Remiremont in the Vosges is a monastery and nunnery under the Rule of Saint Benedict. Saints Romaricus and Amatus founded it in 620 on hills above the present town, whence its name, Romarici Mons. The monastery later became a priory of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine, who gave it in 1623 to the Benedictines of the Congregation of Saint Vannes. In 1768 it held ten monks and a revenue of fifty-five hundred livres.

For three centuries the nunnery stood beside the monastery. In 910, as the Huns wasted the country, the nuns built a fortified convent in the valley with Emperor Louis the Third's help. The town of Remiremont grew around that convent, the relics of Romaricus and Amatus were moved there from the monastery, and Leo the Ninth enriched it with many more relics. Fire destroyed the convent in 1057 and scattered the nuns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reservation-o:
Reservation of the Blessed Sacrament is the keeping, after the Liturgy, of part of the consecrated elements for the Communion of the sick or other pious purposes. Its extreme antiquity is beyond dispute. Justin Martyr's first detailed account of Eucharistic practice already sends a portion by deacons to the absent. Irenaeus records presbyters sending the Eucharist between districts, and Tertullian uses the very word reservare.

The entry draws a firm line about later practice. No reliable evidence shows the Sacrament kept in churches before the year 1000, or even later, so that the faithful might visit it or pray before it. Evidence cited for such a custom tells the other way on inspection. Even Optatus's phrase for the altar, throne of the Body and Blood of Christ, is read by the entry as telling the other way.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacra-jam-spl:
Sacra jam splendent are the opening words of the Matins hymn for the Feast of the Holy Family. The Holy See set up the feast in 1893 as a greater double, placing it on the third Sunday after Epiphany. Leo XIII composed the three hymns of the Breviary Office, for Vespers, Matins, and Lauds. The Matins hymn has nine Sapphic stanzas of classical type. Its first stanza pictures a thousand lights on garlanded shrines and altars.

The Vespers and Lauds hymns are in classical dimeter iambics, four-lined stanzas, six and seven respectively, besides the usual Marian doxology. All three hymns overflow with spiritual warmth, graceful phrasing, and classical dignity of form. They reflect the pope's sentiment in his letter establishing a Pious Association for the Holy Family and in his encyclical on working-men's condition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastian-bra:
Sebastian Brant, German humanist and poet, was born at Strasbourg in 1457 or 1458 and died there in 1521. At Basel university he first studied philosophy, then turned to law, taking his doctorate in canon and civil law in 1489, while lecturing from 1484 and practising at the same time. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a patriot poet of empire and Church.

His Latin and German poems set out religious and political ideals. Maximilian's election as emperor filled Brant and many patriots with hope: emperor as supreme temporal ruler of Christian nations, Church as supreme spiritual ruler, was his great desire, colouring all his verse. He hoped above all for restored imperial power in Germany, but disappointment followed. In 1499 Basel left the empire for the Swiss confederacy, and Brant's position there grew untenable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-servants-of-t:
The Servants of the Most Blessed Sacrament, an order of nuns, was founded in 1858 by Pierre-Julien Eymard. Mother Margaret of the Blessed Sacrament helped him. The Archbishop of Paris authorized the work. Pius IX erected it canonically in 1871, and Leo XIII approved its constitutions in 1885. Its aim is solemn and perpetual adoration of Christ in the Sacrament of the Altar, offered above all else for the love of men.

Each sister makes three adorations in twenty-four hours, two by day and one by night, and the Divine Office is said in choir. The community is contemplative and cloistered, with its mother-house at Angers. Houses followed at Lyons in 1874, Paris in 1876, and Binche in Belgium in 1894, and a Canadian foundation later gained its own novitiate. The entry counts thirteen perpetually professed sisters and fifteen novices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-siger-of-brab:
Siger of Brabant stands as the undisputed leader of Latin Averroism in the 1260s and 1270s. Many arts masters took up his principles, and Dante immortalized him in the Paradiso as the light of Siger who syllogized unwelcome truths. His illustrious colleague Saint Thomas Aquinas expressly refuted his teachings. Few solid details of his life survive.

A master of arts at Paris, he led university agitations for ten years, working with the legate Simon de Brie on discipline. From 1272 to 1275 he held the university rector Alberic of Reims in check, heading an opposition drawn from the Garlande quarter. Condemned in 1270, he kept teaching, and a second condemnation in 1277 ended his career. Hauled before France's Grand Inquisitor and condemned, he appealed to Rome and died at Orvieto between 1281 and 1284, murdered by his secretary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-william-d:
William D'Avenant, poet and dramatist born at Oxford in February 1606, died in London on 7 April 1668. Second son of John D'Avenant, vintner and owner of the Crown Tavern inn where Shakespeare often stayed. He may have been the poet's godson, though the tale making him Shakespeare's natural son lacks foundation. Schooled at Oxford, he became page to Frances, Duchess of Richmond, then entered the service of Fulke Greville, Lord Brooke.

He began writing plays in 1628 and ten years later succeeded Ben Jonson as Poet Laureate. Warmly royalist in the Civil War, he was knighted by Charles I in 1643. After the king's defeat he fled to France in 1644 and became a Catholic. He served Queen Henrietta Maria's correspondence with the king, and faced imprisonment and danger to his life before release in 1651. In 1656 he helped revive English stage performances, silent since 1641, and after the Restoration Charles II patronized his writing and productions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ethelbert-:
Ethelbert, king of Kent from 560 to 616, opened England to the Roman mission by welcoming Augustine with fair dealing. Son of Eormenric and descendant of Hengest, he failed to wrest Britain's overlordship from Ceawlin of Wessex, but his marriage to Bertha, daughter of the Frankish king Charibert, raised his standing. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 24 February 616.

Though himself a worshipper of Odin, he gave Bertha the old Roman church of St. Martin at Canterbury and full freedom for her faith. When Augustine landed in 597, Ethelbert met him with hospitality, caution, and a noble sense of fair play. The entry shows a pagan king whose tolerance prepared the ground for conversion, both his people's and, in time, his own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vigilius-b:
Vigilius, bishop of Trent and martyr, converted Arians and idolaters across the Tyrol. Born about 353, his father is unknown, though some name Theodosius. His mother Maxentia and brothers Claudian and Magorian are all counted saints. Brought young to Trent, he studied at Athens, winning fame for sanctity and learning, and there befriended John Chrysostom.
